fx.source_name: European Central Bank — euro foreign exchange reference rates
fx.note: Three regimes, each dated. Currencies the ECB quotes are ECB reference rates re-based on USD (local units per 1 USD). Currencies pegged to the US dollar carry the official parity published by their own issuing central bank, listed under "pegged" with the authority and the date it was read. Everything else carries the European Commission's monthly accounting rate (InforEuro) for the month shown under "monthly", re-based on the same month's USD value. A monthly rate is fixed for a calendar month, so it is dated by its month and not by a market close. Indicative only; EOR providers apply their own FX margin.

AED.note: The dirham is pegged to the US dollar. The CBUAE rate table gives US Dollar 3.6725, last updated 18 September 2026; the CBUAE's own August 2026 rate file carries that same value on each of the month's 21 business days. The CBUAE states it buys dirhams against dollars at 3.673 and sells at 3.672 with eligible counterparties.

JOD.note: The dinar is pegged to the US dollar. The CBJ's operational framework states that the fixed exchange rate with the US dollar, adopted in 1995, is the nominal pillar of its monetary policy (https://www.cbj.gov.jo/En/Pages/Operational_Framework). Its foreign exchange table, in fils, prints USD 708 and 710 as the lowest and highest rates on every day shown, 2026/09/23 included; 0.709 is the midpoint. InforEuro's September 2026 JOD rate re-based on USD gives 0.709001, the same parity.

QAR.note: The riyal is pegged to the US dollar. QCB states a fixed parity of QR 3.64 per USD, authorised by Amiri Decree No. 34 of 2001, and its own exchange-rate table prints USD 3.64. QCB notes that commercial banks add a margin of 0.24 % to that price when dealing with the public.

SAR.note: The riyal is pegged to the US dollar. SAMA states it remains committed to maintaining the exchange rate at the official rate of 3.75 riyals to the dollar. SAMA's daily rate table is rendered in JavaScript and could not be read at source, so the parity is taken from SAMA's own published exchange-rate policy statement.

monthly.authority: European Commission — InforEuro monthly accounting rate
monthly.note: The European Commission publishes one accounting rate per currency per calendar month and uses it for its own budget. It is the rate of record for currencies the ECB does not quote and no central bank pegs. It is fixed for the month shown, so it carries a month rather than a market close, and it is re-based here on the same month's euro-dollar value.
monthly.volatile_note: These currencies can move by several points inside one month. A monthly rate is still the rate of record, but a figure converted through one of them is as old as its month, and the local caps behind it have to be re-read at least as often.

countries.name: United Arab Emirates

assumptions.label: Foreign full-time employee on a work permit and residence visa
assumptions.notes: Article 51(1) of the Labour Relations Decree-Law sends the national worker to the pension and social security legislation in force, and article 51(2) gives the foreign worker an end-of-service gratuity in its place. An employer-of-record hire in the Emirates is almost always the second case, which is why this ledger carries no pension contribution at all: the employer contribution to the General Pension and Social Security Authority follows Emirati and GCC nationals, and is priced in the note on nationality below rather than in the total. Emiratisation quotas are a hiring constraint on mainland companies rather than a payroll rate, and are not modelled here.

assumptions.label: Basic wage as a share of the total package
assumptions.notes: This is the number that decides the cost of an Emirati hire, and federal law does not fix it. Article 1 of the Decree-Law defines the basic wage as the amount stated in the contract, which 'does not include any other allowances or benefits in kind', and article 51(5) computes the gratuity on the last basic wage alone, so an identical package split differently produces a different bill. Article 66(3)(a) of the DIFC Employment Law does fix one, next door in the same emirate: there the basic wage 'shall not be less than fifty percent of the Employee's Annual Wage'. This ledger takes that floor as its declared point, which makes the figure on this page a floor too: a package where basic pay is 60% of the total carries 3.45% rather than 2.88%, and one paid wholly as basic pay carries the full 5.75%.

employer_contributions.name: End-of-service gratuity, first five years (provision)
employer_contributions.applies: Foreign full-time employees who complete one year or more of continuous service
employer_contributions.notes: Article 51(2) of Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021: the foreign full-time worker who has completed one or more years of continuous service is entitled to a gratuity 'calculated according to the basic wage' of 'twenty-one (21) days for each year of the first five years of service' and 'thirty (30) days for each year in excess of that'. Twenty-one days divided by the 365-day divisor that article 66(3)(b) of the DIFC Employment Law spells out is 5.7534% of annual basic pay, and that is the rate carried here; from the sixth year it rises to 8.22% on the same base. Three conditions are worth knowing: nothing is owed before one full year of continuous service, article 51(3) then pays parts of a year in proportion, and article 51(6) caps the whole award at two years' wage. Days of unpaid absence do not count towards service under article 51(4). On the mainland this is a provision rather than a monthly payment; inside the DIFC the same entitlement is funded month by month - see the note below.

source.name: Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021 Concerning Regulating Labour Relations, consolidated text as updated 29 July 2024

statutory_extras.name: DIFC Qualifying Scheme (DEWS) core benefits
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it applies inside the Dubai International Financial Centre and not on the mainland, and because its rate runs on basic wage rather than on the gross this column measures. Article 66(7) of DIFC Employment Law No. 2 of 2019 replaced the accruing gratuity with a funded plan: the employer pays a Qualifying Scheme, every month, at least 5.83% of the employee's monthly basic wage for the first five years of service and 8.33% for each year after that. Two differences change a budget rather than a percentage. First, it is cash leaving the business every month instead of a liability that waits for a departure, so a DIFC hire costs money from month one. Second, article 66(3)(a) forbids a basic wage below 50% of the annual wage, a floor the federal law does not impose, so a DIFC employer cannot shrink the entitlement by loading the package with allowances. Where the employee is a UAE or GCC national already contributing to the GPSSA, article 65(3) requires a top-up of the difference into the scheme, provided the monthly top-up reaches AED 1,000.

source.name: DIFC Employment Law No. 2 of 2019, consolidated text updated 2024

statutory_extras.name: Cabinet-approved alternative end-of-service systems
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is an option rather than a charge, and because the contribution rate is set by the decision that approves each system. Article 51(8) of the Decree-Law lets the Cabinet approve 'other alternative systems for the end-of-service gratuity system', with the conditions, controls and contribution mechanism specified in the approving decision. It matters to anyone comparing quotes: two providers employing in the same emirate can run the same statutory entitlement through different machinery, one as an unfunded provision and one as a monthly contribution, and only the second shows up as cash in the first year. Ask which of the two a quote reflects.

source.name: Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021 Concerning Regulating Labour Relations, consolidated text as updated 29 July 2024

statutory_extras.name: Work permit and sponsorship
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is an amount per head that does not scale with pay. Article 6(1) of the Decree-Law is categorical: work may not be practised in the State, and the employer may not recruit or employ any worker, 'except after obtaining a work permit from the Ministry'. The permit, the residence visa attached to it and the repatriation at the end are the employer's to arrange and to fund, and they are the reason a Gulf hire is measured in weeks rather than days: Deel quotes 20 days to a first start in the UAE. Article 27 leaves a minimum wage to a Cabinet resolution, and no such resolution is in force.

source.name: Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021 Concerning Regulating Labour Relations, consolidated text as updated 29 July 2024

statutory_extras.name: Health cover, and what a national costs instead
statutory_extras.notes: Health cover is an employer obligation across the Emirates, and it is carried at zero here because it is a premium per person rather than a share of pay. In Dubai, article 10 of Law No. 11 of 2013 on health insurance requires the employer to enrol its employees, bear the cost and not charge it to them. In Abu Dhabi, the government portal u.ae states that employers and sponsors cover their employees and their families (one spouse and three children under 18). In Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah, a Cabinet decision extended the mandate from 1 January 2025: the employer buys the policy as a prerequisite for issuing or renewing the residence permit (work permits issued before that date follow at renewal), and the basic package of the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation costs AED 320 a year. Dubai and Abu Dhabi fix no price, so the premium there is quoted by insurers against age and cover. The national case is the one that changes the percentage: article 4(1) of Federal Decree-Law No. 57 of 2023 on Pension and Social Security, which defines the insured as a national, sets the employer share at 15% of the subscription account salary and the employee share at 11%, and for a private-sector employer the Government bears 2.5 points of the employer share for nationals whose subscription account salary is below AED 20,000, which leaves 12.5% below that line and 15% above it. The Decree-Law, issued on 2 October 2023, applies to nationals insured from its entry into force; those insured under Federal Law No. 7 of 1999 keep that law's rates, which were not read for this page.

source.name: Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation - The Basic Health Insurance Scheme

countries.notice_typical: Article 43 requires written notice of at least 30 days and at most 90 days, as agreed in the contract, with the contract remaining in force and the worker paid in full throughout. Probation runs to six months under article 9, and an employer ending the contract inside it gives 14 days' written notice. A worker who leaves during probation to depart the State gives 14 days' notice, and article 9 puts a compensation on a new employer who hires them back within three months.

countries.name: Albania

employer_contributions.name: Social insurance for sickness, maternity and pension, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on a monthly base between the national minimum wage and the maximum wage for contribution purposes
employer_contributions.notes: Article 10 of Law No. 7703 on Social Insurance sets the contribution to the sickness, maternity and pension funds at 13.8% of the gross payroll for the employer and 9.5% of gross pay for the employee. The same article bounds the base: contributions are calculated on gross pay between the national minimum wage and the maximum wage for contribution purposes, and the maximum rises by the same amount and at the same time as the minimum wage. The General Tax Directorate's notice for 2026 applies that rule: the minimum monthly wage went from ALL 40,000 to ALL 50,000 on 1 January 2026, and the maximum monthly base for social insurance moved by the same ALL 10,000, from ALL 176,416 (in force until 31/12/2025) to ALL 186,416. Carried here as an annual floor of ALL 600,000 and an annual ceiling of ALL 2,236,992, about US$28,227 at the September 2026 accounting rate. The same ceiling bounds the two lines below.

source.name: Law No. 7703 of 11/05/1993 on Social Insurance, article 10, consolidated text published by the Social Insurance Institute (ISSH), as amended up to Law No. 64/2023

employer_contributions.name: Work accident and occupational disease insurance (employer only)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, paid by the employer alone, on the same bounded base as the pension contribution
employer_contributions.notes: Article 14(2)(a) of Law No. 7703 states that the employer pays, in addition, 0.3% of the payroll to the work accident and occupational disease branch. It is part of the employer's 15% of social insurance, not an extra line on top of it. Article 14(3) allows the Social Insurance Institute to differentiate the accident contribution by the risk of the sector, but the Institute's own page on compulsory insurance lists the branch at a single 0.3% alongside 0.3% sickness, 1.40% maternity, 21.6% pension and 0.90% unemployment, for 24.50% of social insurance in total per employee. The accident rate follows the employer of record's own classification, which for an office payroll is the 0.3% shown here.

source.name: Law No. 7703 of 11/05/1993 on Social Insurance, article 14, consolidated text published by the Social Insurance Institute (ISSH)

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (employer only)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, paid by the employer alone, on the same bounded base as the pension contribution
employer_contributions.notes: Article 14(2)(b) of Law No. 7703 puts the 0.9% unemployment contribution on the employer alone. With the 13.8% above and the 0.3% accident branch, it brings the employer's social insurance to 15% of gross, against the employee's 9.5%: the 24.5% combined figure is the one the Social Insurance Institute publishes, and the employer carries 15 of those points.

source.name: Law No. 7703 of 11/05/1993 on Social Insurance, article 14, consolidated text published by the Social Insurance Institute (ISSH)

employer_contributions.name: Compulsory health care insurance, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on the full gross with no ceiling, and never on less than the national minimum wage
employer_contributions.notes: Article 8 of Law No. 10383 on Compulsory Health Care Insurance sets the contribution at 3.4% of the base and splits it 50% employer, 50% employee, so each side pays 1.7%. The base has a floor but no ceiling: the General Tax Directorate's 2026 notice says health contributions for employees are calculated on no less than the ALL 50,000 minimum wage and up to the full gross declared on the payroll. That is the difference with the three social insurance lines above, which stop at ALL 186,416 a month. Above that ceiling the employer's marginal rate falls from 16.7% to 1.7%.

source.name: Law No. 10383 of 24/02/2011 on Compulsory Health Care Insurance, article 8, consolidated text published by the Compulsory Health Care Insurance Fund (FSDKSH)

statutory_extras.name: Seniority award on dismissal - at least 15 days' pay per full year, after three years
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is paid only when the employer ends a contract that has lasted at least three years, and named because it is the Albanian termination cost a flat monthly quote does not show. Article 145 of the Labour Code sets it at no less than 15 days' pay for each full year of work, calculated on the pay in force when the employment ends, and adds it to any award for termination without reasonable grounds. It is lost only where the employee is dismissed with immediate effect for reasonable grounds.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Albania (Law No. 7961 of 12/07/1995), article 145, consolidated text as amended up to Law No. 91/2024, published by the State Labour Inspectorate

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Albanian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code creates no thirteenth-month salary; the consolidated text contains no such entitlement. What it does create are supplements paid only when the hours are actually worked: work on an official public holiday that falls on a working day earns a pay supplement plus paid time off of the same length under article 86 and the articles that follow. A salaried engineering role normally triggers none of them, but they belong in the contract rather than in a surprise invoice.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Albania (Law No. 7961 of 12/07/1995), consolidated text as amended up to Law No. 91/2024, published by the State Labour Inspectorate

countries.notice_typical: After probation, two weeks where the employment has lasted up to six months, one month from six months to two years, two months from two to five years and three months beyond five years, under article 143 of the Labour Code; during an employer's notice the employee is entitled to at least 20 hours of paid leave a week to look for work. During probation either side may terminate on at least five days' notice under article 142.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Albania (Law No. 7961 of 12/07/1995), consolidated text as amended up to Law No. 91/2024, published by the State Labour Inspectorate

countries.name: Armenia

assumptions.label: The hire is at work, not on childcare leave for a child under three
assumptions.notes: This is the only condition under which an Armenian employer pays a social contribution from its own funds. Article 6(10) of the Law on Funded Pensions requires the employer, as tax agent for an employee on childcare leave for a child under three, to calculate and transfer the social payment on that employee's behalf at its own expense, from the month after the leave begins until the month the child turns two. Outside that case the employer withholds and remits, and bears nothing.

employer_contributions.name: Social payment (sotsialakan vchar) - withheld from the employee
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee in the funded scheme; the employer calculates and remits it as tax agent and bears none of it
employer_contributions.notes: Carried at zero because Armenian law places this payment on the employee and makes the employer only its collector. Article 7(1) of the Law on Funded Pensions states that the obligation to calculate and transfer an employee's social payments is borne by employers as tax agents. Article 6(7) then caps what the person owes: 5% of gross where monthly gross does not exceed AMD 500,000, and the difference between 10% of gross and AMD 25,000 above that, with the base itself ceilinged at fifteen times the minimum monthly wage. None of it is an employer charge. Deel's Armenia page corroborates the result from the other side: its employer-cost section shows 0.60% of salary, which is Deel's own administrative fee, with no statutory line beneath it.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Armenia on Funded Pensions, articles 6 and 7, official incorporation on the Armenian Legal Information System

statutory_extras.name: Childcare leave - the employer contributes from its own funds
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it applies to a situation rather than to a salary, and named because it is the single case where an Armenian employer pays a social contribution itself. Article 6(10) of the Law on Funded Pensions requires the employer, acting as tax agent for an employee on childcare leave for a child under three, to calculate and transfer the social payment on that employee's behalf at its own expense, from the month following the start of the leave until the month the child turns two. Ask a provider how it prices that period, because it is the one line that can appear on an Armenian invoice without appearing in any rate table.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Armenia on Funded Pensions, article 6(10)

statutory_extras.name: Military stamp duty - withheld, not charged to the employer
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the employer does not bear it, and named because it is routinely listed as an Armenian employer cost. The law establishing the compensation fund for servicemen describes the amounts as paid by the individuals and withheld by the tax agent from their income, and sets a flat AMD 1,000 per reporting period for employees, against AMD 12,000 for sole traders and notaries. Parents, spouses and children of conscripted or fallen servicemen may reclaim what was withheld from their earnings in the preceding year by applying to the fund in the first two months of the year.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Armenia on compensation for damage caused to the life or health of servicemen during the defence of the Republic, articles 11 and 12

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Armenian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code creates no thirteenth-month salary and no statutory holiday bonus. Annual leave under article 159 is paid leave, with no separate supplement. Bonuses and private medical cover are contractual and common in the Yerevan technology market; price them as market cost, not as a legal charge.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Armenia (09.11.2004, HO-124-N), article 159

statutory_extras.name: Penalty for short notice - one average day's pay per overdue day
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is contingent on the employer getting the notice period wrong, and named because it is the only Armenian employment cost that can exceed the whole statutory ledger - which is nil. Article 115(2) of the Labour Code: where the periods in article 115(1) are not observed, the employer must pay the employee a penalty for each overdue day of notice, calculated on the employee's average daily wage. On a two-month obligation missed in full that is roughly 43 working days of pay. Under an employer of record the legal employer is the provider, so the exposure is the provider's to manage and yours to ask about: confirm in writing who carries it if a termination is mishandled.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Armenia (HO-124-N, 9 November 2004), official incorporation on ARLIS

countries.notice_typical: Two months' written notice for redundancy-type dismissals, and a service-length scale for the rest. Article 115(1) of the Labour Code requires at least two months where the contract ends on the grounds in article 113(1)(1) and (2) - liquidation of the employer, and a change in production volumes, economic or technological conditions. On the other grounds it sets a scale by length of service with that employer: 14 days under one year, 35 days from one to five years, 42 days from five to ten, 49 days from ten to fifteen and 60 days beyond fifteen. A collective or individual contract may lengthen these but not shorten them. Three days during an agreed probation period, under article 93(1). The teeth are in article 115(2): an employer that misses the notice period owes the employee a penalty for every overdue day, calculated on their average daily wage - so notice here is a priced obligation rather than a formality.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Armenia (09.11.2004, HO-124-N), article 159

countries.name: Argentina

assumptions.label: Employer contribution rate taken at 20.40%, the rate for a services or commerce company above the medium-enterprise tranche 2 threshold
assumptions.notes: Article 19 of Ley 27.541 sets two rates: 20.40% for private-sector employers whose main activity falls in 'Servicios' or 'Comercio' and whose total annual sales exceed the limit for categorisation as a medium enterprise, tranche 2; 18% for everyone else. An employer of record is a services company and its Argentine payroll normally puts it above that threshold, so the higher of the two rates is the one modelled. A smaller local employer would pay 2.4 points less.

assumptions.label: The occupational-risk (ART) premium is carried at zero, so the total below is a floor
assumptions.notes: Cover under Ley 24.557 is compulsory and is bought from a licensed ART at a negotiated rate, not at a published statutory percentage. Rather than invent a figure, the line is carried at zero and the total is stated as a minimum.

employer_contributions.name: Employer contributions to the social security subsystems (SIPA, PAMI, family allowances, employment fund)
employer_contributions.notes: One rate covers four subsystems. Article 19 of Ley 27.541: 'Veinte con cuarenta centesimos (20,40%) para los empleadores pertenecientes al sector privado cuya actividad principal encuadre en el sector Servicios o en el sector Comercio ... siempre que sus ventas totales anuales superen ... los limites para la categorizacion como empresa mediana tramo 2'; 18% applies to the rest. Deel's Argentina page splits the same 20.40 into its parts - pension 12.35, Ley 19.032 1.57, family allowances 5.40 and the national employment fund 1.08. Article 22 of the same law lets the employer subtract ARS 7,003.68 per employee per month from the base before applying the rate; that deduction is not applied here, which makes this line slightly conservative, because the peso figure written into the 2019 statute is worth a fraction of a percentage point against a 2026 salary.

source.name: Ley 27.541, articulo 19 (texto actualizado, Argentina.gob.ar / InfoLEG)

employer_contributions.name: Health cover (obra social)
employer_contributions.notes: Article 16(a) of Ley 23.660 reads 5% in its own text, after article 23 of Ley 25.239, but the operative rate is 6%: article 80 of Ley 25.565 (Boletin Oficial 21 March 2002) restored it, and the InfoLEG note records that restoration. The 2026 budget law, Ley 27.802 (Boletin Oficial 6 March 2026), then rewrites the paragraph itself to read 6% for contributions accruing from 1 January 2027, so the rate the employer pays does not move either side of that date. The worker pays a further 3%.

source.name: Ley 23.660, articulo 16 inciso a), with the InfoLEG notes on Ley 25.565 art. 80 and Ley 27.802 art. 165 (texto actualizado, InfoLEG)

statutory_extras.name: 13th-month salary (sueldo anual complementario)
statutory_extras.notes: Article 121 of the Ley de Contrato de Trabajo: 'Se entiende por sueldo anual complementario la doceava parte del total de las remuneraciones ... percibidas por el trabajador en el respectivo ano calendario.' Article 122, as replaced by Ley 27.073, pays it in two instalments due on 30 June and 18 December, each calculated on half of the highest monthly pay of the semester. It is remuneration, so it carries the employer contributions in the line below.

source.name: Ley 20.744 (Ley de Contrato de Trabajo), articulos 121 y 122 (texto actualizado, InfoLEG)

statutory_extras.name: Employer contributions due on the 13th-month salary
statutory_extras.notes: The line most Argentine cost estimates drop. The sueldo anual complementario is pay, so the 20.40% social security contribution and the 6% obra social contribution fall on it as well: 26.40% of 8.33% of annual gross is 2.20% of annual gross. Deel's own Argentina page prints an estimated employer cost of 28.35% and lists no 13th-month line at all, which is what happens when the extra month and its charges are left out.

source.name: Ley 20.744, articulo 121, read with Ley 27.541 articulo 19 and Ley 23.660 articulo 16 (both applied to remuneration, which the SAC is)

statutory_extras.name: Occupational risk insurance (ART)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the premium under Ley 24.557 is agreed with a licensed aseguradora de riesgos del trabajo and varies with the employer's activity and claims record; no statute publishes a rate to quote. It is nonetheless compulsory, and Deel's Argentina page books it at 1.35% of salary plus a fixed ARS 1,227 a month for the profile it sells. Because it is left out, the total on this page is a floor, not a final figure.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Argentina page

statutory_extras.name: Compulsory collective life insurance
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a flat peso premium per employee rather than a share of salary, and at the example salary it is worth far less than a tenth of a point. Deel's Argentina page books it at ARS 334.68 a month per employee. It is listed here so that nothing compulsory is missing from the page, not because it moves the budget.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Argentina page

countries.notice_typical: Article 231(b) of the Ley de Contrato de Trabajo, as replaced by article 48 of Ley 27.802 (Boletin Oficial 6 March 2026), requires the employer to give one month's notice where service does not exceed five years and two months above that; the employee owes fifteen days. No notice is due during the probation period. Notice can be replaced by an indemnity in lieu, which is owed on top of the seniority indemnity.

payments.name: Sueldo anual complementario (aguinaldo), first instalment
payments.deadline: 30 June

payments.name: Sueldo anual complementario (aguinaldo), second instalment
payments.deadline: 18 December

source.quote: El sueldo anual complementario será abonado en dos (2) cuotas: la primera de ellas con vencimiento el 30 de junio y la segunda con vencimiento el 18 de diciembre de cada año

countries.name: Austria

assumptions.label: Place of employment is Vienna (three Austrian employer charges are set by the province, not by the federation)
assumptions.notes: Austria is usually described as having one national employer rate. It does not. Three lines move with the province the job sits in. Vienna tops two of the three - it is alone at 0.75% on the housing levy and alone in charging the employer levy at all - while on the third, the chamber surcharge, it sits mid-table at 0.36% behind Burgenland and Tyrol. The housing subsidy levy (Wohnbauförderungsbeitrag) rose in Vienna alone to 0.75% employer from 1 January 2026 against 0.50% everywhere else. The chamber surcharge (DZ) is set province by province: 0.36% in Vienna in 2026, from 0.31% in Upper Austria to 0.40% in Burgenland. And the Vienna employer levy, the so-called underground-railway tax, exists only inside the city. Net effect: a hire registered in Vienna costs about 0.5 points of salary more than the same hire in Upper Austria. Vienna is modelled because it is where providers register their Austrian examples - Deel prices the Vienna levy on its own Austria page.

assumptions.label: Hire is a white-collar employee (Angestellte), not a manual worker (Arbeiter)
assumptions.notes: The social insurance authority publishes its rate table in four columns, and Arbeiter is not the same column as Angestellte. A manual worker in construction also carries the bad-weather compensation levy (0.70% employer) and, where the night-heavy-work act applies, a 3.80% employer levy that no office role ever pays. Every rate on this page is the Angestellte column.

employer_contributions.name: Pension insurance (Pensionsversicherung), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee above the marginal-earnings threshold of EUR 551.10 a month; charged on pay up to the monthly ceiling of EUR 6,930, which is EUR 83,160 a year
employer_contributions.notes: The largest single line in Austria and the one that makes the country expensive. 22.80% in total under section 51 ASVG, split 10.25% employee and 12.55% employer - the employer carries the bigger half, where the German and Swiss pension lines on this site are both split down the middle. The ceiling is what saves a senior hire: the umbrella body of the Austrian social insurance institutions sets the monthly maximum contribution base at EUR 6,930 for 2026 under section 45(1) and section 108(3) ASVG, so above about EUR 83,160 of annual pay this charge stops growing.

source.name: Dachverband der österreichischen Sozialversicherungsträger - Beitragsrechtliche Werte in der Sozialversicherung 2026, table 3 Beitragssätze ('Pensionsversicherung, § 51 ASVG 22,80 10,25 12,55')

employer_contributions.name: Health insurance (Krankenversicherung), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee above the marginal-earnings threshold; same EUR 6,930 monthly ceiling as pension
employer_contributions.notes: 7.65% in total under section 51 ASVG, 3.87% employee and 3.78% employer. The rate table gives one figure for all Angestellte rather than a schedule by carrier, so unlike Germany - where the employer's half moves with each fund's supplementary rate - there is nothing to compare between providers on this line.

source.name: Dachverband der österreichischen Sozialversicherungsträger - Beitragsrechtliche Werte in der Sozialversicherung 2026, table 3 Beitragssätze ('Krankenversicherung, § 51 ASVG 7,65 3,87 3,78')

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (Arbeitslosenversicherung), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee above the marginal-earnings threshold; same EUR 6,930 monthly ceiling as pension
employer_contributions.notes: 5.90% in total, split evenly 2.95% and 2.95%. The employer half never moves. The employee half does: section 2a AMPFG reduces it to 0% below EUR 2,225 a month, 1% to EUR 2,427 and 2% to EUR 2,630, which is why some payroll summaries print a range here. That relief is on the employee side only and changes nothing for the buyer.

source.name: Dachverband der österreichischen Sozialversicherungsträger - Beitragsrechtliche Werte in der Sozialversicherung 2026, table 3 Beitragssätze ('Arbeitslosenversicherung (AV) 5,90 2,95 2,95')

employer_contributions.name: Accident insurance (Unfallversicherung), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only charge at a single national rate, with no industry risk classes; the levy falls away entirely from the month after the employee turns 60
employer_contributions.notes: 1.10% paid by the employer alone under section 51 ASVG, with nothing from the employee. Austria is the simple case here: unlike Switzerland, Germany or China there is no risk class and no insurer to shop for, so an office role and a building site pay the same rate. One exemption is worth knowing before you compare quotes: the economic chamber's 2026 payroll table states that the accident contribution ceases once the employee has completed their sixtieth year ('Der UV-Beitrag entfällt ab Vollendung des 60. Lebensjahres', wko.at/entlohnung/beitragswesen-dienstnehmer-2026, read 20 September 2026), so a hire over 60 carries 1.10 points less.

source.name: Dachverband der österreichischen Sozialversicherungsträger - Beitragsrechtliche Werte in der Sozialversicherung 2026, table 3 Beitragssätze ('Unfallversicherung, § 51 ASVG 1,10 - 1,10')

employer_contributions.name: Housing subsidy levy (Wohnbauförderungsbeitrag), Vienna rate
employer_contributions.applies: Employees above the marginal-earnings threshold whose place of employment is in the province of Vienna; 0.50% employer in the other eight provinces. Not charged on the 13th and 14th month
employer_contributions.notes: The newest Austrian employer cost, and the one no competitor page has caught up with. The City of Vienna states it plainly: 'Ab 1. Jänner 2026 beträgt die Höhe des Wohnbauförderungsbeitrages für den*die Dienstgeber*in und für den*die Beschäftigte*n jeweils 0,75 Prozent der Bemessungsgrundlage, insgesamt also 1,5 Prozent' - up from 0.50% each, where it had stood since January 2018. The national social insurance rate table carries the same exception in a footnote to its 1.00% national line: 'Der Wohnbauförderungsbeitrag für Wien beträgt ab 01.01.2026 1,5 %'. The health insurance carrier has published the new payroll codes for it. Outside Vienna the employer half is still 0.50%, so this one line is 0.25 points of the roughly 0.5-point Vienna premium. The economic chamber's 2026 payroll table adds that neither this levy nor the chamber of labour dues are charged on the 13th and 14th month ('Kein WBF und AK von Sonderzahlungen', wko.at/entlohnung/beitragswesen-dienstnehmer-2026, read 20 September 2026).

source.name: Stadt Wien - Wohnbauförderungsbeitrag, Höhe und Änderungen ('jeweils 0,75 Prozent der Bemessungsgrundlage, insgesamt also 1,5 Prozent')

employer_contributions.name: Insolvency pay guarantee surcharge (IESG-Zuschlag), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only charge on the same base and ceiling as the four insurances
employer_contributions.notes: 0.10% paid by the employer alone, funding the state guarantee that pays wages when an employer goes insolvent. It is tiny, but it is one of the lines that makes a raw sum of the four headline insurances come out short of what an Austrian payroll actually costs.

source.name: Dachverband der österreichischen Sozialversicherungsträger - Beitragsrechtliche Werte in der Sozialversicherung 2026, table 3 Beitragssätze ('IESG-Zuschlag 0,10 - 0,10')

employer_contributions.name: Severance provision fund (Betriebliche Vorsorge, BV-Kasse), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Every employment relationship beginning after 31 December 2002 that lasts longer than one month; the first month is always contribution-free, and there is no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Austria's answer to severance pay, and the reason Austrian termination is cheap where Brazilian or Italian termination is not. Section 6(1) BMSVG obliges the employer to pay 'einen laufenden Beitrag in Höhe von 1,53 vH des monatlichen Entgelts sowie allfälliger Sonderzahlungen' into a severance fund of the employee's scheme, from the start of the relationship, 'sofern das Arbeitsverhältnis länger als einen Monat dauert. Der erste Monat ist jedenfalls beitragsfrei.' The money belongs to the employee and follows them between jobs, so no provision has to be built for a future payout. Two practical points: it sits outside the social insurance ceiling, so it keeps costing 1.53% however senior the hire, and in a first part-year it is charged on eleven months rather than twelve.

source.name: RIS - Betriebliches Mitarbeiter- und Selbständigenvorsorgegesetz (BMSVG) § 6(1), consolidated text in force

employer_contributions.name: Family burden equalisation levy (Dienstgeberbeitrag zum FLAF)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer with a permanent establishment in Austria, on the whole payroll including the 13th and 14th month, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: A payroll tax rather than a social insurance contribution, which is exactly why it goes missing from cost pages that only read the insurance rate table. The chamber of commerce states the current rate in one sentence: 'Ab dem Jahr 2025 beträgt der Dienstgeberbeitrag 3,7 % der Beitragsgrundlage.' It was 3.9% until the end of 2024, and that stale figure is still in circulation - Deel's Austria page printed 3.90% when this was checked on 20 September 2026, which overstates the levy by 0.2 points of salary. No ceiling applies, so on a senior hire this line keeps growing after the insurances have stopped.

source.name: WKO - Dienstgeberbeitrag zum Familienlastenausgleichsfonds ('Ab dem Jahr 2025 beträgt der Dienstgeberbeitrag 3,7 % der Beitragsgrundlage')

employer_contributions.name: Municipal payroll tax (Kommunalsteuer), 3% to the municipality
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the sum of wages paid at each Austrian permanent establishment, with no ceiling; a monthly base of EUR 1,460 or less is reduced by EUR 1,095
employer_contributions.notes: Three points of salary that almost no English-language Austria guide prints, because it is a municipal tax and never appears in the social insurance schedule. Section 9 of the Kommunalsteuergesetz 1993 is one sentence: 'Die Steuer beträgt 3% der Bemessungsgrundlage.' The rate is federal law and identical in every municipality - what varies is who collects it, the municipality where the establishment sits. There is no ceiling, so it is the second line, after the family levy, that keeps rising once the insurance ceiling has been reached.

source.name: RIS - Kommunalsteuergesetz 1993 § 9 Steuersatz ('Die Steuer beträgt 3% der Bemessungsgrundlage')

employer_contributions.name: Chamber surcharge (Zuschlag zum Dienstgeberbeitrag, DZ), Vienna rate
employer_contributions.applies: Employers that are members of the economic chamber, at the rate of the province where the establishment is registered; 0.36% in Vienna for 2026, 0.31% in Upper Austria to 0.40% in Burgenland
employer_contributions.notes: The second of the three province-dependent lines. The chamber explains the mechanism itself: 'Der DZ-Satz setzt sich aus einem für alle Bundesländer gültigen Bundeskammeranteil von 0,12% und einem von jeder Landeskammer festgesetzten Anteil zusammen', and publishes the resulting 2026 table - Burgenland 0.40%, Carinthia 0.37%, Lower Austria 0.33%, Upper Austria 0.31%, Salzburg 0.35%, Styria 0.34%, Tyrol 0.39%, Vorarlberg 0.33%, Vienna 0.36%. A company with establishments in several provinces applies each province's rate to the staff registered there, which is why a provider operating nationally cannot quote you a single Austrian percentage honestly.

source.name: WKO - Zuschlag zum Dienstgeberbeitrag (DZ), rates by province for 2026

employer_contributions.name: Vienna employer levy (Dienstgeberabgabe, the underground-railway tax)
employer_contributions.applies: Each employment relationship in Vienna, EUR 2 per started week, about EUR 104 a year; not charged for employees over 55 or for contracts of at most ten hours a week
employer_contributions.notes: A flat head tax rather than a percentage, which is why it disappears from every cost page built on rates alone. The City of Vienna states it in one line: 'Die Dienstgeberabgabe beträgt 2 Euro pro Dienstverhältnis und angefangener Woche.' It exists only in Vienna, it is nicknamed the underground-railway tax because the proceeds were earmarked for building the U-Bahn, and it has stood at EUR 2 since 1 June 2012. At EUR 104 a year it is about 0.17% of the example salary on this page - trivial next to the pension line, and the clearest illustration of why an Austrian employer cost cannot be reduced to one national percentage. Because it is a fixed amount, it weighs more on a junior hire than a senior one.

source.name: Stadt Wien - Dienstgeberabgabe ('Die Dienstgeberabgabe beträgt 2 Euro pro Dienstverhältnis und angefangener Woche')

statutory_extras.name: 13th and 14th month (Urlaubsgeld and Weihnachtsgeld) - collective agreement, not law
statutory_extras.notes: The biggest number on this page is the one carried at zero, and the reason is that no Austrian statute imposes it. What imposes it is the Kollektivvertrag of the sector the hire falls under, and nearly every Austrian collective agreement has one, so in practice an offer without a 13th and 14th month is not competitive and often not compliant with the applicable agreement. Budget it. Two extra months of pay is 16.67% of annual gross on top of the ledger above, and those months carry their own charges: the social insurance authority applies the same employer rates minus the housing levy and chamber dues, which is 20.48% - the figure Deel independently prints for Austria as 'Social insurance based on 13th and 14th salaries' - plus the severance fund, the family levy, the chamber surcharge and the municipal tax. Special payments have their own annual ceiling of EUR 13,860, separate from the monthly one. All in, a full 13th and 14th month adds roughly 21 points of annual gross. Ask which Kollektivvertrag your provider will register the hire under before you agree a salary, because the same answer also fixes the minimum pay and the notice scale.

source.name: Dachverband der österreichischen Sozialversicherungsträger - Beitragsrechtliche Werte 2026, monthly maximum contribution bases ('Sonderzahlungen im Kalenderjahr 13.860,00'; no statutory 13th month appears in the rate schedule)

statutory_extras.name: Disability employment levy (Ausgleichstaxe) - assessed on the employer, not the payslip
statutory_extras.notes: A real Austrian employer cost that cannot honestly be written as a percentage of one salary, so it is named here and left out of the total. Employers with 25 or more staff must employ one registered disabled person for every 25 employees, and pay a monthly levy for each position they do not fill. The ministerial order for 2026 sets it at 'monatlich 344 Euro' for employers with 25 to 99 staff, EUR 485 for 100 to 399 and EUR 512 for 400 or more. Every EOR provider is in the largest bracket, so if it fills none of its quota the levy works out at EUR 512 divided by 25, about EUR 20 a month per employee - which is what a provider passes on: Deel lists a 'Disability Levy - 20.19 EUR/month' on its Austria page. A provider that does meet its quota owes nothing. It is a question for the quote, not a rate.

source.name: RIS - Verordnung über die Feststellung der Ausgleichstaxe nach dem Behinderteneinstellungsgesetz für das Kalenderjahr 2026, Art. 1 (BGBl. II Nr. 280/2025)

statutory_extras.name: Social and training fund levy (SWF) - owed by a staff-leasing employer under the AÜG
statutory_extras.notes: 0.35% of the general social-insurance base up to the maximum contribution base of EUR 6,930 a month, with the same rate on the 13th and 14th salaries. Section 22d(1) of the staff-leasing act (Arbeitskräfteüberlassungsgesetz, AÜG) has set it at 0.35% since the second quarter of 2017 and has not been amended since April 2019, so that is the 2026 rate. It is owed by the hirer-out (Überlasser), whether based in Austria or abroad (section 22d(2)), for every employee it employs in order to place with a third party. Section 3 defines that placement as making workers available to perform work for someone else, and the user as whoever deploys them on its own business tasks - which is how an employer of record works: the provider employs, the client directs the work. On the text, the test is that placement, not the licence or the entity: an Austrian subsidiary that places your hire with you is itself a hirer-out. The line stays outside the total for one reason written into the same section: under section 22d(9) the levy rests where section 10(1) makes the client's own binding workplace rules apply to the placed employee, and that turns on the collective agreement the provider applies and on the pay rules at your establishment, which providers do not publish. At the US$70,000 example it would add about US$245 a year. Ask the provider whether it pays the SWF on your hire.

source.name: RIS - Arbeitskräfteüberlassungsgesetz § 22d(1), consolidated text in force since 01.04.2019 ('ab dem zweiten Quartal 2017 0,35 vH der Beitragsgrundlage'), read with § 3 (definitions)

statutory_extras.name: Chamber of labour dues (Arbeiterkammerumlage) - employee side only
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is not an employer cost, and named because it is regularly misfiled as one. The rate table shows 0.50% in the employee column and a dash in the employer column: the employer withholds it and remits it, but it comes out of the employee's pay. It funds the Arbeiterkammer, the statutory body that every Austrian private-sector employee belongs to, and it is not charged on the 13th and 14th month. If a quote shows it on the employer side, the quote is wrong.

source.name: Dachverband der österreichischen Sozialversicherungsträger - Beitragsrechtliche Werte 2026, table 3 Beitragssätze ('Arbeiterkammerumlage 0,50 0,50 -')

countries.notice_typical: Six weeks from the employer, rising to two months after two completed years of service, three after five, four after fifteen and five after twenty-five (Angestelltengesetz § 20(2)). Unless the contract says otherwise the notice must expire at the end of a calendar quarter, which in practice lengthens it; the parties may agree instead that it ends on the fifteenth or the last day of a month. An employee resigning gives one month to the end of a calendar month.

countries.name: Australia

assumptions.label: Employee works in New South Wales (payroll tax 5.45%, icare workers compensation)
assumptions.notes: Each state and territory sets its own payroll tax rate and threshold (roughly 4.75% to 6.85%) and runs its own workers compensation scheme. The provider's grouped Australian payroll is far above every threshold, so the full rate applies to each hire.

assumptions.label: Workers compensation at 0.222% of wages (icare NSW class 783400 Computer Consultancy Services, 2026-27)
assumptions.notes: icare NSW prices each employer by its Workers Compensation Industry Classification (WIC) and, above the small-employer threshold, its claims history; it has confirmed that WIC rates do not change for the 2026-27 policy period. Its published 2026-27 WIC rate table sets class 783400 Computer Consultancy Services (computer consultancy, systems analysis, programming, website design) at 0.218% of wages, plus a Dust Diseases contribution of 0.004% including GST, modelled together as 0.222%. Under an employer of record the provider is a labour hire employer, and the WIC System 2026-27 classes each hired-out worker by the activity most closely associated with that worker's occupation, so a software role sits in 783400, not in the provider's own placement class. Ask the provider for the rate on its NSW policy.

employer_contributions.name: Superannuation guarantee
employer_contributions.applies: All employees; 12% of ordinary time earnings up to the maximum contribution base of AUD 270,830 for 2026-27
employer_contributions.notes: The guarantee reached its legislated 12% on 1 July 2025 and stays there. Since 1 July 2026 (Payday Super) it is paid with each pay run, and the maximum contribution base is an annual figure of AUD 270,830, so the employer's super stops growing at about AUD 32,500 a year.

source.name: ATO — Super guarantee: percentage 12.00% from 1 July 2025, maximum contribution base AUD 270,830 for 2026-27

employer_contributions.name: NSW payroll tax
employer_contributions.applies: Employers, or groups of employers, whose Australian wages exceed the AUD 1,200,000 NSW threshold; superannuation and most allowances count as taxable wages
employer_contributions.notes: 5.45% for 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, unchanged since 2022. The AUD 1.2 million tax-free threshold is a single deduction shared by the whole group, so for a provider's Australian entity it is worth a few dollars per employee; the engine applies the full rate. The tax also applies to the super contribution itself, which the engine leaves out (about 0.65 points).

source.name: Revenue NSW — Payroll tax thresholds and rates (1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027: threshold AUD 1,200,000, rate 5.45%)

employer_contributions.name: Workers compensation insurance (icare NSW), office and IT classification
employer_contributions.applies: Every NSW employer; premium = wages x industry classification rate, adjusted for claims experience above the small-employer threshold
employer_contributions.notes: icare's NSW Workers Compensation Industry Classification (WIC) rates and Dust Disease Contributions 2026-27 list class 783400 Computer Consultancy Services at a WIC rate of 0.218% and a Dust Diseases rate of 0.004% including GST; modelled as 0.222% of wages. icare stated on 27 May 2026 that WIC rates will not change for the 2026-27 policy period. The WIC System 2026-27 (Annexure G, note 10) classes labour hire workers by the activity most closely associated with their occupation, which is how an employer of record's software hire is rated. A larger employer's premium is then adjusted for its claims experience, so the provider's own policy can sit above or below this rate. Until September 2026 this line carried 0.5%, the midpoint of a provider-published range.

source.name: icare NSW - Workers Compensation Industry Classification (WIC) rates and Dust Disease Contributions 2026-27, class 783400

statutory_extras.name: Redundancy pay (NES scale, 4 to 16 weeks)
statutory_extras.notes: Contingent, not recurring: under the National Employment Standards an employee made redundant after at least one year of service receives 4 weeks' pay, rising with service to 16 weeks after 9 years (12 weeks from 10 years). Small businesses with fewer than 15 employees are exempt, but a provider's entity is not.

source.name: Fair Work Ombudsman — Redundancy pay and entitlements (redundancy pay period by years of continuous service)

countries.notice_typical: Under the National Employment Standards the employer gives 1 week's notice in the first year, 2 weeks after 1 year, 3 weeks after 3 years and 4 weeks after 5 years, plus 1 extra week for employees over 45 with at least 2 years' service; unfair-dismissal claims open after 6 months of service (12 months at employers with fewer than 15 staff).

countries.name: Azerbaijan

assumptions.label: The employing entity is in the non-oil, non-state sector
assumptions.notes: This is the assumption that selects the rate schedule. Article 14.4 of the Law on Social Insurance and article 15-10.1.2-1 of the Law on Medical Insurance give reduced banded rates to employers 'not active in the oil and gas field and belonging to the non-state sector'. An EOR provider's local entity is a private company outside oil and gas, so this page prices that schedule. An employer in the oil and gas field or the state sector pays the general rates instead: 22% of the whole payroll for social insurance under article 14.3.1, and medical insurance at 2% up to AZN 8,000 a month and 0.5% above under article 15-10.1.2. At the US$28,000 example that would lift the employer's cost by about 7 points of gross.

assumptions.label: Salary paid in 12 equal monthly instalments
assumptions.notes: Every Azerbaijani threshold is monthly: AZN 200, AZN 2,500 and AZN 8,000 a month. The calculator works on the annual salary and converts each threshold to its yearly equivalent (AZN 2,400, AZN 30,000 and AZN 96,000), which gives the same result only when pay is spread evenly. A bonus paid in one month pushes more of that month into the upper bands, where the social insurance rate is lower, so an uneven pay pattern changes the total slightly.

employer_contributions.name: Social insurance (DSMF), employer share on the first AZN 200 a month
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee of a non-oil private employer, on the first AZN 200 of each month's pay
employer_contributions.notes: The first of three bands in the 2026 schedule. Article 14.4 of the Law on Social Insurance, reworded by Law No. 297-VIIQD of 9 December 2025, sets the employer's share for the non-oil, non-state sector at 22% of monthly income up to AZN 200. That is AZN 44 a month at most, whatever the salary, which is why this line stops growing above AZN 2,400 a year. The same table appears on the State Social Protection Fund's own page and in the State Tax Service's announcement of 21 November 2025, which dates it from 1 January 2026. The employee's share on this slice is 3%, withheld from pay.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan No. 250-IQ on Social Insurance, article 14.4 as reworded by Law No. 297-VIIQD of 9 December 2025 (consolidated text, e-qanun.az)

employer_contributions.name: Social insurance (DSMF), employer share from AZN 200 to AZN 8,000 a month
employer_contributions.applies: The slice of monthly pay between AZN 200 and AZN 8,000
employer_contributions.notes: The band that carries almost all of the Azerbaijani employer bill at a technology salary. Article 14.4 writes it as 'AZN 44 + 15% of the part from AZN 200 to AZN 8,000'; the AZN 44 is the 22% line above, so this line charges 15% on the slice between AZN 2,400 and AZN 96,000 a year. At the US$28,000 example, about AZN 3,967 a month, it is AZN 565 a month. The employee pays 10% on the same slice. Deel's Azerbaijan page applies this 15% to everything above AZN 200 with no upper band, which was the rule until 31 December 2025.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan No. 250-IQ on Social Insurance, article 14.4 as reworded by Law No. 297-VIIQD of 9 December 2025 (consolidated text, e-qanun.az)

employer_contributions.name: Social insurance (DSMF), employer share above AZN 8,000 a month
employer_contributions.applies: Only the part of monthly pay above AZN 8,000 (about US$56,500 a year); not reached at the example salary
employer_contributions.notes: New on 1 January 2026. Before Law No. 297-VIIQD the 15% band ran without an upper limit; since then article 14.4 charges the employer 'AZN 1,214 + 11% of the part above AZN 8,000', and the employee 10%. AZN 1,214 is exactly what the two lower bands produce at AZN 8,000 (44 + 15% of 7,800), so this line only adds 11% on the excess. There is no ceiling on it. The State Tax Service presented the change as a cut of the combined rate above AZN 8,000 from 25% to 21%.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan No. 250-IQ on Social Insurance, article 14.4 as reworded by Law No. 297-VIIQD of 9 December 2025 (consolidated text, e-qanun.az)

employer_contributions.name: Compulsory medical insurance, employer share on the first AZN 2,500 a month
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee of a non-oil private employer, on the first AZN 2,500 of each month's pay
employer_contributions.notes: The ceiling here caps the base, not the amount: 2% on monthly pay up to AZN 2,500, so at most AZN 50 a month, and the part above is charged at 0.5% on the next line. Article 15-10.1.2-1 of the Law on Medical Insurance, inserted by Law No. 297-VIIQD from 1 January 2026, moved the threshold for non-oil private employers from AZN 8,000 down to AZN 2,500. The oil, gas and state sectors keep the AZN 8,000 threshold of article 15-10.1.2. Deel's page still prints the old threshold, with the two rates the wrong way round (0.5% below, 2% above). The employee pays the same 2% and 0.5%.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan No. 725-IQ on Medical Insurance, article 15-10.1.2-1 inserted by Law No. 297-VIIQD of 9 December 2025 (consolidated text, e-qanun.az)

employer_contributions.name: Compulsory medical insurance, employer share above AZN 2,500 a month
employer_contributions.applies: Only the part of monthly pay above AZN 2,500
employer_contributions.notes: 0.5% on the part of monthly pay above AZN 2,500, with no upper limit, under the same article 15-10.1.2-1. At the US$28,000 example it is about AZN 7 a month. The State Tax Service summed up the 2026 change as the combined medical rate on pay between AZN 2,500 and AZN 8,000 falling from 4% to 1%.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan No. 725-IQ on Medical Insurance, article 15-10.1.2-1 inserted by Law No. 297-VIIQD of 9 December 2025 (consolidated text, e-qanun.az)

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on the whole payroll, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Article 9.0.1 of the Law on Unemployment Insurance sets the employer's tariff at 0.5% of the accrued payroll, and article 9.0.2 withholds another 0.5% from the employee. The 2026 reform left it unchanged: the State Tax Service's announcement says it 'continues in the current manner'. It is missing from the employer ledger on Deel's Azerbaijan page.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan No. 765-VQ on Unemployment Insurance, article 9.0.1 (consolidated text, e-qanun.az)

employer_contributions.name: Compulsory occupational accident insurance (office staff, risk class 1)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee; 0.2% for office staff in risk classes 1 to 5
employer_contributions.notes: A premium the employer pays to a licensed insurer rather than to a state fund, but compulsory under the Law on compulsory insurance against loss of professional capacity from occupational accidents and diseases, whose article 13.1 caps tariffs at 2%. The Cabinet of Ministers sets them in decision No. 200 of 5 November 2010, amended most recently on 23 February 2026: software development (code J 62) and employment activities (code N 78, the class that covers staffing and employment services) are both in risk class 1, where the tariff for office staff is 0.2%. A software engineer is office staff: decision No. 192 of 29 October 2010 puts managers, specialists and technical staff in that category, and defines the premium base as twelve times the monthly contract salary, with no ceiling. Manual workers in the same class pay 0.4%.

source.name: Cabinet of Ministers of Azerbaijan, decision No. 200 of 5 November 2010 on occupational accident insurance tariffs, as amended to 23 February 2026 (e-qanun.az)

statutory_extras.name: Employee contributions and income tax - withheld, not a cost to you
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the employee pays them out of gross pay, and named because they explain the gap between a gross offer and take-home pay. In the non-oil private sector the employee pays 3% of social insurance on the first AZN 200 a month and 10% above, 2% of medical insurance up to AZN 2,500 and 0.5% above, and 0.5% of unemployment insurance. Income tax for the same sector was reset on 1 January 2026, when the seven-year income tax privilege introduced in 2019 ended: 3% on monthly income up to AZN 2,500 in 2026 (5% in 2027, 7% from 2028), with AZN 200 of it tax-free for incomes up to AZN 2,500, then 10% from AZN 2,500 to AZN 8,000 and 14% above. A candidate comparing offers made before and after January 2026 is comparing different net pay on the same gross.

source.name: State Tax Service under the Ministry of Economy, announcement of 21 November 2025 on the 2026 income tax and social insurance schedule for the non-oil private sector

statutory_extras.name: Technology park residents - reduced social insurance option, not priced here
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it does not apply to a hire made through an EOR provider unless that provider is itself a registered technology park resident, contractor or direct subcontractor. Article 14.8 of the Law on Social Insurance lets Azerbaijani citizens employed by a technology park resident for software development or system integration choose, for ten years from 1 January 2023, to pay social insurance on four times the monthly minimum wage instead of on their salary. The choice belongs to the employee, is made each year by 15 January and excludes foreigners. For a company that plans a larger engineering team in Baku, that is a reason to price a resident entity against the EOR fee.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan No. 250-IQ on Social Insurance, article 14.8 (consolidated text, e-qanun.az)

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Azerbaijani law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code creates no thirteenth-month salary or holiday bonus. The money it adds on top of ordinary pay is tied to events: average pay during annual leave, and on a redundancy the notice and severance amounts in article 77, which are termination costs rather than recurring ones. Bonuses and private health cover are contractual in the Baku technology market.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Azerbaijan, consolidated text (e-qanun.az)

countries.notice_typical: On a redundancy, notice scales with service under article 77(1) of the Labour Code: at least 2 calendar weeks under one year, 4 weeks from one to five years, 6 weeks from five to ten and 9 weeks beyond ten, with at least one paid day off each week to look for work. With the employee's consent it can be replaced by a payment of 0.5, 0.9, 1.4 or 2 months' average pay. Severance is owed on top under article 77(3): one month's average pay under one year of service, at least 1.4 months from one to five years, 1.7 from five to ten and 2 beyond ten. Either side may end the contract on 3 days' written notice during probation (article 53(1)). An employee resigning gives one calendar month (article 69(1)).

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Azerbaijan, consolidated text (e-qanun.az)

countries.name: Bangladesh

assumptions.label: Basic wage as a share of gross pay
assumptions.notes: Bangladesh has no general social insurance, so what the employer owes is driven entirely by the basic wage rather than by a contribution rate. The Bangladesh Labour Rules, as amended in September 2022, set the floor: where no government-declared minimum wage applies to the job, the worker's basic wage may not be less than 50% of total (gross) pay, and the annual increment may not be less than 5% of basic. Modelled at that floor, so every figure on this page is a minimum: a contract that sets basic at 60% of gross raises both lines below by a fifth.

assumptions.label: Festival allowances modelled at the rule's cap, one month's basic wage each
assumptions.notes: Rule 111(5) of the Bangladesh Labour Rules 2015 requires two festival allowances a year for workers who have completed one continuous year of service, and provides that each one may not exceed a month's basic wage and is paid on top of wages. The rule fixes a ceiling rather than a floor, and paying the full month before each of the two main religious festivals is the settled practice these contracts are written against — so this page models both allowances at the cap and says so rather than quietly pricing them at nothing.

employer_contributions.name: Service-end provision for supplied workers (one month's basic wage per year of service)
employer_contributions.applies: Workers recruited by a contractor organisation and supplied to other establishments — which is what an employer of record is in Bangladeshi law
employer_contributions.notes: This is the line that makes Bangladesh unlike a country with payroll taxes: there is no social insurance contribution to pay, but Rule 17(2) of the Bangladesh Labour Rules 2015 requires a contractor organisation that supplies workers to other establishments to hold, in a bank account and for each worker, an amount equal to one month's basic wage for each completed year of service — or the gratuity under section 2(10) of the Labour Act where that applies — and to pay it to the worker by cheque, directly, whenever the employment ends. Because an EOR is exactly such a supplier, the money is banked from the first year rather than promised at the exit, which is why it belongs in the monthly cost and not in a footnote. At a basic wage of half of gross it is 4.17% of pay; if the contract sets basic higher, so is this line.

source.name: Bangladesh Labour Rules 2015, Rule 17(2) (Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary, 15 September 2015, p. 7325): for every worker recruited by a contractor organisation and supplied to establishments, an amount equal to one month's basic wage for each completed year of service, or gratuity under section 2(10) where applicable, shall be kept in a bank account and paid to the worker directly by cheque on any form of termination

statutory_extras.name: Two festival allowances a year (each up to one month's basic wage)
statutory_extras.notes: Two allowances a year, each capped at a month's basic wage and paid in addition to wages, once the worker has completed a continuous year of service. At a basic wage of half of gross, the pair comes to one month of gross pay a year, which is how it is carried here. The Labour Act was amended to define "festival allowance" and leave the amount to the Rules; Rule 111(5) is where the amount lives. Two points to check in an offer: the entitlement starts only after twelve months of continuous service, and the rule caps each allowance rather than fixing it, so a contract can promise less than a full month unless it says otherwise.

source.name: Bangladesh Labour Rules 2015, Rule 111(5) (Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary, 15 September 2015, pp. 7381-7382): workers who have completed one continuous year of service shall be paid two festival allowances a year, provided that each allowance shall not exceed the monthly basic wage and shall be treated as additional to wages

statutory_extras.name: Statutory gratuity (30 days' wages per year, 45 days after ten years)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero here to avoid counting the same money twice: for an EOR hire the provision above is the banked form of this entitlement. The Labour Act defines gratuity as at least thirty days' wages at the last drawn rate for each completed year of service, or for any service beyond six months, rising to forty-five days' wages a year once service passes ten years, payable when the employment ends. Note that gratuity is calculated on wages rather than on basic wage alone, so where it applies it is larger than the banked month of basic — the gap is worth raising with the provider before signing a long assignment.

source.name: Bangladesh Labour Act 2006, section 2(10) as amended: gratuity means at least thirty days' wages at the worker's last drawn rate for every completed year of service or any part in excess of six months, or forty-five days' wages a year where service exceeds ten years, payable on termination of employment

statutory_extras.name: Workers' Profit Participation Fund
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a share of company profit, not a percentage of one salary, and it cannot honestly be expressed per employee. The Labour Act requires companies above the statutory size thresholds to set aside five per cent of their net profit each year for the participation and welfare funds that pay out to their workers. It never touches an EOR client — the provider is the employer, and the client has no Bangladeshi entity and no Bangladeshi profit — which is one of the few places where using an EOR removes an obligation rather than repackaging it.

source.name: Bangladesh Labour Act 2006, Chapter XV (participation in companies' profits), which requires qualifying companies to pay five per cent of net profit into the workers' participation and welfare funds

statutory_extras.name: Compulsory group insurance (establishments with 100+ permanent workers)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the cost is an insurance premium and it only bites above a headcount an EOR client will not reach on its own. Section 99 of the Labour Act requires an establishment employing at least one hundred permanent workers to run group insurance under the insurance laws, and makes the employer responsible for collecting the claim and paying it to the dependants on a worker's death. The provider's own headcount is what counts here, not the client's, so ask whether it carries the cover and whether the fee includes it.

source.name: Bangladesh Labour Act 2006, section 99(1)-(2) as amended: an establishment with not fewer than one hundred permanent workers shall introduce group insurance under the insurance law, and the employer is responsible for realising the claim and paying it to the dependants

statutory_extras.name: Statutory annual leave (one paid day for every 18 days worked)
statutory_extras.notes: Paid time inside the salary rather than an extra contribution. After one continuous year of service, a worker in a shop, commercial or industrial establishment, factory or road transport undertaking earns one day of paid leave for every eighteen days worked in the preceding twelve months — about seventeen days on Bangladesh's six-day week. Unused annual leave is paid out when employment ends. Casual and sick leave are separate entitlements and do not accumulate into this one.

source.name: Bangladesh Labour Act 2006, section 117(1)(a): every adult worker who has completed one year of continuous service shall be granted paid leave at the rate of one day for every eighteen days of work in a shop, commercial or industrial establishment, factory or road transport undertaking

countries.notice_typical: Notice here is long, and it is the number to plan around. Ending a permanent worker's employment other than by dismissal for misconduct takes 120 days' written notice for a monthly-rated worker, or 60 days for anyone else; for a temporary worker it is 30 days and 14 days respectively. Probation runs six months for clerical work and three months for other work. Public holidays are set by the employer before 31 December for the year ahead and may not be fewer than eleven days.

payments.name: Festival allowance (first of two a year)
payments.deadline: before the religious festival (movable); the Act defines the allowance as payable on the eve of the worker's own religious festival

payments.name: Festival allowance (second of two a year)
payments.deadline: before the second religious festival of the year (movable)

payments.name: Workers' Profit Participation Fund (5 % of prior-year net profit)
payments.deadline: per the Act chapter on the fund (prior year's profit); the 'nine months' deadline was not found in the text read and is not stated here

countries.name: Belgium

assumptions.label: Hire is a white-collar employee (employe / bediende), not a manual worker (ouvrier / arbeider)
assumptions.notes: Belgium still splits its payroll mechanics by collar even though notice periods were unified in 2014. For a manual worker the base of every ordinary contribution is raised to 108% of gross and the employer pays a further 15.84% to fund holiday pay through the national holiday office, which pays the worker directly. For an employee the employer pays holiday pay itself, which is the model priced here because it is what EOR clients hire almost without exception.

assumptions.label: Legal employer has ten or more employees, so the special unemployment contribution applies
assumptions.notes: The 1.69% special unemployment contribution is owed only by employers occupying at least ten workers. Under an EOR the legal employer is the provider, and a provider's Belgian employing entity normally occupies well over ten workers, so expect this line on an EOR hire - ask whether that entity is the provider's own or a partner's. Your own newly incorporated Belgian subsidiary with one or two employees would not pay it - a rare case where the entity route is genuinely cheaper per head on a statutory line, not just on fees.

employer_contributions.name: ONSS employer social security contribution, for-profit private sector
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee of a for-profit private-sector employer, with no salary ceiling found in the official sources read
employer_contributions.notes: The national social security office states it in one line: the employer contribution for the for-profit private sector is 25%. The federal employment department adds that this figure already contains the 7.48% wage moderation contribution, so that is not an extra charge on top. The non-profit private sector pays 32.40% instead. No ceiling on the base is published on either official page; a private payroll bureau mentions a quarterly cap, which is not confirmed by either authority and is therefore not modelled. The wage moderation share is indexed and moves between quarters, so the 25% total is re-read at each data refresh.

source.name: ONSS / socialsecurity.be - which contributions are due ('La cotisation patronale pour le secteur prive a but lucratif est de 25 %')

employer_contributions.name: Special unemployment contribution (employers of ten or more)
employer_contributions.applies: Only employers occupying at least ten workers; always the case when the legal employer is an EOR provider
employer_contributions.notes: 1.60%, or 1.69% once wage moderation is added, charged for unemployment and owed only by employers with ten or more workers. It is the one Belgian line where using a provider costs more than a small entity of your own: the provider is over the threshold by definition, a two-person subsidiary is not. The same official page introduces it as one of 'une serie de petites cotisations' owed on top of the 25%, and names two others without rates - see the line below.

source.name: SPF Emploi - general reduction of wage costs ('1,60 % (1,69 % avec cotisation de moderation salariale) pour le chomage, uniquement pour les employeurs occupant au moins dix travailleurs')

statutory_extras.name: Double holiday pay (double pecule de vacances), 92% of a month's salary
statutory_extras.notes: The Belgian line foreign buyers miss most often. On top of normal salary during the four weeks of leave, an employee is owed a separate annual payment of 92% of the normal monthly salary, which is 7.67% of annual gross - the same 7.67% the social security office itself prints when it decomposes exit holiday pay into a simple and a double half. One detail makes it cheaper than it looks: the social security office states that on this part of holiday pay 'les cotisations de securite sociale ne sont pas dues', so it does not carry the 25% above. What is withheld instead is a special employee contribution of 13.07%, which comes out of the employee's side and not the employer's, and which the office says does not cover the whole amount. It is paid once a year, when the main holiday is taken, pro rata for a partial year.

source.name: ONSS - DmfA instructions, holiday pay ('Le double pecule de vacances legal s'eleve a 92 % du salaire mensuel normal'; on that part 'les cotisations de securite sociale ne sont pas dues')

statutory_extras.name: Company-closure fund and at-risk-group contributions - rates not published
statutory_extras.notes: The reason the Belgian total on this page is a floor rather than a final figure. The federal employment department, on the same page that gives the 25%, says employers also owe 'une serie de petites cotisations sous certaines conditions' and names the ordinary and special contribution to the company-closure fund (fonds de fermeture d'entreprises) and the contributions for at-risk groups, without printing a rate for either. They are carried at zero because no rate is published there, not because they are nil. The gap is small and visible: Deel's Belgium page prints social security at 27.28% against the 26.69% of the two lines above, about 0.6 points. Treat the total on this page as a floor and ask the provider to itemise the rest.

source.name: SPF Emploi - general reduction of wage costs ('Outre cette cotisation patronale de base, les employeurs paient egalement une serie de petites cotisations sous certaines conditions')

statutory_extras.name: Year-end bonus / 13th month - sector agreement, not law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because no Belgian statute imposes a year-end bonus on every employer. What imposes it is the collective agreement of the joint committee the hire falls under, and most committees have one, so in practice it is close to certain. The committee is therefore the question to ask, and for once a provider answers it in public: Deel states that its Belgian EOR employees sit under Joint Committee 200, the catch-all for white-collar staff, and that this raises the applicable minimum from the national EUR 2,070.48 a month to EUR 2,380.64. The same committee also governs the year-end bonus and the voucher rules, so one answer settles three lines of your offer.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Belgium page

statutory_extras.name: Work accident insurance - compulsory, priced by the insurer
statutory_extras.notes: Compulsory for every Belgian private-sector employer under the law of 10 April 1971, from the first day of work and with an authorised insurer.
