Fedris, the federal agency for occupational risks, states that an employer found uninsured is affiliated automatically for the uninsured period, that Fedris pays the victim as an insurer would and recovers everything from the employer, and that criminal proceedings can follow. It is carried at zero because the premium itself is priced by the private insurer according to the risk class, and no authority publishes a tariff or an average. Fedris does publish a bound: the flat contribution charged on automatic affiliation, which it says is higher than the premium of a work accident policy, runs in 2026 from about EUR 124.66 per worker per calendar month for up to three uninsured months to EUR 297.74 beyond twelve. By Fedris's own statement, then, a regular policy costs less than the roughly EUR 124.66 per worker per month of the lowest step.

source.name: Fedris - L'employeur ne s'assure pas (a temps): affiliation d'office et cotisation forfaitaire 2026

statutory_extras.name: Meal vouchers - only where a collective agreement grants them
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because meal vouchers are not a legal entitlement: they exist where a sector or company agreement creates them. Where they do exist the employer's share is capped at EUR 8.91 per voucher and the employee must put in at least EUR 1.09, one voucher per day actually worked. At the ceiling that is roughly EUR 1,900 a year, so it matters to a budget even though it never appears in a statutory rate. Eco-vouchers and sport or culture vouchers work the same way, capped at EUR 250 and EUR 100 a year.

source.name: SPF Emploi - meal vouchers ('L'intervention de l'employeur ne peut exceder 8,91 EUR par titre-repas')

countries.notice_typical: No probation period since 1 January 2014; a probation clause in a contract signed after that date is void. For contracts starting on or after 1 August 2026 the dismissal notice is one week for the first six months of service, then six weeks to nine months, rising by seniority and capped at 52 weeks from seventeen years. Contracts that began before 1 June 2026 follow the older scale, which is uncapped and reaches 65 weeks and beyond.

payments.name: Double holiday pay (employees / employes), 92% of normal monthly salary
payments.deadline: Paid by the employer with the main holiday taken; the month is not fixed by the text (the pay counts the remuneration of the month in which leave is taken)

customary.name: Year-end bonus (prime de fin d'année), Joint Committee 200 sector CBA made binding by royal decree - sector-level, not general
customary.deadline: Paid at the latest at the end of the calendar year (December), unless company-level rules differ

source.quote: Le double pécule de vacances légal s'élève à 92 % du salaire mensuel normal

countries.name: Bulgaria

assumptions.label: The insured employer is registered under employment activities (KID-2025 code 78)
assumptions.notes: Bulgaria sets the work accident and occupational disease rate by the employer's economic activity, not by the job, and under an employer of record the insured employer is the provider rather than you. Annex 2A to the 2026 social security budget act prices code 78, 'Deynosti po naemane i predostavyane na rabotna sila' - the supply of labour, which is what an employer of record is registered as - at 0.5%, and code 62, information technology, at 0.4%. This page models 0.5% because that is the provider's band. Deel's own Bulgaria page prints 0.50% for the same line, which is the corroboration. If you employ directly through a Bulgarian entity of your own with an information technology code, the rate is 0.4% and the ledger below falls by a tenth of a point. Ask the provider which KID-2025 code its Bulgarian entity carries: the annex runs from 0.4% to 1.1%, so the band is worth naming in writing.

employer_contributions.name: State pension fund (fond Pensii), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Employer share for an employee born after 31 December 1959, on insurable income between the statutory floor and ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: The largest line in this ledger, and the one whose rate is assembled from three places in the Social Insurance Code rather than printed anywhere as a single number. Article 6(1)2(a) sets the pension fund contribution at 12.8% for a person born after 31 December 1959; article 6(1)4 adds one percentage point from 1 January 2017 and another from 1 January 2018, each split 0.56 to the employer and 0.44 to the employee; article 6(3)9 splits the 12.8% base 7.1% employer to 5.7% employee. Employer share: 7.1 + 0.56 + 0.56 = 8.22%. For an employee born before 1 January 1960 the same code charges 11.02% here and no second-pillar contribution, so the employer's total is the same 19.02% either way and only the destination of the money changes. That case is now theoretical for a working hire: someone born in 1959 reaches 67 in 2026.

source.name: Kodeks za sotsialno osiguryavane (Social Insurance Code), consolidated text current to State Gazette issue 68 of 28 July 2026, articles 6(1)2, 6(1)4 and 6(3)9

employer_contributions.name: Second-pillar pension (universalen pensionen fond), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Mandatory supplementary pension insurance for employees born after 31 December 1959, on the same insurable income as the state funds
employer_contributions.notes: A funded second pillar, mandatory rather than optional, and an employer cost rather than a deduction. Article 157(1)1(c) sets the universal pension fund contribution at 5% from 2007; article 157(3) splits it 2.8% employer to 2.2% employee. Article 157(6) puts it on the same income as the state social insurance contributions, so the same floor and the same ceiling apply. It is worth separating from the state pension line because the two are paid to different places: this 2.8% goes to a licensed private pension company the employee chooses, and it does not sit in the National Social Security Institute's accounts.

source.name: Kodeks za sotsialno osiguryavane (Social Insurance Code), consolidated text current to State Gazette issue 68 of 28 July 2026, articles 157(1), 157(3) and 157(6)

employer_contributions.name: Health insurance (zdravnoosiguritelna vnoska), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Employer share of the compulsory health insurance contribution, on the same insurable income as the social security funds
employer_contributions.notes: The rate is not in the Health Insurance Act: article 29(3) of that act sends it to the annual budget act of the National Health Insurance Fund, and article 2 of the 2026 fund budget act says 'Razmerat na zadalzhitelnata zdravnoosiguritelna vnoska za 2026 g. e 8 na sto' - 8 per cent for 2026. Article 40(1)1 of the Health Insurance Act splits it 60:40 between employer and insured person from 2010 onwards, which is the 4.8% here, and puts it on the income on which state social insurance contributions are due, so it takes the same floor and the same ceiling.

source.name: Zakon za byudzheta na Natsionalnata zdravnoosiguritelna kasa za 2026 g., article 2, State Gazette issue 68 of 28 July 2026, with Zakon za zdravnoto osiguryavane article 40(1)1 for the 60:40 split

employer_contributions.name: General sickness and maternity fund (obshto zabolyavane i maychinstvo), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Employer share on insurable income between the statutory floor and ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Article 6(1)5 of the Social Insurance Code sets this fund at 3.5% and article 6(3)7 splits it 60:40 between employer and insured person from 1 January 2009, giving 2.1%. This is the fund that pays sickness and maternity cash benefits - but not the first two working days of an illness, which the employer pays directly and which are recorded separately below.

source.name: Kodeks za sotsialno osiguryavane (Social Insurance Code), consolidated text current to State Gazette issue 68 of 28 July 2026, articles 6(1)5 and 6(3)7

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment fund (bezrabotitsa), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Employer share on insurable income between the statutory floor and ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Article 6(1)6 of the Social Insurance Code sets the unemployment fund at 'edno na sto', one per cent, and article 6(3)7 splits it 60:40, giving 0.6% to the employer. The 2026 budget act sets the daily unemployment benefit it funds at a minimum of EUR 9.21 and a maximum of EUR 54.78.

source.name: Kodeks za sotsialno osiguryavane (Social Insurance Code), consolidated text current to State Gazette issue 68 of 28 July 2026, articles 6(1)6 and 6(3)7

employer_contributions.name: Work accident and occupational disease fund (trudova zlopoluka i profesionalna bolest)
employer_contributions.applies: Employer only, at the rate annex 2A sets for the insured employer's economic activity
employer_contributions.notes: Entirely on the employer, and the only rate in this ledger that is not the same for every employer. Article 6(1)7 of the Social Insurance Code fixes the range at 0.4% to 1.1% and leaves the year's assignment to the social security budget act; article 14 of the 2026 act sets one table for 1 January to 31 July and another, annex 2A, for 1 August to 31 December. In annex 2A the 1.1% band holds forestry, mining, construction and land transport; 0.9% holds agriculture and food; 0.7% holds air transport, telecommunications and drinks; 0.5% holds wholesale and retail, hospitality, engineering consultancy and the supply of labour; 0.4% holds information technology, publishing, finance, law and accountancy. The 0.5% modelled here is the band of the activity an employer of record is registered under. See the assumption above for the case where you employ directly.

source.name: Zakon za byudzheta na darzhavnoto obshtestveno osiguryavane za 2026 g., article 14(2) and annex 2A, State Gazette issue 68 of 28 July 2026

statutory_extras.name: Guaranteed claims fund (Garantirani vzemaniya na rabotnitsite i sluzhitelite) - suspended for 2026
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the law suspended it for the year, not because it does not exist, and kept out of the ledger above because a nil rate is not a charge. Article 15(1) of the 2026 social security budget act says 'Za 2026 g. ne se vnasyat vnoski za Fond "Garantirani vzemaniya na rabotnitsite i sluzhitelite"' - no contributions are paid to the guaranteed claims fund in 2026 - while article 15(2) keeps the benefit it pays, capped at EUR 1,550.50, and annex 3 runs the fund on interest income against a EUR 515,900 deficit. The obligation is live, the rate is nil this year, and it is the line to re-read when the 2027 budget act is promulgated. Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia each charge a comparable fund rather than suspending it, so a provider quote built on a neighbouring country's template can carry a charge Bulgarian law is not making in 2026.

source.name: Zakon za byudzheta na darzhavnoto obshtestveno osiguryavane za 2026 g., article 15, State Gazette issue 68 of 28 July 2026

statutory_extras.name: First two working days of sick leave, paid by the employer at 70%
statutory_extras.notes: Contingent, so it is shown and left out of the total. Article 40(5) of the Social Insurance Code, as amended by State Gazette issue 106 of 2023 with effect from 1 January 2024, requires the employer to pay the insured person 70% of the average daily gross pay of the month in which the incapacity began, and not less than 70% of the average daily agreed pay, for the first two working days of each episode of temporary incapacity. The fund picks up day three onwards. Two days at 70% of an engineering salary is roughly a tenth of a per cent of the annual cost per episode, which is small; it matters because it is an employer payment that never appears in a contribution rate, so it is absent from every percentage comparison including this one.

source.name: Kodeks za sotsialno osiguryavane (Social Insurance Code), consolidated text current to State Gazette issue 68 of 28 July 2026, article 40(5)

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Bulgarian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code creates no thirteenth-month salary and no holiday supplement. Annual leave is paid at the employee's own average pay under article 177 of the Labour Code rather than topped up. Bonuses, private health cover and food vouchers are normal in the Bulgarian technology market and are entirely contractual; price them as market cost in a competitive offer, never as a legal charge. Food vouchers have a specific tax treatment here that a provider can explain, and it is a benefit question rather than a statutory one.

source.name: Kodeks na truda (Labour Code), consolidated text current to State Gazette issue 69 of 31 July 2026

countries.notice_typical: Thirty days for an open-ended contract unless the parties agree a longer period, which article 326(2) of the Labour Code caps at three months. A fixed-term contract carries three months' notice, but never more than what is left of the term. The same article lets a collective agreement tie the notice period to length of service with the same employer for redundancy-type dismissals.

source.name: Kodeks na truda (Labour Code), consolidated text current to State Gazette issue 69 of 31 July 2026

countries.name: Brazil

assumptions.label: RAT accident rate at grade 2 = 2% (the employer of record's own activity, CNAE 7830-2/00, supply and management of human resources for third parties)
assumptions.notes: The RAT rate follows the preponderant activity of the employer, and under an EOR the legal employer is the provider, not you. In the official Receita Federal table the closest class to an EOR's own business, 7830-2/00 'Fornecimento e gestao de recursos humanos para terceiros', is grade 2. A software house hiring through its own Brazilian entity would sit at grade 1 (6201-5/01, 1%), so the same engineer can carry a different RAT depending on who employs them. Deel's published Brazil figure implies 1.5%. Ask your provider which CNAE it declares.

assumptions.label: FAP accident-prevention multiplier at its neutral value of 1.0 (legal range 0.5 to 2.0)
assumptions.notes: Every Brazilian establishment gets an individual multiplier on its RAT rate, set from its own accident frequency, severity and cost history. At 0.5 the 2% becomes 1%; at 2.0 it becomes 4%. No provider publishes its FAP, so the ledger uses the neutral 1.0 and the line is worth asking about: it is the only employer charge in Brazil that depends on the provider's own claims record rather than on your hire.

employer_contributions.name: INSS employer contribution (social security)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee and casual worker on the payroll, with no salary ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: The single most misread line in Brazil. The 'teto' that caps Brazilian social security contributions applies only to the employee's own base, the salario-de-contribuicao of articles 20, 21 and 28 paragraph 5. The company's contribution has a different base and no ceiling: article 22 charges 20% on 'o total das remuneracoes pagas, devidas ou creditadas a qualquer titulo'. A senior hire in Brazil therefore carries the full 20% on every extra dollar, unlike Japan, Germany or Poland where the employer charge stops.

source.name: Lei no 8.212 de 24 de julho de 1991 (consolidada), art. 22, I

employer_contributions.name: RAT / SAT work-accident contribution, grade 2 with a neutral FAP
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, at 1%, 2% or 3% of the same uncapped base according to the risk grade of its preponderant activity, then multiplied by its own FAP between 0.5 and 2.0
employer_contributions.notes: Article 22, II of Lei 8.212/1991 sets 1% for light risk, 2% for medium and 3% for high, on the same uncapped base as the 20% above. The grade comes from the employer's CNAE class in Annex I of Instrucao Normativa RFB 971/2009: 6201-5/01 software development is grade 1, while 7830-2/00 human resources supply to third parties and 7020-4/00 management consulting are grade 2. Modelled at grade 2 because under an EOR the provider is the employer of record. Lei 10.666/2003 art. 10 then allows the rate to be cut by up to half or doubled through the FAP.

source.name: Lei no 8.212/1991 art. 22, II and Receita Federal, IN RFB no 971/2009, Anexo I (risk grade by CNAE)

employer_contributions.name: Terceiros / Sistema S levies (FPAS code 515)
employer_contributions.applies: Commerce and services payrolls under FPAS code 515; an industrial payroll (code 507) swaps SENAC and SESC for SENAI and SESI at the same rates, for the same 5.8% total
employer_contributions.notes: Five separate levies collected with the INSS on the same uncapped base: Salario-Educacao 2.5%, INCRA 0.2%, SENAC 1.0%, SESC 1.5% and SEBRAE 0.6%. The 5.8% total and the split are read on the official eSocial FPAS/Terceiros table published by the federal government; the 3.3 points made up of INCRA, SENAC, SESC and SEBRAE are taken from that administrative table rather than from each founding statute read separately. On the old 20-minimum-wage ceiling for these levies, the Superior Tribunal de Justica settled repetitive theme 1.079 on 23 February 2026 against the ceiling for SENAI, SESI, SESC and SENAC, so the line is modelled uncapped.

source.name: gov.br/eSocial, official technical documentation, FPAS and Terceiros tables (code 515: 2.5 + 0.2 + 1.0 + 1.5 + 0.6 = 5.8%)

employer_contributions.name: FGTS severance fund deposit
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, monthly, on pay including the 13th salary; deposited into a blocked bank account in the employee's own name
employer_contributions.notes: Article 15 of Lei 8.036/1990 obliges every employer to deposit 8% of the pay owed for the previous month into a 'conta bancaria vinculada', explicitly including the Christmas bonus of Lei 4.090. It is money the employee eventually draws, not a tax, but it is a real employer outlay from the first payslip. Dismissal without cause adds a 40% penalty on everything deposited over the life of the contract, which is carried separately below.

source.name: Lei no 8.036 de 11 de maio de 1990 (consolidada), art. 15

statutory_extras.name: 13th salary (gratificacao natalina)
statutory_extras.notes: One extra month of pay per calendar year, at 1/12 per month worked, with any fraction of 15 days or more counting as a whole month. Usually paid in two instalments, an advance by the end of November and the balance by 20 December. Because it is pay, it carries its own INSS, RAT and FGTS, which is the line below.

source.name: Lei no 4.090 de 13 de julho de 1962, art. 1 paragraphs 1 and 2

statutory_extras.name: Vacation bonus (one third of a month's salary)
statutory_extras.notes: The 30 days of annual leave are paid at normal salary, so they are already inside the gross above; what is extra is the constitutional bonus of at least one third of normal pay on top of the holiday. One third of one month spread over twelve is 2.78% of annual gross. Modelling the whole vacation month as an extra cost, as several cost guides do, double counts the salary.

source.name: Constituicao Federal de 1988, art. 7, XVII (leave paid with at least one third more than normal salary) and CLT art. 130, I (30 calendar days)

statutory_extras.name: INSS, RAT and FGTS due on the 13th salary and the vacation bonus
statutory_extras.notes: The charge almost every cost page leaves out. The 13th salary is pay, so it attracts the 20% INSS, the 2% RAT and the 8% FGTS: 8.33% x 30% = 2.50% of annual gross. The vacation bonus attracts the employer social contribution as well, which was contested for years and is now settled: on 18 March 2026 the Superior Tribunal de Justica reported that its Second Panel 'readequou seu entendimento para reconhecer a incidencia da contribuicao previdenciaria patronal sobre o terco constitucional de ferias gozadas', following the Supreme Court's general-repercussion ruling in theme 985, and that the Supreme Court limited the effect of the new position to periods from 15 September 2020 onwards. That adds 2.78% x 22% = 0.61%. Total 3.11%. Two amounts are deliberately left out for want of a source read directly: the Terceiros levies on both items, and FGTS on the vacation bonus. The real figure is therefore slightly above this one, never below.

source.name: Superior Tribunal de Justica - Segunda Turma applies STF theme 985 and recognises employer social contribution on the vacation third (REsp 1.559.926)

statutory_extras.name: FGTS termination penalty, 40% of all deposits (dismissal without cause only)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is contingent, not recurring: it falls due only when the employer dismisses without just cause, and then it is 40% of everything deposited over the whole contract, restated for inflation and interest. On a three-year hire that is roughly one month of salary handed over on the way out. It belongs in a severance budget, not in a monthly on-cost, but it is the reason Brazilian termination is expensive and it is worth asking a provider how it funds the line.

source.name: Lei no 8.036/1990 (consolidada), art. 18 paragraph 1

statutory_extras.name: Payroll relief (CPRB) - not available on an EOR hire
statutory_extras.notes: Brazil has an optional sectoral regime, the desoneracao da folha of Lei 12.546/2011, arts. 7 to 9-A, that lets the listed activities pay a percentage of gross revenue (the CPRB, set by sector in arts. 7-A and 8-A) instead of the 20% INSS employer contribution on payroll. Lei 14.973/2024 phases it out: for 1 January to 31 December 2026, a company still in the regime pays 60% of its CPRB rate on revenue plus 50% of the payroll rate, which is 10% of payroll, with no payroll contribution on the 13th salary between 2025 and 2027; in 2027 it pays 40% of the CPRB rate plus 75% of the payroll rate, and the full 20% returns from 2028. The list of eligible activities in the compiled text is closed and identified by activity class, service code or product code (IT and call-centre services, passenger transport, construction, infrastructure, listed manufacturers and a few others), and employment or staffing services are not on it. The line is carried at zero because the employer of record is a human resources supplier, so the relief does not reach your hire even if your own Brazilian subsidiary would qualify; it changes nothing in the total either way.

source.name: Lei no 12.546/2011 (texto compilado), arts. 7, 7-A, 8-A and 9-A as amended by Lei no 14.973/2024, art. 9-A item II (2026 proportions)

countries.notice_typical: Thirty days, plus three days for each year of service with the same employer up to sixty extra days, giving a statutory maximum of ninety days (CLT art. 487 and Lei 12.506/2011).

payments.name: 13th salary (gratificacao natalina)
payments.deadline: 20 Dec

payments.name: Vacation bonus (one third more than normal salary)
payments.deadline: paid with the leave pay, up to 2 days before the leave starts; the leave month is a scenario input, not a date fixed by law

source.quote: será paga pelo empregador até o dia 20 de dezembro de cada ano, compensada a importância que, a título de adiantamento, o empregado houver recebido

countries.name: Canada

assumptions.label: Employee works in Ontario (Employer Health Tax and WSIB apply)
assumptions.notes: Quebec runs its own plans (QPP, QPIP, HSF, CNESST) and is not modelled here

employer_contributions.name: Canada Pension Plan (CPP)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees in Ontario earning above the basic exemption amount
employer_contributions.notes: Employer rate is 5.95% on earnings between basic exemption ($3,500) and YMPE ($74,600)

source.name: CRA — CPP contribution rates, maximums and exemptions

employer_contributions.name: Employment Insurance (EI)
employer_contributions.applies: All insurable employees in Canada
employer_contributions.notes: Employer rate is 1.4 times the employee rate of 1.63% (0.0163 x 1.4 = 0.02282) up to Maximum Insurable Earnings of $68,900. From 1 January 2027 the employer rate is $2.30 per $100 (1.4 x $1.64) and maximum insurable earnings rise to $70,800, confirmed by the Canada Employment Insurance Commission in September 2026; the engine keeps the 2026 figures until then.

source.name: CRA — EI premium rates and maximums

employer_contributions.name: Ontario Employer Health Tax (EHT)
employer_contributions.applies: Employers with Ontario payroll
employer_contributions.notes: Top rate of 1.95% applies; the $1,000,000 exemption is restricted to eligible employers whose total group payroll is under $5,000,000, which an EOR payroll exceeds

source.name: Ontario Ministry of Finance — Employer Health Tax (EHT)

employer_contributions.name: WSIB Workplace Safety Insurance (Ontario Class L)
employer_contributions.applies: Ontario employers in Class L (Professional, Scientific and Technical services / IT)
employer_contributions.notes: Rate is $0.18 per $100 insurable earnings (0.18%) up to maximum insurable earnings ceiling of $121,700

source.name: WSIB — 2026 premium rates

statutory_extras.name: Vacation pay (Ontario ESA minimum)
statutory_extras.notes: Ontario ESA requires minimum 4% vacation pay (2 weeks). For salaried employees, vacation is taken as paid time off inside annual salary

source.name: Ontario Ministry of Labour — Vacation

countries.notice_typical: Statutory notice ranges from 1 week (after 3 months) up to 8 weeks (after 8 years); statutory severance pay applies after 5+ years of service if employer payroll is $2.5M or more.

countries.name: Switzerland

assumptions.label: Employee registered in the canton of Zurich (the family allowance rate is set canton by canton, and within Zurich by the fund)
assumptions.notes: There is no Swiss family allowance rate. The federal social insurance office states the rule itself: 'Les cotisations aux allocations familiales (AFam) dépendent du canton dans lequel votre employeur a son siège... Elles dépendent aussi de la caisse d'allocations familiales à laquelle votre employeur est affilié.' So the figure moves twice - with the canton, and then with which of the competing funds the employer joined inside that canton. Zurich is modelled because it is the largest labour market in the country and the cantonal fund publishes its rate: 1.025% of payroll for 2026. Providers land elsewhere: Deel prints 1.6% for its Swiss family fund on the same date, more than half a point above the Zurich cantonal fund, on exactly the same hire. Ask which canton and which Ausgleichskasse the quote is built on before you compare two Swiss numbers.

assumptions.label: Employee is 35 to 44 years old, so the pension credit is 10% of coordinated salary and the employer's legal minimum is half of it
assumptions.notes: The Swiss second pillar prices the employee's date of birth directly, in steps. Article 16 LPP sets the annual retirement credit as a percentage of coordinated salary by age band: 7% from 25 to 34, 10% from 35 to 44, 15% from 45 to 54 and 18% from 55 to the reference age. Article 66(1) says the employer's total contribution must be at least equal to the employees' total, so the legal minimum on the employer is half: 3.5%, 5%, 7.5% and 9%. On the example salary here that is the difference between about 9.9% and 13.5% of total employer on-cost for the identical role - roughly 3.6 points between the youngest and the oldest band. The 35-44 band is modelled as the declared middle. Nothing else about the hire changes; the candidate's age does.

employer_contributions.name: Old-age, survivors, invalidity and loss-of-earnings insurance (AVS/AI/APG), employer half
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on the whole salary with no ceiling; identical in all 26 cantons
employer_contributions.notes: The first pillar, and the only Swiss employer charge that is genuinely national. The official AVS memento gives the three rates and their sum - AVS 8.7%, AI 1.4%, APG 0.5%, total 10.6% - and then the split: 'En votre qualité d'employeur, vous déduisez 5,3 % du salaire de vos employés pour leur part de cotisation, part que vous versez à votre caisse de compensation AVS avec votre part de l'employeur (également 5,3 %).' There is no ceiling, which is unusual for a contributory pension: a Swiss executive on a million francs carries 5.3% on the whole of it. That is why the Swiss employer cost falls as a share of pay far less steeply than the German or Japanese one, where the main pension lines stop at a ceiling.

source.name: Centre d'information AVS/AI - Mémento 2.01, Cotisations salariales à l'AVS, à l'AI et aux APG ('AVS 8,7 % / AI 1,4 % / APG 0,5 % / Total 10,6 %')

employer_contributions.name: Occupational pension, mandatory minimum (LPP/BVG), employer half at ages 35-44
employer_contributions.applies: Only the slice of annual salary between the coordination deduction of CHF 26,460 and the upper limit of CHF 90,720 is insured; below CHF 22,680 of annual pay there is no compulsory cover at all
employer_contributions.notes: The second pillar, and the line that makes Swiss quotes impossible to compare without two extra facts. Article 8 LPP: 'La partie du salaire annuel comprise entre 26 460 et 90 720 francs doit être assurée. Cette partie du salaire est appelée salaire coordonné.' The federal social insurance office confirms both figures for 1 January 2026, alongside the CHF 22,680 entry threshold and the CHF 3,780 minimum coordinated salary - a floor this model does not apply, since it only bites on very low pay. Article 16 then sets the credit at 10% of that slice for a 35 to 44 year old, and article 66(1) puts at least half on the employer, so 5%. Because the insured slice is capped at CHF 90,720 while salary is not, this line shrinks as a share of pay on every senior hire. Two warnings for a buyer. First, this is the legal minimum, not the market: almost every Swiss employer insures well beyond it, and Deel lists an estimated 8% pension fund contribution among its Swiss employer costs rather than the 5% here, which alone is most of the gap between our figure and a real quote. Second, the same reasoning this site applies to Sweden applies here - what the law imposes goes in the ledger, what a pension plan adds is a contractual benefit and is named instead of guessed.

source.name: Loi fédérale sur la prévoyance professionnelle (LPP, RS 831.40), art. 8 salaire coordonné and art. 16 bonifications de vieillesse, consolidated text

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (AC/ALV), employer half
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on salary up to CHF 148,200 a year, the limit applying per employment contract; nothing at all is charged above it
employer_contributions.notes: 2.2% in total, half each, and the ceiling is the part to re-read. The official memento is explicit that the old solidarity slice is gone: 'Jusqu'à un montant annuel maximal de 148 200 francs, le taux de cotisation à l'AC est de 2,2 %... Depuis le 1er janvier 2023, aucune cotisation à l'AC ne sera plus prélevée sur la part du salaire dépassant ce montant.' Between 2011 and 2022 a further 1% ran on the excess to repay the fund's debt, and cost pages written before 2023 still carry it - if a comparison shows a Swiss employer paying anything on the slice above CHF 148,200, it is three years out of date. The limit applies to each contract separately, so an employee with two Swiss employers reaches it twice.

source.name: Centre d'information AVS/AI - Mémento 2.08, Cotisations à l'assurance-chômage ('le taux de cotisation à l'AC est de 2,2 %'; no contribution above CHF 148,200 since 1 January 2023)

employer_contributions.name: Family allowance contribution (AFam/FAK), canton of Zurich fund
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only charge on the whole AVS-liable payroll, with no ceiling; the rate is set by the canton and by the family allowance fund the employer belongs to
employer_contributions.notes: Employer-only in Zurich - the cantonal table shows a dash in the employee column - and the clearest example of why a single Swiss percentage is a fiction. The canton of Zurich publishes 1.025% for its own family allowance fund in the contribution table it applies from 1 January 2026, next to a dash in the employee column. A provider affiliated to a different fund pays a different rate on the identical hire: Deel's Switzerland page listed a 'Family fund - 1.6%' when it was read on 20 September 2026, 0.575 points above the Zurich cantonal fund. Some cantons fix one rate for every fund instead of letting each set its own, and in some the employee contributes as well, so neither the rate nor the side of the payslip it falls on can be assumed from one canton to the next. There is no ceiling on this line, so it keeps growing after the unemployment insurance has stopped.

source.name: Kanton Zürich - Beiträge an die Sozialversicherungen, Beiträge ab 1.1.2026 ('FAK 1,025%' employer, Familienausgleichskasse des Kantons Zürich)

employer_contributions.name: Occupational accident insurance (LAA, AAP), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only charge on insured earnings up to CHF 148,200 a year; the premium is set by the insurer according to the risk class of the business, so an office rate is far below an industrial one
employer_contributions.notes: Compulsory for every Swiss employee and legally one-sided: article 91(1) LAA puts the premiums for occupational accidents and diseases on the employer, and article 91(2) puts the non-occupational premiums on the employee. Switzerland publishes no general tariff - office and service employers are insured with private insurers rather than SUVA, and each sets its own rate - so a declared point is used instead of a range. The canton of Zurich publishes the rate of its own administrative contract from 1 January 2026: 0.122% employer for occupational accidents with AXA Winterthur, against 0.384% for the non-occupational cover. Deel independently prints 0.1204% on its Switzerland page, within two thousandths of a point of the cantonal figure, which is the best cross-check available for an office role. The ceiling is the maximum insured earnings fixed at CHF 148,200 a year by article 22(1) of the accident insurance ordinance.

source.name: Kanton Zürich - Beiträge an die Sozialversicherungen, Beiträge ab 1.1.2026 (UVG Berufsunfall 0,122% employer, AXA Winterthur; maximum insured earnings CHF 148,200)

employer_contributions.name: Compensation fund administrative levy, modelled at the 1.00% tariff band
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only charge levied as a percentage of the AVS/AI/APG contributions declared for the year, not of salary; the percentage falls as the employer gets bigger
employer_contributions.notes: A small line with a large lesson: it is the one Swiss charge where using a provider is cheaper than running your own subsidiary, and it works the opposite way round to Belgium. The AVS memento notes that 'les caisses de compensation perçoivent en sus une contribution aux frais d'administration qui est à la charge de l'employeur' without giving a rate, because each fund sets its own. The Zurich cantonal fund publishes a sliding scale for 2026, charged on the AVS/AI/APG contributions declared: 5.00% for the smallest employers, then 4.75%, 3.25%, 2.00%, 1.25%, 1.00% from CHF 150,000 of contributions, 0.90% from CHF 200,000 and 0.70% from CHF 500,000, with lower rates again for employers filing online. Modelled here at the 1.00% band, which is an employer declaring roughly CHF 1.5 million of Swiss payroll - about the size of a provider's Swiss book, and deliberately not the cheapest band. Since contributions are 10.6% of salary, 1.00% of them is 0.106% of pay. A two-person subsidiary of your own sits in the 3.25% or 5.00% band and would pay 0.34% to 0.53% of salary on this line; a large employer filing online pays 0.03%.

source.name: SVA Zürich - Verwaltungskostenbeiträge ab 2026, Beitragssätze für Arbeitgebende ('einen prozentualen Verwaltungskostenbeitrag auf Basis der jährlich abgerechneten AHV/IV/EO-Beiträge')

statutory_extras.name: 13th month salary - contract or collective agreement, not law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because Swiss law does not impose it. Article 322d of the Code of Obligations makes the point exactly: where the employer grants a special payment on an occasion such as Christmas or the year end, 'le travailleur y a droit lorsqu'il en a été convenu ainsi' - the entitlement comes from the agreement, not the statute. In practice most Swiss white-collar offers carry one, and it is usually presented as the annual salary divided into thirteen rather than as a bonus on top, which is why it can look like it costs nothing. Confirm which of the two your quote means. If the 13th month is genuinely additional, it adds 8.33% of annual gross plus the charges above on that amount; if the annual figure already contains it, nothing changes.

source.name: Code des obligations (RS 220), art. 322d, gratification ('le travailleur y a droit lorsqu'il en a été convenu ainsi')

statutory_extras.name: Non-occupational accident cover (AANP) - legally the employee's premium
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the law puts it on the other side of the payslip, and named because it is the most common line to be misfiled as an employer cost in Swiss quotes. Article 91(2) LAA: 'Les primes de l'assurance obligatoire contre les accidents non professionnels sont à la charge du travailleur. Les conventions contraires en faveur du travailleur sont réservées.' It is roughly three times the occupational premium - the canton of Zurich publishes 0.384% against 0.122% on the same contract - and many Swiss employers do pay part or all of it as a benefit, which is exactly what that reserved clause allows. So it is a real negotiating item worth about a third of a point of salary, and it should appear on the employer side of a quote only if the provider has chosen to put it there. Ask.

source.name: Loi fédérale sur l'assurance-accidents (LAA, RS 832.20), art. 91(2), obligation de payer les primes

statutory_extras.name: Sickness daily allowance insurance (KTG/APGM) - compulsory only where a collective agreement says so
statutory_extras.notes: No federal statute obliges a Swiss employer to insure sick pay. Article 324a of the Code of Obligations (consolidated text in force since 1 January 2026) sets the underlying duty: an employee prevented from working through illness keeps his salary 'pour un temps limité', three weeks in the first year of service and then 'une période plus longue fixée équitablement', once the job has lasted or was agreed for more than three months. Article 324a(4) lets 'un accord écrit, un contrat-type de travail ou une convention collective' replace that duty with 'des prestations au moins équivalentes' - the legal hook for a daily allowance policy - and an employer may equally self-insure. In practice most employers buy such a policy, and many collective agreements make it compulsory, in which case the employer typically pays at least half the premium. It is carried at zero because there is no public rate: premiums are set per employer by a private insurer. For an order of magnitude on an office role, Deel's Switzerland hiring page (deel.com/hiring/employees/switzerland) listed 'Sickness Insurance - 0.64%' among its Swiss employer costs on 20 September 2026, and on the same page a further 'CBA affiliation cost - 0.3% for employees earning less than CHF 12,350 only'. Both are provider figures, not rates set by a Swiss authority, which is why they are left out of the total. Treat the on-cost on this page as the statutory floor.

source.name: Code des obligations (RS 220), art. 324a, salaire en cas d'empêchement de travailler (version en vigueur au 1er janvier 2026)

statutory_extras.name: Pension cover above the legal minimum - the single largest variable in a Swiss quote
statutory_extras.notes: Named at zero because it is contractual, and it is named because it explains almost the whole spread in Swiss provider numbers. The ledger above carries the mandatory minimum only: 5% of the CHF 26,460 to CHF 90,720 slice for a 35 to 44 year old. A typical Swiss plan insures salary from the first franc, uses a smaller coordination deduction or none, and credits well above the legal percentages, and the employer often pays more than half. Deel models 8% of salary for the Swiss pension fund rather than the roughly 3.2% of salary the legal minimum produces here - a gap of nearly five points, larger than every other difference between our figure and theirs put together. Deel's own summary of Switzerland reads: 'The employer cost is generally estimated between 9.81% to 21.58% of the employee salary. The variation will depend on the canton, age, salary, and multiple conditions.' That range is honest, and this page exists to say where inside it a given hire actually falls.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Switzerland page

countries.notice_typical: One month to the end of a month during the first year of service, two months from the second to the ninth year and three months thereafter (Code of Obligations art. 335c). The probation period is the first month by default with seven days' notice on either side, and may be extended by written agreement, standard contract or collective agreement to at most three months (art. 335b).

source.quote: le travailleur y a droit lorsqu’il en a été convenu ainsi.

countries.name: Chile

assumptions.label: Unidad de Fomento taken at CLP 40,983.58, its value on 21 September 2026
assumptions.notes: Chile writes its contribution ceilings in Unidades de Fomento, an index that is re-published every day, so a ceiling in pesos is only true on the day it is converted. The two ceilings on this page - 90.0 UF a month for pensions, health and accident cover, 135.2 UF a month for unemployment insurance - are converted at the Servicio de Impuestos Internos value for 21 September 2026. Neither binds at the example salary.

assumptions.label: Statutory profit share taken under article 50, at 25% of pay capped at 4.75 monthly minimum incomes a year
assumptions.notes: Article 47 of the Codigo del Trabajo obliges a profitable company to share at least 30% of its liquid profits with its staff. Article 50 lets the employer discharge that obligation instead by paying 25% of the pay earned in the year, capped per worker at 4.75 ingresos minimos mensuales, whatever the profit. Practically every employer takes the article 50 route, which is what this ledger models. With the minimum income at CLP 553,553 the cap is CLP 2,629,376 a year, so the 25% rate only bites on salaries below about CLP 10.5 million a year.

assumptions.label: The activity-rated supplement to the accident insurance is carried at zero, so the total below is a floor
assumptions.notes: Article 15(b) of Ley 16.744 adds a differentiated contribution on top of the 0.90% basic rate, set by decree according to the employer's activity and risk and capped at 3.4%. It depends on the provider's own classification, not on the employee's job, so it is left at zero rather than guessed.

employer_contributions.name: Employer pension contribution (Seguro Social Previsional, disability cover included)
employer_contributions.notes: The rate that changed on 1 August 2026. The Superintendencia de Pensiones states it plainly: 'A partir de las remuneraciones de agosto de 2026, las y los empleadores deben declarar y pagar una cotizacion equivalente al 3,5 % de la remuneracion imponible', split 0.1% to the worker's individual AFP account, 0.9% to the Cotizacion con Rentabilidad Protegida and 2.5% to the Seguro Social Previsional. That 2.5% now finances the Seguro de Invalidez y Sobrevivencia, which ChileAtiende notes is 'ahora recaudado por el IPS' - so the old separate SIS contribution is inside this figure rather than on top of it. Ley 21.735 steps the rate to 4.25% in August 2027 and to 8.5% by 2033. The base is capped at 90.0 UF a month.

source.name: Superintendencia de Pensiones - Cotizacion de cargo del empleador (gradualidad under Ley 21.735)

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (seguro de cesantia), indefinite contract
employer_contributions.applies: Indefinite contracts; a fixed-term or task contract is charged 3% instead
employer_contributions.notes: Article 5 of Ley 19.728: 'b) Un 2,4% de las remuneraciones imponibles, en el caso de los trabajadores con contrato de duracion indefinida y un 3% ... para los trabajadores con contrato a plazo fijo, o por obra, trabajo o servicio determinado. Ambos, de cargo del empleador.' The worker on an indefinite contract adds 0.6%. This contribution has its own, higher ceiling: 135.2 UF a month from 1 February 2026 under Resolucion exenta 236 of the Superintendencia de Pensiones, against 90.0 UF for the pension and accident lines.

source.name: Ley 19.728, articulo 5 (Superintendencia de Seguridad Social, Normativa y jurisprudencia)

employer_contributions.name: Work accident insurance, basic general rate (Ley 16.744)
employer_contributions.notes: Article 15(a) of Ley 16.744 funds the accident and occupational-disease insurance with 'una cotizacion basica general del 0,90% de las remuneraciones imponibles, de cargo del empleador'. Paragraph (b) then adds a differentiated rate of up to 3.4% set by decree on the employer's activity; that supplement is listed outside the total on this page rather than guessed, so this line is the floor of what the insurance costs, not the whole of it.

source.name: Ley 16.744, articulo 15 (Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional, version in force, consulted 21 September 2026)

employer_contributions.name: SANNA contribution (insurance for parents of seriously ill children, Ley 21.063)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the employee's taxable pay up to the contribution ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Article 24(a) of Ley 21.063 funds the insurance 'con una cotizacion mensual de un 0,03% de las remuneraciones o rentas imponibles de los trabajadores dependientes e independientes, de cargo del empleador', the contribution created by article 3 of Ley 21.010. Its phase-in, set by article second transitory of Ley 21.010, rose from 0.01% in 2017 to 0.03% from 1 January 2020, which is the rate in force in 2026. It is collected by the mutual or the Instituto de Seguridad Laboral together with the accident insurance. It is charged on the same capped taxable pay as the basic accident-insurance rate, so it carries the same ceiling here. At the example salary it comes to about US$0.90 a month.

source.name: Ley 21.063, articulo 24 letra a) (BCN LeyChile, version of 28 September 2023, in force), with Ley 21.010 articulos 3 y segundo transitorio

employer_contributions.name: Statutory profit share (gratificacion legal, article 50 route)
employer_contributions.applies: Capped at 4.75 monthly minimum incomes per worker per year, which is CLP 2,629,376 at the 2026 minimum income
employer_contributions.notes: Article 50 of the Codigo del Trabajo: 'El empleador que abone o pague a sus trabajadores el veinticinco por ciento de lo devengado en el respectivo ejercicio comercial por concepto de remuneraciones mensuales, quedara eximido de la obligacion establecida en el articulo 47 ... En este caso, la gratificacion de cada trabajador no excedera de cuatro y tres cuartos (4,75) ingresos minimos mensuales.' The cap is what matters above a modest salary: 4.75 x CLP 553,553 is CLP 2,629,376 a year, reached once annual pay passes CLP 10,517,507, which is the ceiling entered here. The minimum income of CLP 553,553 has applied since 1 May 2026 under Ley 21.830, published in the Diario Oficial on 22 June 2026.

source.name: Codigo del Trabajo, articulos 47 y 50 (BCN, version 23 July 2026), with the minimum income from the Direccion del Trabajo (Ley 21.830)

statutory_extras.name: Work accident insurance, activity-rated supplement
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because article 15(b) of Ley 16.744 sets it by decree on the employer's own activity and risk, anywhere from nothing to 3.4%, so it cannot be read off a salary. The older extraordinary accident-insurance contribution of Ley 19.578 no longer applies: Ley 21.010 phased it down and ended it on 31 December 2019. Deel's Chile page books the whole accident line at 0.93%, three hundredths above the basic rate charged here, the size of the SANNA contribution listed below. Because this supplement is left out, the total on this page is a floor.

source.name: Ley 16.744, articulo 15 inciso b) (Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional)

statutory_extras.name: Contributions falling on the statutory profit share
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it cannot honestly be written as a fixed share of salary. The gratificacion is remuneration, so the pension, unemployment and accident contributions apply to it as well - but the gratificacion is capped in minimum incomes while the contributions are a percentage, so the resulting charge falls as salary rises. At the example salary it is worth about half a point of gross. It is one more reason to read the total here as a minimum.

source.name: Codigo del Trabajo, articulo 50, read with the imponible base of Ley 19.728 articulo 5 and Ley 16.744 articulo 15

countries.probation_note: none by law; fixed-term contract may serve
countries.notice_typical: Article 161 of the Codigo del Trabajo lets an employer end an indefinite contract by invoking 'las necesidades de la empresa, establecimiento o servicio'. Where the contract has run a year or more, article 163 then requires an indemnity equal to thirty days of the last monthly salary for each year of service and for any fraction above six months, unless the parties agreed a larger amount. That indemnity, rather than a notice period, is the number to model before a Chilean exit.

payments.name: Gratificacion legal (article 50 route)
payments.deadline: Not stated in the Código del Trabajo text read: arts. 47 and 50 set the amount, not the payment month.

source.quote: la gratificación de cada trabajador no excederá de cuatro y tres cuartos (4,75) ingresos mínimos mensuales.

countries.name: China

assumptions.label: Employee registered in Shanghai (Chinese contribution rates and bands are set city by city, not nationally)
assumptions.notes: There is no such thing as a Chinese employer rate. The national ministry sets policy ceilings - since 1 May 2019 no province may charge more than 16% for pension - and each city then publishes its own annual schedule of rates, floors and caps. Shanghai is modelled here because it is where almost every provider prices its China example. Deel's own page shows the spread it creates: 34.32% for Shanghai against 40.20% for Beijing and 41% for Tianjin on the same salary. Ask which city your provider will register the hire in before comparing any two quotes.

assumptions.label: Work-injury insurance at band 2 = 0.4% (the band Shanghai assigns to labour-dispatch entities and business services)
assumptions.notes: Shanghai applies the national eight-band industry schedule, 0.2% to 1.9%, in force from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2030. The band follows the registration and main business of the employing entity, not the job: band 1 covers software and IT services and financial services, while business services, professional technical services and every labour-dispatch entity sit in band 2, which is 0.4%. The line is modelled at band 2, since an employer of record usually employs through a dispatch or business-services entity; a provider whose Shanghai entity is registered in band 1 would pay half, 0.2 points of salary less, which is worth asking about when comparing quotes.

assumptions.label: Housing fund at 7%, the top of the 5% to 7% band the employer chooses
assumptions.notes: The Shanghai housing fund committee lets each employer pick a whole-number rate between 5% and 7%, matched by the same rate from the employee. Modelled at 7% because that is the figure Deel publishes for China, and because understating a mandatory employer charge is the more damaging error. A provider contributing at 5% would be 2 points of salary cheaper on this line, so it is worth asking which rate appears in the quote.

employer_contributions.name: Basic pension insurance (yanglao baoxian), Shanghai
employer_contributions.applies: Every urban employee in Shanghai; the base is the real salary between the monthly floor of CNY 7,546 and the monthly cap of CNY 37,731 in force from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027
employer_contributions.notes: The Shanghai human resources and social security bureau states the employer schedule in one sentence: pension 16%, medical 9% including maternity, unemployment 0.5%, work injury base rate 0.2% to 1.9%. The 16% is the national policy ceiling, set by the 2019 State Council reform that ordered every province above 16% down to that level. The band is published separately, and this is the line to re-read every summer: the bureau's notice of 18 August 2026 sets the ceiling at CNY 37,731 a month and the floor at CNY 7,546 with effect from 1 July 2026, on a 2025 city-wide average wage of CNY 12,577 a month (rsj.sh.gov.cn/tgsgg_17341/20260818/t0035_1443203.html, read 20 September 2026). Shanghai's social-insurance year turns on 1 July, not 1 January.

source.name: Shanghai Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau - employer contribution rates

employer_contributions.name: Medical insurance including maternity (yiliao baoxian), Shanghai
employer_contributions.applies: Every urban employee in Shanghai, on the same band as pension
employer_contributions.notes: 9% in Shanghai with maternity insurance merged into it rather than charged separately, per the bureau's own wording: 'medical insurance 9% (maternity included)'. This is the line that varies most between Chinese cities, which is why provider pages quote a range of 6.4% to 10% for the country as a whole and list maternity separately, and why a single national figure would be wrong. Same 2026-27 band as pension, published in the bureau notice of 18 August 2026.

source.name: Shanghai Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau - employer contribution rates

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (shiye baoxian), Shanghai
employer_contributions.applies: Every urban employee in Shanghai, on the same band as pension
employer_contributions.notes: 0.5% from the employer, matched by 0.5% from the employee, on the same 2026-27 band as pension and medical.

source.name: Shanghai Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau - employer contribution rates

employer_contributions.name: Work-injury insurance (gongshang baoxian), industry band 2
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only charge, rate set by the industry risk band of the employing entity: 0.2% for band 1 up to 1.9% for band 8, with labour-dispatch entities placed in band 2 at 0.4%
employer_contributions.notes: Read in the joint Shanghai notice in force from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2030 and in its annex, the industry benchmark rate table. The notice adopts the national eight-band schedule, 0.2, 0.4, 0.7, 0.9, 1.1, 1.3, 1.6 and 1.9 per cent, lets the social insurance agency place each employer in a band from its registration and main business, and classifies labour-dispatch entities uniformly in band 2. The annex puts software and IT services, monetary and capital-market services and insurance in band 1 at 0.2%, and wholesale, retail, internet services, business services, research and development and professional technical services in band 2 at 0.4%. The line is modelled at band 2, because an employer of record in China usually employs through a dispatch or business-services entity, and the notice places both there; a hire employed by an entity registered in software and IT services would pay 0.2% instead. The notice states no separate contribution base for this line, so it is modelled on the same base as the other three insurances, which is standard Chinese practice.

source.name: Shanghai notice on work-injury insurance rates (Hu Ren She Gui 2026 No. 2), in force 2026-2030, with its annex, the industry benchmark rate table

employer_contributions.name: Housing provident fund (zhufang gongjijin), Shanghai, at 7%
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee in Shanghai; the employer picks a whole-number rate from 5% to 7% and the employee matches it. The base shares the CNY 37,731 monthly cap but has its own lower floor of CNY 2,740
employer_contributions.notes: Read in the notice of the Shanghai Housing Provident Fund Management Committee (Hu Gongjijin Guanweihui 2026 No. 3, dated 18 August 2026, marked valid) on the fund's own site. From 1 July 2026 the base moves to the employee's 2025 average monthly wage, capped at CNY 37,731 and floored at CNY 2,740; employer and employee each pay a whole-number rate from 5% to 7% chosen by the employer, which puts the monthly employer amount at 7% between CNY 192 and CNY 2,641 (the notice publishes the combined two-sided figure, CNY 384 to CNY 5,282). A supplementary fund of 1% to 5% each side is voluntary and is not modelled. Deel independently publishes 7% for China. Unlike the four insurances this is a named savings account the employee draws on for housing, not a pure charge, but it leaves the employer's bank account all the same. The fund's domain does not resolve through public resolvers outside China; it answered once resolved through a Chinese one.

source.name: Shanghai Housing Provident Fund Management Committee, notice Hu Gongjijin Guanweihui 2026 No. 3 on the 2026 contribution base, rates and monthly limits

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month or year-end bonus (nianzhongjiang) - customary, not statutory
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because no Chinese statute requires it. The Employment Contract Law only obliges the employer to pay remuneration in full and on time as agreed in the contract and as the state provides; it contains no thirteenth-month clause, and reading the whole text confirms it. In practice a year-end bonus around one month of salary is close to standard in Shanghai and a competitive offer usually has to carry one, so budget it as a market cost rather than a legal charge.

source.name: Employment Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, art. 30 (full text on the State Administration for Market Regulation site)

statutory_extras.name: Disabled employment security fund - assessed on the company, not the payslip
statutory_extras.notes: Read in the Shanghai implementing measures on the disabled employment security fund (Hu Cai Fa 2020 No. 9), extended to 31 December 2030 by Hu Cai Fa 2025 No. 11, and in the Shanghai tax bureau's guide for the 2025 levy, collected from 19 August 2026. It is not a per-payslip contribution like the five insurances: it is an annual levy on an employer that falls short of the 1.5% quota for employing people with disabilities. The levy is (1.5% minus the employer's disabled-staff ratio) times the sum of its prior-year social insurance contribution bases, times 50% if that ratio is at least 1% and 90% if it is below 1%; each wage counts up to twice the Shanghai average wage (CNY 24,868 a month for the second half of 2025). An employer with no disabled staff therefore pays 1.35% of that capped base, and companies with 30 employees or fewer are exempt. Deel's China page quotes a disability fund of 0.50% to 1.60%. The levy falls on the employing entity, so on an EOR hire it is the provider's charge and depends on its whole Shanghai headcount; it is carried at zero here and named because it is part of why a provider's China figure lands above the sum of the five insurances.

source.name: Shanghai implementing measures on the disabled employment security fund (Hu Cai Fa 2020 No. 9), art. 8 and art. 16, extended to 2030 by Hu Cai Fa 2025 No. 11

countries.notice_typical: Thirty days' written notice, or one extra month's salary in place of it, for a no-fault dismissal under article 40 of the Employment Contract Law. An employee resigning also gives thirty days, or three during probation.

countries.name: Colombia

assumptions.label: Occupational risk class I (office work), charged at the initial rate of 0.522%
assumptions.notes: The ARL rate follows the risk class of the job, not of the company, and under an employer of record the policy is taken out by the provider. Class I is the class for office and administrative work; a company entering the system for the first time pays the 'valor inicial' of its class, which is 0.522% for class I. The class I band runs from 0.348% to 0.696%, and classes II to V run higher.

assumptions.label: The employer is a company that files Colombian corporate income tax, which is what triggers the article 114-1 exoneration
assumptions.notes: Article 114-1 of the Estatuto Tributario exonerates 'las sociedades y personas juridicas y asimiladas contribuyentes declarantes del impuesto sobre la renta' from health, SENA and ICBF on employees paid under ten minimum wages. An employer of record's Colombian entity is such a company. An individual employing fewer than two people is outside the exoneration.

employer_contributions.name: Pension (employer share)
employer_contributions.notes: The contribution rate is 16% of the ingreso base de cotizacion and article 20 of Ley 100 de 1993, as replaced by article 7 of Ley 797 de 2003, splits it: 'Los empleadores pagaran el 75% de la cotizacion total y los trabajadores el 25% restante.' That is 12 points for the employer. The base is capped at 25 monthly minimum wages (article 5 of Ley 797 de 2003: 'El limite de la base de cotizacion sera de veinticinco (25) salarios minimos legales mensuales vigentes'), which at the 2026 minimum wage of COP 1,750,905 is COP 43,772,625 a month, COP 525,271,500 a year.

source.name: Ley 100 de 1993, articulo 20, as replaced by articulo 7 de la Ley 797 de 2003 (Secretaria del Senado, compilation updated 31 August 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Family compensation fund (caja de compensacion familiar)
employer_contributions.notes: Article 12 of Ley 21 de 1982 sets the private-sector split of the payroll levy: 'El cuatro por ciento (4%) para proveer el pago de subsidio familiar. 2. El dos por ciento (2%) para el Servicio nacional de aprendizaje (SENA).' The 4% caja share is the one line of the parafiscales that the article 114-1 exoneration does not touch, so it is charged at every salary level. It is calculated on the monthly payroll with no ceiling.

source.name: Ley 21 de 1982, articulo 12 (Funcion Publica, Gestor Normativo)

employer_contributions.name: Occupational risk insurance (ARL), class I
employer_contributions.applies: Office and administrative work (risk class I)
employer_contributions.notes: Article 2.2.4.3.5 of Decreto 1072 de 2015, which consolidates the table set under article 27 of Decreto 1295 de 1994, prints 'TABLA DE COTIZACIONES MINIMAS Y MAXIMAS: CLASE DE RIESGO I 0.348% ... 0.522%' for the minimum and the initial value. A company entering the system pays the initial value of its class. Riskier classes go up to 6.960%, so a warehouse or field role in Colombia does not carry this rate.

source.name: Decreto 1072 de 2015, articulo 2.2.4.3.5 (Funcion Publica, Gestor Normativo)

employer_contributions.name: Health (employer share) - exonerated under ten minimum wages
employer_contributions.applies: Only on salaries of ten monthly minimum wages or more (COP 17,509,050 a month in 2026)
employer_contributions.notes: Article 10 of Ley 1122 de 2007 replaced the first paragraph of article 204 of Ley 100 de 1993: 'La cotizacion al Regimen Contributivo de Salud sera ... del 12,5% del ingreso o salario base de cotizacion ... La cotizacion a cargo del empleador sera del 8.5% y a cargo del empleado del 4%.' Article 114-1 of the Estatuto Tributario then removes the employer's 8.5% for every employee paid less than ten minimum wages. At the 2026 minimum wage that threshold is COP 17,509,050 a month, COP 210,108,600 a year, and the example salary sits below it, so the line is switched off here and comes back in full above the threshold.

source.name: Ley 1122 de 2007, articulo 10, and Estatuto Tributario articulo 114-1 as added by articulo 65 de la Ley 1819 de 2016 (Secretaria del Senado)

employer_contributions.name: SENA training levy - exonerated under ten minimum wages
employer_contributions.applies: Only on salaries of ten monthly minimum wages or more (COP 17,509,050 a month in 2026)
employer_contributions.notes: Two points of payroll to the Servicio Nacional de Aprendizaje under article 12 of Ley 21 de 1982, exonerated by article 114-1 of the Estatuto Tributario for employees paid under ten minimum wages.

source.name: Ley 21 de 1982, articulo 12, with the exoneration in Estatuto Tributario articulo 114-1 (articulo 65 de la Ley 1819 de 2016)

employer_contributions.name: ICBF family welfare levy - exonerated under ten minimum wages
employer_contributions.applies: Only on salaries of ten monthly minimum wages or more (COP 17,509,050 a month in 2026)
employer_contributions.notes: Article 1 of Ley 89 de 1988: 'A partir del 1 de enero de 1989 los aportes para el Instituto Colombiano de Bienestar Familiar -ICBF- ... se aumentan al tres por ciento (3%) del valor de la nomina mensual de salarios.' Exonerated by article 114-1 of the Estatuto Tributario for employees paid under ten minimum wages.

source.name: Ley 89 de 1988, articulo 1 (Funcion Publica, Gestor Normativo)

statutory_extras.name: Severance fund deposit (cesantias)
statutory_extras.notes: Article 249 of the Codigo Sustantivo del Trabajo: 'Todo empleador esta obligado a pagar a sus trabajadores ... como auxilio de cesantia, un mes de salario por cada ano de servicios y proporcionalmente por fraccion de ano.' Since Ley 50 de 1990 it is deposited each February into a fondo de cesantias rather than held by the employer, so it is cash out of the door every year whether or not the employee leaves. It is a prestacion social and not salary, so it does not itself carry pension or health contributions.

source.name: Codigo Sustantivo del Trabajo, articulo 249 (Secretaria del Senado)

statutory_extras.name: Interest on the severance fund (intereses a las cesantias)
statutory_extras.notes: Article 1 of Decreto 116 de 1976, which regulates Ley 52 de 1975: 'todo patrono obligado a pagar cesantia a sus trabajadores, les reconocera y pagara intereses del 12% anual sobre los saldos que en 31 de diciembre de cada ano ... tengan a su favor por concepto de cesantia.' Twelve per cent of one month of salary is one per cent of a full year of salary, paid to the employee in January. It is the line most often dropped from Colombian cost estimates because it is a percentage of a percentage.

source.name: Decreto 116 de 1976, articulo 1 (reglamentario de la Ley 52 de 1975), Funcion Publica Gestor Normativo

statutory_extras.name: Service bonus (prima de servicios)
statutory_extras.notes: Article 306 of the Codigo Sustantivo del Trabajo, as replaced by article 1 of Ley 1788 de 2016: 'la prestacion social denominada prima de servicios que correspondera a 30 dias de salario por ano, el cual se reconocera en dos pagos, asi: la mitad maximo el 30 de junio y la otra mitad a mas tardar los primeros veinte dias de diciembre.' Article 307 adds that it is not salary, so it carries no contributions of its own. Together with the cesantias it is why a Colombian year costs fourteen months of pay, not twelve.

source.name: Codigo Sustantivo del Trabajo, articulo 306, as replaced by articulo 1 de la Ley 1788 de 2016 (Secretaria del Senado)

countries.notice_typical: There is no statutory notice period for dismissing an employee on an indefinite contract; the employer instead owes an indemnity under article 64 of the Codigo Sustantivo del Trabajo, as replaced by article 28 de la Ley 789 de 2002. For an employee paid under ten minimum wages that is thirty days of salary for service of a year or less, plus twenty extra days for each subsequent year; above ten minimum wages it is twenty days, plus fifteen for each subsequent year.

payments.name: Prima de servicios (June instalment)
payments.deadline: by 30 June

payments.name: Prima de servicios (December instalment)
payments.deadline: within the first twenty days of December

source.quote: la mitad máximo el 30 de junio y la otra mitad a más tardar los primeros veinte días de diciembre

assumptions.label: The INS occupational-risk policy is carried at zero, so the total below is a floor
assumptions.notes: Every Costa Rican employer must also insure its staff against occupational risks with the Instituto Nacional de Seguros. That premium is rated by activity and is billed by the INS, not collected by the CCSS with the payroll, so it is not one of the ten lines the CCSS charges. It is left at zero here rather than guessed, which makes the figure below a minimum.

employer_contributions.name: CCSS health insurance (Seguro de Enfermedad y Maternidad)
employer_contributions.notes: The largest single line of the Costa Rican payroll. The CCSS employer calculator prints SEM at 9.25% for the employer and 5.50% for the worker. The base cannot fall below the base minima contributiva, set at CRC 346,789 a month for SEM by Decreto 44756-MTSS, published in La Gaceta 229 of 5 December 2025 and applied from the January 2026 billing; that is the annual floor shown here. There is no ceiling.

source.name: Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social - Calculadora Patronal, Patronos page (2026 rates)

employer_contributions.name: CCSS pensions (Invalidez, Vejez y Muerte)
employer_contributions.notes: Raised from 5.42% to 5.58% for employers with effect from January 2026; the worker's share moved from 4.17% to 4.33% at the same time. The CCSS banner states the plan plainly: 'Desde enero 2026 hasta diciembre 2028, el aporte de IVM sera del 11.66%', that 11.66% being the combined employer, worker and State contribution. The IVM floor is CRC 324,590 a month under the same Decreto 44756-MTSS.

source.name: Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social - Calculadora Patronal, Patronos page (IVM 5,58% patrono from January 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Banco Popular employer levy
employer_contributions.notes: First of the two Banco Popular lines an employer pays. The CCSS groups it under 'Otras Instituciones', the levies it collects on behalf of bodies other than itself.

source.name: Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social - Calculadora Patronal, Otras Instituciones block

employer_contributions.name: Family allowances fund (FODESAF)
employer_contributions.notes: Five points of payroll into the social development and family allowances fund. It is just behind the 5.58% pension line, and it is charged whatever the employee earns.

source.name: Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social - Calculadora Patronal, Otras Instituciones block

employer_contributions.name: IMAS social assistance levy
employer_contributions.notes: Instituto Mixto de Ayuda Social, collected by the CCSS with the rest of the payroll.

source.name: Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social - Calculadora Patronal, Otras Instituciones block

employer_contributions.name: INA vocational training levy
employer_contributions.notes: Instituto Nacional de Aprendizaje, the Costa Rican training levy.

source.name: Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social - Calculadora Patronal, Otras Instituciones block

employer_contributions.name: Banco Popular levy under the Ley de Proteccion al Trabajador
employer_contributions.notes: The second Banco Popular line, this one inside the Ley de Proteccion al Trabajador block. The worker pays 1.00% into the same fund.

source.name: Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social - Calculadora Patronal, Ley de Proteccion al Trabajador block

employer_contributions.name: Labour capitalisation fund (Fondo de Capitalizacion Laboral)
employer_contributions.notes: An individual savings fund the employee can draw on when the relationship ends or, after five years, in part. It is paid monthly by the employer, so unlike a severance provision it is money that leaves the company every month whether or not anyone resigns.

source.name: Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social - Calculadora Patronal, Ley de Proteccion al Trabajador block

employer_contributions.name: Complementary pension (Operadora de Pensiones Complementaria)
employer_contributions.notes: The second pillar. Article 13(c) of Ley 7983 sets the employer's contribution to the Regimen Obligatorio de Pensiones Complementarias at 3%; this 2.00% and the 1.00% line the CCSS labels INS add up to it, which is how this page reads the two lines. It sits on top of the CCSS IVM contribution, so on that reading Costa Rican pension provision costs the employer at least 8.58 points at the example salary, and at least 7.58 even if the INS share funds something else - not the 5.58 that the IVM line alone suggests.

source.name: Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social - Calculadora Patronal, Ley de Proteccion al Trabajador block

employer_contributions.name: Complementary pension, share the CCSS labels INS (Ley 7983 art. 13(c))
employer_contributions.notes: Listed by the CCSS as 'INS' inside the Ley de Proteccion al Trabajador block and collected with the payroll. Ley 7983 creates no levy of that name: article 13(c), as amended by Ley 9906 of 5 October 2020, funds the Regimen Obligatorio de Pensiones Complementarias with 'un aporte de los patronos del tres por ciento (3%) mensual sobre los sueldos, los salarios y las remuneraciones de los trabajadores', and this 1.00% plus the 2.00% complementary-pension line add up to exactly that 3%. That is this page's reading of the label, by arithmetic: neither the CCSS nor the law says what the 'INS' share funds. It is not the occupational-risk policy, which the Instituto Nacional de Seguros bills separately and which this ledger does not price.

source.name: Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social - Calculadora Patronal, Ley de Proteccion al Trabajador block

statutory_extras.name: Aguinaldo (13th-month salary)
statutory_extras.notes: Article 1 of Ley 2412: 'Todo patrono particular esta obligado a conceder a sus trabajadores ... un beneficio economico anual equivalente a un mes de salario.' Article 2, as amended by Ley 3929 of 8 August 1967, computes it on the average of ordinary and extraordinary pay over the twelve months before 1 December, and article 4 requires payment in the first twenty days of December. Article 7 then exempts it from social charges, so unlike the monthly salary it carries none of the ten lines above.

source.name: Ley 2412, Ley Pago de Aguinaldo a Servidores Empresa Privada, articulos 1, 2, 4 and 7 (SCIJ / SINALEVI, version in force, read 21 September 2026)

statutory_extras.name: Occupational risk policy with the INS
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the premium is rated by the insurer on the employer's declared activity rather than fixed by a published percentage, and because the Instituto Nacional de Seguros bills it separately instead of the CCSS collecting it with the payroll. It is a real and compulsory cost: Deel's own Costa Rica page books it at 0.37% of salary under the heading 'Workman Compensation'. Because it is left out, the total on this page is a floor, not a final figure.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Costa Rica page

payments.name: Aguinaldo (13th-month salary)
payments.deadline: 20 Dec (first twenty days of December)

source.quote: dentro de los primeros veinte días de diciembre de cada año

countries.name: Czech Republic

assumptions.label: Role is not risk-classified work, and the employee is not a paramedic or a member of a works fire brigade
assumptions.notes: The Czech employer rate is not single. The pension reform of 2023 opened a second and a third employer rate for hazardous and emergency work, phased in year by year; the ordinary rate stays at 24.8%.

assumptions.label: Statutory work-injury insurance at 5.6 per mille, the residual 'other economic activities' group of decree 125/1993
assumptions.notes: The rate follows the predominant business activity of the legal employer, which under an EOR is the provider. Supplying personnel is not named in any rate group of the decree's annex, so the residual group applies. An entity of your own doing software work would be OKEC 72 at 2.8 per mille.

employer_contributions.name: Social security and employment policy contribution (pojistné na sociální zabezpečení)
employer_contributions.applies: Employees who do not perform risk-classified work and are not paramedics or works fire brigade members
employer_contributions.notes: One payment made of three parts: 2.1% sickness insurance, 21.5% pension insurance and 1.2% employment policy contribution. The Czech Social Security Administration publishes two higher employer rates alongside it, and they exist because of the 2023 pension reform rather than because of the industry: 27.8% in 2026 for employees in risk-classified work, rising to 28.8% in 2027 and 29.8% from 2028, and 29.8% already for paramedics and members of a works fire brigade. The ceiling is 48 times the average wage, CZK 2,350,416 in 2026; the administration states that above it the employer stops paying its own share as well as the employee's, so this line genuinely flattens out rather than only the payslip deduction.

source.name: Česká správa sociálního zabezpečení - Výše a sazba pojistného

employer_contributions.name: Public health insurance (veřejné zdravotní pojištění)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees, with no upper ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: The premium is 13.5% of the assessment base and the employer carries two of the three thirds, which is the 9% here: VZP states that employers remit one third withheld from the employee and two thirds that they pay themselves. There is no maximum assessment base for health insurance - the ceiling that applies to social security was abolished here and never came back - so this line keeps growing with pay while the social security line stops. The floor is the minimum wage, CZK 22,400 a month in 2026 for a minimum premium of CZK 3,024, but where pay falls short the Act puts the top-up on the employee rather than on the employer, except when the shortfall is caused by an obstacle on the employer's side.

source.name: VZP ČR - Splatnost a další zásady pro platbu pojistného (zaměstnavatelé)

employer_contributions.name: Statutory work-injury and occupational-disease insurance
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer with at least one employee, at the rate for its predominant business activity
employer_contributions.notes: The line most cost pages for this country leave out. It is compulsory from the day of the first employment relationship, it is paid quarterly to Kooperativa (or to Česká pojišťovna for employers insured there before 1993), and its rate is fixed by a finance ministry decree rather than by the insurer: from 2.8 per mille for data processing up to 50.4 per mille for coal mining. The rate follows the predominant activity of the legal employer, which under an EOR is the provider, and supplying personnel appears in no rate group of the annex, so the residual 'other economic activities' rate of 5.6 per mille is the declared modelling point here. A Czech entity of your own writing software would be 2.8 per mille. Section 12(2) ties the premium base to the social security assessment base, so the same annual ceiling is applied. The minimum premium is CZK 100 a quarter.

source.name: Vyhláška č. 125/1993 Sb., section 12(2) and annex 2, consolidated text in force since 1 January 2012 - e-Sbírka
