statutory_extras.name: Employer-paid sick pay for the first 14 days
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it follows absence rather than pay. Section 192 of the Labour Code puts the first 14 calendar days of a temporary incapacity or quarantine on the employer, paid for the days that would have been working days and for public holidays that would otherwise have been paid; sickness benefit from the social security system starts after that.

source.name: Zákoník práce (zákon č. 262/2006 Sb.), section 192(1), consolidated text in force on 1 January 2026 - e-Sbírka

statutory_extras.name: Severance on redundancy (odstupné)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is contingent on how the employment ends, not recurring. Section 67 of the Labour Code gives one month's average earnings if the employment lasted under a year, two months from one year and three months from two years, and it is due only where the employer terminates for the reorganisation grounds in section 52(a) to (c), or by agreement for the same reasons. A resignation, a dismissal for cause or the end of a probation period triggers nothing.

source.name: Zákoník práce (zákon č. 262/2006 Sb.), section 67(1), consolidated text in force on 1 January 2026 - e-Sbírka

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth-month pay
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because Czech law does not create it. Nothing in the Labour Code requires a thirteenth month; where one is paid it comes from a collective agreement or the employment contract, and it then counts in full towards both the social security and the health insurance assessment bases.

source.name: Zákoník práce (zákon č. 262/2006 Sb.), consolidated text in force on 1 January 2026, read in full - e-Sbírka

countries.notice_typical: At least two months either way, and since the 2025 amendment the period runs from the day the notice is delivered and ends on the day of the following month bearing the same number, rather than starting on the first day of the next month. One month applies to the narrower grounds in section 52(f) to (h) of the Labour Code. Eight months of probation may be agreed for a managerial employee, against four for everyone else, and either side may end the contract during it in writing without giving a reason.

countries.name: Germany

assumptions.label: Employee's health fund charges the 2026 average supplementary rate of 2.9% (employer half 1.45%)
assumptions.notes: Each Krankenkasse sets its own supplementary rate; the 2026 spread runs from about 2.2% to 4.4%, so the employer's health line moves by up to 0.75 points either way depending on the fund the employee picks.

assumptions.label: Employee works outside Saxony (employer long-term-care share 1.8%, not 1.3%)
assumptions.notes: Saxony kept a public holiday when long-term-care insurance was introduced, so employers there pay 1.3% and employees 2.3%.

assumptions.label: Accident insurance at VBG hazard class 0.70 (staff-leasing tariff item 11.1, office and service work)
assumptions.notes: German EOR employment is staff leasing under the AÜG, insured with the VBG. Hazard class 0.70 covers leased staff in service occupations; leased staff in other occupations sit at 6.24. Deel publishes 1.14% for its German entity.

employer_contributions.name: Statutory pension insurance (Rentenversicherung), employer half
employer_contributions.applies: All employees; base capped at the 2026 contribution ceiling of EUR 8,450 a month
employer_contributions.notes: 18.6% in total, 9.3% employer and 9.3% employee, unchanged for 2026. The ceiling rose from EUR 8,050 to EUR 8,450 a month (EUR 101,400 a year) on 1 January 2026.

source.name: Deutsche Rentenversicherung — Die Sozialversicherungsrechengrößen 2026 (pension 18.6%, 9.3% each; ceiling EUR 8,450 a month; unemployment 2.6%, 1.3% each)

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (Arbeitslosenversicherung), employer half
employer_contributions.applies: All employees; same EUR 101,400 ceiling as the pension line
employer_contributions.notes: 2.6% in total, split 1.3% employer and 1.3% employee, confirmed for 2026.

source.name: BMAS — Das ändert sich im neuen Jahr (2026): unemployment contribution stays at 2.6%; insolvency levy 0.15%

employer_contributions.name: Statutory health insurance (Krankenversicherung), employer half incl. average supplementary rate
employer_contributions.applies: Employees in the statutory scheme; base capped at EUR 5,812.50 a month in 2026. Privately insured employees (above EUR 77,400 a year and opted out) receive an employer subsidy of up to the same amount instead
employer_contributions.notes: General rate 14.6% plus the 2026 average supplementary rate of 2.9% = 17.5%, shared equally (SGB V section 249): 7.3% + 1.45% = 8.75% for the employer. Health funds set their own supplementary rate, so the exact line depends on the employee's fund.

source.name: Bundesministerium für Gesundheit — Beiträge der GKV: general rate 14.6%, average supplementary rate 2.9% for 2026, ceiling EUR 5,812.50 a month / EUR 69,750 a year

employer_contributions.name: Long-term care insurance (Pflegeversicherung), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All employees outside Saxony; same EUR 69,750 ceiling as health insurance
employer_contributions.notes: 3.6% in total since 1 January 2025, split 1.8% employer and 1.8% employee; the childless surcharge (0.6%) and the reductions for parents of several children touch only the employee share. In Saxony the employer pays 1.3%.

source.name: Bundesministerium für Gesundheit — Finanzierung der sozialen Pflegeversicherung (3.6%; employer 1.8%, Saxony 1.3%)

employer_contributions.name: Maternity levy (Umlage U2), Techniker Krankenkasse rate
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, whatever its size, at the rate of the employee's health fund
employer_contributions.notes: Refunds 100% of maternity-pay top-ups. TK charges 0.44% in 2026; other funds sit between roughly 0.2% and 0.7%. The sick-pay levy U1 only applies to employers with up to 30 employees, so an EOR entity is outside it.

source.name: Techniker Krankenkasse — Wie hoch sind die Umlagesätze U1 und U2? (U2 0.44% for 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Insolvency levy (Insolvenzgeldumlage, U3)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer; base capped at the pension ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Set by law at 0.15% (SGB III section 360) and confirmed for 2026.

source.name: SGB III section 360 Umlagesatz (0.15%), gesetze-im-internet.de

employer_contributions.name: Statutory accident insurance (Berufsgenossenschaft VBG), hazard class 0.70
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only, on the full salary; the VBG insures staff-leasing companies and office-based businesses
employer_contributions.notes: Computed from the VBG's published 2025 contribution factor: hazard class 0.70 x EUR 4.40 per 1,000 = 0.31%, plus the cost-sharing surcharges (EUR 1.7851 per 1,000 of pay above a EUR 270,000 allowance and EUR 0.3445 per 1,000 contribution units) = about 0.51%. Secondary source for the hazard class: the VBG 2022 tariff as quoted by zeitarbeit-und-recht.de (item 11.1 = 0.70). Deel's German page shows 1.14% for accident insurance.

source.name: VBG — Ihr Beitrag (contribution factor EUR 4.40 for 2025, cost-sharing factors, worked example with hazard class 0.63)

statutory_extras.name: 18-month staff-leasing limit (AÜG section 1(1b))
statutory_extras.notes: Not a cost line but a hard constraint: an EOR in Germany is a licensed staff-leasing company, and it may not lease the same employee to the same client for more than 18 consecutive months (gaps of up to three months count as continuous). Before month 19 the hire has to move to your own entity or another arrangement. Budget the entity, or the switch, into the total.

source.name: Arbeitnehmerüberlassungsgesetz (AÜG) section 1 paragraph 1b, gesetze-im-internet.de

countries.notice_typical: Four weeks to the 15th or the end of a month during the first two years; the employer's notice then grows with service from one month (after 2 years) to seven months (after 20 years), always to a month end; two weeks during an agreed probation of up to six months (BGB section 622).

source.quote: Dafür kommen verschiedene Möglichkeiten in Betracht: ein Tarifvertrag, eine Betriebsvereinbarung oder eine entsprechende einzelvertragliche Regelung.

countries.name: Denmark

assumptions.label: Salaried monthly employee, business services industry group
assumptions.notes: Two classifications decide a Danish employer's bill, and both are assumed here. The first is that the hire is a funktionaer paid monthly, which is what a software engineer on a permanent contract is: that puts them under the Funktionaer Act for notice and sick pay, and under the holiday act's 1% supplement rather than its 12.5% holiday allowance. The second is the industry group behind the AES charge, modelled at group 71, financing and business services, which is what an employer of record's own Danish entity is. A construction or industrial classification would multiply that one line several times over, but it is small enough that the difference barely moves the total.

employer_contributions.name: ATP labour market supplementary pension (employer share)
employer_contributions.applies: Flat amount per employee working at least 117 hours a month, independent of salary
employer_contributions.notes: This is the whole of Denmark's statutory pension charge on an employer, and it is a fixed sum rather than a percentage. The official rate table for monthly-paid employees on the A-sats gives, for at least 117 hours a month, an employee share of DKK 99.00, an employer share of DKK 198.00 and DKK 297.00 in total per month - so DKK 2,376 a year from the employer, whatever the salary. Below 117 hours the amount steps down in thirds and stops entirely under 39 hours. Because it is flat, ATP is a meaningful cost on a low wage and a rounding error on a high one: on the example salary here it is just over half a percent. The occupational pension of 8% to 12% that appears on most Danish offers is not this charge and is not law; it comes from collective agreements, and it is carried separately below at zero.

source.name: Virk (ATP) - Gaeldende satser for ATP-bidrag, A-sats table for monthly-paid employees

employer_contributions.name: AUB employers' education contribution, including the VEU levy
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer that pays ATP contributions, per full-time employee
employer_contributions.notes: AUB funds Denmark's vocational training system and is charged to every employer that pays ATP. The 2026 figure is stated plainly by the administering body: 'I 2026 skal I betale 2.821 kr. for hver fuldtidsansat medarbejder' - DKK 2,821 for each full-time employee - made up of a quarterly AUB contribution of DKK 596.75 and a VEU adult-training levy of DKK 108.50, DKK 705.25 a quarter in all. Two details matter under an employer of record. There is a deduction for the first employee and for every fiftieth, so a one-person company pays nothing at all - but the legal employer here is the provider, with a Danish payroll far past that threshold, so your hire is charged in full. And the separate Laerepladss-AUB bonus-malus, which rewards employers that take on apprentices, is assessed on the provider's own apprentice record, not on yours.

source.name: Virk (Arbejdsgivernes Uddannelsesbidrag) - Arbejdsgiver, Satser for bidrag 2026

employer_contributions.name: Barsel.dk parental leave equalisation scheme
employer_contributions.applies: Every private-sector employer, per full-time monthly-paid employee
employer_contributions.notes: Barsel.dk spreads the cost of paid parental leave across the private sector, and it rose sharply this year: 'Fra 1. januar 2026 er bidragssatsen til Barsel.dk 2.200 kr. pr. aar (550 kr. pr. kvartal) for en fuldtidsansat, maanedsloennet medarbejder', up from DKK 1,550 in 2025 under Lov nr. 1625 of 16 December 2025. It is collected in proportion to ATP: each full quarterly ATP contribution of DKK 891 triggers one DKK 550 payment. It is compulsory - the scheme's own FAQ answers 'are we forced to pay you' with 'Ja' - unless every employee is covered by another approved parental scheme. What it buys back is a reimbursement when someone does take leave, which matters because the Funktionaer Act separately obliges the employer to pay half salary from the start of maternity leave until fourteen weeks after the birth.

source.name: Virk (Barsel.dk) - Bidrag til Barsel.dk, rate from 1 January 2026

employer_contributions.name: Occupational accident insurance premium (arbejdsskadeforsikring)
employer_contributions.applies: Compulsory for every employer, bought from a private insurer at a market premium
employer_contributions.notes: secondary source: this is the one line in the ledger above whose price the state does not set, so it is modelled from a provider's published figure rather than from an authority. The obligation itself is statutory and was read at source: section 48 of the Workers' Compensation Act says every employer has a duty of cover for the people it employs, and that the duty is met 'ved at tegne forsikring mod foelgerne af arbejdsulykker' - by taking out insurance against workplace accidents - alongside joining AES for occupational disease. No Danish authority publishes a premium, because accident cover is sold on the private market and priced per employer. The amount used here is Deel's published Denmark line item, DKK 184.91 a month, read 20 September 2026, which annualises to DKK 2,219. Treat it as an order of magnitude a provider actually charges, not a rate: your own quote will differ, and a hazardous role will differ a great deal.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Denmark page

employer_contributions.name: AES occupational disease contribution and workplace-injury duty
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer that pays ATP contributions; the amount is set by the company's industry code
employer_contributions.notes: AES covers occupational disease, as distinct from the accident insurance above, and it is collected automatically alongside ATP. The rate is set by industry group rather than by salary, and the published 2026 table gives, for group 71 - financing and business services - an AES contribution of DKK 268 and a workplace-injury duty of DKK 189, DKK 457 a year in all per full-time employee, two kroner of administration included. The spread across industries is wide: DKK 284 for utilities, DKK 2,323 for general construction, DKK 10,892 for defence and policing. Your own figure depends on the industry code of the legal employer, which under an employer of record is the provider's, not yours.

source.name: Arbejdsmarkedets Erhvervssikring - AES-Satser 2026 (PDF), industry group 71 Finansiering og forretningsservice

employer_contributions.name: Financing contribution (finansieringsbidrag), including the wage guarantee fund
employer_contributions.applies: Every private employer registered for VAT or payroll tax, and every foreign company even without a Danish VAT registration, per person with a full ATP contribution
employer_contributions.notes: A small joint charge with an unusually transparent breakdown. The 2026 rate is DKK 82.00 per full-time employee per quarter, DKK 328 a year, and the administering body publishes what each krone funds: DKK 55.00 to the wage guarantee fund that pays salary, pension and holiday money if an employer goes bankrupt, DKK 19.75 towards sickness benefit, DKK 13.25 towards unemployment benefit and adult-training allowance, and two negative entries, minus DKK 5.00 for parental benefit and minus DKK 1.00 for job-clarification allowance, which are refunds of earlier over-collection. Public employers do not pay it; foreign companies do, even without a Danish VAT registration.

source.name: Virk (Samlet Betaling) - Finansieringsbidrag, Satser 2026 with the per-scheme breakdown

statutory_extras.name: Holiday supplement (ferietillaeg), 1% of salary
statutory_extras.notes: The only part of a Danish employer's bill that is a percentage of pay, and the one line here that is genuinely additional rather than a reshuffling of salary. Section 16(1) of the Holiday Act says a monthly-paid employee entitled to full pay on public holidays and sick days 'faar loen under ferie samt et ferietillaeg paa 1 pct. af loennen' - salary during holiday plus a 1% supplement. Read the alternative carefully before comparing this figure with anyone else's. The two subsections are the Act's two regimes for the same thing - the chapter is headed 'the payment during holiday' - and they are mutually exclusive: section 16(2) gives a holiday allowance of 12.5% to an employee 'som ikke er omfattet af stk. 1', who is not covered by subsection 1. So 12.5% is what the holiday itself is paid with where there is no salary during it, not a supplement stacked on twelve months of pay. Before accepting a Danish quote that shows 12.5% above a full monthly salary, ask which of the two regimes the contract is under. The 1% supplement is paid with the May and August salaries, or as each holiday begins.

source.name: Holiday Act (Ferieloven), LBK nr. 152 of 20 February 2024, section 16(1) and 16(2)

statutory_extras.name: Occupational pension of 8-12% - collective agreement, not law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because no Danish statute requires it, and named because it is the largest number anyone will quote you for Denmark. The pension the law puts on an employer is ATP, the flat contribution in the ledger above. The 8% to 12% arbejdsmarkedspension on most Danish offers comes from a collective agreement or from the individual contract, which is why it varies by sector and why a provider can price it only once it knows which agreement applies. Budget it as market cost if you want a competitive offer - on this example salary a 10% employer pension would cost several times everything in the table above put together - but do not read it as a statutory charge, and do not accept it in a quote without asking which agreement obliges it.

source.name: Virk (ATP) - ATP Livslang Pension, the statutory labour market pension and its employer rates

statutory_extras.name: Full salary during sickness - paid by the employer
statutory_extras.notes: A real and potentially large employer cost that cannot honestly be a rate, so it is named here and left out of the total. The Funktionaer Act treats illness as lawful absence, and its section 5(2) allows an employer to give one month's notice only once a salaried employee 'har oppebaaret loen under sygdom i ialt 120 dage' within twelve consecutive months - has drawn salary during sickness for 120 days - which is the Act stating, in the course of limiting it, that the employer pays. Denmark therefore differs from countries that fund sick pay through an employer contribution: here the charge arrives as salary you keep paying. Municipal sickness benefit reimburses part of it after the first weeks, and how much you end up paying depends on the person, not on the payroll.

source.name: Salaried Employees Act (Funktionaerloven), LBK nr. 1002 of 24 August 2017, section 5(2)

statutory_extras.name: Holiday fund administration fees - DKK 68 a year
statutory_extras.notes: Named for completeness and carried at zero because it is too small to survive rounding, not because it does not exist. Two administration fees ride along with the quarterly Samlet Betaling collection: DKK 4 a month per employee for FerieKonto, and DKK 5 a quarter for Loenmodtagernes Feriemidler, the fund holding the holiday pay frozen during the 2019 transition. Together they come to DKK 68 a year, about US$10, or under a dollar a month - less than a rounding step on any figure on this page. The FerieKonto fee applies only where holiday pay is actually routed through FerieKonto, which is not the case for a monthly-paid employee taking paid holiday, although providers commonly bill it anyway.

source.name: Virk (Samlet Betaling) - Satser for Samlet Betaling 2017-2026, contribution rates for 2026

countries.notice_typical: One month in the first six months of service, three months after six months, then one month more for every three years of service up to a maximum of six, all under section 2 of the Salaried Employees Act. During an agreed probation of no more than three months the employer's notice is fourteen days; the employee gives one month throughout.

countries.name: Dominican Republic

assumptions.label: Contribution ceilings taken on the TSS national minimum wage of RD$23,223 a month, in force since 1 February 2026
assumptions.notes: The Tesoreria de la Seguridad Social sets its ceilings in multiples of a national minimum wage of its own, not a company-size minimum wage. Its Resolution 01-2025 put that reference at RD$21,674.80 from 1 April 2025 and at RD$23,223.00 from 1 February 2026, which gives ceilings of RD$92,892 (4 minimum wages) for occupational risk, RD$232,230 (10) for health and RD$464,460 (20) for pensions. At the example salary, about RD$175,463 a month, only the occupational-risk ceiling binds.

assumptions.label: Christmas salary capped at five times the large-company minimum wage, RD$29,988 a month since 1 February 2026
assumptions.notes: Article 219 of the Codigo de Trabajo caps the salario de Navidad at 'cinco salarios minimos legalmente establecido'. For the private non-sectorised sector, Resolution CNS-01-2025 of the Comite Nacional de Salarios sets four minimum wages by company size; from 1 February 2026 the large-company one is RD$29,988.00 (151 workers or more, or gross sales above RD$202 million). This page takes the large-company minimum as the provider's; a provider classed as a medium company (RD$27,489.60) would pay a lower cap. The Code lets an employer pay more than the cap, and many pay a full month.

assumptions.label: Occupational-risk insurance taken at 1.1%: the fixed 1% plus the minimum variable share of 0.1%, so the total below is a floor
assumptions.notes: IDOPPRIL, the institute that runs the Seguro de Riesgos Laborales, states two components: 'una cuota basica fija del uno por ciento (1%)' and 'una cuota adicional variable desde cero punto uno (0.1%) hasta cero punto tres por ciento (0.3%), establecida en funcion de la rama de actividad y del riesgo de cada empresa'. Under an employer of record the insured employer is the provider, an office-based services business, and no public table gives each provider's variable share; the page carries the minimum, 0.1%, so the line can be up to 0.2 points of the capped base higher.

assumptions.label: Profit sharing (article 223) is carried at zero because it depends on the provider's profit, so the total below is a floor
assumptions.notes: Article 223 of the Codigo de Trabajo obliges every company to share 10% of its net annual profit among its indefinite-term workers, with a ceiling per worker of 45 days of ordinary salary under three years of service and 60 days from three years. What it costs depends on the provider's net profit, not on the employee's salary, so it cannot honestly be written as a percentage of one salary.

employer_contributions.name: Family health insurance (Seguro Familiar de Salud, SFS), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: On the cotizable salary up to 10 national minimum wages, RD$232,230 a month since 1 February 2026
employer_contributions.notes: The TSS answer to 'Cuales son los porcentajes de retencion y aporte de trabajador y empleadores?' gives the Seguro Familiar de Salud at 3.04% for the worker and 7.09% for the employer, and its ceilings table sets the SFS ceiling at 10 SMN, RD$232,230.00, effective 01/02/2026; the annual cap entered here is twelve times that. The TSS defines the cotizable salary as 'salario ordinario + comisiones + vacaciones por ley', so the Christmas salary is outside it. The ceiling sits about a third above the example salary and does not bind.

source.name: Tesoreria de la Seguridad Social - Preguntas frecuentes, questions 13 and 14 (percentages and ceilings effective 1 February 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Old-age, disability and survivors' pension (Seguro de Vejez, Discapacidad y Sobrevivencia), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: On the cotizable salary up to 20 national minimum wages, RD$464,460 a month since 1 February 2026
employer_contributions.notes: The TSS gives the Seguro de Vejez, Discapacidad y Sobrevivencia at 2.87% for the worker and 7.10% for the employer, with a ceiling of 20 SMN, RD$464,460.00, effective 01/02/2026. The 7.10% is the whole employer share: some payroll guides add a separate 0.4% for the Fondo de Solidaridad Social on top, which the TSS table does not. The ceiling is more than twice the example salary.

source.name: Tesoreria de la Seguridad Social - Preguntas frecuentes, questions 13 and 14 (percentages and ceilings effective 1 February 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Occupational risk insurance (Seguro de Riesgos Laborales, SRL)
employer_contributions.applies: On the cotizable salary up to 4 national minimum wages, RD$92,892 a month since 1 February 2026; fixed 1% plus the minimum variable share of 0.1%
employer_contributions.notes: The TSS table: the worker pays nothing ('Lo cubre el empleador 100%'), and the employer pays '1% cuota fija mas un porciento variante de 0.10-0.30 dependiendo el factor de riesgo de la empresa establecido por IDOPPRIL'; the IDOPPRIL FAQ states the same two components. The ceiling is 4 SMN, RD$92,892.00, effective 01/02/2026, which binds at the example salary: the line comes to about 0.58% of gross rather than 1.1%. The variable share is the provider's, since the provider is the insured employer; this page carries the minimum, 0.1%.

source.name: Tesoreria de la Seguridad Social - Preguntas frecuentes, questions 13 and 14, with IDOPPRIL - Preguntas frecuentes ('Cual es el porcentaje a cotizar?')

employer_contributions.name: Vocational training levy (INFOTEP, Ley 116-80)
employer_contributions.notes: Article 24 of Ley 116-80 finances the Instituto Nacional de Formacion Tecnico Profesional with 'el uno por ciento (1%) que sobre el monto total de las planillas de sueldos o salarios fijos que paguen mensualmente las empresas', and with a half per cent charged to the workers on their profit share and bonuses, withheld once a year. The TSS, which collects it, defines the INFOTEP salary as 'salario ordinario + comisiones', so there is no ceiling and the Christmas salary is outside the base.

source.name: Ley 116-80 que crea el INFOTEP, articulo 24 (text published by INFOTEP), with the TSS definition of the INFOTEP salary

employer_contributions.name: Christmas salary (salario de Navidad, article 219), capped at five minimum wages
employer_contributions.applies: One twelfth of the year's ordinary salary, never more than five minimum wages: RD$149,940 at the large-company minimum of RD$29,988
employer_contributions.notes: Article 219 of the Codigo de Trabajo: the employer pays in December 'la duodecima parte del salario ordinario devengado por el trabajador en el ano calendario', but 'en ningun caso el salario de Navidad sera mayor del monto de cinco salarios minimos legalmente establecido'. The cap is on the amount, so it is entered as a cap on the base of five minimum wages divided by one twelfth: 5 x RD$29,988 x 12 = RD$1,799,280 a year. At the example salary it binds, and the bonus comes to about 85% of one month's pay. It is due by 20 December (article 220), is free of income tax (article 222) and falls outside the TSS cotizable salary, so no contribution is charged on it.

source.name: Codigo de Trabajo (Ley 16-92) y normas complementarias, articulos 219-222 (Ministerio de Trabajo edition), with Resolucion CNS-01-2025, articulo tercero (large-company minimum from 1 February 2026)

statutory_extras.name: Profit sharing (participacion en los beneficios, article 223)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero and left out of the total because it cannot be read off a salary. Article 223 of the Codigo de Trabajo: every company shares 'el diez por ciento de las utilidades o beneficios netos anuales' among its indefinite-term workers, each worker's share capped at 45 days of ordinary salary under three years of service and 60 days from three years. It is paid 90 to 120 days after the financial year closes (article 224), and article 226 exempts free-zone companies and some agricultural and industrial ones. Under an employer of record the profit is the provider's; ask whether its fee already covers this line.

source.name: Codigo de Trabajo (Ley 16-92) y normas complementarias, articulos 223-226 (Ministerio de Trabajo edition)

countries.holidays_note: in 2026; 16 August falls on a Sunday
countries.probation_note: none by law; no notice due in first 3 months
countries.notice_typical: Articles 76 and 80 of the Codigo de Trabajo tie both notice and severance (auxilio de cesantia) to continuous service, and neither is owed in the first three months. Notice is at least 7 days after three to six months, 14 days after six months to a year and 28 days after a year. The cesantia an employer owes on ending an indefinite contract without cause is 6 days of ordinary salary after three to six months, 13 days after six months to a year, 21 days per year of service from one to five years and 23 days per year from five years.

payments.name: Salario de Navidad (Christmas salary)
payments.deadline: 20 December at the latest

payments.name: Participación en los beneficios (profit sharing, art. 223)
payments.deadline: between 90 and 120 days after the close of each financial year; the calendar month depends on the company's year-end

source.quote: consistente en la duodécima parte del salario ordinario devengado por el trabajador en el año calendario

countries.name: Ecuador

assumptions.label: Costs shown for the first year of service; the fondo de reserva adds 8.33% of pay from the thirteenth month
assumptions.notes: Article 196 of the Codigo del Trabajo gives every worker 'que preste servicios por mas de un ano' a sum equal to one month of pay 'por cada ano completo posterior al primero de sus servicios'. A new hire therefore costs nothing on this line for twelve months, then one twelfth of pay every month. The total on this page is the first-year figure, which keeps it a floor for every year of employment; the fondo de reserva is listed beside it at 8.33% so the second-year step is visible.

assumptions.label: The 15% workers' profit share is carried at zero, so the total below is a floor
assumptions.notes: Article 97 of the Codigo del Trabajo has the employer pay its workers 15% of its 'utilidades liquidas'. Under an employer of record the employer is the provider's Ecuadorian entity, so the amount depends on that entity's profit and headcount for the year, not on any one salary. It cannot honestly be written as a percentage of pay and sits outside the total.

employer_contributions.name: Employer social security contribution (aporte patronal, IESS)
employer_contributions.applies: Private-sector employees (sector privado bajo relacion de dependencia)
employer_contributions.notes: IESS Consejo Directivo resolution C.D. 515, annex 5, 'Ano 2021 en adelante', table for private-sector employees: 'Total Aportes' personal 9,45, patronal 11,15, total 20,60. The employer's 11.15% is split between pensions (3.82), health (5.16), work risks (0.38), unemployment (1.00), peasant social insurance (0.35) and administration (0.44); the Consejo Directivo has reallocated that split between branches several times (resolution C.D. 501 of 2016 used a different one) without changing the 11.15% the employer pays. The work-accident cover is inside this rate, so no separate activity-rated premium applies. Article 11 of the Ley de Seguridad Social sets the contribution base as all regular pay and puts a floor at the basic wage; that article sets no ceiling.

source.name: IESS - Resolucion No. C.D. 515, anexo 5 (ano 2021 en adelante), with Resolucion C.D. 501 (Registro Oficial 703, 2 March 2016)

employer_contributions.name: Payroll contribution formerly for IECE and SECAP (0.5% + 0.5%)
employer_contributions.notes: Codigo Organico Monetario y Financiero, eleventh general provision: 'La contribucion de 1% de las planillas de pago al Instituto Ecuatoriano de Seguridad Social, que se estan transfiriendo al Instituto Ecuatoriano de Credito Educativo y Becas, IECE (0,5%) y al Servicio Ecuatoriano de Capacitacion Profesional SECAP (0,5%) ... sera depositada en la Cuenta Unica del Tesoro Nacional ... a partir del 1 de enero de 2015.' The employer still pays it on the IESS payroll; only its destination changed. El Universo reported on 23 May 2026 that a bill to return the SECAP half to SECAP had not yet been examined by the Asamblea, so the charge stands as it is.

source.name: Codigo Organico Monetario y Financiero (Registro Oficial 332, 12 September 2014; consolidated to Registro Oficial 309, 21 August 2018), disposicion general decima primera

employer_contributions.name: Fourteenth salary (decimocuarta remuneracion), one basic wage a year
employer_contributions.notes: Article 113 of the Codigo del Trabajo: a monthly bonus 'equivalente a la doceava parte de la remuneracion basica minima unificada para los trabajadores en general', which the worker may ask to receive in one sum by 15 March (Costa and Galapagos) or 15 August (Sierra and Amazonia). Twelve twelfths make one basic wage a year, whatever the salary. The Ministerio del Trabajo announced on 15 December 2025 that the Salario Basico Unificado for 2026 is USD 482. Article 95 excludes this bonus from remuneration, so no contribution falls on it.

source.name: Ministerio del Trabajo - Salario Basico Unificado 2026 fixed at USD 482 (15 December 2025), with Codigo del Trabajo article 113

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth salary (decimotercera remuneracion)
statutory_extras.notes: Article 111 of the Codigo del Trabajo: employers pay 'mensualmente, la parte proporcional a la doceava parte de las remuneraciones que perciban durante el ano calendario', or in one sum by 24 December at the worker's written request, calculated under article 95. Article 95 in turn excludes 'la decimotercera y decimocuarta remuneraciones' and the fondo de reserva from remuneration, so for a fixed salary this is one month a year. It carries no IESS contribution: article 11 of the Ley de Seguridad Social does not list it among the parts of the contribution wage.

source.name: Codigo del Trabajo, articulos 95 y 111 (Codificacion 17, Registro Oficial Suplemento 167 of 16 December 2005, as last amended 22 June 2020)

statutory_extras.name: Reserve fund (fondo de reserva), from the thirteenth month of service
statutory_extras.notes: Article 196 of the Codigo del Trabajo: one month of pay 'por cada ano completo posterior al primero de sus servicios', paid to the IESS or to the worker each month. That is 8.33% of pay, due only once the employee has served more than a year. It is left out of the first-year total above; add it from the second year, when the statutory bill moves from about 21.8% to about 30.2% of gross at the example salary.

source.name: Codigo del Trabajo, articulo 196 (Codificacion 17, as last amended 22 June 2020)

statutory_extras.name: Workers' profit share (participacion en utilidades, 15%)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because article 97 of the Codigo del Trabajo sets it at 15% of the employer's net profit, 10% split equally among the workforce and 5% by family dependants. Under an employer of record that is the provider's entity, so it depends on the provider's profit and headcount rather than on this salary. Deel's Ecuador page lists it among the payroll costs; ask any provider how it is handled and billed.

source.name: Codigo del Trabajo, articulo 97 (Codificacion 17, as last amended 22 June 2020)

countries.holidays_note: midweek dates can move to Monday or Friday
countries.notice_typical: Article 184 of the Codigo del Trabajo gives the worker's resignation (desahucio) at least 15 days' written notice, which the employer may shorten. The employer has no notice route: a dismissal without legal cause is a despido intempestivo under article 188, owed three months of pay up to three years of service and one month per year beyond, capped at 25 months, with a part year counted as a full one. The 25% bonus of article 185, a quarter of the last monthly pay per year of service, is owed on top, and also when the contract ends by resignation or by agreement. Probation, up to 90 days on a first indefinite contract (article 15), can be ended freely by either side.

payments.name: Thirteenth salary (decimotercera remuneracion)
payments.deadline: 24 Dec (lump sum on the worker's written request)

payments.name: Fourteenth salary (decimocuarta remuneracion), one basic wage a year
payments.deadline: 15 Mar (Costa and Insular) / 15 Aug (Sierra and Amazonica), lump sum on request

source.quote: Los trabajadores tienen derecho a que sus empleadores les paguen mensualmente, la parte proporcional a la doceava parte de las remuneraciones que perciban durante el año calendario.

countries.name: Estonia

assumptions.label: The hire works full months on an open-ended contract
assumptions.notes: Estonia sets a minimum monthly base for social tax rather than a ceiling, so the charge can only ever be larger than the rate suggests, never smaller. In 2026 that base is EUR 886 a month, which is below the national minimum wage and far below an engineering salary, so it does not bind here. It does bind on part-months and on very low pay, where the employer still owes social tax on the full monthly rate.

employer_contributions.name: Social tax (sotsiaalmaks)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on the whole of gross pay with no ceiling, subject to a minimum monthly base
employer_contributions.notes: One tax, no ceiling, and that is what makes Estonia expensive on the employer side however simple it looks. The tax authority states the rate plainly: social tax is levied on income from employment in order to finance pension insurance and state health insurance, and the rate is 33% of the taxable amount, citing section 7 of the Social Tax Act. Nothing above a threshold escapes it, so the percentage an employer pays is the same at EUR 30,000 and at EUR 300,000. The floor carried here is the other half of the rule: the tax authority states that in 2026 the monthly rate on which the minimum social tax liability is based is EUR 886, giving a minimum liability of EUR 292.38 a month, which the employer owes even when the wage paid is lower. Modelled here as an annual floor of EUR 10,632 on the base.

source.name: Estonian Tax and Customs Board (EMTA) - Social tax, rate and minimum monthly base for 2026

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance premium (employer share)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, uncapped; the employer share continues even for an employee past pensionable age, when the employee's own 1.6% stops
employer_contributions.notes: The tax authority's rate page states that the unemployment insurance premium rates are 1.6% for the employee and 0.8% for the employer, unchanged from 2025. The asymmetry is worth knowing for an older hire: the obligation to withhold the employee's 1.6% ends on the last day of the month in which the employee reaches pensionable age or is granted an early or flexible old-age pension, while the employer keeps paying its 0.8%.

source.name: Estonian Tax and Customs Board (EMTA) - Tax rates applicable from 1 January 2026

statutory_extras.name: Occupational health check on hiring
statutory_extras.notes: A real cost of hiring in Estonia that is a fee per employee rather than a share of pay, so it is carried at zero and kept out of the total. Deel's Estonia page prices the medical check at EUR 160 on onboarding, repeated every three years. Deel also adds an administrative fee of 0.60% of salary, which is what separates its 34.40% estimate from the 33.8% of statutory charges in the ledger above: the gap is a provider fee, not a levy.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Estonia page

countries.notice_typical: 15 to 90 calendar days by length of service

countries.name: Egypt

employer_contributions.name: Old-age, disability and death insurance, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the contributory wage between the statutory floor and ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Article 19 of Social Insurance and Pensions Law 148 of 2019 sets the employer share at 12% of the monthly wages of the insured employees, against 9% for the employee. The same article carries the escalator: contribution rates rise by one percentage point every seven years from the date the law took effect, split equally between employer and employee, until total contributions reach 26%. The law came into force on 1 January 2020, so the first step falls due on 1 January 2027 and would take this line to 12.5%.

source.name: National Organization for Social Insurance (NOSI) - Social Insurance and Pensions Law 148 of 2019, article 19 (employer 12%, employee 9%; +1% every seven years, capped at 26% in total)

employer_contributions.name: Sickness insurance, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Private-sector employees, on the contributory wage between floor and ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Article 70 of Law 148 of 2019 splits the employer's sickness contribution by category of insured person: 3% for the categories listed at items 1 and 2 of the article 2 schedule, which are state administration and public-sector staff, and 3.25% for items 3, 4 and 5. Item 3 is 'private-sector employees subject to the Labour Law', so a private employer pays 3.25%, not 3%. The employee's own share is 1% of wages. Article 70 opens by preserving the Comprehensive Health Insurance Law 2 of 2018, which is being rolled out governorate by governorate and changes how health cover is financed where it has arrived.

source.name: National Organization for Social Insurance (NOSI) - Social Insurance and Pensions Law 148 of 2019, articles 2 and 70 (employer 3.25% for private-sector employees; employee 1%)

employer_contributions.name: Work-injury insurance, medical treatment share
employer_contributions.applies: Employees not yet covered by the Comprehensive Health Insurance system
employer_contributions.notes: Article 46(1) of Law 148 of 2019 requires a monthly employer contribution of 1% of the contributory wage, paid to the health insurance authority against treatment and medical care, and it is expressly written for employees not subject to the Comprehensive Health Insurance Law 2 of 2018. Egypt is phasing that system in by governorate, so in a governorate already switched over this 1% is superseded by the new scheme's financing rather than added to it. Ask a provider which regime covers the governorate your hire lives in.

source.name: National Organization for Social Insurance (NOSI) - Social Insurance and Pensions Law 148 of 2019, article 46(1)

employer_contributions.name: Work-injury insurance, cash benefits share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, at the base rate for a low-risk activity
employer_contributions.notes: Article 46(2) of Law 148 of 2019 sets a monthly employer contribution of 0.5% of the contributory wage against the cash rights the fund owes, and then adds that the rate 'is increased up to 1% according to the risks of the establishment's activity' as prescribed by the executive regulation. This ledger prices a software or office employer at the 0.5% base rate and says so rather than picking the middle of a band: a hazardous activity carries up to 1%, which would take the Egyptian employer total from 18.75% to 19.25%. The rate is a property of the establishment, not of the individual hire.

source.name: National Organization for Social Insurance (NOSI) - Social Insurance and Pensions Law 148 of 2019, article 46(2) (0.5%, rising to 1% with the activity's risk)

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Private and public-sector employees; employer pays the whole of it
employer_contributions.notes: Article 86 of Law 148 of 2019 finances unemployment insurance from 'the share borne by the employer at 1% of the wages of the insured persons employed by him, monthly'. There is no employee share of this branch. Article 85 applies the chapter to the categories at items 2 and 3 of the article 2 schedule, which includes private-sector employees under the Labour Law, while excluding casual, seasonal and contracting labour.

source.name: National Organization for Social Insurance (NOSI) - Social Insurance and Pensions Law 148 of 2019, articles 85 and 86

employer_contributions.name: Gratuity scheme, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Employees in the article 2 'employees of others' category
employer_contributions.notes: Article 36 of Law 148 of 2019 creates a gratuity scheme funded by two equal shares of 1% of the contributory wage, one from the employee and one from the employer. The money is held in a personal account in the employee's name and invested by the authority, and the balance is paid out when the insurance entitlement falls due. At 1% it is one of the smaller employer lines and the least familiar to anyone reading Egypt through an older payroll guide.

source.name: National Organization for Social Insurance (NOSI) - Social Insurance and Pensions Law 148 of 2019, article 36

statutory_extras.name: Contributory wage floor and ceiling for 2026: EGP 2,700 and EGP 16,700 a month
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is the band the rates apply to, not a charge of its own - but it is the number that decides the Egyptian employer cost. NOSI announced on 30 November 2025 that from 1 January 2026 the minimum contributory wage rises from EGP 2,300 to EGP 2,700 and the maximum from EGP 14,500 to EGP 16,700, under Law 148 of 2019 and its executive regulation. Because the ceiling is low against a software salary, the whole 18.75% applies to at most EGP 16,700 a month: the employer charge stops at EGP 3,131 a month no matter how high the salary goes. The band is revised each January, so a page quoting EGP 14,500 is a year out of date.

source.name: National Organization for Social Insurance - 'Raising the minimum and maximum contributory wage from 1 January 2026' (minimum EGP 2,300 to 2,700; maximum EGP 14,500 to 16,700), 30 November 2025

statutory_extras.name: Employee contribution of 11% - deducted from pay, not an employer charge
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it comes out of the employee's pay. Law 148 of 2019 puts 9% on the employee for old-age, disability and death (article 19), 1% for sickness (article 70) and 1% for the gratuity scheme (article 36), which is the 11% usually quoted next to the employer's 18.75%. Both are charged on the same capped contributory wage, so the two together stop at EGP 4,968 a month.

source.name: National Organization for Social Insurance (NOSI) - Social Insurance and Pensions Law 148 of 2019, articles 19, 36 and 70

statutory_extras.name: Per-head fixed fees a provider may add on top of the percentage
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because these are amounts in Egyptian pounds per employee per month rather than a share of salary, and because they are the provider's list rather than a single statutory schedule. Deel publishes four of them next to the 18.75%: a training and rehabilitation fund contribution of EGP 0.833, an emergency fund contribution of EGP 29.80, a social, health and cultural services fund contribution of EGP 1.33, and a disability workforce contribution of EGP 425 per employee per month. The last one dwarfs the others and relates to Egypt's disability employment quota, so it is worth asking any provider whether it is charging it and on what basis.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Egypt page

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month pay - not required by Egyptian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because Labour Law 14 of 2025 does not require a thirteenth month. What it does require is an annual periodic raise, and a three-month notice period on an open-ended contract that applies from the first day after probation rather than building up with seniority.

source.name: Ministry of Labour - Labour Law 14 of 2025, Official Gazette issue 18 (bis), 3 May 2025

countries.notice_typical: Three months on an open-ended contract, for either side, under article 156 of Labour Law 14 of 2025 - a flat period that does not step up with seniority. Article 161 forbids agreeing a shorter one or waiving it, though the parties may agree a longer one and the employer may release a resigning employee from serving it. The contract stays alive throughout the notice period under article 160.

source.name: Ministry of Labour - Labour Law 14 of 2025, Official Gazette issue 18 (bis), 3 May 2025

countries.name: Spain

employer_contributions.name: Common contingencies (contingencias comunes)
employer_contributions.notes: Employer share of the main Regimen General contribution; employee pays an additional 4.70% (28.30% combined). Applied to the monthly contribution base, capped at EUR 5,101.20/month (group 1 floor: EUR 1,989.30/month for titled engineers/graduates).

source.name: Seguridad Social — Tipos de Cotizacion Regimen General 2026 (Orden PJC/297/2026)

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (desempleo)
employer_contributions.applies: Rate for open-ended contracts (contrato indefinido), incl. part-time and fijo-discontinuo — employee pays 1.55% (7.05% combined). Fixed-term (temporal) contracts pay a higher 6.70% employer / 1.60% employee (8.30% combined).
employer_contributions.notes: Official table shows this rate under the indefinite-contract column of the 2026 unemployment section.

source.name: Seguridad Social — Tipos de Cotizacion Regimen General 2026 (Orden PJC/297/2026)

employer_contributions.name: Wage Guarantee Fund (FOGASA)
employer_contributions.notes: Employer-only contribution (0% employee share) funding wage/severance guarantees in case of employer insolvency.

source.name: Seguridad Social — Tipos de Cotizacion Regimen General 2026 (Orden PJC/297/2026)

employer_contributions.name: Vocational training (formacion profesional)
employer_contributions.notes: Employee pays an additional 0.10% (0.70% combined).

source.name: Seguridad Social — Tipos de Cotizacion Regimen General 2026 (Orden PJC/297/2026)

employer_contributions.name: Intergenerational Equity Mechanism (MEI)
employer_contributions.notes: Pension-sustainability levy on the common-contingencies base. Total MEI rate is 0.90% (employer 0.75% / employee 0.15%) in 2026, up from 0.80% (0.67%/0.13%) in 2025 — it rises 0.1 pt/year through 2029 per the 2021 pension reform.

source.name: Seguridad Social — Tipos de Cotizacion Regimen General 2026 (Orden PJC/297/2026)

employer_contributions.name: Occupational accidents and diseases (AT y EP)
employer_contributions.applies: Varies by CNAE economic activity (tarifa de primas, Real Decreto-ley 3/2026 amending LGSS disposicion adicional 61). The rate shown (1.50% = 0.80% IT + 0.70% IMS) applies to CNAE 62, 'Programacion, consultoria y otras actividades relacionadas con la informatica', one of the lowest-risk tiers and the classification used for the example software-engineer role.
employer_contributions.notes: The 1.50% figure is corroborated by three independent secondary sources: a legal-database mirror of the relevant LGSS provision, Deel's Spain payroll-cost page, and the mutua Fraternidad-Muprespa. The official Social Security tariff PDF and BOE table were not directly retrievable when checked, so this line is high-confidence but not primary-source verified.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Spain page

statutory_extras.name: Two extra payments (pagas extraordinarias)
statutory_extras.notes: Article 31 ET grants employees two extra payments a year (Christmas + one set by collective agreement), which can be prorated over 12 monthly payments by collective agreement. In practice Spanish salaries are quoted, and this engine's example_salary_usd is treated, as an ANNUAL GROSS that already includes these two extra payments — they are not added on top of the 12 monthly base salaries.

source.name: Estatuto de los Trabajadores, Real Decreto Legislativo 2/2015 — Articulo 31

statutory_extras.name: Severance pay — objective/economic dismissal (despido objetivo)
statutory_extras.notes: 20 days' salary per year of service, prorated by month for periods under a year, capped at 12 monthly payments. Statutory minimum for a lawful objective/economic dismissal only (Article 53.1.b ET); not an automatic annual accrual, so it is NOT added to the yearly employer-cost total by default — shown here as a contingent termination-cost reference only.

source.name: Estatuto de los Trabajadores, Real Decreto Legislativo 2/2015 — Articulo 53.1

countries.notice_typical: 15 calendar days for an objective/economic dismissal (despido objetivo, Art. 53.1.c ET); no statutory notice is required to resign or dismiss during the probation period, or for disciplinary dismissal.

source.quote: El trabajador tiene derecho a dos gratificaciones extraordinarias al año, una de ellas con ocasión de las fiestas de Navidad y la otra en el mes que se fije por convenio colectivo o por acuerdo entre el empresario y los representantes legales de los trabajadores.

countries.name: Finland

assumptions.label: Employee is 35 years old, so all three Finnish employer contributions apply in full
assumptions.notes: Age is a switch in Finland rather than a rate, and the three lines switch at different ages. Earnings-related pension (TyEL) must be insured from the calendar month after the employee turns 17, up to an upper age limit that depends on the year of birth. The unemployment insurance contribution is paid only for employees aged 18 to 64, so it falls away entirely at 65. The employer's health insurance contribution is paid for employees aged 16 to 67. At 35 all three are due, which is the ordinary case and the one priced here. Hiring a 66-year-old removes the unemployment line and about 0.31 points of the total. One thing age no longer changes in 2026: the employee's own TyEL share is a flat 7.30% at every age, where in 2025 it was 7.15% under 53 and 8.65% between 53 and 62 - and the employer's share, being the rest of the contribution, moved with it. Any page still quoting a 7.15/8.65 split is quoting 2025.

assumptions.label: TyEL priced at the published average employer rate for a contract employer, 17.10% of wages in 2026
assumptions.notes: Finland does not publish one TyEL employer rate, so a point is declared here rather than left as a band. The Finnish Centre for Pensions states that the basic contribution of an employer with an insurance contract is 24.85% of wages in 2026, that the worker's share of it is 7.30 percentage points, and that 'the average employer's share under the Employees Pensions Act is 17.10 per cent of wages in 2026'. The Tax Administration prints the same 17.10% as the average rate for an employer with an insurance contract. A particular employer's rate moves around that average in two ways: the pension company's own management cost is added, its client bonuses are deducted, and an employer whose payroll two years earlier exceeded EUR 2.4555 million also carries a disability component rated on the disability pensions granted to its own staff. An employer of record is normally in that larger bracket, so its disability component is experience-rated rather than flat - which can put its true TyEL cost either side of 17.10%. An employer that does not employ continuously and paid under EUR 10,272 of wages in six months is an occasional employer instead and pays a flat 25.85% with no client bonus.

assumptions.label: Unemployment insurance priced at the lower tier, 0.31%, on the assumption the legal employer's Finnish payroll stays under EUR 2,509,500 a year
assumptions.notes: The Finnish unemployment contribution has two tiers, and the threshold is on the employer's total annual payroll, not on your employee's salary. In 2026 the employer pays 0.31% up to EUR 2,509,500 of wages and 1.23% on the part above it. Under an employer of record the legal employer is the provider, so the tier is a fact about the provider's Finnish payroll that no provider page we read discloses. The lower tier is priced here because it is the rate every employer pays on the first EUR 2.5 million and because Deel's published Finland breakdown, read 20 September 2026, prices the lower tier too. If your provider is already above the limit, every euro of your hire's salary is charged at 1.23% instead: 0.92 points more, about US$600 a year on this page's example salary. That is a question worth putting in writing to a provider, and it is the same trap Belgium sets - a statutory line where hiring through a large provider costs more than hiring through a small entity of your own. Deel's own Finland page compounds the confusion by printing the threshold as 'up to an annual salary of EUR 2,337,000', which reads as an individual salary limit; no employee earns that, and the figure is in any case the 2024 limit.

employer_contributions.name: Earnings-related pension insurance (TyEL, employer share)
employer_contributions.applies: Employees from the month after their 17th birthday to the upper age limit set by year of birth, with no ceiling on the contribution base
employer_contributions.notes: Four fifths of the Finnish employer cost, and it is paid to a private pension company rather than to the state. The Finnish Centre for Pensions publishes the 2026 figures: the average total contribution under the Employees Pensions Act is 24.40% of wages, the basic contribution for an employer with an insurance contract is 24.85%, the worker's share is 7.30 percentage points, and the average employer's share is 17.10%. The Tax Administration's own table gives the same 17.10% as the average rate for a contract employer. The employer pays the whole contribution to the insurer and withholds the employee's 7.30% from the payslip, so the 17.10% modelled here is the employer's own cost. There is no ceiling: unlike Germany or Japan, the rate applies to the whole salary however high it goes. The rate fell from 17.38% in 2025. Two things move a real invoice off the average and neither is published per employer: the pension company's management cost, added, and its client bonuses, deducted. See the assumptions above for the size effect.

source.name: Finnish Centre for Pensions (ETK) - Private Sector ('The average employer's share under the Employees Pensions Act is 17.10 per cent of wages in 2026'; basic contribution 24.85%, worker's share 7.30 percentage points)

employer_contributions.name: Employer's health insurance contribution (sairausvakuutusmaksu)
employer_contributions.applies: Employees aged 16 to 67 covered by Finnish social insurance, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Paid to the Tax Administration rather than to an insurer, which makes it the one Finnish employer line with a single published national rate and no company-specific variation. The Tax Administration's rate table gives 1.91% for 2026, up from 1.87% in 2025. It is due for employees aged 16 to 67 and is payable even when no tax can be withheld, for instance where pay is given as a fringe benefit. Vendor pages are behind on this one: Deel's Finland page still lists a 'Social Security' line of 1.16%, the rate from two years ago.

source.name: Finnish Tax Administration - Social insurance contributions, rate tables for 2026 (employers' health insurance contribution 1.91%; pension average rate 17.10%; unemployment 0.31% / 1.23%), page updated 8 December 2025

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance contribution (tyottomyysvakuutusmaksu, employer share)
employer_contributions.applies: Employees aged 18 to 64, where the employer's total wages for the year exceed EUR 1,500
employer_contributions.notes: Paid to the Employment Fund, which publishes the rates itself: for 2026 the employer's contribution is 0.31% of wages up to a payroll limit of EUR 2,509,500 and 1.23% on the part above it, with the employee paying 0.89%. The Tax Administration prints the same pair. The limit is on the employer's total annual payroll rather than on the individual salary, which is why it is modelled as a declared assumption above rather than as a cap on this line. It rose sharply from 2025, when the employer paid 0.20% and 0.80%. It may fall again: on 27 August 2026 the Employment Fund's Supervisory Board approved a proposal to the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health to cut the aggregate contribution by 0.3 percentage points for 2027, which would put the employer's lower rate at 0.26% and the higher at 1.04%. That is a proposal, not law, so the engine keeps the 2026 rates until it is confirmed.

source.name: Employment Fund - Contribution percentages 2026 ('The employer's contribution percentage is 0,31%, or 1,23% for the part exceeding the payroll limit (EUR 2 509 500)')

statutory_extras.name: Workers' compensation insurance (tyotapaturmavakuutus)
statutory_extras.notes: Compulsory for every Finnish employer whose wages for the year exceed EUR 1,500, and effective from the day employment begins - but there is no rate to publish for one employer, so it is named here and left out of the total. The Tax Administration states that 'the accident insurance contribution varies by line of business and by company' and that the insurance company invoices it. The Workers' Compensation Center (TVK), which coordinates the scheme, says the premium is set by each insurer and varies between them, and publishes only an average across all employers: 0.48% of wages for 2026, a forecast last updated on 13 August 2026 (0.51% in 2024, 0.50% forecast for 2025). That average mixes every line of business, office work and construction alike, so it describes the market rather than your hire; at 0.48% the example hire would cost about US$310 a year. Deel's Finland page, read 20 September 2026, prices it at 0.324% of salary, below that average. Ask the provider for the rate its own policy carries.

source.name: Workers' Compensation Center (TVK), Tyotapaturmatieto - Average insurance premium: compulsory workers' compensation 0.48% of wages for 2026 (forecast updated 13 August 2026), premium set by each insurer

statutory_extras.name: Employees' group life insurance (ryhmahenkivakuutus)
statutory_extras.notes: Small, usually unavoidable and still not statutory in its own right. The Tax Administration's wording is precise: you may have to take out a group life policy 'if it is so agreed in the collective labour agreement that applies to you', and the insurer collects it together with the workers' compensation contribution. So it exists because of a collective agreement rather than because of a statute. The Workers' Compensation Center (TVK) publishes the average premium, weighted by the member insurers' market shares: 0.053% of wages for 2026 (a forecast added on 12 January 2026) and 0.054% for 2025, roughly US$34 a year on this page's example hire. Carried at zero because whether it is owed depends on the collective agreement the provider applies, and the average is not the rate any one policy carries.

source.name: Workers' Compensation Center (TVK), Tyotapaturmatieto - Average insurance premium: employees' group life 0.053% of wages for 2026 (forecast added 12 January 2026), 0.054% for 2025

statutory_extras.name: Holiday bonus (lomaraha)
statutory_extras.notes: A Finnish cost that often surprises a foreign buyer, and one this site genuinely cannot price. Finnish employees commonly receive a holiday bonus on top of holiday pay, but it does not come from the Annual Holidays Act. The occupational safety authority says so in terms: the holiday bonus 'ei perustu vuosilomalakiin', is not based on the Annual Holidays Act, and is an addition agreed in collective agreements, 50% of holiday pay being its example, usually paid with the summer holiday. Both whether a holiday bonus is owed and how big it is therefore come from the collective agreement that applies to the role, and which agreement applies to an employer-of-record hire is for the provider to state. It is carried at zero rather than estimated because guessing an agreement would be inventing the number. Put it in writing when you ask for a quote: which collective agreement the provider applies, and whether a holiday bonus sits inside the quoted employer cost or outside it.

source.name: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (tyosuojelu.fi) - Lomapalkka ja lomakorvaus: 'Lomaraha tai lomaltapaluuraha ei perustu vuosilomalakiin. Se on tyoehtosopimuksissa sovittu lisa (esim. 50 prosenttia lomapalkasta)' (page updated 15 October 2025)

statutory_extras.name: Occupational health care (tyoterveyshuolto)
statutory_extras.notes: secondary source: a per-head service fee rather than a payroll percentage, which is why it is carried at zero. Finnish employers arrange preventive occupational health care for their staff and are billed for it by the provider of that care; a share of the cost is reimbursed by the social insurance institution. Deel bills EUR 3.00 for it on its Finland page, about EUR 36 a year, and lists occupational health insurance among the benefits included for Finnish hires. It is small enough not to change a decision and large enough to belong on an invoice line rather than inside a blended percentage.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Finland page

countries.notice_typical: Set by the Employment Contracts Act unless the contract or the collective agreement says otherwise. The employer gives 14 days up to one year of service, one month from one to four years, two months from four to eight, four months from eight to twelve and six months beyond twelve. The employee gives 14 days up to five years of service and one month after that. An agreed notice period may never exceed six months, and the employee's may never be longer than the employer's.

countries.name: France

assumptions.label: Example salary is above 3 x SMIC (EUR 65,629 a year in 2026), so no general reduction of employer contributions applies
assumptions.notes: France replaced its old reduced rates with a single degressive relief on 1 January 2026, the reduction generale degressive unique (RGDU), which stops at a gross salary of 3 x SMIC. URSSAF computes the annual SMIC as hourly SMIC x 35 x 52, so 12.02 EUR x 1,820 = 21,876.40 EUR and the ceiling is 65,629 EUR (the June revaluation to 12.31 EUR is handled by a 2.9293 coefficient that lands on the same ceiling). The example is deliberately set above it, at 69,808 EUR, because the RGDU is a single coefficient applied to the whole employer block rather than a rate on any one line: the engine cannot subtract it, so every ledger below is exact only above the ceiling. Set a salary under 65,629 EUR in the calculator and the total is overstated by roughly 2 to 3 points of gross.

assumptions.label: Hire is a cadre (executive status), which adds the APEC levy and the 1.50% tranche 1 death-benefit contribution
assumptions.notes: Cadre status is the norm for an engineer hired through an EOR. It costs the employer two extra lines: the APEC levy (0.036% employer share) and the contribution of 1.50% of tranche 1 that the 1947 executives' agreement, restated by the national agreement of 17 November 2017, puts entirely on the employer. Both disappear for a non-cadre, which is worth about 1.1 points of gross at this salary.

assumptions.label: Legal employer has 50 or more employees, so Fnal is 0.50% of all pay and the training levy is 1%
assumptions.notes: Under an EOR the legal employer is the provider, and a provider's French employing entity is normally far past the French headcount thresholds - ask whether it is the provider's own entity or a partner's. Below 50 employees Fnal falls to 0.10% and is capped at the social security ceiling; below 11 employees the training levy falls to 0.55% and the versement mobilite is not due at all. Those three thresholds are the main reason a small French subsidiary of your own can be cheaper per head on statutory lines than an EOR.

assumptions.label: Employee works in Paris, so the versement mobilite is the Ile-de-France Mobilites inner-zone rate of 3.20%
assumptions.notes: The transport levy is set by the local transport authority and is the single most location-dependent line in France. URSSAF's own rate file gives 3.20% for the 143 communes of the Ile-de-France inner zone (Paris, Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis), which is the highest rate in the country; the outer Ile-de-France rings sit at 2.01% and 1.60%, Bordeaux, Nantes and Marseille at 2.00%, and many rural areas at nothing. Paris is modelled because that is where the providers' French entities and most EOR hires sit, not because it is representative of France; outside the inner zone, take 1.2 to 1.6 points off the total.

assumptions.label: Work-accident insurance at the 2026 national average net rate of 2.08%
assumptions.notes: France notifies an AT-MP rate per establishment, computed from the employer's own claims record and activity, and no provider page we read publishes the rate of its French entity. The only official figure that can be quoted is article 2 of the tarification order of 30 December 2025: the national average net rate is 2.08%. Office and software work sits below that average - Deel's own France page shows 0.75% for its entity - so this line is modelled at the average rather than at the bottom of the range, and a 0.75% rate would take about 1.3 points off the total.

employer_contributions.name: Health, maternity, invalidity and death insurance (assurance maladie), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All employees, on the whole salary, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: URSSAF states it plainly: "Dans la majorite des cas, le taux de la cotisation patronale maladie est fixe a 13 %." The 7% reduced rate that most provider guides still quote no longer exists for an ordinary private employer in 2026 - URSSAF now restricts it to employers holding a zoned or overseas exemption and to special-regime staff outside the general reduction. This single change is worth 6 points of gross against the figures published on most EOR country pages.

source.name: URSSAF - La cotisation maladie-maternite-invalidite-deces (13% standard rate; reduced rate restricted to zoned, Lodeom and special-regime employers), updated 17 June 2026

employer_contributions.name: Basic state pension, capped portion (assurance vieillesse plafonnee), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Charged on pay up to the 2026 social security ceiling of EUR 48,060 a year (EUR 4,005 a month)
employer_contributions.notes: The ceiling, the plafond annuel de la securite sociale, is the hinge of the whole French ledger: it fixes this line, the Agirc-Arrco tranches, the Fnal base for small employers and the executives' death-benefit contribution. It rose from EUR 47,100 to EUR 48,060 on 1 January 2026.

source.name: URSSAF - Taux de cotisations, secteur prive: assurance vieillesse 2.11% sur la totalite et 8.55% dans la limite du plafond (at 01/01/2026)

employer_contributions.name: Basic state pension, uncapped portion (assurance vieillesse deplafonnee), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All employees, on the whole salary, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Employer 2.11% on the whole salary on top of the capped 8.55%. URSSAF's own page on the general reduction adds the two together and calls the result 10.66%, which is the cross-check that both figures are read correctly.

source.name: URSSAF - Taux de cotisations, secteur prive: assurance vieillesse 2.11% sur la totalite et 8.55% dans la limite du plafond (at 01/01/2026)

employer_contributions.name: Family benefits contribution (allocations familiales)
employer_contributions.applies: Employer only, on the whole salary, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: "Le taux de la cotisation patronale d'allocations familiales est generalement fixe a 5,25 %." The 3.45% reduced rate below 3.5 SMIC that most provider pages still show was narrowed in 2026 to employers holding a zoned, overseas or home-help exemption, and to special-regime staff the general reduction does not reach. An ordinary EOR provider is none of those.

source.name: URSSAF - La cotisation d'allocations familiales (5.25% standard; 3.45% restricted to zoned, Lodeom, home-help and special-regime cases), updated 10 June 2026

employer_contributions.name: Mandatory occupational pension Agirc-Arrco, tranche 1, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Pay up to one social security ceiling, EUR 48,060 a year in 2026
employer_contributions.notes: The called rate on tranche 1 is 7.87% in 2026, split 60% employer and 40% employee by the scheme's own rule, so 4.72% for the employer. Agirc-Arrco is not optional and not a company benefit: it is the second statutory pension pillar and it is what makes France expensive relative to its neighbours.

source.name: Agirc-Arrco - Le calcul des cotisations de retraite complementaire: taux appeles 2026 T1 7.87%, T2 21.59%, employer 60% / employee 40%; tranche 1 up to EUR 48,060, tranche 2 EUR 48,060 to EUR 384,480

employer_contributions.name: Mandatory occupational pension Agirc-Arrco, tranche 2, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Only the slice of pay between one and eight social security ceilings, EUR 48,060 to EUR 384,480 a year
employer_contributions.notes: The called rate on tranche 2 is 21.59%, employer 60% of it, so 12.954%. This is why the French employer rate does not fall away above the ceiling the way the German or Dutch one does: the tranche 2 pension rate is larger than the capped basic pension line it replaces, so the marginal employer rate stays near 47% on every euro between EUR 48,060 and EUR 192,240.

source.name: Agirc-Arrco - Le calcul des cotisations de retraite complementaire: taux appeles 2026 T1 7.87%, T2 21.59%, employer 60% / employee 40%; tranche 1 up to EUR 48,060, tranche 2 EUR 48,060 to EUR 384,480

employer_contributions.name: Agirc-Arrco general balance contribution (CEG), tranche 1, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Pay up to one social security ceiling, EUR 48,060 a year
employer_contributions.notes: Funds retirement before 67. Total 2.15% on tranche 1, of which the employer pays 1.29% and the employee 0.86%. Adding it to the 4.72% pension line gives the 6.01% that URSSAF itself uses for Agirc-Arrco when it lists the contributions covered by the general reduction - a second independent check on both rates.

source.name: Agirc-Arrco - Le calcul des cotisations: CEG tranche 1 total 2.15% (employer 1.29%), tranche 2 total 2.70% (employer 1.62%)

employer_contributions.name: Agirc-Arrco general balance contribution (CEG), tranche 2, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Only the slice of pay between one and eight social security ceilings
employer_contributions.notes: Total 2.70% on tranche 2, employer 1.62% and employee 1.08%.

source.name: Agirc-Arrco - Le calcul des cotisations: CEG tranche 1 total 2.15% (employer 1.29%), tranche 2 total 2.70% (employer 1.62%)

employer_contributions.name: Agirc-Arrco technical balance contribution (CET), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Only for employees whose pay exceeds the social security ceiling, and then on the whole of tranches 1 and 2
employer_contributions.notes: A threshold line rather than a band line: it does not apply at all below EUR 48,060, and above it is charged on the whole salary up to eight ceilings. Total 0.35%, employer 0.21% and employee 0.14%. The engine switches it on at exactly EUR 48,060 where the scheme's wording is "superieur au plafond"; the difference is a rounding artefact worth a few cents on one payslip.

source.name: Agirc-Arrco - Le calcul des cotisations: CET 0.35% on tranches 1 and 2 for employees paid above the ceiling (employer 0.21%)

employer_contributions.name: APEC levy for executives (cadres)
employer_contributions.applies: Cadres only, on tranches 1 and 2 capped at four social security ceilings (EUR 192,240)
employer_contributions.notes: Funds the executives' employment agency. Total 0.06%, employer 0.036% and employee 0.024%. Tiny in money, but it is one of the two lines that make a cadre contract measurably more expensive than a non-cadre one.

source.name: Agirc-Arrco - Le calcul des cotisations: APEC 0.06% on tranches 1 and 2 limited to four ceilings (employer 0.036%)

employer_contributions.name: Executives' death-benefit contribution (prevoyance cadres, 1.50% of tranche 1)
employer_contributions.applies: Cadres only, on pay up to one social security ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: The national agreement of 17 November 2017 is explicit: "Les employeurs s'engagent a verser, pour tout beneficiaire vise a l'article 2 du present accord, une cotisation a leur charge exclusive, egale a 1,50 % de la tranche de remuneration inferieure au plafond fixe pour les cotisations de securite sociale", allocated first to death cover. An employer that cannot show it paid owes the survivors three times the annual ceiling. The 1.50% is a floor: Deel's France page prices its own scheme at 0.89% of tranche 1 plus 1.45% of the slice above, which is more, so treat this line as the minimum an EOR will bill.

source.name: Legifrance - Accord national interprofessionnel du 17 novembre 2017 relatif a la prevoyance des cadres, article 1er (en vigueur etendu)

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (assurance chomage), employer contribution
employer_contributions.applies: Pay up to four social security ceilings, EUR 192,240 a year in 2026
employer_contributions.notes: Employer-only in France; employees pay nothing towards unemployment. The rate is 4.00% in 2026, down from the 4.05% that provider pages still print.

source.name: URSSAF - Taux de cotisations, secteur prive: contribution assurance chomage 4.00% dans la limite de 192 240 EUR en 2026

employer_contributions.name: Wage guarantee scheme (AGS)
employer_contributions.applies: Pay up to four social security ceilings; 0.03% instead for temporary-work agencies
employer_contributions.notes: Pays your employee's wages if the legal employer - which under an EOR is the provider, not you - goes into administration or liquidation. Employer-only, 0.25% in 2026.

source.name: URSSAF - Taux de cotisations, secteur prive: cotisation AGS 0.25% dans la limite de 192 240 EUR en 2026

employer_contributions.name: Work accidents and occupational illness (AT-MP), national average net rate
employer_contributions.applies: Employer only, on the whole salary; the real rate is notified to each establishment by its Carsat
employer_contributions.notes: URSSAF publishes no rate here, only "taux notifie par la Carsat": the rate depends on the establishment's activity and size and, above 150 employees, on its own claims record. The one official figure is article 2 of the tarification order of 30 December 2025, "Le taux net moyen national de cotisation est de 2,08 %", and that is what is modelled. Office work sits below it; Deel publishes 0.75% for its French entity, which would take about 1.3 points off this page's total. Ask your provider for its notified rate in writing - it is the one statutory line an EOR can legitimately differ on.
