source.name: Legifrance - Arrete du 30 decembre 2025 relatif a la tarification des risques d'accidents du travail et de maladies professionnelles pour l'annee 2026, article 2 (JORF n°0306 du 31 decembre 2025, NOR SFHS2536273A)

employer_contributions.name: Autonomy solidarity contribution (CSA)
employer_contributions.applies: Employer only, on the whole salary, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Funds care for elderly and disabled people; the counterpart of the unpaid solidarity day. Flat 0.30%.

source.name: URSSAF - Taux de cotisations, secteur prive: contribution solidarite autonomie (CSA) 0.30% (at 01/01/2026)

employer_contributions.name: Housing fund contribution (Fnal), employers with 50 or more staff
employer_contributions.applies: Employers of 50 or more: 0.50% of the whole salary. Below 50 it is 0.10% capped at the social security ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: URSSAF gives the two formulas verbatim: "totalite de la remuneration x taux de 0,50 %" at 50 employees and over, "remuneration limitee au plafond de la Securite sociale x taux de 0,10 %" below. At this salary the difference between the two regimes is about 0.43 points of gross - a rare case where the provider's size makes your hire dearer.

source.name: URSSAF - La contribution au Fonds national d'aide au logement (Fnal): 0.50% of total pay at 50 employees and over

employer_contributions.name: Transport levy (versement mobilite), Ile-de-France Mobilites inner zone
employer_contributions.applies: Employers of 11 or more staff in a zone that has instituted the levy; charged on all pay subject to social security contributions
employer_contributions.notes: URSSAF's official rate file for payroll software lists ILE-DE-FRANCE MOBILITES at 3.2%, in force since 1 February 2024, for the 143 communes of Paris, Hauts-de-Seine and Seine-Saint-Denis. That is the highest rate in France: the outer Ile-de-France rings are 2.01% and 1.60%, Bordeaux, Nantes and Marseille 2.00%, Lyon's urban core 2.00%, and a great many areas charge nothing. Modelled at Paris because that is where the providers' French entities sit, not because it is a French average.

source.name: URSSAF - official versement mobilite rate file used by payroll software, tauxTransport.20260710.csv: ILE-DE-FRANCE MOBILITES 3.2, date d'effet 20240201 (file last modified 20 September 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Vocational training levy (contribution a la formation professionnelle)
employer_contributions.applies: Employers of 11 or more: 1% of pay. Below 11 employees it is 0.55%
employer_contributions.notes: "Il est de 0,55 % si vous employez moins de 11 salaries et de 1 % si vous employez 11 salaries et plus." Charged on the same base as social security contributions. A further 1% CPF-CDD levy applies to fixed-term contracts only, which an EOR hire on a CDI does not pay.

source.name: URSSAF - Les contributions a la formation professionnelle (CFP et CPF-CDD): 1% at 11 employees and over

employer_contributions.name: Apprenticeship tax (taxe d'apprentissage, main part plus balance)
employer_contributions.applies: Main part 0.59% plus balance 0.09% for establishments in mainland France outside Alsace-Moselle
employer_contributions.notes: URSSAF sets the main part at 0.59% and the balance at 0.09% on the same base as the contributions, so 0.68% in total. Establishments in Bas-Rhin, Haut-Rhin and Moselle pay 0.44% and owe no balance.

source.name: URSSAF - La taxe d'apprentissage et la contribution supplementaire a l'apprentissage: part principale 0.59%, solde 0.09% (mainland, outside Alsace-Moselle), updated 4 June 2026

employer_contributions.name: Social dialogue contribution (contribution au dialogue social)
employer_contributions.applies: All private employers, on the whole salary
employer_contributions.notes: Funds unions and employers' federations. 0.016% - about EUR 11 a year on this salary, included because a French payslip shows it and an honest ledger should not quietly round it away.

source.name: URSSAF - Taux de cotisations, secteur prive: contribution au dialogue social 0.016% (at 01/01/2026)

statutory_extras.name: General degressive reduction (RGDU) - nil at this salary
statutory_extras.notes: From 1 January 2026 France merged its reduced health and family rates and its old general relief into one degressive reduction that stops at 3 x SMIC, EUR 65,629 of annual gross. This page's example is above that ceiling, so the reduction is nil and every line above is charged in full. Below the ceiling it is real money: the coefficient is 0.0200 + 0.3821 x [0.5 x (3 x annual SMIC / gross - 1)] to the power 1.75 for an employer of 50 or more, which is worth about 2.4 points of gross at EUR 56,700 and about 3.0 points at EUR 52,400. The engine cannot net it off, because it is one coefficient applied to the whole employer block rather than a rate on any single line, so treat any result below EUR 65,629 as an upper bound and ask your provider whether it passes the relief through.

source.name: URSSAF - La reduction generale degressive unique (RGDU): ceiling of 3 SMIC, covered contributions, coefficient formula, updated 13 July 2026

statutory_extras.name: Compulsory group health cover, employer share - real cost, not a percentage of pay
statutory_extras.notes: Every French employer must offer a collective health plan and, in the words of the law that created article L. 911-7 of the social security code, "L'employeur assure au minimum la moitie du financement de cette couverture". The cost is a premium per head, not a share of salary, so it is carried at zero here rather than guessed as a rate. For scale, Deel's France page (read 20 September 2026) prices its employer share at EUR 74.26 per employee per month, described as an estimate to be adjusted at onboarding - about EUR 891 a year, or 1.3 points of gross at this salary. It is usually inside the EOR quote; get it in writing.

source.name: Legifrance - LOI n° 2013-504 du 14 juin 2013 relative a la securisation de l'emploi, article 1 creating article L. 911-7 of the code de la securite sociale (employer funds at least half)

statutory_extras.name: Occupational health service and payroll admin fees - per head, not a percentage of pay
statutory_extras.notes: A French employer must join an occupational health service (SPST) and pay a per-employee subscription, and it must issue and archive payslips electronically. None of this is a percentage of salary, so it sits at zero in the ledger. Deel's France page lists them as separate employer costs: occupational medicine at 0.41% capped at the monthly ceiling plus a EUR 9.53 fixed fee, an annual medical fee of EUR 50, a mandatory electronic safe fee of EUR 3.46, time-tracking software at EUR 3.00 and an employer liability administration fee of 0.60%. Together these are worth roughly one point of gross and they are the part of a French quote that varies most between providers.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the France page

statutory_extras.name: Portage business allowance of 5% - provider-specific, excluded from the total
statutory_extras.notes: The largest number missing from this ledger, and it is not statutory. Deel states that its French collective agreement is portage salarial, that "there is a mandatory business allowance cost as per collective bargaining agreement of 5% of the employee's salary", and that its employer costs are computed on gross salary plus that 5%. On this example that is about EUR 3,490 of extra pay plus roughly EUR 1,650 of charges on it, at the 47.2% marginal rate that applies above the ceiling - near 7.4 points of gross. It is carried at zero because it follows the provider's chosen collective agreement, not French law, and no other provider page we read says which agreement it uses. Ask every French quote two questions: which convention collective, and is a business allowance added on top of the salary you quoted.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the France page

countries.notice_typical: Article L1234-1 of the code du travail sets the employer's notice on dismissal other than for gross misconduct: for less than six months of service, whatever the law, the collective agreement or local practice provides; one month between six months and two years; two months from two years. Those are floors - a branch agreement, the contract or established practice may give more, and for a cadre the applicable agreement commonly gives three months from the start. Statutory probation for a cadre is four months (article L1221-19), and the code allows one renewal where a branch agreement provides for it.

source.quote: Leur versement est obligatoire s'il est prévu par l'un des dispositifs suivants

countries.name: United Kingdom

assumptions.label: Employing entity belongs to a group with a UK pay bill above GBP 3 million (Apprenticeship Levy 0.5% applies)
assumptions.notes: Every large EOR provider is above the threshold, so the levy is passed through. A small company employing directly, with a pay bill under GBP 3 million, does not pay it.

employer_contributions.name: Employer Class 1 National Insurance (secondary contributions)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees aged 21 and over; charged on earnings above the secondary threshold of GBP 5,000 a year (GBP 417 a month), with no upper limit
employer_contributions.notes: Rate 15% for the 2026 to 2027 tax year (6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027). The GBP 10,500 Employment Allowance is shared across connected companies and is negligible per employee for a large provider. Under-21s and apprentices under 25 attract 0% up to GBP 50,270.

source.name: GOV.UK — Rates and thresholds for employers 2026 to 2027 (secondary threshold GBP 5,000 a year; employer rate 15%)

employer_contributions.name: Workplace pension, employer minimum (automatic enrolment)
employer_contributions.applies: Eligible jobholders aged 22 to State Pension age earning over GBP 10,000 a year; contributions on qualifying earnings between GBP 6,240 and GBP 50,270 (2026 to 2027 band)
employer_contributions.notes: Statutory minimum 3% employer, 5% employee (8% total) on the qualifying earnings band. Employees can opt out, and many providers offer schemes above the minimum on request.

source.name: GOV.UK — Workplace pensions: what you, your employer and the government pay (employer minimum 3%; earnings between GBP 6,240 and GBP 50,270)

employer_contributions.name: Apprenticeship Levy
employer_contributions.applies: Employers and connected companies with an annual pay bill above GBP 3 million; the GBP 15,000 allowance is shared across the group
employer_contributions.notes: 0.5% of the pay bill that is subject to employer National Insurance. Providers pass it through because their UK pay bill is far above the threshold.

source.name: GOV.UK — Pay Apprenticeship Levy (0.5% of annual pay bill above GBP 3 million; GBP 15,000 allowance)

statutory_extras.name: Unfair-dismissal protection after 6 months (from 1 January 2027)
statutory_extras.notes: Not a payroll line but a termination-cost driver. The Employment Rights Act 2025 cuts the qualifying period for ordinary unfair dismissal from two years to six months for dismissals from 1 January 2027 and removes the cap on compensatory awards. Paternity and unpaid parental leave are day-one rights since 6 April 2026, and statutory sick pay is paid from the first day of illness with no lower earnings limit.

source.name: GOV.UK — Plan to Make Work Pay and Employment Rights Act: timeline update (unfair dismissal qualifying period 6 months from 1 January 2027; SSP and day-one leave changes from 6 April 2026)

countries.notice_typical: Statutory minimum notice from the employer is one week after one month's service, then one week per full year of service from two years, up to 12 weeks; contracts usually set one to three months. Unfair-dismissal protection starts after two years of service until 31 December 2026 and after six months for dismissals from 1 January 2027.

countries.name: Georgia

assumptions.label: The hire is enrolled in the funded pension scheme
assumptions.notes: This is the assumption that decides whether the Georgian employer pays anything at all. Article 3(2) of the Law on Funded Pension makes enrolment and contributions mandatory for every employee on salary income, excluding only those who had already turned 60 (men) or 55 (women) before the law took effect. Article 3(5) then lets an employee who had turned 40 before the law took effect leave the scheme. For someone who left, the employer's 2% stops with them: there is no other statutory employer charge to fall back on, so that hire costs the employer exactly the gross salary. A software engineer hired today is almost always inside the scheme, which is what this page prices, but the question is worth asking a provider for an older hire, because it is the difference between 2% and nothing.

employer_contributions.name: Funded pension contribution (employer share)
employer_contributions.applies: Every enrolled employee, on the whole of taxable salary, with no ceiling on the employer's share
employer_contributions.notes: The whole of the Georgian employer ledger is this one line. Article 3(6)(a) of the Law on Funded Pension requires the employer, at its own expense and in favour of the employee, to transfer a pension contribution 'in the amount of 2% of the taxable salary paid to the employee within the accounting period'. A separate 2% is withheld from the employee under subparagraph (b), and the state adds its own share under subparagraph (e), which is where most published summaries of Georgia go wrong. The state's share is the part that is capped: 2% within the first GEL 24,000 of annual salary, 1% on the slice from GEL 24,000 to GEL 60,000, and under paragraph (f) nothing at all above GEL 60,000 a year. Those thresholds are frequently repeated as if they capped the employer too. They do not. The employer's 2% is written without a ceiling and is owed on the same percentage at any salary, which is why this line carries no cap. Rate read on the consolidated Georgian text in force; the English translation published alongside it is still the 27 June 2024 edition and carries a banner saying so.

source.name: Law of Georgia on Funded Pension, article 3(6), consolidated version in force (Legislative Herald of Georgia, matsne.gov.ge, publication of 16 September 2026, marked 'final')

statutory_extras.name: State co-contribution - paid by the budget, not by you
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a payment by the Georgian state into the employee's pension account, not a cost to the employer, and named because it is the line that makes Georgian payroll look like a 6% scheme when the employer side is 2%. Article 3(6)(e) sets the state's share at 2% of taxable salary within the first GEL 24,000 of annual income and 1% on the slice up to GEL 60,000; article 3(6)(f) stops it above GEL 60,000. At the US$28,000 example, roughly GEL 73,200 a year, the state has already stopped paying. Nothing about that changes the employer's bill, but it changes what the employee receives, and it is worth knowing before you repeat a '2+2+2' summary to a candidate.

source.name: Law of Georgia on Funded Pension, article 3(6)(e) and 3(6)(f), consolidated version in force

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Georgian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code of Georgia creates no thirteenth-month salary, no holiday bonus and no severance fund. Annual leave is paid leave under article 31, and the only money the Code adds on top of ordinary pay is the dismissal compensation in article 48, which is a termination cost rather than a recurring one. Bonuses and private health cover are contractual in the Tbilisi technology market; price them as market cost in a competitive offer, not as a legal charge.

source.name: Organic Law of Georgia - Labour Code of Georgia, consolidated version in force (matsne.gov.ge, marked 'final')

countries.notice_typical: 30 calendar days with compensation of at least one month's pay, or 3 calendar days with compensation of at least two months' pay, at the employer's choice under article 48(1) and 48(2) of the Labour Code. An employee resigning gives 30 calendar days.

source.name: Organic Law of Georgia - Labour Code of Georgia, consolidated version in force (matsne.gov.ge, marked 'final')

countries.name: Ghana

assumptions.label: Basic salary as a share of gross
assumptions.notes: SSNIT charges the employer on the worker's basic salary: 'Deduct 5.5% from the worker's monthly salary and add 13% of their basic salary to total an 18.5% contribution.' Ghanaian packages are often paid as one basic figure, which is what this ledger models at 100%, and that is also the most the contribution can cost. Where a package is split into basic plus allowances, only the basic part carries the 13% and the line falls in proportion. Move the selector to price a split package.

employer_contributions.name: SSNIT first-tier pension, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer of one or more workers, on basic salary between the minimum and maximum insurable earnings
employer_contributions.notes: SSNIT states the split plainly for employers: 'Worker - 5.5% of workers' basic salary. Employer - 13% workers' basic salary. Total - 18.5% of workers' basic salary.' The employer's own charge is therefore 13%, and the 13.5% that often appears in provider price lists is something else: it is the slice of the combined 18.5% that is remitted to SSNIT for the first tier, with the remaining 5% going to a licensed second-tier scheme. Half a point of that 13.5% comes out of the worker's 5.5%, not out of the employer. Both tiers are funded inside the same 18.5%, so an employer that pays 13% has paid for both.

source.name: SSNIT - Become an employer, and Frequently asked questions ('Worker - 5.5% of workers' basic salary; Employer - 13% workers' basic salary; Total - 18.5%'; 13.5% remitted to SSNIT, 5% to Tier 2)

statutory_extras.name: Maximum and minimum insurable earnings for 2026: GHS 69,000 and GHS 587.80 a month
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is the band the 13% applies to, not a charge of its own. SSNIT's public notice of 13 January 2026 raised the maximum insurable earning for 2026 from GHS 61,000 to GHS 69,000 under section 63(3) of the National Pensions Act 2008 (Act 766), and the minimum from GHS 539.19 to GHS 587.80 following the rise in the national daily minimum wage: 'from 1 January 2026, the maximum and minimum contributions payable to SSNIT will be GHS 9,315.00 and GHS 79.40 respectively.' The ceiling is high enough that a software salary sits well under it, so the 13% behaves as a flat rate here - but SSNIT's own FAQ page still says the maximum contribution is on a salary of GHS 25,000, a figure the notice supersedes. Read the notice, not the FAQ.

source.name: SSNIT - Public notice, Maximum and Minimum Insurable Earnings for 2026, 13 January 2026 (maximum GHS 69,000 from GHS 61,000; minimum GHS 587.80 from GHS 539.19)

statutory_extras.name: Worker contribution of 5.5% - deducted from pay, not an employer charge
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it comes out of the worker's salary. It matters here more than in most countries because of how Ghanaian contributions are described: the familiar 18.5% is the combined figure, and it is routinely quoted where an employer cost is meant. Of that 18.5%, the employer bears 13 points and the worker 5.5. Anyone comparing Ghana against another country on an 18.5% basis is comparing an employer charge with a total.

source.name: SSNIT - Frequently asked questions ('Deduct 5.5% of the workers salary every month and add 13% of worker's basic salary to make 18.5%')

statutory_extras.name: Second-tier occupational scheme - funded inside the 18.5%, not added to it
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is not an extra employer charge. SSNIT instructs employers to 'Remit 13.5% of the total contribution to SSNIT within 14 days of the following month. 5% to Tier 2.' The 5% is carved out of the same 18.5% and paid to a licensed corporate trustee rather than to SSNIT, so an employer that has paid 13% has funded its share of both tiers. A third tier exists and is voluntary. This is the most common way Ghana gets over-priced: 13% and 5% are added together to produce an 18% employer cost that does not exist.

source.name: SSNIT - Become an employer ('Remit 13.5% of the total contribution to SSNIT within 14 days of the following month. 5% to Tier 2.')

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month pay - not required by Ghanaian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651) contains no thirteenth month or annual bonus obligation. What it does fix is fifteen working days of paid annual leave per calendar year of continuous service under section 20, and a notice ladder under section 17 that tops out at one month.

source.name: Ghana Investment Promotion Centre - Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651), sections 17 and 20

countries.notice_typical: By contract length, under section 17(1) of the Labour Act, 2003: one month's notice or one month's pay in lieu for a contract of three years or more, two weeks for a contract of less than three years, and seven days for a week-to-week engagement. Notice must be in writing, and the day it is given counts towards the period. The Act recognises a probationary period 'of reasonable duration determined in advance' without fixing a maximum, so the length is a matter for the contract.

source.name: Ghana Investment Promotion Centre - Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651), sections 17 and 20

countries.name: Greece

assumptions.label: The annual salary is the Greek fourteen-payment total, not twelve monthly payments
assumptions.notes: Greece pays a Christmas bonus of one month, an Easter bonus of half a month and a holiday allowance of half a month on top of the twelve monthly salaries, so a full year is fourteen payments. As on the Spanish and Italian pages of this site, the example annual figure already contains them: US$40,000, about EUR 34,904, is fourteen payments of about EUR 2,493, not twelve of EUR 2,909. This is the single most common mistake in a Greek budget. If a recruiter quotes you a monthly salary, multiply by fourteen before using this page, or the total here will be a sixth too low.

assumptions.label: Ordinary business, coverage package KPK 101 (employer 21.79%, employee 13.37%)
assumptions.notes: e-EFKA groups every contribution into a coverage package. KPK 101, mikta IKA-TEAM, is the full-insurance package for an ordinary private employee and is what an office or software hire falls under. Businesses listed in the 1961 occupational-hazard decree pay one point more (KPK 102, 22.79%), and the heavy-and-unhealthy schedule adds 0.75 points on top of that; neither reaches a desk job. If a Greek quote shows 22.79% or more, ask which package the provider has registered your employee under.

employer_contributions.name: Main state pension (kyria syntaxi), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All private-sector employees, on every payment, up to the insurable earnings ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: The Ministry of Labour states it directly: the main pension contribution for private-sector employees insured with e-EFKA is 20% in total, of which the employee bears 6.67% and the employer 13.33%. It is by far the largest of the five Greek employer lines - more than half the package on its own.

source.name: Ypourgeio Ergasias kai Koinonikis Asfalisis - Asfalistikes Eisfores: main pension 20%, employee 6.67%, employer 13.33%; ceiling EUR 7,761.94 a month from 1-1-2026

employer_contributions.name: Health care in kind (asthenia se eidos), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All private-sector employees; 4.75% instead for construction work
employer_contributions.notes: Cut on 1 January 2025 by article 12 of law 5162/2024. e-EFKA's circular gives the new split for ordinary businesses: 1.65% employee and 3.80% employer, 5.45% together. Construction sites pay 4.75% on the employer side, which is why builders' quotes look different.

source.name: e-EFKA circular 38/2024 (ADA 971Y46MAPS-348), health branch table for koines epicheiriseis from 01.01.2025: asthenia se eidos employee 1.65% / employer 3.80% / total 5.45%

employer_contributions.name: Sickness cash benefit (asthenia se chrima), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All private-sector employees, on every payment, up to the ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: The smaller half of the health branch and the one line in Greece where the employee pays more than the employer: 0.40% against 0.25%, 0.65% together. Funds the cash paid during sick leave rather than the treatment itself.

source.name: e-EFKA circular 38/2024 (ADA 971Y46MAPS-348), health branch table for koines epicheiriseis from 01.01.2025: asthenia se chrima employee 0.40% / employer 0.25% / total 0.65%

employer_contributions.name: Auxiliary pension (epikouriki asfalisi, TEKA), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All private-sector employees, on the same earnings as the main pension, up to the ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Greece's second pension pillar is compulsory, not a benefit: 6% in total since 1 June 2022, split equally between employer and employee. Anyone first insured from 1 January 2022 is enrolled in TEKA, the funded auxiliary scheme, rather than the old pay-as-you-go one; the rate is the same either way.

source.name: Ypourgeio Ergasias kai Koinonikis Asfalisis - Asfalistikes Eisfores: auxiliary pension contributions total 6% since 01/06/2022, split equally (3+3%), article 97 of law 4387/2016

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment and other DYPA funds, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All private-sector employees, on every payment, up to the ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: The balance of the official package, and the one line here that is a subtraction rather than a quotation. e-EFKA publishes the KPK 101 employer total, 21.79%, but not a public breakdown of this last item; 21.79 minus pension 13.33, health 3.80 + 0.25 and auxiliary 3.00 leaves 1.41%, which funds unemployment benefit and the smaller DYPA schemes. Deel's own Greece page lists exactly 1.41% for unemployment, so the subtraction lands where a provider's payroll lands.

source.name: e-EFKA circular 38/2024 (ADA 971Y46MAPS-348), Pinakas 1 of active coverage packages from 01.01.2025: KPK 101 MIKTA, IKA-TEAM - employee 13.37%, employer 21.79%, total 35.16%

statutory_extras.name: Christmas and Easter bonuses and the holiday allowance - inside the annual salary, not on top
statutory_extras.notes: Greece pays fourteen times a year. The Ministry of Labour, applying the 1981 joint ministerial decision, gives a Christmas bonus "equal to one monthly salary" and an Easter bonus "equal to half a monthly salary"; the holiday allowance rests on paragraph 16 of article 3 of law 4504/1966 and adds the other half. The Ministry's own severance page puts the arithmetic beyond doubt: the monthly proportion of the bonuses and the holiday allowance increases regular pay by one sixth, which is exactly two extra months. They are carried at zero here because the example annual salary already contains them, the same convention this site uses for Spain and Italy - and they do carry the full 21.79% of employer contributions, which the ledger above already charges.

source.name: Ypourgeio Ergasias kai Koinonikis Asfalisis - Epidomata Eorton (KYA 19040/1981, FEK B 742): Christmas bonus one monthly salary, Easter bonus half a monthly salary

statutory_extras.name: Teleworking allowance - a monthly amount, not a share of pay
statutory_extras.notes: Article 67 of law 4808/2021 makes the employer carry the cost teleworking imposes on the employee - equipment, telecommunications, maintenance and repairs - and states that these sums are not pay, are exempt from tax and carry no social contributions for either side. Because it is a fixed monthly amount rather than a percentage, it is carried at zero here. Deel prices it at EUR 28 per employee per month on its Greece page, about EUR 336 a year. Almost every EOR hire in Greece is a home worker, so expect this line in the quote.

source.name: Law 4808/2021 (FEK A 101/19.06.2021), article 67 paragraph 4: the employer bears the cost of equipment, telecommunications, maintenance and repairs; the sums are not pay and carry no employer or employee contributions

statutory_extras.name: Severance on dismissal - contingent, not a running cost
statutory_extras.notes: Not a monthly charge, but the Greek number most often missed at budget time. The Ministry's table gives, for dismissal without notice, two months' pay after one completed year, three after four years, four after six, six after ten, and twelve from sixteen years. Give notice instead - one month between one and two years of service, two months to five, three months to ten, four months beyond - and the payment halves. Because the severance base includes the monthly proportion of the bonuses and the holiday allowance, it is a sixth larger than a month's salary looks.

source.name: Ypourgeio Ergasias kai Koinonikis Asfalisis - Lysi Symvasis Ergasias, PINAKAS APOZIMIOSEOS YPALLILON (laws 2112/1920, 3198/1955, 4093/2012, 4808/2021)

statutory_extras.name: Occupational hazard contribution of 1% - not owed for office work
statutory_extras.notes: An employer-only contribution of 1% paid by businesses listed in the 1961 royal decree, where the work itself endangers life or health. Software and office work is not among them, so it is carried at zero - but it is the difference between coverage package 101 at 21.79% and package 102 at 22.79%, and it is worth checking which one a provider has used, because a point of gross is a point of gross.

source.name: Ypourgeio Ergasias kai Koinonikis Asfalisis - Asfalistikes Eisfores: occupational risk contribution of 1%, employer only, for businesses covered by paragraph 1 of article 1 of royal decree 473/1961

countries.notice_typical: Greece abolished the distinction between salaried staff and manual workers for notice and termination on 1 January 2022, so one scale applies to everyone. The Ministry's table sets the employer's notice at one month once a year of service is complete, two months from two years, three months from five and four months from ten; giving notice halves the severance otherwise due. Below one completed year there is no statutory notice and no severance. Probation is capped at six months on an open-ended contract: article 4 of law 5053/2023 inserted article 1A into the Individual Labour Law Code, allowing the parties to agree a trial period 'of up to six (6) months', after which a successful hire's service counts from the original start date and an unsuccessful one ends automatically with the time served counting for accrued rights and on what legal basis.

payments.name: Christmas bonus (Δώρο Χριστουγέννων)
payments.deadline: 21 Dec (the part for 21-31 Dec may be paid by 31 Dec)

payments.name: Easter bonus (Δώρο Πάσχα)
payments.deadline: Holy Wednesday (the part from Holy Wednesday to 30 April may be paid by 30 April); the month moves with the date of Easter, so no month is given

payments.name: Holiday allowance (Επίδομα αδείας)
payments.deadline: Paid in advance at the start of the annual leave; the month depends on when leave is taken, so no month is given

source.quote: Επίδομα εορτών Χριστουγέννων ίσο με ένα μηνιαίο μισθό για τους αμειβόμενους με μισθό

countries.name: Hong Kong

assumptions.label: The hire is aged 18 to 64 and stays longer than 60 days
assumptions.notes: MPF covers employees aged 18 to 64. An employee engaged for fewer than 60 days is exempt, and so is an employee aged 65 or over, for whom neither side contributes. Those are the two cases where the single line on this page falls to nothing; both are unusual for a salaried engineering hire, so the full charge is modelled.

employer_contributions.name: MPF mandatory contribution (employer share)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee aged 18 to 64 engaged for 60 days or more, on relevant income up to HKD 30,000 a month
employer_contributions.notes: The whole employer side of a Hong Kong payslip is this one line, and the ceiling is what makes it small. The MPFA states that employers and employees each contribute 5% of relevant income, and that the current maximum relevant income level is HKD 30,000 a month, which caps the employer at HKD 1,500 a month whatever the salary. Those levels have applied to contribution periods commencing from 1 June 2014, per the MPFA's own table of legislative amendment history; the minimum level of HKD 7,100 a month governs the employee's contribution, not the employer's, who pays 5% of relevant income below it too. Relevant income is all monetary payments including a 13th month where the contract provides one, and it expressly excludes severance payments and long service payments. The practical consequence is worth stating plainly: Deel's Hong Kong page estimates the employer cost at about 5.777% of salary with 'Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) - 5%' listed uncapped, but the ceiling means that at the example salary on this page the MPF is nearer 1.5% of gross, and it keeps falling as pay rises.

source.name: MPFA - Mandatory Contributions for regular employees, and the summary table of legislative amendment history for the minimum and maximum relevant income levels

statutory_extras.name: Long service payment and severance payment
statutory_extras.notes: Real, statutory, and impossible to express honestly as a share of one salary, so it is carried at zero and left out of the total. The Employment Ordinance makes a long service payment or a severance payment due on certain terminations after a qualifying period of service, and the MPFA states that both are excluded from relevant income, so no MPF is charged on them. What they cost depends on why and when the employment ends, not on what the job pays this year. Ask any provider how it funds them before signing.

source.name: MPFA - Mandatory Contributions, relevant income definition excluding severance and long service payments

statutory_extras.name: Employees' compensation insurance
statutory_extras.notes: Compulsory for every employer in Hong Kong, but it is an insurance premium set by an insurer rather than a rate set by statute, so there is no official percentage to publish and it is carried at zero. Deel's Hong Kong page prices it at about 0.4% of salary as part of its own 5.777% estimate, and adds a 0.60% administrative fee of its own on top; neither figure is a statutory charge, which is why neither is in the ledger above.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Hong Kong page

countries.notice_typical: 1 month after probation; 7 days minimum during probation after the first month

source.quote: How many months of pay an employee receives is determined by his/her employment contract

countries.name: Croatia

assumptions.label: The hire is not a first-time employee under article 20(2) of the Contributions Act
assumptions.notes: Article 20(2) of the Contributions Act provides that for an insured person employed for the first time ('osiguranik koji se prvi put zapošljava' - written here without diacritics as 'prvi put zaposljava') only the contributions taken out of gross pay are calculated, which removes the employer's 16.5% health contribution, and article 20(3) limits this to monthly bases covering a period of up to one year. Article 7 point 54 defines a person employed for the first time on an employment contract as someone the employer registers on an open-ended contract who had no open-ended employment contract before. An experienced software engineer does not qualify, so this page charges the full 16.5%. For a graduate on a first open-ended contract the employer side can be close to nothing for the first year; ask the provider whether it applies the relief and whether its quote passes it on.

employer_contributions.name: Compulsory health insurance contribution (doprinos za obvezno zdravstveno osiguranje)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the full gross pay of an employee, as a contribution 'on' the base (na osnovicu)
employer_contributions.notes: This single line is the whole statutory employer side of a Croatian payslip. Article 14(1) point 1 of the Contributions Act sets the health insurance contribution at 16.5%, and article 20(1) lists it as the one contribution calculated on top of the base, while the pension contributions (20%, or 15% plus 5% for a member of the second pillar) are calculated out of it and paid by the employee. The Tax Administration's contributions page states the same split: 'doprinos na osnovicu: doprinos za zdravstveno osiguranje po stopi od 16,5%'. No ceiling is applied, and that is not a simplification: article 7 point 18 and article 204 limit the maximum monthly base to the pension contributions only. For 2026 that base is EUR 11,958 a month (six times the average gross wage of EUR 1,993, Narodne novine 150/2025), and it caps what the employee pays, not the employer's health line. For an insured person in an employment relationship, article 20(1) lists no other contribution on the base: no separate employer pension, unemployment or payroll tax line is added.

source.name: Zakon o doprinosima (Contributions Act), consolidated text NN 84/08 to 152/24, in force from 1 January 2025, articles 14(1) and 20(1); cross-checked on the Tax Administration (Porezna uprava) contributions page updated 8 January 2025

statutory_extras.name: Minimum monthly contribution base - employer pays on at least EUR 757.34
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it never binds at a full-time professional salary. Article 21(2) of the Contributions Act says the monthly base for full-time work cannot be lower than the minimum monthly base, and the 2026 order published in Narodne novine 150/2025 sets it at EUR 757.34 (0.38 times the average wage of EUR 1,993). It matters only on a low or unusual full-time wage, where the 16.5% is charged on the floor rather than on actual pay.

source.name: Naredba o iznosima osnovica za obracun doprinosa za obvezna osiguranja za 2026. godinu, Narodne novine 150/2025, article 3

statutory_extras.name: Statutory severance (otpremnina) after two years - not an annual cost
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a liability on dismissal, not a payroll charge. Article 126 of the Labour Act gives an employee dismissed after two years of continuous work a severance of not less than one third of the average monthly pay of the last three months for each completed year of service, and caps the statutory amount at six average monthly salaries unless a law, collective agreement, work rules or the contract set otherwise. It is not owed on dismissal for the employee's conduct. Under an employer of record the provider pays it and invoices it back, so read the termination clause of the service agreement before signing.

source.name: Zakon o radu (Labour Act), consolidated text NN 93/14 to 64/23, in force from 14 June 2023, article 126

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month or Christmas bonus - not required by Croatian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Act creates no thirteenth salary and no holiday bonus. Christmas bonuses (bozicnica), holiday pay (regres) and meal or commuting allowances are common in Croatian offers and often come from collective agreements or work rules; they are contractual, so price them as market cost in a competitive offer, not as a legal charge.

source.name: Zakon o radu (Labour Act), consolidated text NN 93/14 to 64/23, in force from 14 June 2023

countries.notice_typical: Under article 122(1) of the Labour Act the minimum notice on an ordinary dismissal grows with service: two weeks under one year, one month after one year, one month and two weeks after two years, two months after five years, two months and two weeks after ten years, and three months after twenty years, with two weeks or a month more for an employee of 50 or 55 with twenty years of service. Notice is halved for a dismissal caused by the employee's conduct. An employee who resigns for a particularly important reason cannot be held to more than one month.

source.name: Zakon o radu (Labour Act), consolidated text NN 93/14 to 64/23, in force from 14 June 2023

countries.name: Hungary

assumptions.label: No employer tax credit applies to this hire
assumptions.notes: The social contribution tax carries a long list of credits, but each one targets a category of worker rather than an employer: unskilled and agricultural roles, people entering the labour market, workers with reduced capacity, researchers, apprenticeship contracts. A software engineer on an open-ended contract matches none of them, so the full 13% is modelled. If your hire does fall into one of those categories, the credit is worth asking the provider about, because it is applied by the employer of record and not by you.

employer_contributions.name: Social contribution tax (szocialis hozzajarulasi ado)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on the same base as the employee's own social security contribution, with no ceiling on employment income
employer_contributions.notes: This is the only charge levied on the payslip, and that is the point of the country. The tax authority's own rate table gives the general rate as 13% from 1 January 2022, down from 15.5% before it, and its 2026 guidance states it plainly: 'Az ado merteke az adoalap 13 szazaleka' - the rate is 13% of the base. The same date removed the second employer levy: NAV's notice opens 'On 1 January 2022 the vocational training contribution ceased', with its training tax credit moved into the social contribution tax (nav.gov.hu/ado/szocialis_hozzajarulasi_ado/uj-szochokedvezmeny-2022.-januar-1-jetol, read 20 September 2026). One rate is not a simplification we have made; it is what Hungary now charges. For an employee the base is the same as the base of the social security contribution. There is a statutory minimum base, HUF 96,840 a month in 2026, stated in NAV's information booklet 49 of 16 January 2026 rather than on the rate table (nav.gov.hu/pfile/file?path=/ugyfeliranytu/nezzen-utana/inf_fuz/rejtett/Informacios-fuzetek---Aktualis/49.-A-szocialis-hozzajarulasi-ado). It sits far below any full-time minimum wage in Hungary, so it cannot bind for the kind of hire this page prices. The ceiling the law sets on social contribution tax applies to an individual's own liability on capital-type income, not to wages, so the employer rate does not fall away as salary rises.

source.name: NAV (Hungarian Tax and Customs Administration) - rate table of the social contribution tax, and information booklet 49 published 16 January 2026

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Hungarian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code creates no thirteenth-month entitlement. Hungarian employers commonly pay a bonus, and the cafeteria benefit system (SZEP card and similar) is close to standard in the market, but neither is statutory. Budget them as market cost if you need a competitive offer, not as a legal charge.

source.name: Act I of 2012 on the Labour Code (Munka Torvenykonyve), consolidated text on the National Legislation Database

statutory_extras.name: Local business tax (up to 2%) and innovation contribution (0.3%) - charged on the provider, not on the payslip
statutory_extras.notes: The cost most likely to appear on a Hungarian EOR invoice without appearing in any employer rate. Two taxes fall on the provider's Hungarian company, not on the payslip. The local business tax (helyi iparűzési adó) is set by each municipality with a ceiling in the Local Taxes Act: section 40(1)(c) caps it at 2% of the tax base from 2000 onwards, and section 39(1) defines that base as net turnover less the cost of goods sold and mediated services, subcontractor work, material costs and direct research costs - wages are not among the deductions, so the salaries an EOR re-invoices sit inside its taxable turnover. The innovation contribution adds 0.3% of the same base under section 16(2) of Act LXXVI of 2014, and section 15(2)(a) exempts micro and small enterprises, so whether it applies depends on the size of the provider's Hungarian entity. Both are carried at zero because they tax the provider's turnover rather than one salary, and named because somebody pays them. Deel's Hungary page also lists a monthly 'additional employer cost' of HUF 15,700 and a one-off pre-employment medical examination at HUF 17,800 as provider line items; neither is traced to a Hungarian official source here. Ask whether any of these reaches your invoice.

source.name: Nemzeti Jogszabálytár - 1990. évi C. törvény a helyi adókról (Htv.), text in force from 31.07.2026, § 40(1)(c) ('2000. évtől az adóalap 2%-a') and § 39(1); with 2014. évi LXXVI. törvény §§ 15-16 (innovation contribution 'a járulékalap 0,3%-a')

statutory_extras.name: Age-based extra leave, one to ten extra days
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it buys time, not money, and because it depends on the employee's age rather than the job. The Labour Code adds one working day of leave from the age of 25, two from 28, three from 31, four from 33, five from 35, and continues upward. A hire in their late thirties therefore starts with several days more than the twenty-day base, which matters for capacity planning and for any handover you are costing, and which no provider quote will mention.

source.name: Act I of 2012 on the Labour Code, section 117(1) (age supplements to annual leave)

countries.notice_typical: Thirty days, the statutory base under section 69 of the Labour Code. On the employer's notice it lengthens with service: five days more after three years, fifteen after five, twenty after eight, twenty-five after ten.

source.name: Act I of 2012 on the Labour Code (Munka Torvenykonyve), consolidated text on the National Legislation Database

countries.name: Indonesia

assumptions.label: Work accident (JKK) class: very low risk, 0.24%
assumptions.notes: BPJS Ketenagakerjaan charges JKK on five risk grades — 0.24%, 0.54%, 0.89%, 1.27% and 1.74% of monthly wages — set by the employer's line of business. Modelled at the very-low grade because the legal employer under an EOR is an office-based services company; BPJS's own worked example puts a restaurant one grade higher, at low risk. If the provider's registered activity sits in a higher grade the difference is up to 1.5 points of pay, so ask which grade the quote assumes.

employer_contributions.name: Old-age savings JHT (Jaminan Hari Tua), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All wage-earning workers registered with BPJS Ketenagakerjaan
employer_contributions.notes: The heaviest contribution line at this page's salary, and the one with no ceiling at all: 5.7% of monthly wages in total, 3.7% from the employer and 2% from the employee, on the whole salary however high it goes. The health line carries a higher rate, 4%, but its base stops at IDR 12,000,000 a month, so in money JHT costs the employer roughly three times as much here. Wages here mean basic pay plus fixed allowances, which is the base BPJS calls upah.

source.name: BPJS Ketenagakerjaan — Wage-earning participants (Penerima Upah), contribution calculation: JHT employer 3.7% of monthly wages, worker 2%

employer_contributions.name: Work accident insurance JKK (Jaminan Kecelakaan Kerja), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only cover; rate set by the employer's risk grade
employer_contributions.notes: Five grades published by BPJS: very low 0.24%, low 0.54%, medium 0.89%, high 1.27%, very high 1.74% of monthly wages. Modelled at the very-low grade for an office-based provider entity, on the assumption shown above. No ceiling: unlike the pension and health lines, JKK is charged on the whole salary.

source.name: BPJS Ketenagakerjaan — Wage-earning participants (Penerima Upah): JKK 0.24% very low risk, 0.54% low, 0.89% medium, 1.27% high, 1.74% very high, of monthly wages

employer_contributions.name: Death benefit JKM (Jaminan Kematian), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only cover for death outside work
employer_contributions.notes: 0.3% of monthly wages, employer only, uncapped. It pays a lump sum and a funeral grant to the family, and a schooling benefit for the children of a worker who has paid in long enough.

source.name: BPJS Ketenagakerjaan — Wage-earning participants (Penerima Upah): JKM 0.3% of monthly wages

employer_contributions.name: Pension JP (Jaminan Pensiun), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: 3% of monthly wages in total, employer 2% and worker 1%, charged up to a wage ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: The ceiling is what makes this line small on a professional salary: BPJS states the contribution base is capped at IDR 10,547,400 of monthly wages, so the employer's 2% stops at about IDR 211,000 a month. The cap is reviewed each year, and the same page publishes 2026 pension benefits of IDR 411,400 to IDR 4,932,300 a month, so check the figure with the provider before signing a long quote.

source.name: BPJS Ketenagakerjaan — Wage-earning participants (Penerima Upah): JP employer 2%, worker 1%, contribution base capped at IDR 10,547,400 of monthly wages

employer_contributions.name: Health insurance JKN (BPJS Kesehatan), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: 5% of monthly pay in total, employer 4% and worker 1%, on pay capped at IDR 12,000,000 a month
employer_contributions.notes: A separate fund from BPJS Ketenagakerjaan, with its own ceiling written into the presidential regulation: article 30 sets the contribution at 5% of monthly pay, 4% on the employer and 1% on the worker, and article 32 caps the pay used for the calculation at IDR 12,000,000 a month. The employer's share therefore stops at IDR 480,000 a month. The floor is the local minimum wage. Cover extends to the worker's spouse and up to three children at no extra premium.

source.name: Presidential Regulation 64/2020 amending Regulation 82/2018 on health insurance, art. 30(1) (5% of monthly pay: 4% employer, 1% participant) and art. 32(1) (pay ceiling IDR 12,000,000 a month)

statutory_extras.name: THR religious holiday allowance (Tunjangan Hari Raya Keagamaan)
statutory_extras.notes: A legal obligation, not a custom, and the biggest employer line in this ledger — at the example salary it is worth more than the five contribution lines put together. The wage regulation makes the religious holiday allowance compulsory and requires payment no later than seven days before the religious holiday; the ministerial regulation sets the amount at one month of wages for twelve months of continuous service, prorated by months worked below that, and is owed from one month of service. Wages for this purpose are clean wages, or basic pay plus fixed allowances. It adds 8.33% to annual cost. Note what does not follow: the wage regulation classifies the THR as non-wage income, and BPJS contributions are charged on monthly wages, so the THR itself carries no social security on top.

source.name: Government Regulation 36/2021 on wages, art. 8(1) (religious holiday allowance is non-wage income) and art. 9 (employers are required to give it, paid no later than seven days before the holiday); Minister of Manpower Regulation 6/2016, art. 2–3 (one month of wages at twelve months of service, prorated from one month)

statutory_extras.name: Statutory severance and long-service pay on termination
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is contingent on the contract ending, not a monthly charge, but it is the largest single exposure of an Indonesian hire. Ending an indefinite contract triggers a statutory package — severance pay, long-service reward and compensation for rights — whose multiples depend on the reason for the termination and the length of service. It belongs in an exit budget rather than in an on-cost, and it is the first thing to ask a provider about: whether it funds the accrual monthly or invoices it when the hire ends.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Indonesia page

statutory_extras.name: Statutory annual leave (12 days after one year)
statutory_extras.notes: Paid time inside the salary rather than an extra contribution. Twelve working days a year once twelve months of continuous service are complete, accruing at one day a month. Indonesian employers also observe collective leave days (cuti bersama) fixed each year by joint ministerial decree, which are normally deducted from this entitlement.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Indonesia page

countries.notice_typical: Probation of up to three months, and only on an indefinite contract — a fixed-term contract cannot carry one. No minimum notice period is set by statute; thirty days is the general practice for either side, seven days during probation. What matters financially is not the notice but the termination package: ending an indefinite contract triggers statutory severance, long-service reward and compensation for rights, scaled by the reason and the length of service.

payments.name: THR religious holiday allowance
payments.deadline: no later than 7 days before the religious holiday (the holiday date moves each year, so no fixed month)

source.quote: Pekerja/Buruh yang telah mempunyai masa kerja 12 (dua belas) bulan secara terus menerus atau lebih, diberikan sebesar 1 (satu) bulan upah

countries.name: Ireland

employer_contributions.name: Employer PRSI (Class A0/AX/AL, reduced band)
employer_contributions.applies: weekly gross pay of €552 or less (annualised at 52 weeks/year to approx. €28,704)
employer_contributions.notes: Employer PRSI is charged on the full amount of weekly gross pay, not just the excess, so pay at or below the €552/week threshold is charged at 9.15% rather than 11.40%. This rate already includes the National Training Fund levy, which is collected jointly with employer PRSI rather than billed separately. It rose from 9.00% on 1 October 2026 (gov.ie, 'Class A from 1 October 2026').

source.name: gov.ie — Department of Social Protection, PRSI Class A rates (from 1 October 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Employer PRSI (Class A1, standard rate)
employer_contributions.applies: weekly gross pay above €552 (annualised at 52 weeks/year to approx. €28,704)
employer_contributions.notes: No ceiling on the employer PRSI base: the 11.40% rate applies to all gross pay once weekly earnings exceed €552, with no annual contribution cap. Already includes the National Training Fund levy (collected jointly with employer PRSI). It rose from 11.25% on 1 October 2026 (gov.ie, 'Class A from 1 October 2026').

source.name: gov.ie — Department of Social Protection, PRSI Class A rates (from 1 October 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Auto-enrolment pension — My Future Fund (Phase 1, employer share)
employer_contributions.applies: employees aged 23-60 earning more than €20,000/year across all employments who are not already contributing to a qualifying occupational pension through payroll
employer_contributions.notes: Auto-enrolment started 1 January 2026. Employer matches the employee's 1.5% contribution (plus a 0.5% state top-up) on gross earnings up to an €80,000 annual cap. Rates are scheduled to rise to 3% in year 4, 4.5% in year 7 and 6% in year 10 (mirrored by the employee rate). secondary source: gov.ie ("My Future Fund update for employers and employees") and citizensinformation.ie auto-enrolment pages returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch during this research session; figures were confirmed via Mercer Ireland's employer guide and cross-checked against pensionplanner.ie and Lockton.

source.name: Mercer Ireland — An Employer's Guide to Auto-Enrolment (secondary source)

countries.notice_typical: 1 week (13 weeks–2 years of service) rising to 8 weeks (15+ years), per the Minimum Notice and Terms of Employment Act 1973–2005

source.quote: A Christmas bonus is not automatically a legal entitlement in Ireland.

countries.name: Israel

assumptions.label: Israeli resident aged 18 to retirement age (column 1 of form 102)
assumptions.notes: National insurance rates in Israel are set per category of worker, and the reporting form 102 has a column for each. This ledger models column 1, the ordinary Israeli-resident employee aged 18 up to retirement age, which is the normal employer-of-record hire. Every other column costs the employer less: 2.12% flat above the age of entitlement to the old-age pension, 2.12% for an employee under 18, and slightly reduced rates for a controlling shareholder in a closely held company. Health insurance is deducted from the employee only and never costs the employer anything.

employer_contributions.name: National insurance (Bituach Leumi), reduced rate
employer_contributions.applies: Israeli resident employees aged 18 to retirement age, on the part of the salary below the reduced collection step
employer_contributions.notes: The employer pays 4.51% on the part of the salary up to the reduced collection step, which the National Insurance Institute sets at ILS 7,703 a month from 1 January 2026, so ILS 92,436 a year. The employer rate for this band has been 4.51% since 1 January 2025. There is no employer health-insurance contribution in Israel: the health levy of 3.23% and 5.17% is deducted from the employee alone, which is why the employee side of an Israeli payslip is far heavier than the employer side.

source.name: National Insurance Institute - rates and amounts of insurance contributions for salaried employees

employer_contributions.name: National insurance (Bituach Leumi), full rate
employer_contributions.applies: The slice of salary between the reduced collection step and the maximum income liable for contributions
employer_contributions.notes: The employer pays 7.6% only on the slice of salary between the reduced step (ILS 7,703 a month) and the maximum income liable for contributions, which the same table sets at ILS 51,910 a month from 1 January 2026, so ILS 622,920 a year. Nothing is charged above that ceiling, and the employer rate for this band has been 7.6% since 1 January 2019. Because both ends are fixed in shekels, the effective national-insurance rate on a senior Israeli salary is well under 7.6% and keeps falling as pay rises.

source.name: National Insurance Institute - rates and amounts of insurance contributions for salaried employees

employer_contributions.name: Compulsory pension, employer contributions (tagmulim)
employer_contributions.applies: Insured salary, which is the salary paid or the national average wage, whichever is lower
employer_contributions.notes: Israel has no pension law: the obligation comes from an extension order issued under the Collective Agreements Law, which is why guides miss it. The employer deposits 6.5% to the retirement component, a rate in force since 1 January 2017 and recited in a Supreme Court judgment of 4 November 2025 as part of the 18.5% minimum (6% employer severance, 6.5% employer contributions, 6% employee). The base is capped: section 6(c) of the consolidated order applies the duty to 'the salary paid to the employee, or the average wage in the economy as updated from time to time, whichever is the lower'. That average wage, under section 2 of the National Insurance Law, is ILS 13,769 a month from 1 January 2026, so nothing is statutory above ILS 165,228 a year. Israeli employers customarily insure the whole salary; the part above the cap is contractual, not statutory, and is not modelled here.

source.name: Supreme Court of Israel - judgment of 4 November 2025 stating the pension extension-order rates in force

employer_contributions.name: Compulsory severance provision (pitzuim)
employer_contributions.applies: Insured salary, which is the salary paid or the national average wage, whichever is lower
employer_contributions.notes: The same extension order makes the employer deposit 6% to the severance component every month, at the rates in the section 6(d) table since 1 January 2014, on the same insured salary capped at the average wage. This is a real monthly cash cost, not a provision you can postpone. Section 7 is the catch: those deposits stand in place of severance under section 14 of the Severance Pay Law only 'in respect of the salary, the components, the periods and the rates for which the provision was made', so an employer who deposits the 6% minimum on a capped base has not discharged the whole severance entitlement. See the severance top-up line below.

source.name: Ministry of Labour - Extension Order for Compulsory Pension, consolidated text (2011)

statutory_extras.name: Severance top-up to 8.33% - the gap this page does not add
statutory_extras.notes: Section 9 of the extension order lets the employer raise the severance component to 8.33% of the pay elements it contributes on, and section 7 limits the substitution for statutory severance to what was actually provisioned. Provider quotes for Israel carry the full 8.33% on the whole salary, which is the single largest reason their published statutory range (Deel: 19.34% to 23.43%) sits above the figure on this page. The 2.33 points shown here are the gap inside the extension order, on the same capped insured salary; the uncapped part of the severance entitlement is a further liability that falls due on dismissal. Ask any provider whether its Israeli quote provisions 6% or 8.33%, and on the capped or the whole salary - the answer is worth several points of payroll.

source.name: Ministry of Labour - Extension Order for Compulsory Pension, consolidated text (2011)

statutory_extras.name: Travel allowance (dmei nesiaa)
statutory_extras.notes: The extension order on the employer's share of travel to and from work, signed on 8 August 2016 and applying to all employees and employers in Israel from 1 February 2016, sets the reimbursement at up to ILS 22.60 per working day. Every employee who needs transport to reach the workplace is entitled to it for each day actually worked, priced at the discounted bus fare or discounted monthly pass from home to work; it is not paid to an employee the employer transports, and it is halved when transport is provided one way. It is carried at zero because it is a reimbursement per day of attendance, capped in shekels, not a percentage of salary, and it does not scale with pay. It is named because it is a genuine employer cost that appears on an Israeli EOR invoice and in none of the top-ranked guides for this query. A provider guide prints it as a flat ILS 323 a month, a figure the order does not contain.

source.name: Ministry of Labour - Extension order on employer participation in travel expenses to and from work (2016), ILS 22.60 per working day

statutory_extras.name: Convalescence pay (dmei havraa)
statutory_extras.notes: Owed to private-sector employees once they complete a first year of service, then pro rata for part years, normally paid once a year between June and September. The days come from the 2016 extension order on convalescence and recreation expenses: 5 days in the first year, 6 in years two and three, 7 in years four to ten, 8 in years eleven to fifteen, 9 in years sixteen to nineteen and 10 from the twentieth year, pro rata for part-time. The day rate is set each year: an extension order signed by the Minister of Labour on 16 August 2026, extending the general collective agreement of 22 June 2026, fixes the rate for the 2026 convalescence year at ILS 451.50 a day, so a full-time employee in the second year of service is owed ILS 2,709. It is carried at zero because it is a number of days at a shekel rate, not a percentage of salary. Budget it as a real annual cost from the first full year of service.

source.name: Ministry of Labour - Extension order on employer participation in convalescence and recreation expenses, signed 16 August 2026 (ILS 451.50 a day for 2026)

statutory_extras.name: Study fund (keren hishtalmut) - not required by law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because no Israeli statute or general extension order requires it. Deel's Israel guide describes it as an optional but common tech-sector benefit with an employer contribution around 7.5%, either capped at a salary of ILS 15,712 or uncapped. It is close to unavoidable in a competitive Tel Aviv offer, so treat it as market cost, not as a legal charge - the same treatment this site gives the Swedish occupational pension.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Israel page

countries.notice_typical: Notice builds up during the first year - one day for each of the first six months of service, then 2.5 days for each further month - and is 30 days once a full year is complete. Payment in lieu or garden leave is allowed. There is no statutory probation period in Israel; probation is whatever the contract says.

payments.name: Convalescence pay (dmei havra'a)
payments.deadline: annual; payment month not stated on the pages read

source.quote: הזכאות לתשלום משכורת 13 אינה קבועה בדיני העבודה

countries.name: India

assumptions.label: Basic wage as a share of gross
assumptions.notes: Basic wage is typically 40-50% of CTC (Cost to Company) in Indian payroll structures; adjustable per employer pay-structure design. All 'basic' contributions below are computed on this share.

employer_contributions.name: EPF employer contribution (Employees' Provident Fund)
employer_contributions.applies: Applies to basic wage plus dearness allowance, capped at the statutory wage ceiling of Rs 25,000/month (in force since 17 September 2026)
employer_contributions.notes: 3.67% is the residual of the 12% statutory employer EPF+EPS contribution after removing the 8.33% EPS share; EPFO's wage-ceiling FAQ (Q39) now states the split verbatim: 12% split as 3.67% towards EPF and 8.33% towards EPS, capped at the revised Rs 25,000 wage ceiling. The ceiling was raised from Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000 per month by Gazette of India notification S.O. 5109(E) of 17 September 2026 (Code on Social Security, 2020, section 2(89), for the purposes of Chapter III), in force from its publication that day: https://egazette.gov.in/WriteReadData/2026/276299.pdf. Contributions on wages above the ceiling under an existing higher-wage arrangement may continue (FAQ Q22) and are not modelled here.

source.name: Employees' Provident Fund Organisation - FAQs on the revision of the EPFO statutory wage ceiling (Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000, S.O. 5109(E))

employer_contributions.name: EPS employer contribution (Employees' Pension Scheme)
employer_contributions.applies: Diverted from the same 12% employer EPF contribution; capped at the Rs 25,000/month wage ceiling (in force since 17 September 2026)
employer_contributions.notes: The 8.33% EPS share was confirmed verbatim on two EPFO pages (epfo.gov.in and pmvbry.epfindia.gov.in) and again in EPFO's wage-ceiling FAQ (Q39). The same FAQ applies the revised ceiling to EPS as well as EPF and EDLI (Q5): from 17 September 2026 EPS wages count up to Rs 25,000 (Q9), under Gazette notification S.O. 5109(E) of 17 September 2026 (https://egazette.gov.in/WriteReadData/2026/276299.pdf).

source.name: Employees' Provident Fund Organisation - FAQs on the revision of the EPFO statutory wage ceiling (Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000, S.O. 5109(E))

employer_contributions.name: EDLI employer contribution (Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance)
employer_contributions.applies: Applies to the same capped basic wage as EPF/EPS; premium paid entirely by the employer, no deduction from the employee
employer_contributions.notes: EDLI administrative charges (separate from this 0.5% insurance premium) were reduced to nil with effect from 1 April 2017 per EPFO circular. EPFO's wage-ceiling FAQ (Q5, Q7) applies the Rs 25,000 ceiling to EDLI from 17 September 2026 and computes the 0.50% EDLI contribution (A/c 21) on wages up to that ceiling.

source.name: Employees' Provident Fund Organisation - FAQs on the revision of the EPFO statutory wage ceiling (Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000, S.O. 5109(E))

employer_contributions.name: EPF administrative charges (employer-borne)
employer_contributions.applies: Charged on the same capped basic wage; funds EPFO scheme administration, borne solely by the employer
employer_contributions.notes: The rate has remained unchanged since 1 June 2018; it was 0.65% from 1 April 2017 and 0.85% before that. No official revision of the rate was found when checked. EPFO's wage-ceiling FAQ (Q7) computes the 0.50% administrative charges (A/c 2) on wages up to the Rs 25,000 ceiling in force since 17 September 2026. Payroll-compliance sites commonly cite a minimum monthly charge of Rs 500, but that minimum was not confirmed on an EPFO web page and is not modelled here.

source.name: Employees' Provident Fund Organisation - FAQs on the revision of the EPFO statutory wage ceiling (Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000, S.O. 5109(E))

employer_contributions.name: ESIC employer contribution (Employees' State Insurance)
employer_contributions.applies: Applies only when the employee's gross monthly wage is at or below Rs 21,000 (Rs 25,000/month for persons with disabilities)
employer_contributions.notes: The employee's own 0.75% share is separate and not an employer cost. Employees with an average daily wage up to Rs 176 are exempt from their own contribution, but the employer's 3.25% share remains payable for them.

source.name: Employees' State Insurance Corporation - Contribution

statutory_extras.name: Gratuity accrual (Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 / Code on Social Security, 2020)
statutory_extras.notes: Derived from 15 days of basic wages per completed year: (monthly basic / 26 days) x 15 days, equal to approximately 4.81% of annual basic pay. The percentage is calculated rather than stated verbatim on a government page. Gratuity is payable after five years of continuous service but is commonly accrued as an ongoing employer provision. Secondary sources commonly cite a Rs 20 lakh private-sector ceiling. A 2024 circular raised the ceiling to Rs 25 lakh for central government employees; no official confirmation was found that this increase extends to private-sector or EOR employees.

source.name: Ministry of Labour & Employment - Additional FAQs on Labour Codes (gratuity: 15 days' wages per year, 5-year eligibility)

statutory_extras.name: Statutory bonus (Payment of Bonus Act, 1965)
statutory_extras.notes: The official minimum statutory bonus is 8.33% of wages and the maximum is 20%. It applies to employees earning up to Rs 21,000 per month in basic pay plus dearness allowance; this exact threshold was corroborated by secondary payroll-compliance sources but was not found verbatim on the official pages checked. The calculation uses a Rs 7,000 monthly wage ceiling or the applicable minimum wage if higher, as described in secondary coverage of the 2015 amendment. The item is excluded from this example because its USD 30,000 annual salary is above the eligibility threshold.

source.name: Ministry of Labour & Employment - Compliance Handbook for Employers Under the Four Labour Codes

countries.notice_typical: 30 days minimum by law (Industrial Disputes Act); commonly 30-90 days in practice depending on seniority, especially in IT/tech roles

payments.name: Statutory bonus (Code on Wages, replacing the Payment of Bonus Act 1965)
payments.deadline: within eight months from the close of the accounting year; the MoLE handbook says the accounting year starts on 1 April, which would put the limit at 30 November (derived, not quoted); extendable by order to a total of two years

source.quote: shall be paid by crediting it in the bank account of the employee by his employer within a period of eight months from the close of the accounting year

countries.name: Italy

assumptions.label: Employing entity averages more than 15 employees and sits in the general FIS scheme (FIS 0.80% and CIGS 0.90% both apply)
assumptions.notes: Set by the EOR's Italian entity, not by the client. Below 16 employees the CIGS line falls away; up to 5 employees the FIS rate drops to 0.50%. Entities covered by a sector bilateral solidarity fund follow that fund's rates instead.

assumptions.label: Employee first insured after 31 December 1995 (pension base capped at EUR 122,295 in 2026)
assumptions.notes: Workers already insured on 31 December 1995 have no pension ceiling; the minor contributions are due on the full salary in both cases.

employer_contributions.name: Pension fund (FPLD, IVS contribution)
employer_contributions.applies: All private-sector employees insured with INPS
employer_contributions.notes: 33% combined: 23.81% employer, 9.19% employee. For workers first insured after 1995 the base stops at the 2026 ceiling of EUR 122,295 (INPS circular 6/2026); above that only this pension line stops, the lines below continue.

source.name: INPS — Circular 82 of 14 July 2022 (IVS 33%: 23.81% employer, 9.19% employee)

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (NASpI, ordinary)
employer_contributions.applies: Open-ended contracts; fixed-term contracts pay a further 1.40%, not modelled
employer_contributions.notes: Ordinary financing contribution of 1.31%. No ceiling applies to this line.

source.name: INPS — Circular 82 of 14 July 2022 (NASpI ordinary contribution 1.31%)

employer_contributions.name: Vocational training levy (art. 25, Law 845/1978)
employer_contributions.applies: All employers subject to unemployment insurance
employer_contributions.notes: Supplementary 0.30% collected with NASpI; employers can route it to an inter-professional training fund. Often shown together with NASpI as 1.61%.

source.name: INPS — Circular 82 of 14 July 2022 (supplementary contribution 0.30%, art. 25 Law 845/1978)

employer_contributions.name: TFR guarantee fund (Fondo di garanzia, Law 297/1982)
employer_contributions.applies: Employees whose severance accrual (TFR) follows article 2120 of the Civil Code; 0.40% for industrial executives
employer_contributions.notes: Employer-only. Insures the severance accrual if the employer becomes insolvent. Waived on the share of TFR paid into a pension fund or the INPS treasury fund.

source.name: INPS — Circular 12 of 5 February 2026 (guarantee fund 0.20%, or 0.40% for industrial executives)

employer_contributions.name: Family allowance fund (CUAF)
employer_contributions.applies: General rate for employers of INPS-insured employees
employer_contributions.notes: 2.48% statutory rate less 1.80 points of standing relief = 0.68%. Some sectors carry further relief.

source.name: INPS — Circular 82 of 14 July 2022 (CUAF 0.68% = 2.48% less 1.80%)

employer_contributions.name: Sickness insurance (commerce and services, office staff)
employer_contributions.applies: White-collar employees of commerce and service-sector employers; industrial office staff pay 0%
employer_contributions.notes: Due even when the collective agreement makes the employer pay full salary during sick leave (Law 133/2008, art. 20).

source.name: INPS — Circular 82 of 14 July 2022 (sickness, commerce/services, white-collar: 2.44%)

employer_contributions.name: Maternity insurance (commerce and services)
employer_contributions.applies: White-collar employees of commerce and service-sector employers (industry: 0.46%)
employer_contributions.notes: Finances maternity, paternity and parental-leave benefits under Legislative Decree 151/2001.

source.name: INPS — Circular 82 of 14 July 2022 (maternity, commerce/services, white-collar: 0.24%)

employer_contributions.name: Wage integration fund (FIS), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Employers averaging more than 5 employees that are not covered by an industry CIGO scheme or a sector bilateral fund
employer_contributions.notes: 0.80% in total, split 0.53% employer and 0.27% employee. Employers with up to 5 employees pay 0.50% (0.33% employer).

source.name: INPS — Circular 101 of 12 December 2023 (FIS 0.80%: 0.53% employer, 0.27% employee)

employer_contributions.name: Extraordinary wage guarantee (CIGS), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Employers in the FIS scheme averaging more than 15 employees (Legislative Decree 148/2015, art. 20 par. 3-bis)
employer_contributions.notes: 0.90% in total, split 0.60% employer and 0.30% employee since 1 January 2023. Falls away below 16 employees.

source.name: INPS — Circular 101 of 12 December 2023 (CIGS 0.90%: 0.60% employer, 0.30% employee; scope above 15 employees)

employer_contributions.name: INAIL work-accident insurance (tariff item 0722, office work)
employer_contributions.applies: Office and remote desk work classified under item 0722, services tariff (Gestione Terziario)
employer_contributions.notes: Average rate 4 per thousand for the services tariff (industry 5, crafts 6). INAIL adjusts each employer's rate for claims history, so the invoiced rate can sit above or below 0.40%. Software development is item 0726.

source.name: INAIL — Circular 38 of 24 June 2025, office work under tariff item 0722 (average rate 4 per thousand, services tariff)

statutory_extras.name: Severance accrual (TFR, trattamento di fine rapporto)
statutory_extras.notes: Accrues at 7.41% of pay (1/13.5, Civil Code art. 2120) less the 0.50% Law 297/1982 contribution already paid with the pension line, so 6.91% net. Paid out at termination, or monthly to the INPS treasury fund for employers averaging 60+ employees in 2026-2027 (50+ from 2028).

source.name: INPS — Circular 12 of 5 February 2026 (TFR 7.41% = 1/13.5, net of the 0.50% contribution)

statutory_extras.name: 13th and 14th monthly salaries
statutory_extras.notes: The commerce and services agreement (CCNL Terziario) pays one extra month in December and one in June. The annual gross entered above already contains both: providers quote Italian salaries as 14 instalments, so nothing is added here.

source.name: Confcommercio — CCNL Terziario, Distribuzione e Servizi (13th and 14th month)

countries.notice_typical: Set by the collective agreement, level and seniority. Under the CCNL Terziario an employer dismissing a level 6-7 employee gives 15 to 20 days; for a Quadro or level 1 it is 60 days rising to 120 days after ten years. Notice runs from the 1st or 16th of the month. Severance (TFR) is paid on every exit, resignation included.

countries.name: Jordan

assumptions.label: Full old-age contribution, no under-30 reduction claimed
assumptions.notes: The ledger charges the old-age, disability and death branch at the full 11% employer rate of article 59 of the Social Security Law. Regulation No. 45 of 2024 lets a small or medium private establishment cut that contribution for a Jordanian employee under 30 with no earlier compulsory coverage, but the size test is applied to the establishment that employs the worker, which under an employer of record is the provider's Jordanian entity and not your company. Whether the reduction is available is therefore a question for the provider, and this page does not assume it.

employer_contributions.name: SSC old-age, disability and death insurance
employer_contributions.applies: Every insured worker aged 16 or over, Jordanian or not, on wages up to JOD 3,733 a month in 2026
employer_contributions.notes: Article 59(a)(1) of Social Security Law No. 1 of 2014, as amended by Law No. 11 of 2023: the establishment pays 11% of insured wages, and article 59(a)(2) has it withhold a further 6.5% from the employee.
