Article 4(a) brings every worker under the Labour Law into the scheme 'without any discrimination due to nationality', whatever the length or form of the contract, so a foreign hire costs the same percentage as a Jordanian one. Article 20(a) sets the wage ceiling at JOD 3,000 a month and article 20(b) indexes it to inflation every January; the Social Security Corporation announced on 14 May 2026 that the 2026 ceiling is JOD 3,733 a month, up from JOD 3,668 in 2025 after 1.77% inflation, which is the JOD 44,796 a year carried here. Some provider pages still print an older ceiling.

source.name: Social Security Law No. 1 of 2014, consolidated by the Social Security Corporation with amendments to 16 April 2023, articles 4, 20 and 59

employer_contributions.name: SSC work injury insurance
employer_contributions.applies: Every insured worker, on wages up to the SSC ceiling, paid by the employer alone
employer_contributions.notes: Article 24(a) of the Social Security Law: work injury insurance is financed by 'monthly contributions paid by the establishment at two percent of the wages of the insured'. Nothing is withheld from the employee for this branch. Article 32(b) makes an establishment that breaches occupational safety rules repay the medical costs the Corporation has paid for an injury caused by the breach, which is a liability on top of the rate rather than a change to it.

source.name: Social Security Law No. 1 of 2014, consolidated by the Social Security Corporation with amendments to 16 April 2023, article 24

employer_contributions.name: SSC maternity insurance
employer_contributions.applies: Every insured worker, men included, on wages up to the SSC ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Article 42(a)(1) of the Social Security Law, as amended in 2019: the establishment pays 'three quarters of one percent' of insured wages. Article 43(a) applies the branch to all insured persons, so the charge is due for a male software engineer exactly as for a female one. The design matters to an employer: article 45 pays the maternity allowance out of the fund at the employee's last insured wage, so the ten weeks of leave in article 70 of the Labour Law are not a wage the employer carries itself.

source.name: Social Security Law No. 1 of 2014, consolidated by the Social Security Corporation with amendments to 16 April 2023, articles 42 to 45

employer_contributions.name: SSC unemployment insurance
employer_contributions.applies: Every insured worker, on wages up to the SSC ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Article 48 of the Social Security Law: the establishment pays half of one percent of insured wages and withholds one percent from the employee. The unemployment benefit is drawn from the worker's own savings account in the fund, and article 58(b) stops it for a non-Jordanian insured person whose account is not in credit, so a foreign hire pays into this branch on the same terms while drawing on it under narrower ones.

source.name: Social Security Law No. 1 of 2014, consolidated by the Social Security Corporation with amendments to 16 April 2023, article 48

statutory_extras.name: End-of-service award under the Labour Law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it does not arise for a worker enrolled with the Social Security Corporation. Article 32 of Labour Law No. 8 of 1996, in the version in force since 16 May 2019, grants an end-of-service award of one month's wage per year of service only to 'the worker who is not subject to the provisions of the Social Security Law'. Since article 4(a) of the Social Security Law enrols every worker covered by the Labour Law regardless of nationality, a salaried hire made through an employer of record is insured, and the pension contributions above take the place of the award. This is the line that separates Jordan from the Gulf ledgers on this site, where the end-of-service accrual is the employer's main charge. Separate company provident funds under article 33 remain possible by agreement and are not modelled.

source.name: Labour Law No. 8 of 1996 and its amendments, consolidated text published by the Ministry of Labour (file dated 24 July 2025), article 32

statutory_extras.name: Old-age contribution reduction for Jordanians under 30
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it lowers a cost and depends on the provider rather than on you. Regulation No. 45 of 2024, in force from 1 August 2024 under the new article 59(c) of the Social Security Law, reduces the old-age, disability and death contributions an establishment pays by 40% for a small establishment of up to 25 workers and by 20% for a medium one of 26 to 50, on request, for an insured person who is Jordanian, has had no earlier compulsory coverage and has not reached 30. An establishment above 50 workers gets nothing, and one that grows past 50 loses the reduction for new hires. The article 59(c) ceiling on any such reduction is 50% of the contribution. Before 2023, article 4(d) instead allowed young workers in new small firms to be left out of old-age insurance altogether; the 2023 amendment removed that clause, so guides written before it describe an exemption that no longer exists.

source.name: Regulation No. 45 of 2024 on reducing old-age, disability and death contributions for workers in private-sector establishments, Social Security Corporation

statutory_extras.name: Work permit fee for a non-Jordanian employee
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is an amount per head, not a share of pay, and applies only to a foreign hire. Article 2 of the Regulation on work permit fees for non-Jordanians No. 142 of 2019, as amended in 2025 and reproduced in the Ministry of Labour's comprehensive guide dated 20 August 2026, sets the fee for issuing or renewing a permit at JOD 350 per worker for a year or part of a year in most sectors, about US$494 at the CBJ parity. A specialised-skills permit above the permitted share of foreign workers costs JOD 1,500 for a year. The same guide makes engineering professions subject to the prior approval of the Jordan Engineers Association. A Jordanian hire triggers none of this.

source.name: Ministry of Labour, comprehensive guide to the rules for issuing work permits for non-Jordanian workers (20 August 2026), including Regulation No. 142 of 2019 as amended

statutory_extras.name: SSC health insurance branch
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the law names the branch but sets no rate for it. Article 3(a)(5) of the Social Security Law lists health insurance among the five branches, and article 3(c) makes it apply only from a Council of Ministers decision fixing its start date, the groups covered and the regions of each phase, with the contribution rates left to a special regulation under article 3(e). This review found no such decision or regulation in force. Private health cover is therefore a benefit the employer chooses to offer, priced per person, and not a statutory charge.

source.name: Social Security Law No. 1 of 2014, consolidated by the Social Security Corporation with amendments to 16 April 2023, article 3

countries.notice_typical: Article 23 of the Labour Law: either party ending an indefinite-term contract must give the other written notice of at least one month, and the contract runs throughout the notice period. Where the employer gives notice, the worker may stop working for the last seven days of it and is still paid in full. Probation under article 35 may not exceed three months, pay during it may not fall below the minimum wage, and the employer may end it without notice or compensation; a worker kept on after probation is on an indefinite contract with the probation counted as service.

countries.name: Japan

employer_contributions.name: Employees' Pension Insurance (kosei nenkin)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees at an applicable workplace, under 70
employer_contributions.notes: Total rate 18.300%, split in half between employer and employee, unchanged since September 2017. The base is the standard monthly remuneration, which tops out at grade 32 = JPY 650,000 a month (JPY 7.8 million a year): the official Tokyo table says that for pension purposes grade 35(32) is read as 'JPY 635,000 and above'. That ceiling is what makes Japan comparatively cheap for senior hires. Bonuses are charged separately up to JPY 1,500,000 per payment.

source.name: Japan Health Insurance Association (Kyokai Kenpo) - Tokyo branch premium table, applicable from the March 2026 payroll month

employer_contributions.name: Health insurance (kenko hoken), Tokyo rate
employer_contributions.applies: Employees enrolled in Kyokai Kenpo; the rate is set per prefecture
employer_contributions.notes: Total 9.85% in Tokyo, split in half, in force from the March 2026 payroll month. This rate is prefectural, not national: an employee registered in another prefecture carries a different one, so a Japan-wide 'employer rate' does not exist. The standard-remuneration ceiling is higher than the pension one, grade 50 = JPY 1,390,000 a month, and annual bonuses are charged up to JPY 5,730,000.

source.name: Japan Health Insurance Association (Kyokai Kenpo) - Tokyo branch premium table, health insurance rate applicable from March 2026

employer_contributions.name: Employment insurance (koyo hoken), general business
employer_contributions.applies: General business; agriculture, forestry, fisheries, sake brewing and construction carry higher rates
employer_contributions.notes: Employer share 8.5/1,000 for fiscal 2026 (1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027), made up of 5/1,000 for unemployment and parental-leave benefits plus 3.5/1,000 for the two employment services. Down from 9/1,000 in fiscal 2025. Uncapped, so unlike pension and health it keeps growing with salary. The employee pays a further 5/1,000.

source.name: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare - Employment insurance contribution rates for fiscal 2026

employer_contributions.name: Child allowance contribution (kodomo kosodate kyoshutsukin)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, whether or not the employee has children
employer_contributions.notes: Paid entirely by the employer: the official table states plainly that the insured person bears none of it. Charged on the pension base, so it stops at the same JPY 650,000 monthly ceiling. Rate unchanged since April 2020.

source.name: Japan Health Insurance Association (Kyokai Kenpo) - Tokyo branch premium table, child allowance contribution note

employer_contributions.name: Workers' accident compensation insurance (rosai hoken), other businesses
employer_contributions.applies: Rate class 94, 'other businesses' - the class an office or software role normally falls into
employer_contributions.notes: Borne entirely by the employer, with no employee share, and uncapped. The rate is set by industry class and runs from 2.5/1,000 to 88/1,000; 3/1,000 is the 'other businesses' class that covers office and information-services work. The class follows the activity the employer declares to the labour bureau, so a provider that has registered a different activity may carry a different rate - worth asking when comparing quotes.

source.name: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare - Workers' accident compensation insurance rate table, in force since 1 April 2024

employer_contributions.name: Child support levy (kodomo kosodate shienkin), new in 2026
employer_contributions.applies: All employees enrolled in health insurance
employer_contributions.notes: Brand new line: first charged on the April 2026 payroll month, paid in May 2026. Total 0.23% split in half with the employee, collected alongside health insurance and on the same base. Do not confuse it with the older child allowance contribution above, which is 0.36% and entirely on the employer. Because 2026 is its first year there is no track record on how the rate will move, so it is re-checked at each monthly data refresh.

source.name: Japan Health Insurance Association (Kyokai Kenpo) - Tokyo branch premium table, child support levy rate applicable from the April 2026 payroll month

statutory_extras.name: Nursing care insurance (kaigo hoken), employees aged 40 to 64
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it depends on the employee's age, not on the job. The official Tokyo table states that category-2 insured persons are those aged 40 to 64, and that a nursing care rate of 1.62% is added to the 9.85% health rate and the 0.23% child support levy for them. The employer half is therefore a further 0.81% of the health insurance base for an employee in that age band, and nothing at all outside it. A provider quoting one flat Japanese employer rate is quietly assuming an age.

source.name: Japan Health Insurance Association (Kyokai Kenpo) - Tokyo branch premium table, nursing care footnote

statutory_extras.name: Summer and winter bonus (shoyo) - customary, not statutory
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because no Japanese statute requires a bonus: the Labour Standards Act only requires that, where a bonus exists, the rules governing it are written into the rules of employment. In practice most Japanese employers pay a summer and a winter bonus worth several months of salary, and a competitive offer usually has to include one. Treat it as a market cost to budget, not a legal charge - and note that bonuses do attract social insurance, capped at JPY 1,500,000 per payment for pension and JPY 5,730,000 a year for health.

source.name: Japan Health Insurance Association (Kyokai Kenpo) - Tokyo branch premium table, bonus contribution ceilings

countries.notice_typical: Thirty days' notice, or pay in lieu of the shortfall, under article 20 of the Labour Standards Act. Article 21 exempts a worker on trial during the first 14 days of employment from that requirement; the Act sets no maximum length for the trial period itself.

countries.name: Kenya

employer_contributions.name: National Social Security Fund (NSSF), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on pensionable earnings up to the Upper Earning Limit
employer_contributions.notes: Section 20(1)(a) of the NSSF Act sets the employer contribution at six per centum of monthly pensionable earnings, and pensionable earnings are defined as the lower of the employee's monthly wages and the Upper Earning Limit. The limit is what moved: the Act's Third Schedule phases it in over five years, and NSSF's notice to employers puts Year 4 into effect in February 2026 with a Lower Earning Limit of KES 9,000 and an Upper Earning Limit of KES 108,000 a month. The employer therefore pays at most KES 540 on the lower band plus KES 5,940 on the band above it, KES 6,480 a month in all, which is the figure this ledger caps at. Providers' own Kenya pages have not all followed the schedule: Deel's still prices NSSF against a maximum salary of KES 36,000, the Year 2 limit, which understates the charge by two thirds at this salary.

source.name: NSSF Kenya - Notice to employers, Year 4 (2026) NSSF contribution rates (Lower Earning Limit KES 9,000; Upper Earning Limit KES 108,000; maximum monthly employer contribution KES 6,480)

employer_contributions.name: Affordable Housing Levy, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the employee's gross monthly salary, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: The Affordable Housing Act, 2024 makes the Kenya Revenue Authority the collector and splits the levy in two equal halves. KRA's public notice states it as 'One point five per centum (1.5%) of the employee's monthly gross salary by the employer', alongside the same rate deducted from the employee. There is no ceiling, so this line grows with pay while the NSSF line stops at KES 108,000 a month - above roughly KES 108,000 the housing levy becomes the larger of the two employer charges. KRA also notes the employer's share is an allowable deduction under section 15 of the Income Tax Act.

source.name: Kenya Revenue Authority - Collection of Affordable Housing Levy by Kenya Revenue Authority (public notice, Affordable Housing Act 2024)

statutory_extras.name: NITA industrial training levy (KES 600 per employee per year)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the amount is too small to show as a ledger line, not because it is optional. The Industrial Training (Training Levy) Order requires that 'an employer shall remit to the Director a levy of six hundred shillings per employee per year or pro rata for their term of service'. At the example salary that is about USD 4.63 a year, or 39 cents a month, too small to show as its own row. It is a real employer charge - the Industrial Training Act states that 'a training levy shall not be deducted from the emoluments of an employee' - and it is worth knowing it is a flat amount per head: it is often quoted as 'KES 50 a month', which is the same figure paid annually. Newly registered businesses are exempt for their first twelve months.

source.name: Kenya Law - The Industrial Training (Training Levy) Order, Legal Notice 113 of 2007 as amended by LN 10 of 2020 and LN 62 of 2021, consolidated to 2022-12-31

statutory_extras.name: Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF), 2.75% - deducted from the employee
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a payroll deduction, not an employer charge. The Social Health Authority sets contributions at 2.75% of gross monthly income with a floor of KES 300 a month and no ceiling, and describes the mechanism plainly: 'Contributions are automatically deducted from employees' gross salaries by their employers at a rate of 2.75%. Employers are responsible for calculating and remitting these payments.' SHIF replaced the NHIF in 2024, and because the employer does the remitting it is easy to find it counted inside an employer cost figure. It reduces the employee's net pay, not your invoice.

source.name: Social Health Authority - Premium rates (SHIF: 2.75% of gross monthly income, deducted by the employer, minimum KES 300, no upper limit)

statutory_extras.name: Work Injury Benefits Act (WIBA) cover - insurance premium, not a percentage charge
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is an insurance premium whose rate depends on the insurer and the occupation, not a statutory percentage of one salary. The Work Injury Benefits Act obliges every employer to hold approved cover for its employees against work injury, and providers price it as a line on the invoice: Deel publishes 0.91% for Kenya. Under an employer of record the policy is the provider's, so what you see is whatever margin and class rating it applies, which is why this ledger will not present a single number as if it were the law.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Kenya page

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month pay - not required by Kenyan law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Employment Act, 2007 does not require a thirteenth month or any annual bonus. Bonuses in Kenya are contractual. What the Act does require on the way out is service pay under section 35(5) and, on redundancy, severance of not less than fifteen days' pay for each completed year of service plus one month's notice or pay in lieu - costs that fall at termination rather than in the monthly run rate.

source.name: Kenya Law - Employment Act, 2007 (consolidated to 2024-04-26), sections 35 and 40

countries.notice_typical: Twenty-eight days for a salary paid monthly, under section 35(1)(c) of the Employment Act, 2007, which makes a contract paying wages at intervals of a month or more terminable at the end of the twenty-eight days following written notice. A probationary contract may be ended on seven days' notice or seven days' wages in lieu. On redundancy the employer owes at least one month's notice or a month's wages in lieu, plus severance of fifteen days' pay for each completed year of service.

source.name: Kenya Law - Employment Act, 2007 (consolidated to 2024-04-26), sections 35 and 40

countries.name: South Korea

assumptions.label: Provider's Korean entity has 150 to 999 employees (employment-security rate 0.65%)
assumptions.notes: The employment-security and vocational-training half of employment insurance is charged on the legal employer's headcount, and under an EOR the legal employer is the provider, whose Korean payroll includes every worker it hosts. The decree sets four rates: 0.25% under 150 staff, 0.45% at 150 or more when the business is a priority-support company, 0.65% from 150 to 999 otherwise, 0.85% at 1,000 or more. A smaller provider would land at 0.25% or 0.45% and a very large one at 0.85%, a spread of 0.6 points of pay; ask the provider which bracket its Korean entity is in.

employer_contributions.name: National Pension (국민연금), employer half
employer_contributions.applies: All workplace subscribers; charged on the standard monthly income between KRW 410,000 and KRW 6,590,000
employer_contributions.notes: The headline rate rose on 1 January 2026. The National Pension Service states that a 9% rate applied from 1998 to 2025 and that from 2026 the rate rises by 0.5 point a year for eight years to reach 13% in 2033, and its own worked example is charged at 9.5%. Employer and employee each pay half, so the employer side is 4.75% in 2026 and will be 4.875% in 2027. The standard monthly income is capped at KRW 6,590,000 from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027 (KRW 6,370,000 in the year before), which is why the employer share stops at KRW 313,025 a month however high the salary goes.

source.name: National Pension Service — Pension contributions: standard monthly income ceiling KRW 6,590,000 for 2026.7.1–2027.6.30, floor KRW 410,000; rate 9% to 2025, +0.5pt a year from 2026 to 13% in 2033, split half and half

employer_contributions.name: National Health Insurance (국민건강보험), employer half
employer_contributions.applies: All employees; 7.19% of monthly remuneration, shared equally between employer and employee
employer_contributions.notes: The Health Insurance Policy Deliberation Committee set the 2026 rate at 7.19% on 28 August 2025, up 0.1 point from 7.09%, and the enforcement decree states the rate as 719 ten-thousandths. Half falls on the employer. A ceiling exists but is far above an engineer's pay: the monthly remuneration premium is capped at KRW 9,183,480 a month for employer and employee together, which is reached only above roughly KRW 128 million of monthly pay, so it is not modelled here.

source.name: Ministry of Health and Welfare — 2026 health insurance contribution rate set at 7.19% (press release, 15th Health Insurance Policy Deliberation Committee of 2025)

employer_contributions.name: Long-term care insurance (노인장기요양보험), employer half
employer_contributions.applies: All health insurance subscribers; a surcharge collected with the health premium and shared equally
employer_contributions.notes: This line is not a percentage of pay in the statute: it is charged as a percentage of the health insurance premium. The Long-Term Care Committee decided on 4 November 2025 that the 2026 rate is 13.14% of the health premium, which the ministry itself restates as 0.9448% of income (0.9182% in 2025). Half of that 0.9448% is the employer's, which is the 0.4724% modelled here. Because it rides on the health premium, it follows the same base and the same ceiling.

source.name: Ministry of Health and Welfare — 2026 long-term care insurance rate 0.9448% of income (13.14% of the health insurance premium), press release of 4 November 2025

employer_contributions.name: Employment insurance (고용보험) — unemployment benefit, employer half
employer_contributions.applies: All insured employees; 1.8% of pay, split equally between employer and employee
employer_contributions.notes: Article 12 of the enforcement decree of the Act on the Collection of Insurance Premiums sets the unemployment-benefit rate at 18 thousandths of pay. Employer and employee each carry 0.9%. Uncapped: unlike pension and health, there is no ceiling on the base, so this line keeps growing with the salary.

source.name: Act on the Collection of Insurance Premiums for Employment Insurance and Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance, Enforcement Decree art. 12 (Presidential Decree 35935, in force 23 December 2025) — unemployment benefit rate 18/1,000

employer_contributions.name: Employment insurance — employment security and vocational training, employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only branch; rate set by the legal employer's headcount
employer_contributions.notes: The same decree article sets four rates by the employer's number of regular employees: 25 ten-thousandths under 150 staff, 45 at 150 or more for a priority-support company, 65 from 150 to 999 otherwise, 85 at 1,000 or more and for the State. Modelled at 0.65% on the declared assumption that the provider's Korean entity employs 150 to 999 people including the workers it hosts; the ministry's own 2026 employment insurance booklet prints the same four brackets. No employee share and no ceiling.

source.name: Act on the Collection of Insurance Premiums, Enforcement Decree art. 12 (Presidential Decree 35935, in force 23 December 2025) — employment security and vocational training rates 25/45/65/85 ten-thousandths by headcount

employer_contributions.name: Industrial accident compensation insurance (산재보험), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only cover; rate set by the employer's registered business type, plus a flat commuting-accident rate
employer_contributions.notes: Two components of the ministry's 2026 notice: 8 per thousand for facility management and business support services, the class a staffing and payroll provider registers under, plus the commuting-accident rate of 0.6 per thousand which is the same for every business type. Neighbouring classes in the same notice show what the choice is worth: professional, health, education and leisure services pay 6 per thousand, finance and insurance 5, construction 35. The 2026 average across all 28 classes is 1.47% including the commuting rate.

source.name: Ministry of Employment and Labour Notice 2025-91 of 31 December 2025 — 2026 industrial accident insurance rates by business type (facility management and business support services 8/1,000; commuting-accident rate 0.6/1,000 for all types), in force 1 January to 31 December 2026

statutory_extras.name: Statutory severance / retirement benefit (퇴직금)
statutory_extras.notes: The largest employer line in this ledger, ahead of the pension. The Employee Retirement Benefit Security Act requires the employer to run a scheme paying at least 30 days of average wages for each year of continuous service, so one month of pay accrues every year, which is 8.33% of annual salary. It is included in the total because it accrues from the first year and providers fund it monthly, unlike a redundancy payment that only falls due on dismissal. Two things push the real figure slightly higher: average wages are the last three months' total pay divided by the days in that period, so bonuses and unused-leave pay enter the base, and a defined-contribution plan obliges the employer to pay in at least one twelfth of total annual remuneration.

source.name: Employee Retirement Benefit Security Act art. 8(1) (Act 21475, in force 18 September 2026) — at least 30 days of average wages for each year of continuous service

statutory_extras.name: Statutory annual leave (15 days from the second year)
statutory_extras.notes: Paid time inside the salary rather than an extra contribution, so it is listed here and left out of the total. Fifteen days a year once one year of service is complete, accruing at one day a month during the first year, with an extra day for every two further years of service. Unused days are paid out, and that payment enters the average wage used for severance.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the South Korea page

countries.notice_typical: Dismissal needs 30 days' written notice or 30 days of ordinary wages in lieu, and no notice is owed in the first three months of employment; dismissal itself must have just cause, which is the harder constraint. Severance is not a dismissal cost in Korea: the statutory retirement benefit of one month per year of service is owed however the contract ends, including resignation, and is payable within 14 days of leaving.

countries.name: Kazakhstan

assumptions.label: Social contribution base: gross less the employee's 10% pension withholding
assumptions.notes: Kazakhstan does not apply its employer charges to one base, it applies them to four. Article 245 of the Social Code defines the base for social contributions as the employee's taxable income minus the mandatory pension contributions withheld from it, and those are 10% of pay under article 249, so the social contribution line runs on 90% of gross. That share is what this assumption carries. The other three lines use their own bases and are expressed directly: employer pension contributions and health deductions apply to gross, and the social tax applies to gross less both the 10% pension withholding and the employee's 2% health contribution, which is why it appears below as an effective 5.28% rather than its statutory 6%.

assumptions.label: The hire was born on or after 1 January 1975
assumptions.notes: Article 248 of the Social Code releases the agent from employer pension contributions for several categories, and the last of them is 'persons born before 1 January 1975'. For an older hire the 3.5% line below simply does not arise, which changes the employer's bill by a fifth. Retirement-age employees and several disability categories are exempt on the same article. A software engineer hired today is almost always inside the charge, which is what this page prices.

employer_contributions.name: Employer pension contribution (ОПВР)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee born on or after 1 January 1975, on monthly income between one and fifty minimum wages
employer_contributions.notes: The newest line in Kazakh payroll and the one that is scheduled to keep rising. Article 251 of the Social Code states that employer pension contributions are made 'at the expense of the agent's own funds' and sets the rate year by year: 1.5% from 1 January 2024, 2.5% from 1 January 2025, 3.5% from 1 January 2026, 4.5% from 1 January 2027 and 5% from 1 January 2028. The 2026 step was enacted by the amending law of 18 July 2025, No. 215-VIII. A multi-year engagement therefore gets more expensive without anyone renegotiating anything: the same salary carries 3.5% this year and 5% from 2028. The base is the income used for the employee's own pension contributions, bounded at one and fifty minimum wages a month, so with the minimum wage at KZT 85,000 for 2026 the ceiling is KZT 4,250,000 a month, far above the salary priced here. Provider pages still showing 2.5% are quoting the 2025 step.

source.name: Social Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan, article 251, rate and procedure for employer pension contributions

employer_contributions.name: Social contributions (социальные отчисления)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on gross less the 10% pension withholding, bounded at one and seven minimum wages a month
employer_contributions.notes: Article 244 of the Social Code sets the rate at 3.5% and then at '5 per cent of the object of calculation of social contributions from 1 January 2025'. What makes this line unusual is its ceiling: article 245 caps the monthly base at seven minimum wages, which is KZT 595,000 for 2026, and floors it at one minimum wage. Because the base is gross less the employee's 10% pension withholding, the cap is reached at about KZT 661,000 of monthly gross - roughly US$17,100 a year at the September 2026 accounting rate. Above that the contribution stops being a percentage and becomes a fixed KZT 29,750 a month, about US$64. On the salary priced here it is already a flat amount, which is why the effective rate of this line falls as pay rises while the other three do not.

source.name: Social Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan, articles 244 and 245, rate and object of calculation of social contributions

employer_contributions.name: Mandatory health insurance deductions (ОСМС), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on the employer's expenditure paid to the employee, capped at forty minimum wages a month
employer_contributions.notes: Kazakh health financing uses two words that translate the same way and mean opposite things. Отчисления are, in the words of article 1 of the health insurance law, 'money paid by employers at the expense of their own funds' - that is this line, at 3% since 1 January 2022 under article 27. Взносы are paid by the insured person and are withheld from pay at 2%; they are not an employer cost and are excluded from the ledger here, though they do reduce the social tax base below. The monthly object is capped at forty minimum wages, KZT 3,400,000 for 2026, which is well above the salary priced here.

source.name: Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 405-V on Mandatory Social Health Insurance, articles 1, 27 and 28

employer_contributions.name: Social tax (социальный налог), effective rate on gross
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on the employer's expenditure on employee income less the 10% pension withholding and the 2% health contribution
employer_contributions.notes: This line changed on 1 January 2026 and most published figures for Kazakhstan have not caught up. The new Tax Code, adopted on 18 July 2025 and in force from 1 January 2026, sets the social tax at 6% in article 557(1), against the 9.5% of the code it replaced, and article 556(2) reduces the taxable object by the mandatory pension contributions and by the employee's mandatory health insurance contributions. Article 558(1) then applies the rate to the object net of those exclusions. Two consequences are worth stating plainly. The statutory 6% lands on 88% of gross - 100 less the 10% pension withholding and the 2% health contribution - so the effective charge on gross is 5.28%, which is the rate carried here. And the old rule that let an employer deduct the amount of its social contributions from the social tax due has not been carried into the new code, so the two are now paid in full side by side. Provider pages quoting 'Social Tax 11%' are describing neither the old rate nor the new one.

source.name: Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan on Taxes and Other Obligatory Payments to the Budget (Tax Code), articles 556, 557 and 558, in force from 1 January 2026

statutory_extras.name: Compulsory employee accident insurance - a premium, not a levy
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a commercial insurance premium whose rate is set by the insurer against the employer's occupational risk class, not a statutory percentage of pay, and named because it is a real legal obligation that an employer of record carries on your behalf. Kazakh law requires every employer to insure its employees against accidents in the course of their duties, and the premium for a low-risk office activity sits at the bottom of the scale: Deel's Kazakhstan page prices it at 0.49% of salary, which would be roughly US$11 a month on the salary here. Expect it either as its own invoice line or folded into the monthly fee, and ask which, because at this size it is easy to miss.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Kazakhstan page

statutory_extras.name: Scheduled employer pension increases - 4.5% in 2027, 5% in 2028
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a future cost rather than a current one, and named because it is the only line on this page that is already legislated to rise. Article 251 of the Social Code sets employer pension contributions at 3.5% from 1 January 2026, 4.5% from 1 January 2027 and 5% from 1 January 2028. On the salary priced here each step adds about US$23 a month. If you are signing a three-year engagement, model the 2028 rate, not this year's.

source.name: Social Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan, article 251(1)

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Kazakh law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code creates no thirteenth-month salary and no statutory annual bonus. Paid annual leave of 24 calendar days under article 88 is paid at average earnings, with no separate holiday supplement. Bonuses and private medical cover are contractual and common in the Almaty technology market; price them as market cost, not as a legal charge.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan, article 88

countries.notice_typical: One month for liquidation of the employer or a reduction in headcount under article 53(1) of the Labour Code, unless the employment or collective agreement sets a longer period, and fifteen working days where the termination follows a fall in production volumes under article 53(2). By agreement the notice period may be replaced by a payment. Probation may not exceed three months under article 36(2), extended to six only for directors, their deputies, chief accountants and heads of branches.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan, article 88

countries.name: Sri Lanka

employer_contributions.name: Employees' Provident Fund (EPF), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee of a covered employer; charged on total monthly earnings with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Twelve per cent of total monthly earnings, and the Central Bank writes it as a floor — "a minimum amount equivalent to 12%" — paid entirely by the employer on top of the employee's own 8%, for a fund of at least 20% of earnings. There is no ceiling and no grade table, so the rupee amount rises with every rupee of salary: at four times the example salary the employer pays four times as much, which is not true of a country whose contributions stop at a grade. "Total earnings" is defined by the fund and is not the same as gross pay: it includes salary, cost-of-living and similar allowances, holiday pay, food allowances and the cash value of food provided, and it excludes overtime, reimbursed travel and incentive or bonus payments — so a bonus-heavy package carries less EPF than a salary-heavy one of the same value.

source.name: Central Bank of Sri Lanka, Employees' Provident Fund — Remitting Contributions: employee's contribution a minimum of 8% of total monthly earnings, employer's contribution a minimum amount equivalent to 12% of total monthly earnings paid totally by the employer, total 20%

employer_contributions.name: Employees' Trust Fund (ETF), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Every private-sector employee; charged on total monthly earnings with no ceiling, and nothing may be deducted from the employee
employer_contributions.notes: Three per cent of total monthly earnings, paid by the employer alone under the Employees' Trust Fund Act No. 46 of 1980. The Board is explicit that it may not be recovered from the employee's pay, which makes it a pure employer cost rather than a shared one — the Board itself calls it non-contributory for the member. It uses the same definition of total earnings as the EPF and, like the EPF, has no ceiling. Employers remit it separately from the EPF, to the ETF Board rather than to the Central Bank, so it is two filings a month, not one.

source.name: Employees' Trust Fund Board — Employer Details: employer's contribution 3% of the total monthly earnings, not to be deducted from the employee's monthly salary or wages; About the Board: employers remit 3% of gross earnings monthly and only the employer contributes

statutory_extras.name: Statutory gratuity on termination (half a month per year, after five years)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is contingent on both a headcount test and a service test, not because it is small. The Payment of Gratuity Act No. 12 of 1983 applies to an employer who has employed fifteen or more workmen on any day in the twelve months before a termination, and it is owed to a worker with at least five completed years of service — however the job ends, including resignation, retirement and death. The rate for a monthly-rated worker is half a month's last-drawn salary for each completed year, payable within thirty days. An EOR hire that lasts under five years never triggers it; one that lasts ten years carries five months of salary at the exit. Ask the provider whether it accrues this monthly or bills it at the end.

source.name: Payment of Gratuity Act No. 12 of 1983, sections 5(1) and 5(2)(a), as reproduced in the Department of Labour's labour code: fifteen or more workmen, five completed years of service, half a month's wage or salary for each year of completed service for a monthly rated workman

statutory_extras.name: Termination compensation under the Commissioner's formula
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it only arises when the employer ends the contract, but it is the number to know before hiring here. Under the Termination of Employment of Workmen (Special Provisions) Act an employer may not end a covered worker's employment without either the worker's prior written consent or the Commissioner's prior written approval, which the Commissioner may grant or refuse at absolute discretion and must answer within three months. The Commissioner's published formula prices the consent: 2.5 months of salary for each year of service in the first five years, then 2.0 months a year to year 14, tapering to 0.5, with a cumulative cap of 48 months and an overall ceiling of LKR 1,250,000 set by that order. The Act does not apply to employers averaging fewer than fifteen workmen, or to a worker with fewer than 180 days of service.

source.name: Termination of Employment of Workmen (Special Provisions) Act No. 45 of 1971, sections 2(1) and 3(1), with the Commissioner of Labour's Order under section 6D of 15 March 2005 (compensation formula: 2.5 months per year for years 1-5, 2.0 for years 6-14, 1.5, 1.0 then 0.5, cumulative maximum 48 months, no payment above LKR 1,250,000), as reproduced in the Department of Labour's labour code

statutory_extras.name: Statutory annual leave (14 days after a completed year)
statutory_extras.notes: Paid time inside the salary rather than an extra contribution. Shop and office employees are entitled to fourteen days of holiday with full remuneration for each year of continuous employment, of which at least seven must be consecutive; in the first year the entitlement is earned at one day per completed two months of service. Seven days of casual leave for private business, ill health or other reasonable cause sit on top of that.

source.name: Shop and Office Employees (Regulation of Employment and Remuneration) Act, annual holiday and casual leave provisions as published by the Department of Labour: fourteen days with full remuneration, not less than seven consecutive, plus casual leave not exceeding seven days

countries.notice_typical: There is no statutory notice period that buys an employer out of a dismissal. Under the Termination of Employment of Workmen (Special Provisions) Act, an employer with fifteen or more workmen on average may not end the employment of a worker with 180 days or more of service without the worker's prior written consent or the Commissioner of Labour's prior written approval; the Commissioner decides at absolute discretion, within three months; section 2 of the 1971 Act calls the decision final, but section 10B, inserted by Act No. 23 of 2022, now lets an employer apply to the Court of Appeal for a writ against an order under section 6 or 6A, on depositing cash security. In practice the exit is negotiated against the Commissioner's compensation formula, which starts at 2.5 months of salary per year of service. Probation has no statutory maximum and is set in the contract.

countries.name: Lithuania

assumptions.label: The contract is open-ended rather than fixed-term
assumptions.notes: The employer's unemployment insurance rate here depends on the kind of contract rather than on the job. Sodra's 2026 rate table gives 1.31% for an open-ended contract (neterminuota darbo sutartis) and 2.03% for a fixed-term one (terminuota darbo sutartis), a gap of 0.72 of a point that is charged for the whole life of the contract. An employer of record normally issues an open-ended contract for a permanent role, which is what this page models. If the provider proposes a fixed-term contract - some do for a first year, or for a project - ask for the unemployment line to be repriced at 2.03%.

assumptions.label: The employer sits in accident insurance group I
assumptions.notes: The accident and occupational disease rate is set per employer, not per job. Sodra publishes four groups for 2026 - 0.14%, 0.49%, 0.7% and 1.4% - and states that a company normally belongs to the first ('Iprastai imone priklauso pirmajai draudeju grupei'), which is why 0.14% is modelled here. The assignment is made each year by order of the Sodra board, and a company lands in group II or above only by appearing on the published lists. Under an employer of record the insured employer is the provider, so the rate that applies is the provider's group, not yours: a provider that has had accident claims across its Lithuanian payroll could sit higher. It is a question worth putting in writing, because the difference between group I and group IV is 1.26 points - most of the whole employer ledger again.

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment social insurance (nedarbo socialinis draudimas)
employer_contributions.applies: Employer share on the employee's calculated pay, at the open-ended contract rate
employer_contributions.notes: The largest of the four employer lines, and the only one whose rate moves with the type of contract: Sodra's 2026 rate table prints 'Neterminuota darbo sutartis - 1,31 proc.' against 'Terminuota darbo sutartis - 2,03 proc.'. No ceiling applies to it. Lithuania does have a contribution ceiling - 60 times the projected average wage, EUR 138,729 for 2026 - but Sodra states in the same place that since 2021 it reaches only the insured person's own contributions: 'nuo 2021 metu VSD imoku lubos taikomos tik apdraustuju VSD imokoms, darbdavio mokamai imoku daliai lubos netaikomos', the ceiling does not apply to the part paid by the employer. So the employer rate on this page is flat whatever the salary, which is the opposite of Japan, Germany or Singapore, where the employer share fades as pay rises.

source.name: Sodra (State Social Insurance Fund Board) - contribution rates for employed persons, 2026 table

employer_contributions.name: Accident at work and occupational disease insurance, group I
employer_contributions.applies: Employers in group I, which Sodra describes as the normal case
employer_contributions.notes: Sodra's 2026 table gives four employer groups - I 0.14%, II 0.49%, III 0.7%, IV 1.4% - assigned each year by order of the Sodra board under article 29(3) of the Law on Social Insurance of Accidents at Work and Occupational Diseases. The 2026 assignment orders are V-531 of 18 December 2025, V-23 of 19 January 2026 and V-26 of 22 January 2026, and the group II and III member lists are published as spreadsheets next to the rate table. An employer is in group I in 2026 if it is not on those lists or if it started trading in 2026. Note what changed between years: group II moved from 0.43% in 2025 to 0.49% in 2026 while group I stayed at 0.14%, as it has since at least 2022.

source.name: Sodra - contribution rates for employed persons, accident insurance groups 2026

employer_contributions.name: Guarantee Fund contribution (imoka i Garantini fonda)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer other than the Bank of Lithuania, budget institutions, political parties, trade unions and religious communities
employer_contributions.notes: Sodra states it in one line: '0,16 proc. nuo asmeniui priskaiciuoto darbo uzmokescio', 0.16% of the pay calculated for the person. The fund pays wages owed when an employer becomes insolvent, so it is the Lithuanian equivalent of Poland's FGSP or Belgium's company-closure fund. The exemption list is short and none of it applies to a commercial employer of record.

source.name: Sodra - contribution rates for employed persons, Guarantee Fund

employer_contributions.name: Long-Term Employment Benefits Fund (Ilgalaikio darbo ismoku fondas)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer other than the Bank of Lithuania and budget institutions, on a base of at least the statutory minimum monthly wage
employer_contributions.notes: The wording carries a floor that the other three lines do not: '0,16 proc. nuo asmeniui priskaiciuoto darbo uzmokescio, ne mazesnio kaip minimalioji menesine alga' - 0.16% of the pay calculated for the person, that pay being not less than the minimum monthly wage. The minimum monthly wage for 2026 is EUR 1,153 a month, so the floor is EUR 13,836 a year and it binds only on part-time or very low-paid work; at the salary on this page it changes nothing. Government Resolution No. 509 of 1 July 2026 sets the minimum monthly wage at EUR 1,245 from 1 January 2027, which will lift this floor to EUR 14,940 a year; the ledger keeps the 2026 figure until then. The fund pays a long-service benefit to employees dismissed after five or more years with the same employer, which is a real thing to know before a redundancy, and it is the newest of the four lines.

source.name: Sodra - contribution rates for employed persons, Long-Term Employment Benefits Fund; minimum monthly wage 2026

statutory_extras.name: Contribution floor - employer funds both sides below the minimum wage
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it never bites at a full-time professional salary, and named because it is expensive when it does. Sodra's rule on contribution floors states that where an insured person's monthly pay is below the statutory minimum monthly wage, the employer must calculate and pay not only the employer's but also the insured person's contributions on a base of at least that minimum, and its own worked example, which Sodra still runs on the 2025 minimum of EUR 1,038, says the shortfall is met 'darbdavio lesomis' - out of the employer's funds. Transposed to the 2026 minimum of EUR 1,153, a EUR 100 month means the employer funds both sides of EUR 1,053. Part-time hires, mid-month starts and unpaid leave are where this shows up; the exemptions are narrow and mostly personal (under 24, drawing a pension, receiving parental benefit, or insured through another employer). That last case narrows on 1 January 2027: Law No. XV-1065 of 25 June 2026, amending article 10 of the State Social Insurance Law, provides that where a person's pay from all employers together is below the minimum monthly wage, each employer paying less than its share of that minimum (the minimum divided by the number of employers) pays additional employee and employer contributions out of its own funds, on an amount Sodra's territorial office calculates and prorates for the days worked. In 2027 that minimum is EUR 1,245 under Government Resolution No. 509 of 1 July 2026; the 2026 rule is the one modelled here.

source.name: Sodra - employment, reporting, contributions and rates: contribution floors and ceilings

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Lithuanian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code creates no thirteenth-month salary and no statutory holiday bonus. Annual leave is paid at the employee's average pay under the same code, not topped up by a holiday supplement of the kind Sweden, Belgium or Finland add. Bonuses, private health cover and a remote-work allowance are normal in the Lithuanian technology market and are entirely contractual; price them as market cost in a competitive offer, never as a legal charge.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Lithuania (Law No XII-2603), consolidated version in force 7 June 2026 to 31 October 2026

statutory_extras.name: Second-pillar pension saving - deducted from the employee, not added by the employer
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is not an employer cost at all, and named because provider pages in several countries fold a pension line into the employer ledger. Sodra lists the 2026 employee contributions as pension 8.72%, sickness 1.99%, maternity 1.81% and health insurance 6.98%, and adds that where the employee takes part in supplementary pension accumulation a further 3% is deducted - 'Jei darbuotojas dalyvauja papildomame pensiju kaupime papildomai priskaiciuojama 3 proc. imoka'. All of it comes out of the employee's pay. Nothing on the Lithuanian employer side funds a pension.

source.name: Sodra - contribution rates for employed persons, employee contributions 2026

countries.notice_typical: One month, or two weeks where the employment has lasted less than a year, under article 57(7) of the Labour Code for dismissal on the employer's initiative without fault on the employee's part. The same provision doubles those periods for employees within five years of pension age and triples them for parents of a child under fourteen, pregnant employees and employees with a disability.

source.name: Labour Code of the Republic of Lithuania (Law No XII-2603), consolidated version in force 7 June 2026 to 31 October 2026

countries.name: Latvia

assumptions.label: The employee is insured for every branch of social insurance
assumptions.notes: Latvia does not have one employer rate, it has a grid. The State Revenue Service publishes the employer's share for each category of insured person, and 23.59% is the line for an ordinary employee insured for all branches. The same table drops the employer to 20.77% for an employee who has reached state pension age, and lower still for several service-pension and disability categories. A software engineer on an open-ended contract is the first line, which is what this page models. If your hire is at or past pension age, the employer side falls by 2.82 points and neither the provider's quote nor most comparison pages will mention it.

employer_contributions.name: Mandatory state social insurance contributions (VSAOI), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the full pay of an employee insured for all branches of social insurance
employer_contributions.notes: This single rate is the whole employer side of a Latvian payslip. The State Revenue Service states it in one sentence - 'Obligato iemaksu likme, ja darba nemejs tiek apdrosinats visiem socialas apdrosinasanas veidiem, ir 34,09 %, no kuriem 23,59 % maksa darba devejs un 10,50 % - darba nemejs' - a total rate of 34.09%, of which the employer pays 23.59% and the employee 10.50%. One line covers pensions, health, unemployment, disability, maternity, sickness, parental cover and accidents at work; Latvia does not bill them separately the way Germany or Poland do. The modelling decision worth stating: no ceiling is applied here even though one exists. The VSAOI base is capped at EUR 105,300 a year for 2026 (it was EUR 78,100 as recently as 2024), but the same VID page explains what happens above it - 'Obligato iemaksu objekts, kas parsniedz maksimalo apmeru, ir solidaritates nodokla objekts un no si objekta veiktas obligatas iemaksas tiek novirzitas solidaritates nodoklim' - the base above the ceiling becomes the object of the solidarity tax, and the contributions paid on it are redirected to that tax. The employer keeps paying; only the name of the payment changes. Capping the line at EUR 105,300 would therefore understate a senior salary, so the rate is carried flat and the solidarity tax is named instead.

source.name: State Revenue Service (Valsts ienemumu dienests) - mandatory state social insurance contributions; rate table updated 2 September 2026

statutory_extras.name: Business risk state fee (uznemejdarbibas riska valsts nodeva)
statutory_extras.notes: Cabinet of Ministers Regulation No. 651 of 4 November 2025, in force from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2026, point 2: 'Valsts nodevas apmers parskata menesi ir 0,36 euro' - the fee is EUR 0.36 per reporting month for each employee with whom an employment relationship has been established; point 3 sets payment by the 23rd of the following month. Regulation No. 533 of 8 September 2026, in force from 1 January 2027, keeps the same EUR 0.36. The State Revenue Service adds that since 1 October 2023 natural persons who employ staff owe it too. It is carried at zero rather than as a contribution line for two reasons: on a EUR 33,000 salary EUR 4.32 a year is about 0.013% of pay, too small to show as its own line at any salary this page prices, and it is a flat head-count fee rather than a share of pay. Its purpose is the insolvency fund that pays wages owed when an employer fails, so under an employer of record the fee follows the provider's payroll, not yours. Expect it as a line on the invoice or folded silently into the monthly fee.

source.name: Cabinet of Ministers Regulation No. 651 (4 November 2025) on the business risk state fee in 2026, point 2, consolidated text in force (likumi.lv)

statutory_extras.name: Minimum contribution object - employer tops up below the floor
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it never binds at a full-time professional salary, and named because it is the Latvian trap on part-time work. Since 1 July 2021 contributions are owed on a minimum object regardless of what was actually paid: VID gives the 2026 figure as EUR 2,340 a quarter, that is EUR 780 a month, calculated by the State Social Insurance Agency and billed to the employer afterwards. A half-time hire at EUR 600 a month is charged as though paid EUR 780. It is worth asking a provider how it handles part-time Latvian contracts, because the top-up arrives as a separate assessment rather than in the ordinary monthly run.

source.name: State Revenue Service - mandatory state social insurance contributions: minimum and maximum contribution object

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Latvian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Law creates no thirteenth-month salary and no statutory holiday bonus. Annual leave is paid at average earnings under the same law, with no separate holiday supplement of the kind Sweden, Belgium or Finland add on top. Bonuses, private health insurance and a remote-work allowance are normal in the Latvian technology market and are contractual; price them as market cost in a competitive offer, not as a legal charge.

source.name: Labour Law (Darba likums), consolidated text on the official legal portal likumi.lv

countries.notice_typical: One month under article 103(1)(3) of the Labour Law for the ordinary employer grounds, including a reduction in the number of employees. The same article sets ten days for several fault-based grounds, immediate notice for the gravest, and two months where the employee has been recognised as a person with a disability. An employee resigning gives one month under article 100(1) unless the contract sets a shorter period.

source.name: Labour Law (Darba likums), consolidated text on the official legal portal likumi.lv

countries.name: Morocco

employer_contributions.name: Family allowances (prestations familiales), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer affiliated to the CNSS, on the whole of pay, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Article 1 of decree 2-01-2723 of 12 March 2002 on CNSS contribution rates, as last amended on 10 December 2014 (Official Bulletin 6317 of 15 December 2014), sets the employer contribution for family allowances at 6.40% of the employee's total gross monthly pay. The MAD 6,000 ceiling in article 4 of the same decree covers only the short-term and long-term lines, so this one runs on the whole of pay. Read in the consolidated collection of social security texts the CNSS publishes, dated 7 January 2026 (Arabic text). It is the largest uncapped employer line in Morocco, and the reason Moroccan employer cost does not collapse at higher salaries the way Egypt's does. The benefit it funds is a flat amount per child, not a percentage.

source.name: CNSS - Recueil des textes legislatifs et reglementaires relatifs au regime de securite sociale (07/01/2026), decree 2-01-2723 of 12 March 2002, article 1

employer_contributions.name: Short-term social benefits (sickness, maternity, death, job loss), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on pay up to the CNSS ceiling of MAD 6,000 a month
employer_contributions.notes: Article 2 of decree 2-01-2723 of 12 March 2002, as amended on 10 December 2014 (Official Bulletin 6317), sets short-term benefits at 1.57% of gross monthly pay: 0.57% for the job-loss allowance (IPE), of which 0.38% employer and 0.19% employee, and 1% for the other short-term benefits, of which 0.67% employer and 0.33% employee. That is 1.05% for the employer and 0.52% for the employee, and article 4 limits the pay taken into account to MAD 6,000 a month. Read in the consolidated collection of social security texts the CNSS publishes, dated 7 January 2026 (Arabic text); the CNSS page on paying contributions gives the same IPE split. More than a third of this employer line is the unemployment benefit.

source.name: CNSS - Recueil des textes legislatifs et reglementaires relatifs au regime de securite sociale (07/01/2026), decree 2-01-2723 of 12 March 2002, articles 2 and 4

employer_contributions.name: Long-term social benefits (retirement, invalidity, survivors), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on pay up to the CNSS ceiling of MAD 6,000 a month
employer_contributions.notes: Article 3 of decree 2-01-2723 of 12 March 2002 sets long-term benefits at 11.89% of gross monthly pay, 7.93% for the employer and 3.96% for the employee, and article 4 limits the pay taken into account to MAD 6,000 a month. Read in the consolidated collection of social security texts the CNSS publishes, dated 7 January 2026 (Arabic text). This is the largest rate of the five and the one the ceiling bites hardest on: at MAD 6,000 a month it is worth MAD 475.80, and it stays at MAD 475.80 whatever the salary. Above roughly MAD 6,000 of monthly pay the uncapped lines - family allowances, health insurance and the training tax - do all the growing.

source.name: CNSS - Recueil des textes legislatifs et reglementaires relatifs au regime de securite sociale (07/01/2026), decree 2-01-2723 of 12 March 2002, articles 3 and 4

employer_contributions.name: Compulsory health insurance (AMO), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the whole of pay, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Article 1 of decree 2-05-734 of 18 July 2005, as amended by decree 2-14-707 of 10 November 2014 (Official Bulletin 6310 of 20 November 2014) with effect from 1 January 2016, sets the AMO contribution for private-sector employees at 4.52% of total pay, split 50% employer and 50% employee, and adds 1.85% of total gross monthly pay borne by the employer alone: 2.26% plus 1.85%, or 4.11%, with no ceiling. Read in the consolidated collection of AMO texts the CNSS publishes, dated 10 September 2025 (Arabic text). The CNSS also publishes the partial exemption under which firms that already held group medical cover before Law 65.00 came into force 'restent uniquement redevables de la cotisation de solidarite, fixee a 1,85%, conformement a l'article 114 de la loi n° 65.00'. That exemption is worth 2.26 points of payroll and is claimed each year on form 325-1-03, so it is worth asking a provider which rate it is actually charging.

source.name: CNSS - Recueil des textes legislatifs et reglementaires relatifs a l'assurance maladie obligatoire de base (10/09/2025), decree 2-05-734 of 18 July 2005, article 1

employer_contributions.name: Vocational training tax (taxe de formation professionnelle)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the whole of pay, with no ceiling; collected by the CNSS
employer_contributions.notes: Article 3 of decree 2-73-633 of 22 May 1974, as amended by decree 2-86-820 of 31 December 1986, sets the vocational training tax at 1.6% of pay, and article 4 assesses it on each employee's total gross monthly pay, allowances and bonuses included, with no ceiling. Read in the consolidated collection of social security texts the CNSS publishes, dated 7 January 2026 (Arabic text). The CNSS collects this tax and publishes the exemptions: embassies and diplomatic missions, mining companies already subject to the mining training fund, and public establishments listed under decree 2.98.523, each on production of specified evidence. A private employer of record is none of those, so the tax applies.

source.name: CNSS - Recueil des textes legislatifs et reglementaires relatifs au regime de securite sociale (07/01/2026), decree 2-73-633 of 22 May 1974, articles 3 and 4

statutory_extras.name: Work-accident insurance - a private policy, not a CNSS contribution
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because Moroccan work-accident cover is bought from a private insurer rather than paid to the CNSS, so its price is a premium set by the insurer and the occupational class, not a statutory percentage. Providers do quote a number: Deel publishes 0.85% of salary for Morocco. Under an employer of record the policy belongs to the provider, so what you pay is its rating and its margin. Adding it would take the Moroccan employer figure on this page from about 15.3% to about 16.0% at the example salary.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Morocco page

statutory_extras.name: Employee contributions of about 6.7% - deducted from pay, not an employer charge
statutory_extras.notes: Read in the same decrees: 0.52% for short-term benefits (0.19% job-loss allowance plus 0.33%) and 3.96% for long-term benefits under decree 2-01-2723 of 12 March 2002, both capped at MAD 6,000 a month, plus 2.26% uncapped for AMO, the employee half of 4.52% under decree 2-05-734 of 18 July 2005, for 6.74% in all. The employee pays nothing towards family allowances or the training tax. The Moroccan employer and employee rates together come to about 27.8% of pay before the ceiling is applied.

source.name: CNSS - Recueil des textes legislatifs et reglementaires relatifs au regime de securite sociale (07/01/2026), decree 2-01-2723 of 12 March 2002, articles 2 to 4; AMO share from decree 2-05-734, article 1

statutory_extras.name: Partial AMO exemption for firms with group cover predating Law 65.00
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a reduction some employers can claim, not a charge. The CNSS states that firms holding group medical cover with an insurer, a mutual or an internal fund before Law 65.00 took effect are only liable for the solidarity contribution of 1.85% under article 114 of that law, and that to keep it they must file form 325-1-03, an 'attestation de benefice d'une couverture medicale' stamped by their insurer, every year. An employer of record set up after 2006 will not hold this exemption, so the 4.11% applies - but it explains why two Moroccan quotes can differ by 2.26 points of payroll and both be correct.

source.name: CNSS - Paiement des cotisations, 'Exoneration partielle du taux de cotisation AMO' (solidarity contribution 1.85%, article 114 of Law 65.00, annual form 325-1-03)

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month pay - not required by Moroccan law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code, Law 65-99, requires no thirteenth month. What it does require at the end of the relationship is notice under article 43 and the decree that sets its length, which for a cadre reaches three months after five years of service - a real cost at exit rather than a monthly one.

source.name: Centre Regional d'Investissement Casablanca-Settat - Code du travail (Law 65-99), articles 43 and 231

countries.notice_typical: Set by decree 2-04-469 of 29 December 2004 under article 43 of the Labour Code, and graded by category and seniority. For cadres et assimiles, the grade a software engineer falls into: one month below a year of service, two months from one to five years, three months beyond five years. For employees and workers: eight days, one month and two months over the same bands. Article 43 of the Code voids any clause setting a shorter period than the regulation allows, and voids outright any clause below eight days.

source.name: Centre Regional d'Investissement Casablanca-Settat - Code du travail (Law 65-99), articles 43 and 231

countries.name: Myanmar

employer_contributions.name: Social Security Board, Health and Social Care Fund, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Insured employees of a registered establishment; charged on monthly wages up to MMK 300,000 a month
employer_contributions.notes: Two per cent from the employer and two per cent from the worker under rule 55(a)(i) of the Social Security Rules 2014, rising to 2.5% each for a person first registered after the age of 60. The base stops at MMK 300,000 a month, the ceiling set by Social Security Board Notification No. 56/2014 and not adjusted since, so any salary above it pays the same MMK 6,000 a month from the employer: a flat amount in practice, well under one per cent of this page's example salary. Rule 55 also writes a further 3% employer contribution to a disability, superannuation and survivors' fund and 1% to an unemployment fund, but rule 56(b) makes those payable only from a date the Ministry fixes by notification, and the unemployment scheme had not been implemented when the ILO reviewed it in 2022. They are not in this total; if they are switched on, the employer rate on the capped base goes from 3% to 7%. Secondary source for the ceiling: the ILO paper cited here, which reads Notification No. 56/2014 section 3(a); the notification itself was not read.

source.name: Social Security Rules 2014 (Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Security Notification No. 41/2014, 2 April 2014), rule 55(a)(i): two per cent by the employer and two per cent by the worker; secondary source: ILO, Policy design for unemployment benefits in Myanmar (2022), p. 12: ceiling of insurable earnings of 300,000 kyats per month (SSB Notification No. 56/2014, section 3(a)), not adjusted since 2014

employer_contributions.name: Social Security Board, Employment Injury Benefit Fund, employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Insured employees of a registered establishment; employer only, on the same capped monthly wage
employer_contributions.notes: One per cent of monthly wages, paid by the employer alone. Rule 58(a) calls it the basic contribution for an establishment when it first registers; rule 58(b) and (c) then move the rate with that establishment's own record of permanent disability and survivors' claims. Under an employer of record the establishment is the provider's Myanmar entity, so the rate that applies is the provider's, not the client's. The MMK 300,000 monthly ceiling is applied here as providers and payroll guides apply it to the whole 3% (a maximum employer payment of MMK 9,000 a month); the ILO paper that cites the ceiling names only the Health and Social Care Fund, so treat the cap on this line as secondary source: provider practice.

source.name: Social Security Rules 2014 (Notification No. 41/2014), rule 58(a): one per cent of the wages or income obtained by the insured person in a month as the basic contribution for the business centre initially registered; rules 58(b)-(c): rate adjusted with the establishment's claims record

statutory_extras.name: Severance pay on termination by the employer (0.5 to 13 months by length of service)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is owed only when the employer ends the contract, not because it is small. The scale in Ministry Notification No. 84/2015 runs by continuous months with the same employer: 0.5 month of pay for 6 to 11 months, 1 month for 12 to 23, 1.5 for 24 to 35, 3 for 36 to 47, 4 for 48 to 71, 5 for 72 to 95, 6 for 96 to 119, 8 for 120 to 239, 10 for 240 to 299 and 13 months from 300 months. Nothing is owed on resignation or on dismissal for misconduct after the third warning. The notification does not say which wage components count. Secondary source: the scale as tabulated by the ILO; the notification itself was not read.

source.name: Secondary source: ILO, Policy design for unemployment benefits in Myanmar (2022), table 28, severance pay by duration of employment under MOLIP Notification No. 84/2015, and table 27, entitlement by reason for termination under the Employment Contract Template (Notification No. 140/2017)

statutory_extras.name: Earned leave (10 days after twelve months of continuous service)
statutory_extras.notes: Paid time inside the salary rather than an extra contribution. Ten days of earned leave once a worker has completed twelve months of continuous service, with proportional leave before that under rule 34 of the Leave and Holidays Rules 2018. On top: up to six days of casual leave a year, and medical leave for a worker with at least six months of service. Secondary source: the ILO summary of the Leave and Holidays Act 1951 and Rules 2018; the Act was not read on an official portal.

source.name: Secondary source: ILO, Myanmar labour laws and COVID-19, frequently asked questions (2021): ten days earned leave after 12 months of continuous service (Leave and Holidays Act 1951, s. 4(1)-(2)), proportional leave under Rule 34, casual leave of a maximum of six days per year

countries.notice_typical: Thirty days' written notice from the employer, with a sound reason, under clause 15(b)(3) of the Ministry's Standard Employment Contract Template (Notification No. 140/2017), and severance on the Notification No. 84/2015 scale on top. A worker usually resigns on 30 days' notice, or 7 days during probation. Probation may not exceed three months and cannot be extended (secondary source: ILO labour law FAQ, 2021, and Duane Morris employment guide, 2018).

countries.name: Malta

assumptions.label: Basic weekly wage as a share of gross
assumptions.notes: Malta's Class 1 contribution and the Maternity Leave Trust Fund levy are both charged on the basic weekly wage: the MTCA's 2026 Class 1 table is laid out by basic weekly wage and reaches its maximum at EUR 559.31 a week. This ledger models basic pay at 100% of gross, which is the most either line can cost. At the example salary, about EUR 755 a week, the ceiling still binds as long as basic pay is at least about 74% of the package, so the figure here only moves for a package paid mostly in allowances. Once basic pay falls below EUR 559.31 a week, about US$33,330 a year, both lines fall in proportion to it.

assumptions.label: The employee was born on or after 1 January 1962 and earns above the Category D threshold
assumptions.notes: Malta's Class 1 table has two columns by date of birth. For a person born from 1 January 1962 the 2026 maximum is reached at a basic weekly wage of EUR 559.31 (Category D, EUR 55.93 a week from the employer); for a person born up to 31 December 1961 it is reached at EUR 490.39 (EUR 49.04 a week). A software engineer on this page's example earns about EUR 755 a week, so the later column and Category D apply. The engine models the weekly cap as an annual base of 52 weeks, and 2026 has 52 Mondays - Deel describes the monthly charge as depending on the number of Mondays in the month.

employer_contributions.name: Class 1 social security contribution, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the basic weekly wage of an employee aged 18 or over, up to the weekly maximum
employer_contributions.notes: The Malta Tax and Customs Administration's 2026 Class 1 table sets the employer's share at 10% of the basic weekly wage in Category C, between EUR 229.45 and EUR 559.30 a week for a person born from 1 January 1962, and at a fixed EUR 55.93 a week in Category D, from EUR 559.31 upwards. The law therefore caps the base, not the rate: 10% of EUR 559.31 is EUR 55.93. The annual cap here is EUR 559.31 times 52 weeks, EUR 29,084.12, which gives about EUR 2,908 a year from the employer whatever the salary above it. Two consequences follow. The effective rate falls as pay rises - at this page's example salary the line is about 7.4% of pay, not 10% - and a pay rise above roughly EUR 29,000 a year costs the employer nothing more in social security. The table was 2025's EUR 54.43 a week at EUR 544.28 before this year's update, and the base is the basic wage, so overtime and bonuses do not enter it.

source.name: Malta Tax and Customs Administration (MTCA) - Class 1 Social Security Contribution Rates, 2026

employer_contributions.name: Maternity Leave Trust Fund contribution, employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the same basic weekly wage and up to the same weekly maximum as Class 1
employer_contributions.notes: The same MTCA table carries a separate 'Maternity' column paid by the employer alone: 0.30% of the basic weekly wage in Category C, and a fixed EUR 1.68 a week in Category D for a person born from 1 January 1962. The table has no separate column by sex, so it is charged on every employee. Capped on the same base as Class 1, it comes to about EUR 87 a year.

source.name: Malta Tax and Customs Administration (MTCA) - Class 1 Social Security Contribution Rates, 2026 (Maternity column)

employer_contributions.name: Government bonuses: statutory bonus and weekly allowance
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, paid by the employer on top of salary; pro rata for part of a period
employer_contributions.notes: Two fixed payments the employer owes every whole-time employee in addition to the agreed salary. The weekly allowance is set by the Weekly Allowance National Standard Order (S.L. 452.62, consolidated version in force, read on legislation.mt): EUR 4.66 for each week of whole-time employment, paid on the last working day of March and of September for the six months before, which is EUR 121.16 for 26 full weeks. The statutory bonus rests on article 23 of the Employment and Industrial Relations Act (Cap. 452, version in force from 2 April 2026): it is paid between 15 and 30 June and between 15 and 23 December, pro rata to annual hours worked for part of a year, and each payment may not be less than half of what the Government announces in the General Estimates for its own employees. The Act does not print the amount; the Department for Industrial and Employment Relations gives it as EUR 135.10 for each payment, so EUR 512.52 a year for a full year of service. For part periods DIER gives EUR 0.74 a calendar day for the bonus. They are flat, so they weigh about 1.3% of pay at this page's example salary and more on a lower one. Many salary quotes state an annual package that already includes them; check whether yours does before adding them again.

source.name: Department for Industrial and Employment Relations (DIER) - Bonus and Weekly Allowances

statutory_extras.name: Extra leave day for each public holiday falling on a weekend
statutory_extras.notes: Regulation 8(1) of the Organisation of Working Time Regulations (S.L. 452.87, consolidated version in force since 26 November 2024) gives a whole-time employee, with effect from 1 January 2021, an additional day of vacation leave in the same calendar year for each national or public holiday that falls on a Saturday, Sunday or weekly day of rest; article 6(c) of the National Holidays and Other Public Holidays Act (Cap. 252) says the same. That Act lists five national holidays and nine public holidays besides Sundays.
