In 2026 three of the fourteen fall on a weekend - 7 June (Sette Giugno) on a Sunday, 15 August (the Assumption) on a Saturday and 13 December (Republic Day) on a Sunday - so a full-time employee has 24 days of basic leave plus 3, or 27 paid days off beside the holidays. Shown for planning rather than added to the total, because the salary already pays for these days; the count changes every year with the calendar.

source.name: Organisation of Working Time Regulations (S.L. 452.87), regulation 8(1), version in force since 26 November 2024

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Maltese law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because Malta has no statutory thirteenth salary. What it has instead are the fixed government bonuses (EUR 512.52 a year), which are priced in the ledger above, and the yearly cost-of-living adjustment that DIER describes as added to the basic wage - EUR 4.66 a week for 2026 - which becomes part of salary rather than a separate charge.

source.name: Department for Industrial and Employment Relations (DIER) - National Minimum Wage (2026 COLA example)

countries.notice_typical: Set by continuous service, per DIER: one week after more than one month, two weeks after more than six months, four weeks after more than two years, eight weeks after more than four years, then one more week for each further year after seven years up to twelve weeks; longer periods may be agreed for technical, administrative, executive or managerial posts. During probation, one week applies once the employee has worked more than one month.

source.name: Department for Industrial and Employment Relations (DIER) - National Minimum Wage (2026 COLA example)

employer_contributions.name: IMSS — Sickness & maternity, fixed quota (cuota fija)
employer_contributions.applies: Fixed amount per employee, independent of salary
employer_contributions.notes: 20.40% of one UMA per day, paid for every employee regardless of salary (LSS Art. 106 / Decreto DOF 16-12-2020). Modelled as a flat amount: 0.2040 x the 2026 daily UMA of MXN 117.31 x 365 = MXN 8,734.90 per year. This percentage is supported by a secondary source citing the law; the JS-rendered IMSS and DOF percentage pages were not directly retrievable when checked.

source.name: IDC Online — "Factores de las cuotas y aportaciones 2026" (cites LSS + Decreto DOF 16-dic-2020)

employer_contributions.name: IMSS — Sickness & maternity, excess quota (cuota adicional)
employer_contributions.notes: 1.10% employer share on the part of the contribution base (SBC) above three times the daily UMA (the first 3 UMA are covered by the fixed quota), up to the general 25-UMA/day ceiling. Modelled exactly as a band: 3 x UMA 117.31 x 365 = MXN 128,454.45 to 25 x UMA x 365 = MXN 1,070,453.75 per year. Secondary source (see cuota fija note). Base: the SBC, not the gross salary. LSS Art. 27 builds the SBC from every payment for the work, including "gratificaciones" and "primas" (Ley del Seguro Social, Camara de Diputados, texto vigente, last reform DOF 15-01-2026, read 2026-10-02), so the 15-day aguinaldo and the first-year vacation premium (25% of 12 days) enter it. Integration factor: (365 + 15 + 12 x 0.25) / 365 = 383/365 = 1.049315, applied to gross before the floor and the 25-UMA cap. This is the legal minimum: richer benefits (more aguinaldo days, a longer vacation, taxable vouchers) raise the SBC further, so the cost is at least this.

source.name: IDC Online — "Factores de las cuotas y aportaciones 2026" (cites LSS + Decreto DOF 16-dic-2020)

employer_contributions.name: IMSS — Medical expenses for pensioners
employer_contributions.notes: 1.05% employer share of the salario base de cotizacion (SBC), capped at 25 UMA/day. Secondary source (see cuota fija note). Base: the SBC, at least gross x 1.049315 (LSS Art. 27, see the excedente note).

source.name: IDC Online — "Factores de las cuotas y aportaciones 2026" (cites LSS + Decreto DOF 16-dic-2020)

employer_contributions.name: IMSS — Sickness & maternity, cash benefits (en dinero)
employer_contributions.notes: 0.70% employer share of the SBC, capped at 25 UMA/day. Secondary source (see cuota fija note). Base: the SBC, at least gross x 1.049315 (LSS Art. 27, see the excedente note).

source.name: IDC Online — "Factores de las cuotas y aportaciones 2026" (cites LSS + Decreto DOF 16-dic-2020)

employer_contributions.name: IMSS — Disability & life insurance
employer_contributions.notes: 1.75% employer share of the SBC, capped at 25 UMA/day. Secondary source (see cuota fija note). Base: the SBC, at least gross x 1.049315 (LSS Art. 27, see the excedente note).

source.name: IDC Online — "Factores de las cuotas y aportaciones 2026" (cites LSS + Decreto DOF 16-dic-2020)

employer_contributions.name: IMSS — Daycare & social benefits
employer_contributions.notes: 1.00% employer share of the SBC, capped at 25 UMA/day. Secondary source (see cuota fija note). Base: the SBC, at least gross x 1.049315 (LSS Art. 27, see the excedente note).

source.name: IDC Online — "Factores de las cuotas y aportaciones 2026" (cites LSS + Decreto DOF 16-dic-2020)

employer_contributions.name: IMSS — Retirement (Retiro)
employer_contributions.notes: 2.00% employer share of the SBC, capped at 25 UMA/day. Also confirmed independently by PwC Tax Summaries ("2% on the base salary of the employee is paid by the employer for the concept of retirement"). Secondary source. Base: the SBC, at least gross x 1.049315 (LSS Art. 27, see the excedente note).

source.name: IDC Online — "Factores de las cuotas y aportaciones 2026" (cites LSS + Decreto DOF 16-dic-2020)

employer_contributions.name: IMSS — Old-age & unemployment-in-old-age (Cesantia y Vejez, CEAV)
employer_contributions.notes: Employer CEAV quota is progressive by SBC/UMA ratio under the 2020 pension reform (Decreto DOF 16-12-2020, Art. Segundo Transitorio), rising every year to 2030. 2026 table: 1 SM = 3.150%; 1.01-1.50 UMA = 3.676%; 1.51-2.00 UMA = 4.851%; 2.01-2.50 UMA = 5.556%; 2.51-3.00 UMA = 6.026%; 3.01-3.50 UMA = 6.361%; 3.51-4.00 UMA = 6.613%; 4.01+ UMA = 7.513%. A gross salary above roughly 4.01 UMA (~$171,700 MXN, ~$10,100 USD/year at the 2026 UMA) falls in the top 7.513% bracket -- true for effectively every salary this calculator models, including the $36,000 example. Secondary sources, cross-confirmed. Base: the SBC, at least gross x 1.049315 (LSS Art. 27, see the excedente note).

source.name: Manuel Nevarez y Asociados — "Tabla para el calculo de las cuotas patronales de Cesantia en Edad Avanzada y Vejez aplicable en 2026" (cites Decreto DOF 16-dic-2020)

employer_contributions.name: IMSS — Occupational risk insurance (prima de riesgo)
employer_contributions.applies: Class I (ordinary/office risk) minimum premium — applies to desk-based roles such as software engineers
employer_contributions.notes: Employer-only premium set by risk class (LSS Art. 73), ranging roughly 0.5%-15% of the SBC depending on the employer's accident record and industry. Shown here is the Class I minimum premium (0.54355%), the class for low-risk office work, capped at 25 UMA/day. A logistics, manufacturing or field-labor employer would fall into a higher class. Secondary source (specialized payroll firm). Base: the SBC, at least gross x 1.049315 (LSS Art. 27, see the excedente note).

source.name: SDV — "Cuotas IMSS 2026: Tabla Obrero-Patronal Completa" (Clases de Riesgo de Trabajo, Art. 73 LSS)

employer_contributions.name: INFONAVIT — Housing fund contribution
employer_contributions.notes: 5.00% employer contribution to the national housing fund on the same SBC used for IMSS, capped at 25 UMA/day. Confirmed on INFONAVIT's own site ("el empleador debe aportar el 5% del salario") and by Ley del INFONAVIT Art. 29-II ("cinco por ciento sobre el salario de los trabajadores a su servicio"; "En lo que corresponde a la integración y cálculo de la base y límite superior salarial para el pago de aportaciones, se aplicará lo contenido en la Ley del Seguro Social", Camara de Diputados, texto vigente, last reform DOF 21-02-2025, read 2026-10-02), independently corroborated by PwC Tax Summaries ("5% ... for the concept of housing must be paid by the employer"). Base: the SBC, at least gross x 1.049315 (LSS Art. 27, see the excedente note).

source.name: INFONAVIT — "Aportaciones patronales a Mi Ahorro"

employer_contributions.name: State payroll tax (impuesto sobre nominas)
employer_contributions.applies: Levied by the state where the employee works; rate set by each state
employer_contributions.notes: Modelled at 3%. Each state sets its own rate (roughly 2-4% of payroll); PwC's Mexico summary (reviewed 6 Aug 2026) cites Mexico City as the example, and Mexico City raised its rate to 4% from 2025 (Codigo Fiscal CDMX art. 158, per CDMX business-chamber sources). The EOR bills the rate of the state where the employee works. Secondary source. Base: all pay for the work, aguinaldo and vacation premium included, as in Mexico City, whose Codigo Fiscal art. 156 lists "Premios, primas, bonos, estímulos e incentivos" and "Gratificaciones y aguinaldos" among the taxed payments (Congreso CDMX copy, last reform published 02-09-2021, read 2026-10-02). Modelled as gross x (1 + 0.5/12 + 0.0082) = 1.049867, the same aguinaldo and vacation-premium extras this page adds below.

source.name: PwC Tax Summaries - Mexico, Corporate, Other taxes (Payroll tax)

statutory_extras.name: Aguinaldo (13th-month bonus)
statutory_extras.notes: 15 days of salary minimum, paid before 20 December (LFT Art. 87: "un aguinaldo anual ... equivalente a quince dias de salario, por lo menos"). Modeled as 15/30 = 0.5 extra month of gross pay.

source.name: Ley Federal del Trabajo, Articulo 87 (Orden Juridico Nacional, gob.mx)

statutory_extras.name: Vacation premium (prima vacacional)
statutory_extras.notes: 25% premium on the pay corresponding to vacation days (LFT Art. 80: "prima no menor de veinticinco por ciento sobre los salarios"), on top of the vacation pay itself. First-year minimum is 12 paid vacation days (LFT Art. 76, "vacaciones dignas" reform, in force since 2023). Calc: 12 days x 25% = 3 days' pay equivalent = 3/365 = 0.82% of annual gross.

source.name: Ley Federal del Trabajo, Articulos 76 y 80 (Orden Juridico Nacional, gob.mx)

statutory_extras.name: Profit sharing (PTU)
statutory_extras.notes: 10% of the company's adjusted taxable income is distributed among employees (LFT Art. 117-120 sets the obligation; the 10% figure is fixed by the Comision Nacional para la PTU). Per-employee payout is capped at the higher of 3 months' salary or the average PTU received over the last 3 years; not due in a company's first year of operation. Not computable from an individual salary alone, so excluded from the total (in_total: false). Secondary source (PwC Tax Summaries, an approved fallback per project rules).

source.name: PwC Tax Summaries — Mexico, Corporate, Other taxes (Employees' statutory profit sharing)

payments.name: Aguinaldo
payments.deadline: before 20 December

payments.name: Prima vacacional
payments.deadline: with the vacation pay; leave is granted within 6 months after the service anniversary (art. 81), so the cash month is a scenario input

payments.name: PTU (profit sharing)
payments.deadline: within 60 days after the annual tax payment date; the month (May for companies filing the annual return in March) is inferred, the LISR deadline was not read today

source.quote: un aguinaldo anual que deberá pagarse antes del día veinte de diciembre, equivalente a quince días de salario, por lo menos

countries.name: Malaysia

assumptions.label: Employee is a Malaysian citizen or permanent resident
assumptions.notes: This is the decisive assumption for Malaysia, and it moves the total by about ten points. The EPF Third Schedule puts Malaysians, permanent residents and non-Malaysians who registered as members before 1 August 1998 in Part A, where the employer pays 12% or 13%. A non-Malaysian who first registered from 1 August 1998 falls under Part F: employer 2% and employee 2%, with no wage limit, for the October 2025 salary month onwards. SOCSO, the Employment Insurance System and the HRD Corp levy are not affected in the same way - the levy is charged on Malaysian employees, and SOCSO covers foreign workers under the Third Schedule of Act 4. If your hire is a foreign national in Malaysia, ask the provider for a Part F quote instead of this one.

assumptions.label: Employee is under 60 years old
assumptions.notes: Age changes two lines at once. From 60, a Malaysian employee's EPF drops to an employer share of 4% with no employee share (Third Schedule Part E), and SOCSO moves from the First Category, which is 1.75% for the Employment Injury and Invalidity Schemes, to the Second Category, which is 1.25% and covers Employment Injury only. The Employment Insurance System applies to employees aged 18 to 60. A hire aged 60 or over therefore costs roughly nine points less than the figure on this page.

employer_contributions.name: EPF employer contribution (monthly wages above MYR 5,000)
employer_contributions.applies: Malaysians, permanent residents and pre-1998 non-Malaysian members under 60, on monthly wages above MYR 5,000
employer_contributions.notes: Employer 12%, employee 11%, under Part A of the EPF Third Schedule in force for the October 2025 salary month onwards. There is no wage ceiling on EPF, which is what makes Malaysia's employer cost rise steadily with pay while SOCSO and the Employment Insurance System stop at MYR 6,000 a month. One detail no guide prints: employers are not allowed to apply the exact percentage except above MYR 20,000 a month - below that the ringgit amount comes from the wage ranges in the Third Schedule and is rounded up to the next ringgit, so the real deduction is a few ringgit above the percentage this engine computes. EPF's own example puts RM816 against RM805.30 on a wage of RM6,710.80.

source.name: EPF (KWSP) - Mandatory Contribution, employer responsibilities, section 43(1) EPF Act 1991

employer_contributions.name: EPF employer contribution (monthly wages of MYR 5,000 or less)
employer_contributions.applies: Only when monthly wages are MYR 5,000 or less; above that the employer rate falls to 12%
employer_contributions.notes: Employer 13%, employee 11%, under the same Part A of the Third Schedule. The rate is not a band: at MYR 5,000 a month and below the whole wage carries 13%, and one ringgit higher the whole wage carries 12%, so an employer just above the line pays less in total than one just below it. Move the salary slider below MYR 60,000 a year in local currency and this line replaces the 12% one.

source.name: EPF (KWSP) - Mandatory Contribution, employer responsibilities, section 43(1) EPF Act 1991

employer_contributions.name: SOCSO, First Category (Employment Injury and Invalidity)
employer_contributions.applies: Employees under 60, for both the Employment Injury Scheme and the Invalidity Scheme
employer_contributions.notes: PERKESO states that the First Category rate 'comprises 1.75% of employer's share and 0.5% of employees' monthly wages according to the contribution schedule'. From 1 October 2024 the wage ceiling for contributions rose from MYR 5,000 to MYR 6,000 a month, so MYR 72,000 a year, and above it the contribution is frozen at the ceiling amount. The published schedule works in wage bands rather than a straight percentage, and its top band gives a maximum employer contribution of MYR 104.15 a month, a little under the MYR 105 this engine computes at the ceiling.

source.name: PERKESO (SOCSO) - Contributions under the Employees' Social Security Act 1969

employer_contributions.name: Employment Insurance System (EIS/SIP)
employer_contributions.applies: Private-sector employees aged 18 to 60
employer_contributions.notes: Contributions to the Employment Insurance System total 0.4% of the assumed monthly salary, 0.2% from the employer and 0.2% from the employee, under the Second Schedule and section 18 of the Employment Insurance System Act 2017. The same MYR 6,000 monthly ceiling applies from 1 October 2024, so MYR 72,000 a year, and the schedule's maximum employer contribution is MYR 11.90 a month. It is the smallest line on any Malaysian payslip and the one most often left out of a foreign employer's budget.

source.name: PERKESO - Employment Insurance System Act 2017, coverage and contribution rates

employer_contributions.name: HRD Corp levy (human resources development)
employer_contributions.applies: Employers with 10 or more Malaysian employees, which every employer of record in Malaysia is
employer_contributions.notes: HRD Corp states that 'for employers with 10 or more Malaysian employees, it is COMPULSORY to register with HRD Corp. The monthly levy is charged at the rate of 1% of the monthly wages of employees.' Employers with five to nine Malaysian employees may register instead at 0.5%. Because the legal employer under an employer-of-record arrangement is the provider, and a provider's Malaysian employing entity normally has well over ten Malaysian employees, the 1% rate is the one that reaches your invoice - even though you would be in the optional band, or outside the scheme entirely, if you hired one person through your own entity. There is no wage ceiling. The levy funds training claims the provider, not you, is entitled to make.

source.name: HRD Corp - Registered Employers, terms and conditions for new registration (PSMB Act 2001)

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Malaysian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Employment Act 1955 creates no thirteenth-month or annual-bonus entitlement. A contractual bonus is common in the Malaysian market and, once it is paid, it is wages: EPF, SOCSO, the Employment Insurance System and the HRD Corp levy all fall on it. Budget a bonus as market cost plus about 13% of itself, not as a legal charge.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Malaysia page

statutory_extras.name: Termination and lay-off benefits
statutory_extras.notes: Under regulation 6(1) of the Employment (Termination and Lay-Off Benefits) Regulations 1980, the payment is not less than ten days' wages for every year of service below two years, fifteen days' wages a year from two to five years, and twenty days' wages a year from five years, pro rata for an incomplete year to the nearest month. It is owed once the employee has twelve months of continuous service and the contract ends for any reason other than retirement at a contractual age, dismissal for misconduct after due inquiry, or a voluntary resignation. Paragraph 1A of the First Schedule to the Employment Act 1955 disapplies section 60J, under which these Regulations are made, to an employee whose wages exceed MYR 4,000 a month, so above that line the exit cost is whatever the contract says. Deel's Malaysia guide of 9 June 2026 adds that a redundancy termination is generally not available for an employee held through an employer of record, mutual termination being the route used instead. It is carried at zero because it falls due on termination rather than monthly.

source.name: Employment (Termination and Lay-Off Benefits) Regulations 1980, regulations 3, 4 and 6 (P.U. (A) 338/83 as last amended by P.U. (A) 92/2011, in force from 1 April 2011), with the Employment Act 1955, section 60J and First Schedule paragraph 1A (Attorney General's Chambers updated text as at 1 January 2023), both as published by the Department of Labour of Peninsular Malaysia

countries.notice_typical: Where the contract is silent, the Employment Act ladder applies: four weeks below two years of service, six weeks from two to five years, eight weeks beyond five. Payment in lieu or garden leave is allowed. Probation length is not fixed by statute; contracts commonly run three to six months.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Malaysia page

countries.name: Nigeria

assumptions.label: Pension contribution base as a share of gross
assumptions.notes: The Pension Reform Act 2014 charges the employer on 'monthly emoluments', which it defines as 'total emoluments as may be defined in the employee's contract of employment but shall not be less than a total sum of basic salary, housing allowance and transport allowance'. The law therefore sets a floor on the base, not a ceiling. This ledger models the base at 100% of pay, which is what a single all-in salary produces and the most the Act can cost; a Nigerian package split into basic plus housing and transport allowances narrows the base towards that statutory floor, and the pension line falls with it. Move the selector to see the effect - it changes only the pension line, because the NSITF and ITF levies are charged on total payroll either way.

employer_contributions.name: Contributory Pension Scheme, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Employers with three or more employees, on the employee's monthly emoluments, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Section 4(1) of the Pension Reform Act 2014 sets the rates 'relating to his monthly emoluments' at 'a minimum of ten per cent by the employer' and a minimum of eight per cent by the employee. Two words in that sentence do work. 'Minimum' means an employer may agree to more, and section 4(4) lets one carry the whole scheme at no less than 20% of monthly emoluments. 'Monthly emoluments' is defined in the Act as total emoluments under the contract, but never less than basic salary plus housing and transport allowances - a floor on the base rather than a cap. There is no earnings ceiling, so this line is a straight percentage at every salary.

source.name: National Pension Commission (PenCom) - Pension Reform Act 2014, section 4(1) and the definition of 'monthly emoluments'

employer_contributions.name: Employees' Compensation Fund (NSITF), employer contribution
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on total monthly payroll, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Section 33(1) of the Employees' Compensation Act 2010 obliges an employer to pay into the Employees' Compensation Fund managed by the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund. The National Industrial Court of Nigeria states the obligation in those terms in a judgment it published on 7 May 2025: an employer 'is obligated to make a minimum monthly contribution of 1% of its total monthly payroll into the Employees' Compensation Fund managed by the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund Management Board'. It is charged on payroll rather than on a capped insurable wage, and it is the Nigerian equivalent of the work-injury cover that many countries buy from a private insurer.

source.name: National Industrial Court of Nigeria - 'Employer is obligated to pay minimum 1% contribution of total monthly payroll into Employees' Compensation Fund', judgment reported 7 May 2025 (Employees' Compensation Act 2010, s. 33(1))

employer_contributions.name: Industrial Training Fund levy
employer_contributions.applies: Employers with five or more employees, or fewer than five but with annual turnover of NGN 50m or above
employer_contributions.notes: The Industrial Training Fund (Amendment) Act 2011 substitutes a new section 6(1): 'Every employer having either 5 or more employees in his establishment, or having less than 5 employees but with a turnover of N50m and above per annum, shall, in respect of each calendar year and or the prescribed date, contribute to the Fund one per centum of his total annual payroll.' The threshold is why this line is sometimes said not to apply to a first hire. Under an employer of record it always applies: the employer of record is the employer, and it is well past both tests. The Act also lets the Ministry vary the rate by order published in the Gazette.

source.name: Industrial Training Fund - Industrial Training Fund (Amendment) Act 2011 (No. 19), section 6 substituting section 6 of the Principal Act

statutory_extras.name: Group life insurance of three times annual emoluments - premium, not a percentage charge
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is an insurance premium, not a rate fixed by law. Section 4(5) of the Pension Reform Act 2014 requires that 'every employer shall maintain a Group Life Insurance Policy in favour of each employee for a minimum of three times the annual total emolument of the employee'. The law fixes the cover, the insurer fixes the price, so what appears on an invoice is a commercial number: Deel publishes 1.8% of salary for Nigeria. On a USD 20,000 salary that single line would be nearly as large as the NSITF and ITF levies combined, 1.8% against 2%, which is why it is worth asking a provider to quote it separately rather than reading it as part of the statutory total.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Nigeria page

statutory_extras.name: National Housing Fund, 2.5% - deducted from the employee
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the private-sector National Housing Fund contribution is a deduction from the employee's monthly income that the employer withholds and remits, with no matching employer share. Deel lists a National Housing Development Fund among Nigerian benefits without putting a percentage against it in the employer cost, which is consistent: the money comes out of pay.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Nigeria page

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month pay - not required by Nigerian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Act contains no thirteenth month or annual bonus obligation. Bonuses are contractual, and in practice a Nigerian offer that competes for software engineers usually carries one by contract rather than by law.

source.name: Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment (NELEX) - Labour Act, Cap L1 LFN 2004, Part I

countries.notice_typical: By length of service, under section 11(2) of the Labour Act: one day where the contract has run three months or less, one week between three months and two years, two weeks between two and five years, and one month at five years or more. Notice of a week or more must be in writing. The statute is a floor - contracts for senior staff commonly provide one to three months - and a Nigerian hire of under two years' standing can be released on a week.

source.name: Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment (NELEX) - Labour Act, Cap L1 LFN 2004, Part I

countries.name: Netherlands

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (AWf, low rate for permanent contracts)
employer_contributions.applies: Applies when the employment contract is for an indefinite period, is in writing, and is not an on-call (oproep) contract — the standard case for a full-time permanent EOR hire modelled here. This is the calculator's default AWf rate.
employer_contributions.notes: 2.74% in 2026 (unchanged from 2025), capped at the 2026 maximumpremieloon of EUR 79,409 (same cap for AWf, Aof, Whk and Zvw). Fixed-term or on-call contracts pay the high AWf rate of 7.74% instead; EOR hires modelled here are indefinite contracts.

source.name: Belastingdienst — Premiedifferentiatie WW: lage en hoge AWf-premie (2026)

employer_contributions.name: Disability fund contribution (Aof, medium/large employer rate)
employer_contributions.applies: Applies to medium and large employers (payroll above the small-employer threshold). Used as the calculator's default Aof rate, since EOR providers are typically classified as medium/large employers by total payroll.
employer_contributions.notes: 7.63% in 2026 (down from 7.64% in 2025), capped at EUR 79,409. Small employers pay 6.27%; EOR providers are classified as medium/large employers by total payroll, so the high rate is the realistic one for an EOR hire. For 2027 the draft budget of the Ministry of Social Affairs (Rijksbegroting SZW 2027, proposed, not yet final) puts the Aof rate at 8.03% for larger employers and 6.67% for small ones; the engine keeps the 2026 rate.

source.name: Belastingdienst — Calculating employed persons' insurance contributions (rates 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Return to Work Fund contribution (Whk — WGA + Ziektewet-flex, sector average)
employer_contributions.applies: National average of the two differentiated Whk components for 2026: WGA (0.96%) + Ziektewet-flex (0.56%). The employer's actual rate is set individually by the Belastingdienst per year based on sector and company size (small/medium/large), and can be materially higher or lower than this average.
employer_contributions.notes: The average WGA percentage rose from 0.83% in 2025 to 0.96% in 2026, while the average Ziektewet percentage rose from 0.50% to 0.56%. Their combined average is used as an indicative modelling assumption; the provider's actual Whk rate can differ. UWV has set the 2027 average Whk premium at 1.67% (+0.15 point), per the same budget memorandum; the engine keeps the 2026 rate until 1 January 2027.

source.name: UWV — Gedifferentieerde premies WGA en Ziektewet 2026

employer_contributions.name: Healthcare Insurance Act employer levy (Zvw)
employer_contributions.applies: Standard employer-paid healthcare levy on wages from current employment (the case modelled here). A different, lower 'bijdrage Zvw' rate applies to some other income categories (e.g. certain benefit payments) and is not modelled.
employer_contributions.notes: 6.10% in 2026, down from 6.51% in 2025. Maximumbijdrage-inkomen (contribution wage cap) for 2026 is €79,409, up from €75,864 in 2025 — same cap family as AWf/Aof/Whk.

source.name: Belastingdienst — Percentages inkomensafhankelijke bijdrage Zvw (2026)

statutory_extras.name: Holiday allowance (vakantiegeld)
statutory_extras.notes: Statutory minimum of 8% of gross annual salary, added on top of 12 monthly salaries (Wet minimumloon en minimumvakantiebijslag). Caution: Dutch salary figures are sometimes quoted inclusive of vakantiegeld and sometimes exclusive — confirm before stacking this on top of an already-inclusive salary figure.

source.name: Business.gov.nl — Holiday allowance

statutory_extras.name: Supplementary company pension
statutory_extras.notes: There is no general legal obligation for every employer to offer a pension scheme. A pension can become mandatory under a CAO (collective labour agreement), a compulsory sectoral pension fund (bedrijfstakpensioenfonds), or an occupational scheme; employer contributions then commonly vary between 8% and 20% of pensionable salary. This item is excluded because no single national rate exists. The applicable sector and CAO must be checked before treating the total as final.

source.name: Business.gov.nl — Pension schemes in the Netherlands

statutory_extras.name: Transition payment (transitievergoeding) on termination
statutory_extras.notes: Statutory severance owed on dismissal (not an annual cost): 1/3 of one month's gross salary per full year of service, pro-rated for partial years, from day one of employment. Capped in 2026 at €102,000 gross, or one gross annual salary if that is higher. Excluded from the annual total because it is a contingent liability triggered only by termination.

source.name: Rijksoverheid.nl — Hoe hoog is de transitievergoeding als ik word ontslagen?

countries.notice_typical: Employee: 1 month statutory minimum (can be extended by contract, up to 6 months). Employer: scales with tenure — 1 month under 5 years of service, 2 months at 5–10 years, 3 months at 10–15 years, 4 months at 15+ years.

countries.name: Norway

assumptions.label: Employer registered in Oslo, which is zone I for the employer's national insurance contribution
assumptions.notes: The rate follows the zone in which the employer (or its registered sub-unit) sits, not where the employee lives. Zone I carries the full 14.1%; the other zones carry 10.6%, 6.4%, 5.1%, 7.9% and, in zone V, nothing at all.

assumptions.label: Occupational pension funded at the legal minimum of 2% of pay up to 12 G
assumptions.notes: The Mandatory Occupational Pension Act sets a floor, not a rate. Many Norwegian employers fund 5% or more, and a provider that already runs a scheme will quote whatever that scheme pays.

assumptions.label: Holiday pay modelled as a 2.19% surplus over the pay withheld for the 25 statutory holiday days
assumptions.notes: Holiday pay of 10.2% replaces salary for the leave period rather than being added to it. Deducting 25 of 26 virkedager of a month's salary, which is 8.01% of annual pay, leaves 2.19% as new money. This is a declared modelling point, not a rate printed in the Act.

employer_contributions.name: Employer's national insurance contribution (arbeidsgiveravgift)
employer_contributions.applies: Employers registered in zone I, which includes Oslo
employer_contributions.notes: The Storting sets the rate annually rather than the National Insurance Act, and it is differentiated by geography: the 2026 decision gives 14.1% in zone I, then 10.6%, 6.4%, 5.1% and 7.9% by zone, and 0% in zone V. A company with registered sub-units computes the rate per sub-unit, and work performed mainly in another zone is charged at that zone's rate unless it is remote work in a cheaper zone. There is no pay ceiling and no surcharge above a salary threshold anywhere in the 2026 text: the NOK 850,000 figure that appears in it is the de-minimis state-aid limit for reduced-rate zones, which is a limit per company and not a threshold per employee.

source.name: Stortingsvedtak om fastsetting av avgifter mv. til folketrygden for 2026 (FOR-2025-12-18-2748), sections 1 to 4 - Lovdata

employer_contributions.name: Mandatory occupational pension contribution (OTP)
employer_contributions.applies: Every company with at least two staff working 75% of full time, or one employee without an ownership interest at that level
employer_contributions.notes: Section 4(1) of the Mandatory Occupational Pension Act requires an annual contribution of at least 2% of the pay each member receives up to 12 G, and since the 2022 amendment it runs from the first krone rather than from 1 G. The base amount G is NOK 136,549 from 1 May 2026, so the ceiling is NOK 1,638,588 of pay. Two further costs sit in the same section and are not in this line because neither is a percentage of pay: the premium for contribution waiver on disability, and the scheme's administration costs, both of which the Act puts on the employer on top of the contribution.

source.name: Lov om obligatorisk tjenestepensjon (LOV-2005-12-21-124), section 4 first paragraph - Lovdata

employer_contributions.name: Employer's contribution on the pension premium
employer_contributions.applies: Charged on the pension contribution itself, so it stops where the pension contribution stops, at 12 G of pay
employer_contributions.notes: Section 23-2 of the National Insurance Act says in terms that the employer's contribution is due on employers' payments into annuity and pension schemes. The 14.1% therefore falls on the OTP premium as well as on salary: 14.1% of the 2% minimum is 0.282% of pay. Cost pages that show a pension line and a national insurance line side by side usually leave this compounding out, which understates the Norwegian employer by roughly a quarter of a point before anything else is counted.

source.name: Folketrygdloven (LOV-1997-02-28-19), section 23-2 sixth paragraph - Lovdata

statutory_extras.name: Holiday pay above the salary it replaces (feriepenger)
statutory_extras.notes: Section 10(2) of the Holidays Act sets holiday pay at 10.2% of the previous year's pay basis, and section 11(1) shows how it works: it speaks of "the part of the holiday pay that exceeds pay for normal working hours during the holiday", so the first tranche stands in for wages the employee does not receive while on leave. Statutory leave is 25 virkedager counted on a six-day week, and Norwegian monthly payroll withholds 25 of 26 virkedager of a month's salary for it, which is 8.01% of annual pay. 10.2% less 8.01% leaves 2.19%, the figure carried here. Employees who have five weeks and 12% under a collective agreement reach a similar surplus by a different route, and employees over 60 add 2.3 percentage points on the part of the basis up to 6 G.

source.name: Ferieloven (LOV-1988-04-29-21), sections 5(1), 10(2) and 11(1) - Lovdata

statutory_extras.name: Employer's contribution on the holiday pay surplus
statutory_extras.notes: Holiday pay is ordinary contributory remuneration, so the 14.1% applies to it. The contribution line above already charges twelve months of pay; what remains to add is the contribution on the 2.19% surplus, which is 0.31% of annual pay.

source.name: Folketrygdloven (LOV-1997-02-28-19), section 23-2 first paragraph - Lovdata

statutory_extras.name: Occupational injury insurance (yrkesskadeforsikring)
statutory_extras.notes: Compulsory, and carried at zero because no statute sets its price. Section 3 of the Occupational Injury Insurance Act obliges every employer to take out cover, and section 4 requires it to be bought from an approved insurer or insurance pool, so the premium is whatever that insurer quotes for the role and the payroll. It is a real line on a Norwegian payroll: ask a provider what it charges rather than assuming it is inside the headline percentage.

source.name: Yrkesskadeforsikringsloven (LOV-1989-06-16-65), sections 3 and 4 - Lovdata

statutory_extras.name: Employer-paid sick pay for the first 16 days
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it follows absence rather than pay. Section 8-19 of the National Insurance Act puts the first 16 calendar days of a sickness absence on the employer, and a fresh absence starting within 16 days of the last one falls inside the same employer period rather than starting a new one. NAV pays after that.

source.name: Folketrygdloven (LOV-1997-02-28-19), section 8-19 - Lovdata

countries.notice_typical: One month either way by default (Working Environment Act, section 15-3(1)), two months after five continuous years with the same employer and three months after ten. From ten years of service the employer's notice is at least four months once the employee has turned 50, five months after 55 and six months after 60, while the employee may still leave on three. Fourteen days either way during an agreed probation period.

countries.name: New Zealand

assumptions.label: The employee is a KiwiSaver member
assumptions.notes: This is the single largest assumption on the page and it is about the employee, not about you. The compulsory employer contribution is owed only for employees who are in KiwiSaver. New employees aged 18 to 64 are automatically enrolled and may opt out between weeks 2 and 8; existing members stay in; an employee on a savings suspension, or one who opted out, carries no employer contribution at all. So the same salary can cost 3.5% or 0% depending on one decision your hire makes in their first two months, and no provider quote can tell you in advance which it will be. Two further carve-outs from Inland Revenue's employer guide: no compulsory employer contribution is required for employees under 16, and contributions to an existing complying superannuation scheme can reduce what is owed. Budget for 3.5% and treat an opt-out as a windfall, not the other way round.

assumptions.label: The ACC Work levy is priced at an office classification unit
assumptions.notes: ACC charges the Work levy per $100 of liable payroll at a rate set by the employer's classification unit (CU). The rate modelled is 0.02%, the rate that Schedule 2 of the Accident Compensation (Work Account Levies) Regulations 2025 sets for 2026/27 for CU 78340 'Computer systems design and related services', and that ACC's Levy Guidebook 2026/27 prints for the same CU. Two things follow. Rates differ sharply between office work and physical trades, so this line is not transferable to a warehouse or field role. And under an employer of record the levied employer is the provider, whose classification and whose claims history drive the rate - ACC's Experience Rating programme adjusts a Work levy up or down on past claims once a business has paid three invoices. Ask which CU your provider is registered under.

employer_contributions.name: Compulsory KiwiSaver employer contribution
employer_contributions.applies: Employees who are KiwiSaver members and aged 16 or over
employer_contributions.notes: Inland Revenue's KiwiSaver employer guide, edition of April 2026, states it in one line: 'The compulsory employer contribution rate is 3.5% of your employee's gross salary or wages.' The rate rose from 3% with effect from the start of the 2026-27 year, and the same guide lists the member's own choices as 3.5%, 4%, 6%, 8% or 10% with 3.5% as the default. There is no ceiling on it - the contribution is a flat share of gross pay however senior the hire, which is the opposite of the ACC line below. Employer superannuation contribution tax is taken out of this contribution rather than added to it; see the ESCT entry in the notes below, because getting that wrong is the most common way a New Zealand quote is overstated.

source.name: Inland Revenue - KiwiSaver employer guide KS4, April 2026 edition

employer_contributions.name: ACC Work levy (Workplace Cover), office classification
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on each employee's liable earnings up to the annual maximum
employer_contributions.notes: The Accident Compensation (Work Account Levies) Regulations 2025, version as at 1 April 2026, Schedule 2 'Classifications and Work Account levy rates for 2026/27 tax year', set the levy for CU 78340 'Computer systems design and related services' at 0.02 per $100 of earnings, that is 0.02%, exclusive of GST; ACC's Levy Guidebook 2026/27 prints the same $0.02 for employers, or $0.02144 for an employer in the Experience Rating programme. Until September 2026 this line carried 0.21%, a provider figure. The ceiling is read from ACC's page 'Calculating your levies': 'You'll only pay levies on an individual's earnings up to the maximum level. If an employee on your payroll earns more than the maximum, we'll only levy you for the maximum', with the maximum liable income for employees set at NZD 156,641 for the year starting 1 April 2026, up from NZD 152,790 the year before. Provider pages have not all caught up - Deel's own New Zealand page still prints the 2025-26 figure of NZD 12,732.50 a month. The practical effect is that the Work levy fades as pay rises while the KiwiSaver line does not, so a senior New Zealand hire gets slightly cheaper as a percentage, not dearer.

source.name: Accident Compensation (Work Account Levies) Regulations 2025 (SL 2025/17), version as at 1 April 2026, Schedule 2, CU 78340

employer_contributions.name: Working Safer levy (funds WorkSafe New Zealand), billed with the ACC Work levy
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on liable earnings up to the ACC maximum
employer_contributions.notes: ACC's Levy Guidebook 2026/27 states that the Working Safer levy 'is a flat rate, currently $0.08 per $100 of your liable earnings', that is 0.08% of pay up to the same ceiling - on an office classification that is four times the Work levy itself. ACC's own description of what an employer is invoiced names three levies - 'ACC will send you an invoice for Earners', Work and Working Safer levies' - and the Working Safer levy funds WorkSafe New Zealand rather than ACC. It is charged per $100 of the same liable payroll as the Work levy and adds about US$4 a month on this salary. Ask the provider to show the Work and Working Safer lines separately on a sample invoice.

source.name: ACC - Calculating your levies: levies invoiced to an employer

statutory_extras.name: ESCT - taken out of the employer contribution, not added to it
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it costs the employer nothing extra, and named because treating it as an extra cost is the single most common error in New Zealand EOR comparisons. Employer superannuation cash contributions are liable for employer superannuation contribution tax, and Inland Revenue's own worked example shows where the money comes from: an employee on $2,600 a month, 'The net compulsory employer contribution will be: $2,600 x 3.5% = $91; $91 x 17.5% = $15.93 (ESCT); $91 - $15.93 = $75.07'. The employer pays 3.5% of gross; the tax is deducted from that 3.5% and the balance reaches the employee's scheme. Adding an ESCT rate on top of 3.5% - which several comparison pages do - overstates a New Zealand hire by a point or more. The ESCT rate itself is set from the employee's total pay plus employer contributions, so it changes what the employee receives, never what you pay.

source.name: Inland Revenue - KiwiSaver employer guide KS4, April 2026 edition, ESCT worked example

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by New Zealand law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because New Zealand law creates no thirteenth-month salary and no holiday supplement. What the Holidays Act 2003 does create instead is worth knowing when you compare: annual holidays are paid at the greater of ordinary weekly pay and average weekly earnings, an employee who works a public holiday must be paid at least time and a half and given an alternative day off, and the four-week entitlement arrives as a block after twelve months of continuous employment rather than accruing month by month. None of that is an employer contribution, but the public holiday rule is a real cost for any role with weekend or on-call work.

source.name: Holidays Act 2003, version as at 20 December 2023, New Zealand Legislation

countries.notice_typical: Whatever the individual employment agreement specifies. New Zealand sets no statutory minimum notice period for an ordinary resignation or dismissal, which moves the whole question into the contract; one month is the usual market term for a professional role. Inside the first 90 days a trial provision under section 67A of the Employment Relations Act 2000 lets the employer dismiss without the employee being able to bring a personal grievance over the dismissal, provided the employee has not worked for that employer before and the provision is written into the agreement before work starts.

source.name: Holidays Act 2003, version as at 20 December 2023, New Zealand Legislation

countries.name: Peru

assumptions.label: Severance deposit (CTS) taken at one and one sixth of a monthly salary a year
assumptions.notes: Article 21 of the CTS law has the employer deposit, in May and November, 'tantos dozavos de la remuneracion computable percibida por el trabajador en los meses de abril y octubre respectivamente, como meses completos haya laborado en el semestre'. A full year is therefore one monthly salary. Article 16 then adds one sixth of the gratificaciones to the computable pay, which brings the annual deposit to seven sixths of a month, or 9.72% of annual gross.

assumptions.label: The compulsory life policy and the profit share are carried at zero, so the total below is a floor
assumptions.notes: The Seguro de Vida Ley premium is priced by the insurer on the employee's age, and the profit share is a slice of the company's taxable income rather than of any one salary. Neither can honestly be written as a percentage of a salary, so both sit outside the total and the figure below is a minimum.

employer_contributions.name: EsSalud health contribution
employer_contributions.notes: Article 6(a) of Ley 26790: 'El aporte de los trabajadores en actividad ... equivale al 9% de la remuneracion o ingreso. Es de cargo de la entidad empleadora que debe declararlos y pagarlos.' There is no ceiling, so the charge scales with salary. Ley 32503, published on 19 November 2025, adds a third paragraph to that same article, but it concerns construction workers only: 'En el caso de los trabajadores de construccion civil, el porcentaje de aporte debe cubrir lo estipulado en los articulos 10 y 11.' The 9% general rate is unchanged. EsSalud is charged on the monthly salary alone: the gratificaciones are exempt, which is what the next two lines are about.

source.name: Ley 26790, Ley de Modernizacion de la Seguridad Social en Salud, articulo 6 (text hosted by EsSalud), with Ley 32503 (El Peruano, 19 November 2025)

statutory_extras.name: Two statutory bonuses (gratificaciones de Fiestas Patrias y Navidad)
statutory_extras.notes: Article 1 of Ley 27735 gives private-sector employees the right 'a percibir dos gratificaciones en el ano, una con motivo de Fiestas Patrias y la otra con ocasion de la Navidad'. Article 2 sets the amount: 'El monto de cada una de las gratificaciones es equivalente a la remuneracion que perciba el trabajador en la oportunidad en que corresponde otorgar el beneficio.' Article 5 has them paid in the first fortnight of July and of December. Two full months of pay a year, and under Ley 30334 they carry no social contributions of their own.

source.name: Ley 27735, articulos 1, 2 y 5 (El Peruano facsimile, 28 May 2002, hosted by the Congreso de la Republica)

statutory_extras.name: Severance deposit (compensacion por tiempo de servicios)
statutory_extras.notes: Money that leaves the company twice a year whether or not anyone resigns. Article 21 of the CTS law requires a deposit in May and November of one twelfth of the computable pay for each complete month worked in the half year, and article 22 fixes the deadline at the first fifteen calendar days of those months. Article 16 puts one sixth of the gratificaciones into the computable pay, so the year's deposits come to seven sixths of a monthly salary, which is 9.72% of annual gross.

source.name: Texto Unico Ordenado de la Ley de Compensacion por Tiempo de Servicios, D.S. 001-97-TR, articulos 16, 21 y 22 (Ministerio de Trabajo y Promocion del Empleo)

statutory_extras.name: Extraordinary bonus of 9% on the two gratificaciones
statutory_extras.notes: The Peruvian quirk that costs the employer exactly what exempting the bonuses saved it. Article 1 of Ley 30334 puts the gratificaciones outside contributions altogether, and article 3 then redirects the money: 'El monto que abonan las entidades empleadoras por concepto de aportaciones al Seguro Social de Salud (Essalud) con relacion a las gratificaciones de julio y diciembre son abonados a los trabajadores bajo la modalidad de bonificacion extraordinaria.' Nine per cent of two months of pay is 1.50% of annual gross, paid to the employee instead of to EsSalud. Where the employee is covered by an EPS rather than by EsSalud the rate is lower.

source.name: Ley 30334, articulos 1 y 3 (Congreso de la Republica del Peru)

statutory_extras.name: Compulsory life cover (Seguro de Vida Ley)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the premium is rated by the insurer on the employee's age rather than fixed by a published percentage. It is compulsory from the first day of employment, and Deel's Peru page books it at an estimated 1.11% of salary while noting that 'the rate varies depending on the employee's age and ranges from 0.14% (employees aged 18-36) to 11% (employees aged 70+)'. Because it is left out, the total on this page is a floor.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Peru page

statutory_extras.name: Family allowance (asignacion familiar)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is owed only to employees who have a dependent child, so it cannot be charged to every hire. When it is due it is a flat monthly amount set at a tenth of the minimum wage, and it joins the base on which the other charges are calculated. Deel's Peru page records the mechanism: 'If the employee is entitled to receive the family bonus (PEN 113), the monthly costs will be calculated on the sum of the employee's salary and the family bonus.' At the example salary that would add about a point.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Peru page

statutory_extras.name: Profit share (participacion en las utilidades)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a share of the company's taxable income distributed across its workforce, not a percentage of any one salary, and it changes with each financial year. Deel's Peru page puts the per-employee figure at 'approximately PEN 190 for 2023, but it changes every fiscal year'. Ask the provider whether its Peruvian entity distributes one and, if so, how it is billed.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Peru page

countries.notice_typical: Peru front-loads the cost of leaving rather than charging it at the exit. The compensacion por tiempo de servicios is deposited into the employee's own account every May and November under articles 21 and 22 of D.S. 001-97-TR, so by the time a contract ends the severance fund is already outside the company and outside the employer's reach. Notice and dismissal procedure are governed by the Ley de Productividad y Competitividad Laboral and are not priced on this page. Article 10 of that law (TUO, D.S. 003-97-TR) sets the trial period at three months, after which the worker is protected against arbitrary dismissal; the parties may extend it in writing when the role needs training or carries responsibility, up to six months in total for qualified or trusted staff (the bracket that would cover a software engineer) and up to a year for management. The six months shown is that written maximum, not the default.

payments.name: Gratificación de Fiestas Patrias (July)
payments.deadline: first fortnight of July (MTPE, citing Ley 27735 and its regulation)

payments.name: Gratificación de Navidad (December)
payments.deadline: first fortnight of December (MTPE, citing Ley 27735 and its regulation)

payments.name: Bonificación extraordinaria (9 % of each gratificación)
payments.deadline: paid with the July and December gratificaciones

source.quote: El monto de la gratificación equivale a un sueldo completo, siempre que se haya laborado durante todo el semestre en la oportunidad que corresponda otorgar el beneficio.

countries.name: Philippines

assumptions.label: Employee is rank-and-file (13th-month pay applies)
assumptions.notes: The 13th-month decree covers rank-and-file employees; managerial staff are outside it by law, though most providers pay it to every EOR hire. Set to 0 in your own model if the role is managerial and the provider says so.

employer_contributions.name: Social Security System (SSS), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All private-sector employees; computed on the Monthly Salary Credit (MSC) between PHP 5,000 and PHP 35,000
employer_contributions.notes: 15% of the MSC from 2025 onward: 10% employer, 5% employee. The MSC stops at PHP 35,000 a month (PHP 420,000 a year), so the employer share peaks at PHP 3,500 a month; MSC above PHP 20,000 funds the mandatory provident fund. SSS rounds pay into PHP 500 brackets, which this engine ignores (difference under PHP 50 a month).

source.name: Republic Act No. 11199 (Social Security Act of 2018), section 4 contribution schedule: 2025, 15%, employer 10%, employee 5%, MSC PHP 5,000-35,000

employer_contributions.name: PhilHealth premium, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All employed members; premium of 5% of monthly basic salary between the PHP 10,000 floor and the PHP 100,000 ceiling, shared equally
employer_contributions.notes: 2026 rate confirmed at 5% under the Universal Health Care Act schedule: employer 2.5%, employee 2.5%. The employer share peaks at PHP 2,500 a month once basic pay reaches PHP 100,000.

source.name: Philippine Information Agency — PhilHealth sets 5% premium contribution rate for 2026 (equal employer/employee sharing, PHP 10,000 floor, PHP 100,000 ceiling)

employer_contributions.name: Pag-IBIG Fund (HDMF), employer counterpart
employer_contributions.applies: All employees; 2% of the monthly fund salary up to the PHP 10,000 maximum fund salary
employer_contributions.notes: Since February 2024 (Pag-IBIG Circular No. 460) the maximum fund salary is PHP 10,000, so the employer counterpart is PHP 200 a month for anyone earning above that. The employee pays 2% as well (1% below PHP 1,500).

source.name: Department of Budget and Management — Circular Letter No. 2024-2 on Pag-IBIG Fund Circular No. 460 (maximum fund salary PHP 10,000; employer 2%)

statutory_extras.name: Employees' Compensation (EC) contribution, PHP 30 a month
statutory_extras.notes: Employer-only work-injury insurance collected with SSS: PHP 30 a month for a monthly salary credit of PHP 15,000 and above, PHP 10 below that. PHP 360 a year, under half a US dollar a month, so it is listed here rather than as a ledger line.

source.name: SSS — Employees' Compensation Program, payment of ECP contribution (PHP 10 below MSC 15,000; PHP 30 from MSC 15,000)

statutory_extras.name: 13th-month pay (Presidential Decree 851)
statutory_extras.notes: One twelfth of the basic salary earned in the calendar year, due on or before 24 December to every rank-and-file employee with at least one month of service; prorated for partial years. Paid on top of the 12 monthly salaries, so it adds 8.33% to the annual cost.

source.name: DOLE — Workers should get 13th-month pay on time (advisory: all rank-and-file employees with at least one month of service, not less than one-twelfth of total basic salary, not later than 24 December)

statutory_extras.name: Service incentive leave (5 days)
statutory_extras.notes: Statutory minimum of five paid leave days a year after one year of service (Labor Code art. 95). Paid time inside the salary, not an extra contribution; providers usually offer more vacation and sick leave in their standard contract.

source.name: DOLE — Labor Code of the Philippines, Book 3, art. 95 Right to Service Incentive Leave

countries.notice_typical: Dismissal for authorized causes (redundancy, retrenchment, closure) needs one month's written notice to the employee and to DOLE plus separation pay of at least one month's pay per year of service for redundancy, or half a month per year for retrenchment; just-cause dismissal needs due process but no separation pay; an employee resigns on one month's notice.

payments.name: 13th-month pay
payments.deadline: 24 Dec

source.quote: a 13th-month pay not later than December 24 of every year

countries.name: Pakistan

assumptions.label: Sindh minimum wage, the SESSI base in PKR a month (EOBI uses the federal rate of PKR 40,700)
assumptions.notes: Social security in Pakistan is provincial, and the minimum wage that drives it is notified province by province; the old-age scheme is federal and runs on the federal rate. This page models Sindh, where the Labour and Human Resources Department raised the monthly minimum wage for unskilled adult, juvenile and adolescent workers from PKR 40,000 to PKR 43,000 with effect from 1 July 2026 (notification of 17 August 2026). The Islamabad Capital Territory set PKR 40,700 from the same date, and Balochistan's last notified figure read here, from July 2025, is PKR 37,000, where the two lines below would be about 14% smaller. A hire in Punjab pays the equivalent Punjab institution rather than the Sindh one, at the same 6%.

employer_contributions.name: EOBI old-age benefits contribution, employer share (5% of the notified minimum wage)
employer_contributions.applies: Federal old-age pension scheme; charged on the federal minimum wage, not on the salary actually paid, so it stops at PKR 40,700 a month of base
employer_contributions.notes: secondary source: the Employees' Old-Age Benefits Institution's circular setting the FY2026-27 contribution base could not be read (every eobi.gov.pk page tried on 2026-09-24 returned an empty document); a payroll practitioner's post reproducing it gives a monthly minimum wage of PKR 40,700 from 1 July 2026, an employer share of PKR 2,035 and an employee share of PKR 407, and the Centre for Labour Research describes the base as the minimum wage notified for the Islamabad Capital Territory, which is PKR 40,700 from the same date. The Institution states the split as employer 5% and employee 1% of the worker's minimum wages, 6% in total. The base is the point most cost models get wrong: the Act defines "wages" for this purpose as the rates declared under the Minimum Wages for Unskilled Workers Ordinance, a federal instrument, so the charge is 5% of the federal rate - PKR 2,035 a month - whether the employee earns PKR 40,700 or PKR 460,000, and it does not follow the Sindh minimum wage that drives the SESSI line below. On the wording, note that section 9(1) of the Act fixes at 6% what the employer must remit each month and section 9B makes 1% of wages the insured person's own share, which the employer withholds from pay; the Institution publishes the same arithmetic as 5% plus 1%. This ledger carries the employer's 5%.

source.name: Employees' Old-Age Benefits Institution — Enactment page: "RATES: Employer's Contribution @ 5 % of the worker's minimum wages. Employee's Contribution @ 1 % of the worker's minimum wages. Total Contribution per Employee 5% + 1% = 6% Per Month"; EOB Act 1976 section 2(p) defines wages as the rates declared under the Minimum Wages for Unskilled Worker Ordinance 1969

employer_contributions.name: Sindh Employees' Social Security (SESSI) contribution, employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Provincial medical and cash-benefit scheme; charged on the Sindh minimum wage prevailing when the contribution is paid, so it stops at PKR 43,000 a month of base
employer_contributions.notes: Section 20(1) of the Act sets the employer contribution at six per cent, and section 20(2) forbids deducting any part of it from the employee. The Sindh Employees' Social Security (Amendment) Act 2018 replaced the proviso to section 20(1) with two: no contribution is payable on so much of an employee's wages as exceeds the upper wage limit determined under section 75, and the contribution is to be calculated on the minimum wage rate prevailing under the Sindh Minimum Wages Act 2015 at the time of payment. The ceiling therefore applies to the base, not to the amount: 6% of PKR 43,000, the Sindh minimum wage from 1 July 2026, or PKR 2,580 a month, the larger of this ledger's two lines. The Sindh High Court read the Act the same way when no separate limit had been notified, holding that contributions are due on the minimum wage notified for the year. An employee does not leave the scheme by earning more than the limit: the proviso to section 2(9), as substituted in 2018, says so expressly.

source.name: Sindh Employees' Social Security Act 2016 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2016), sections 20(1)-(2), 21 and 75, with the provisos to section 20(1) and section 2(9)(e) as substituted by the Sindh Employees Social Security (Amendment) Act 2018 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2018, sections 4 and 8), both on the Sindh Law Department's Sindh Code; wage base from the Labour and Human Resources Department notification No. SO(L-II)/13-3/2016-II of 17 August 2026 (PKR 43,000 a month from 1 July 2026)

statutory_extras.name: Gratuity on termination (one month's wages per year of service)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it falls due when the job ends rather than every month, but it is the largest employer obligation on this page by some distance — one month's wages for every completed year of service, and for any part of a year beyond six months, payable to a worker who resigns or whose services are terminated for any reason other than misconduct. At one month a year it is worth about 8.3% of salary, roughly eight times the recurring contributions above. The same Standing Order removes it for any period covered by a provident fund to which the employer contributes at least as much as the worker, provided the fund pays out no less than the gratuity would have, which is why some employers run a fund instead. Ask the provider whether it accrues gratuity monthly, funds a provident fund in its place, or invoices the whole amount at the exit.

source.name: Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), Standing Order 16(6): gratuity equivalent to one month's wages for every completed year of service or any part in excess of six months, on resignation or termination other than for misconduct, unless a qualifying provident fund exists; Sindh Law Department, Sindh Code

statutory_extras.name: Statutory profit bonus
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is owed only in a profitable year and its size follows the profit, not the salary. Standing Order 13 requires an employer that made a profit in a year to pay, within three months of the year closing, a bonus to every worker with at least ninety days of continuous service in that year. Where the profit is at least the workers' combined monthly wages, the bonus pool is at least one month's wages, subject to a maximum of 30% of the profit; where the profit is smaller, the pool is at least 15% of it, shared in proportion to monthly wages. It is not a thirteenth month and it has no fixed rate, but it is a statutory entitlement rather than a discretionary gesture, so it belongs in a budget for a profitable local entity.

source.name: Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), Standing Order 13(1)-(3): profit bonus for workers with not less than ninety days of continuous service in the year, at least one month's aggregate wages up to 30% of profit, or at least 15% of a smaller profit; Sindh Law Department, Sindh Code

statutory_extras.name: Compulsory group insurance for permanent workers
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the cost is an insurance premium rather than a percentage of one salary. In an industrial or commercial establishment with twenty or more workers, the employer must insure every permanent worker against natural death and disability and against death or injury not already covered by the Workmen's Compensation Act or provincial social security, for at least the compensation set in Schedule IV of that Act, pays the whole premium, and is liable for the payout itself if the worker was not insured. An EOR's fee normally covers this because the provider is the employer of record; a company opening its own entity has to buy the policy.

source.name: Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), Standing Order 12(1)-(4): compulsory group insurance for permanent workers where twenty or more workers are employed, premium on the employer, cover not below Schedule IV of the Workmen's Compensation Act 1923, employer liable for what the insurer would have paid; Sindh Law Department, Sindh Code

statutory_extras.name: Statutory annual leave (14 days)
statutory_extras.notes: Paid time inside the salary rather than an extra contribution. An office hire works in a commercial establishment, where the Sindh Shops and Commercial Establishment Act 2015 grants fourteen days of leave on full wages after twelve months of continuous employment; untaken leave carries forward until the balance reaches thirty days, or can be paid out at the employee's request. The same Act adds ten days of casual leave a year and eight days of sick leave, which can accumulate to sixteen. A factory worker has the same fourteen days under the Sindh Factories Act 2015, with sick leave of sixteen days a year. Both are generous by the standards of the contracts EOR providers draft, so check what the offer actually promises. Public holidays are separate. The Cabinet Division's circular of 19 January 2026 lists the 2026 holidays, and the Muslim festivals are fixed later by moon-sighting notifications. As notified, 2026 has 14 public holiday dates for all employees: two days of Eid-ul-Fitr, three of Eid-ul-Azha (the third coinciding with Youm-e-Takbeer on 28 May), two of Ashura, and seven single days, with 26 December added for Christian employees only. Standing Order 9(2) gives every worker covered by the Standing Orders Act paid holidays on all days the provincial or federal government declares festival holidays; the Shops Act's own floor is ten festival holidays a year, dated by the employer at the start of the year.

source.name: Sindh Shops and Commercial Establishment Act 2015 (Sindh Act No. XII of 2016), sections 14 (annual leave), 15 (casual and sick leave) and 16 (festival holidays), on the Sindh Law Department's Sindh Code; Sindh Factories Act 2015, sections 73 and 79; Standing Order 9 of the Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act 2015; Cabinet Division circular F.No. 10-1/2025-Min-II of 19 January 2026 and its Eid-ul-Fitr (15 March), Eid-ul-Azha (20 May), Ashura (22 June) and Eid Milad-un-Nabi (21 August 2026) notifications

countries.notice_typical: One month's notice, or one month's wages in lieu, is the standing-order default for ending the employment of a permanent worker, and the employer must give the reason in writing. Probation for a permanent post runs three months. The money at the exit is not the notice but the gratuity: one month's wages for every completed year of service, and for any part of a year beyond six months, owed whenever employment ends for any reason other than misconduct.

countries.name: Poland

assumptions.label: Accident insurance at the category-2 activity-group rate of 0.67% (IT, finance, professional services; the rate Deel publishes for Poland)
assumptions.notes: ZUS sets each employer's accident rate from its PKD activity group once it reports 10 or more insured people: 0.93% for employment agencies (PKD 78), up to 3.33% for mining. Payers with up to 9 insured people pay a flat 1.67%. The provider's Polish entity, not the client, decides which applies.

assumptions.label: Employee stays enrolled in the PPK pension plan (employer 1.5%)
assumptions.notes: Enrolment is the default; an employee who files an opt-out declaration stops the employer contribution from that month, and the on-cost falls by 1.5 points.

employer_contributions.name: Old-age pension insurance (ubezpieczenie emerytalne), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All employees on an employment contract (umowa o pracę)
employer_contributions.notes: 19.52% in total, split equally: 9.76% employer, 9.76% employee. The base stops at the 2026 annual ceiling of PLN 282,600 (30 times the forecast average monthly wage of PLN 9,420).

source.name: Biznes.gov.pl (Polish government business portal) — ZUS contributions an employer pays for an employee, 2026 split table and annual ceiling

employer_contributions.name: Disability insurance (ubezpieczenie rentowe), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: All employees on an employment contract
employer_contributions.notes: 8.00% in total: 6.50% employer, 1.50% employee. Shares the PLN 282,600 annual ceiling with the pension line.

source.name: Biznes.gov.pl (Polish government business portal) — ZUS contributions an employer pays for an employee, 2026 split table and annual ceiling

employer_contributions.name: Accident insurance (ubezpieczenie wypadkowe), activity-group rate
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only; rate set by ZUS from the payer's PKD activity group (0.67% to 3.33%), or 1.67% flat for payers with up to 9 insured people
employer_contributions.notes: 0.67% is the category-2 rate for information and communication (PKD J), finance, real estate and professional services. Employment agencies (PKD 78) are category 3 at 0.93%. No annual ceiling.

source.name: ZUS — Guide to setting the accident-insurance contribution rate (activity-group table in force from 1 April 2025, edition of 1 January 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Labour Fund and Solidarity Fund (Fundusz Pracy 1.00% + Fundusz Solidarnościowy 1.45%)
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only, on pay of at least the minimum wage; not due for women aged 55+ and men aged 60+, nor for some hires returning from parental leave or referred by a labour office
employer_contributions.notes: Collected together as 2.45%. The PLN 282,600 ceiling does not apply. The minimum-wage test is PLN 4,806 a month in 2026 under the Council of Ministers regulation of 11 September 2025 (Dz.U. 2025 poz. 1242); the Council of Ministers regulation of 14 September 2026 (Dz.U. 2026 poz. 1213) raises it to PLN 4,950 from 1 January 2027.

source.name: ZUS — Contributions to the Labour Fund, Solidarity Fund and Guaranteed Employee Benefits Fund (FP, FS i FGŚP)

employer_contributions.name: Guaranteed Employee Benefits Fund (FGŚP)
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only
employer_contributions.notes: Insures wages if the employer becomes insolvent. No annual ceiling.

source.name: ZUS — Contributions to the Labour Fund, Solidarity Fund and Guaranteed Employee Benefits Fund (FP, FS i FGŚP)

employer_contributions.name: Employee Capital Plan (PPK), employer basic contribution
employer_contributions.applies: Every enrolled employee; enrolment is the default and the employee can opt out in writing
employer_contributions.notes: The employer must pay 1.5% of gross pay and may add up to 2.5% voluntarily; the employee pays 2%. Employer PPK payments are not subject to ZUS contributions. Some providers only bill this line while the employee stays enrolled.

source.name: MojePPK.pl (official PPK portal) — For employers: who pays what into PPK

statutory_extras.name: PFRON disability-employment levy (pass-through)
statutory_extras.notes: Employers with 25 or more full-time equivalents whose disabled-employee share is under 6% pay 40.65% of the national average wage for each missing position. PFRON applies the previous quarter's average wage published in Monitor Polski: PLN 9,233.13 for September to November 2026 (Monitor Polski of 11 August 2026, item 779), after PLN 9,562.88 for June to August. With no disabled staff that is about PLN 225 a month per employee (0.4065 x 9,233.13 x 6%). Most EOR entities cross the 25-FTE line, and some providers bill it as a variable monthly line; ask before signing.

source.name: PFRON — Average wage applied to mandatory payments (PLN 9,233.13 for September to November 2026) and amount of payments (40.65% formula)

countries.notice_typical: Statutory notice on a fixed-term or open-ended contract is 2 weeks under 6 months of service, 1 month from 6 months and 3 months from 3 years, always ending on a Saturday or the last day of a month; a probation contract ends on 3 working days to 2 weeks' notice depending on its length.

customary.name: Annual additional pay (13th salary) for budget-sector employees only

source.quote: o dodatkowym wynagrodzeniu rocznym dla pracowników jednostek sfery budżetowej

countries.name: Portugal

assumptions.label: The annual gross entered is the employee's whole year of pay, paid in fourteen instalments: twelve months plus the holiday and Christmas subsidies
assumptions.notes: This is the single modelling choice that decides whether Portugal looks like a 24% country or a 45% one, so it is stated rather than assumed. Portuguese pay is quoted monthly and the year contains fourteen of those months, because the Labour Code gives the employee a Christmas subsidy equal to one month (art. 263) and a holiday subsidy on top of holiday pay (art. 264). Deel states the convention plainly on its own Portugal page: 'Please note that 13th and 14th month salaries are paid to the employee in monthly instalments and are included in the total annual salary.' Playroll puts it the same way, 'splitting annual pay into 12 regular months plus holiday and Christmas allowances', and Rippling writes that Portuguese salaries 'are split into 14 payments throughout the year rather than 12'. So the annual figure you enter above is divided by fourteen to set the monthly wage, exactly as Italian and Spanish salaries are treated on this site. Adding the two subsidies a second time would count the same euros twice and would overstate the hire by about twenty points. If instead you mean a monthly wage times twelve, enter fourteen times that monthly wage here.

employer_contributions.name: Social security contribution (Taxa Social Unica, employer share)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee on a Portuguese contract, on the whole remuneration, with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: This is the whole employer side of a Portuguese payslip, and there is no second line. The social security institute's own practical guide states it in one sentence: 'Na maioria dos casos, a taxa e de 34,75%: 23,75% sao pagas pela entidade empregadora; 11% sao pagos pelo/a trabalhador/a', and its rate table repeats 23,75% / 11% / 34,75% for trabalhadores por conta de outrem. The base is the whole remuneration and it explicitly includes the two extra months: the declaration guide files the Christmas and holiday subsidies under article 46(2)(h) of the contributions code as remuneration subject to contributions. Because the annual gross entered here already contains those two months (see the assumption above), this one rate already carries the contributions on them, and a separate charge line would double count. Uncapped: neither the rate table nor the declaration guide sets a maximum contribution base for an employee, so the rate does not fade as salary rises. Reduced rates exist, but for non-profit employers and specific hiring incentives, not for a commercial employer of record.

source.name: Instituto da Seguranca Social - Guia Pratico 1001 (v5.40), Inscricao, Vinculacao e Cessacao de Atividade de Trabalhador por Conta de Outrem, p. 15-16 ('23,75% sao pagas pela entidade empregadora; 11% sao pagos pelo/a trabalhador/a')

statutory_extras.name: Holiday and Christmas subsidies (13th and 14th month)
statutory_extras.notes: Statutory, not customary, and still not an addition to the figure above. The Labour Code is explicit on both: art. 263(1), 'O trabalhador tem direito a subsidio de Natal de valor igual a um mes de retribuicao, que deve ser pago ate 15 de Dezembro de cada ano', and art. 264(2), which grants a holiday subsidy on top of the pay the employee receives while on leave. Together they are the thirteenth and fourteenth months. They are carried at zero here because the annual gross entered above is the whole year of pay including them, which is how Portuguese salaries are quoted and how Deel, Playroll and Rippling all describe the arrangement. They do attract social security, and the 23.75% line above is already charged on them. What to watch in a quote: both are proportional in the year of joining and the year of leaving, so a hire starting in July costs roughly half of each in that first calendar year, and a provider that pays them in twelve monthly instalments rather than in June and December changes your cash timing, not the total.

source.name: Codigo do Trabalho (Lei 7/2009), arts. 263 and 264 - consolidated text published by the Procuradoria-Geral Distrital de Lisboa ('subsidio de Natal de valor igual a um mes de retribuicao')

statutory_extras.name: Labour compensation funds (FCT and FGCT)
statutory_extras.notes: Nothing is owed, and this is a figure provider pages still get wrong: Oyster prints 'roughly 0.925% of gross to the Fundo de Compensacao do Trabalho (FCT)' and Rippling prints a 'Wage Guarantee Fund 1% of gross income'. Decreto-Lei 115/2023 of 15 December ended it. The official fund portal describes the change in its own FAQ: the FCT becomes a closed fund, 'cessando definitivamente ... a obrigacao de realizar entregas para o Fundo', with employers' existing FCT debts extinguished; and for the guarantee fund, 'Ficam suspensas as obrigacoes de admissao de novos trabalhadores e de pagamento de entregas para o FGCT'. The decree took effect on 1 January 2024, so no Portuguese employer has paid into either fund for the salary years this page prices. The obligations behind them did not disappear: half of the statutory termination compensation the funds used to reimburse is now simply an employer cost when it falls due.
