The two halves differ in kind. The FCT end is definitive (art. 4(a): 'Sao extintas as obrigacoes de adesao e de pagamento de entregas ao FCT'). The FGCT is only suspended, 'ate ao final da vigencia do Acordo de Medio Prazo de Melhoria dos Rendimentos, dos Salarios e da Competitividade' (art. 4(b)), an agreement signed in October 2022 whose targets run from 2023 to 2026. The consolidated decree still carries that wording unamended, and the fund portal's FAQ (item 27) still states the suspension, so a contract signed in 2026 owes nothing to the FGCT. What changes if the suspension ends is set in the same law: 0.075% of base pay and seniority allowances (Lei 70/2013, art. 12(2)). Whether it ends after 2026 is not settled in any text read, so this line is re-read at each monthly review.

source.name: Decreto-Lei 115/2023 of 15 December, art. 4(a)-(b) and art. 11 (in force 1 January 2024), consolidated text published by the Procuradoria-Geral Distrital de Lisboa ('O diploma ainda nao sofreu alteracoes'); consistent with the Fundos de Compensacao FAQ, items 2 and 27

statutory_extras.name: Work accident insurance (seguro de acidentes de trabalho)
statutory_extras.notes: secondary source: compulsory for every Portuguese employer and genuinely large, but there is no public rate to quote, so it is named here and left out of the total. The work accidents law, Lei 98/2009, art. 79(1), requires the employer to transfer liability 'para entidades legalmente autorizadas a realizar este seguro' - a private insurer - and art. 81(2) says the standard policy 'obedece ao principio da graduacao dos premios de seguro em funcao do grau de risco do acidente', by the nature of the activity and the prevention in place. So the premium is that insurer's quote, graded by activity and risk; the law sets no percentage and no authority publishes one. The percentages in circulation are provider figures. Deel and Rippling both print a number, and they disagree by almost half: Deel's Portugal page charges 3.15% of salary for it, Rippling's guide states 1.75% of gross income, and Boundless says only that premiums are 'typically a small percentage of gross salary'. On a US$45,000 hire the difference between those two is about US$630 a year, which is why it is a question for the quote rather than a number to publish. Occupational health and safety services are a second charge of the same kind: mandatory, and billed by the provider rather than rated by law. Deel lists EUR 150 a year for it. Deel's headline 27.50% for Portugal is this site's 23.75% plus its own 3.15% accident policy and a 0.60% liability administration fee, all three of which are priced by Deel, not by the state.

source.name: Lei 98/2009 of 4 September (work accidents regime, version after DL 87/2024), arts. 79(1) and 81(2) - liability transferred to an authorised insurer, premiums graded by risk; consolidated text published by the Procuradoria-Geral Distrital de Lisboa

statutory_extras.name: Meal allowance (subsidio de refeicao)
statutory_extras.notes: Not an entitlement the Labour Code creates, and in practice not optional either. It exists where a collective agreement or the employment contract creates it, and in the Portuguese market that is almost everywhere, which is why providers treat it as mandatory: Deel's Portugal page lists a 'Mandatory meal allowance - EUR 6.15 per working day'. That figure is the public-sector rate, which the Directorate-General for Public Administration and Employment lists as 'Subsidio de Refeicao EUR 6,15 (a partir de 1-01-2026)', set by Portaria 51-B/2026/1 of 30 January with effect from 1 January 2026. The same figure is the private-sector tax threshold: the IRS Code, art. 2(3)(b)(2), taxes the allowance only 'na parte em que exceder o limite legal estabelecido ou em que o exceda em 70% sempre que o respetivo subsidio seja atribuido atraves de vales de refeicao'. So in 2026 it is tax-free up to EUR 6.15 a day in cash and about EUR 10.46 a day on a meal card, which is why Portuguese employers use cards. Carried at zero because it is a daily amount attached to days actually worked, not a share of one salary; at EUR 6.15 over about 220 working days it is roughly EUR 1,350 a year, near 3% of the example salary on this page. Assume it is in your invoice and ask for the daily rate and the payment method.

source.name: Direcao-Geral da Administracao e do Emprego Publico - Suplementos ('Subsidio de Refeicao EUR 6,15 (a partir de 1-01-2026)', Portaria 51-B/2026/1 of 30 January); tax threshold in Codigo do IRS art. 2(3)(b)(2), wording of Lei 45-A/2024, on the Autoridade Tributaria portal

statutory_extras.name: Telework expense compensation
statutory_extras.notes: The cost that exists precisely because an employer of record hire is a remote one. Article 168(2) of the Labour Code makes the employer liable for all the additional expenses the teleworker demonstrably bears from using the equipment and systems the work needs, energy and connection costs included, and art. 168(3) requires the contract or the collective agreement to fix the amount when the telework agreement is signed. There is no statutory amount to pay; Deel sets EUR 50 a month on its Portugal page, about EUR 600 a year. Carried at zero because the amount is contractual rather than rated, and because it is paid to the employee rather than to the state. What the state does fix is how much of it escapes tax and social security: Portaria 292-A/2023, art. 2(1), sets the exempt limit at EUR 0.10 a day for home electricity, EUR 0.40 for internet and EUR 0.50 for a personal computer, EUR 1.00 a day in all, raised by 50% when the amount comes from a negotiated collective agreement (art. 2(2)), and counted only on full telework days under a written agreement (art. 4). At about 21 full telework days a month that is roughly EUR 21 exempt, so on a EUR 50 flat amount the rest is taxed as pay. Ask your provider what it fixes, because the article makes silence expensive: without an agreed fixed amount, the reference becomes the employee's actual documented extra spending.

source.name: Portaria 292-A/2023 of 29 September (Diario da Republica, 1st series, no. 190), arts. 2 and 4 - exempt limits EUR 0.10 / 0.40 / 0.50 a day, in force 1 October 2023, copy hosted by Pessoas 2030 (gov.pt); duty to compensate in Codigo do Trabalho art. 168(2)-(3)

countries.notice_typical: Resignation takes 30 days' notice up to two years of service and 60 days after that (Labour Code art. 400). On the employer's side a dismissal for economic reasons is notified 15 days under one year of service, 30 days from one to five years, 60 days from five to ten and 75 days beyond ten (art. 363), and carries compensation of 14 days of base pay per complete year (art. 366). Probation is the practical exit: during it either side ends the contract without notice or compensation.

payments.name: Subsidio de Natal (Christmas subsidy)
payments.deadline: 15 Dec

payments.name: Subsidio de ferias (holiday subsidy)
payments.deadline: with the holiday period (art. 264 CT); no calendar month stated

source.quote: O trabalhador tem direito a subsídio de Natal de valor igual a um mês de retribuição, que deve ser pago até 15 de Dezembro de cada ano.

countries.name: Qatar

assumptions.label: Non-Qatari employee on a work visa and residence permit
assumptions.notes: Qatar's retirement system is written for Qataris. Law No. 24 of 2002 on Retirement and Pensions applies, in its own words, to 'Qatari employees subject to the provisions of the Civil Service Law' and to 'Qatari public servants in public authorities, institutions and corporations', and its definitions speak throughout of 'the Qatari beneficiary'. An expatriate employed through a provider therefore generates no employer pension contribution, and the Labour Law's end-of-service gratuity is what remains. Qatarisation targets are a hiring constraint rather than a payroll rate and are not modelled here.

assumptions.label: Basic wage as a share of the total package
assumptions.notes: Article 54 of the Labour Law settles the gratuity on 'the last Basic Wage', and article 1 defines the Basic Wage as the remuneration for the work 'including only the annual allowance and no other payment', against a Remuneration that adds every allowance and compensation on top. No Qatari statute fixes a ratio between the two for a salaried professional. Two reference points help. The statutory minimum wage is structured as QAR 1,000 of basic pay, QAR 500 of housing and QAR 300 of food, which puts basic pay at 56% of that package; and article 66(3)(a) of the DIFC Employment Law, in Dubai, forbids a basic wage below 50% of the annual wage. This ledger declares 50% and therefore publishes a floor; raise the share and the cost rises with it in direct proportion.

employer_contributions.name: End-of-service gratuity (provision)
employer_contributions.applies: Workers who have completed one year or more of employment, paid at the date of termination
employer_contributions.notes: Article 54 of Law No. 14 of 2004: 'The Employer shall pay at date of termination the end of service gratuity in addition to any amounts due to the Worker who spent one year or more in employment. This gratuity shall be agreed upon by the two parties, provided that it is not less than a three-week Remuneration for every year of employment... The last Basic Wage shall be taken as the basis of the calculation of the gratuity.' Three weeks in fifty-two is 5.7692% a year, and this ledger applies it to the basic wage because that is what the article's own calculation sentence says. The tension inside the article is worth knowing before signing anything: the floor is expressed in Remuneration, which includes every allowance, while the base of the calculation is the Basic Wage, which includes none of them. Read it the first way on a package split evenly and the provision doubles. Fractions of a year are owed in proportion once a full year is complete, and the employer may deduct from the gratuity what the worker owes it. Nothing in the Law requires the amount to be funded month by month, so this is a provision rather than a payment.

source.name: Law No. 14 of 2004 promulgating the Labour Law, article 54, consolidated text on the Al-Meezan legal portal (status: in force)

statutory_extras.name: Qatari retirement and pensions contribution
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it does not reach the employee an employer of record places. Law No. 24 of 2002 on Retirement and Pensions states that its provisions apply to Qatari employees subject to the Civil Service Law and to Qatari public servants in public authorities, institutions and corporations; the beneficiary it defines is 'the Qatari beneficiary'. Nothing in it extends to a foreign worker in the private sector. This line is named rather than omitted because a reader comparing Qatar with Germany or France will look for the payroll contribution first and find nothing, and a missing line is easier to trust when it says why it is missing.

source.name: Law No. 24 of 2002 on Retirement and Pensions, scope of application, Al-Meezan legal portal

statutory_extras.name: Mandatory health cover and workmen's compensation
statutory_extras.notes: secondary source for the prices, not the obligation: the obligation itself is read in Law No. 22 of 2021 regulating healthcare services, in force, in its official Arabic text on Al-Meezan. Health insurance is mandatory for expatriates and visitors (art. 8), no expatriate may be employed or have a residence permit issued or renewed without proof of cover for the whole stay (art. 10), and the employer pays the premiums for its workers' basic healthcare and may not recover the cost from them (art. 13). Neither the law nor its executive regulation (Minister of Public Health Decision No. 8 of 2022) sets a premium amount, so the prices rest on Deel's Qatar hiring page, read on 20 September 2026: local health insurance at QAR 3,330 to about QAR 5,150 per employee, workmen's compensation insurance at QAR 350 billed annually, and social security at 14% of basic salary and housing allowance for Qatari and GCC nationals only, which is consistent with what Law No. 24 of 2002 says about its own scope. All of it is carried at zero because each item is a price per head rather than a share of pay. At the QCB peg those charges are between about US$1,010 and US$1,510 a year for one employee, which is larger than it looks against a statutory percentage under three points.

source.name: Secondary source, cited on the Qatar page

countries.notice_typical: Article 49 gives a worker paid monthly one month's written notice where service is five years or less, and two months where it is more. Probation may not exceed six months under article 39 and may not be imposed twice by the same employer. Article 10 is worth knowing on the way out: a claim for worker benefits is free of judicial fees and lapses one year after the contract ends.

countries.name: Romania

assumptions.label: The role is classified as normal working conditions
assumptions.notes: Romania keeps one employer pension charge in reserve for hazardous work. Article 138 of the Fiscal Code sets it at 4% for conditii deosebite de munca and 8% for conditii speciale de munca, both payable by the employer, both defined by the pensions act rather than by the tax authority. An office role does not fall into either class, so neither rate is modelled. The list of qualifying activities sits in the pensions act rather than in the tax code and is not reproduced here. If there is any chance your hire's role is classified as deosebite or speciale, add 4 or 8 points to the figure on this page and ask the provider which classification it will file.

employer_contributions.name: Work insurance contribution (contributia asiguratorie pentru munca)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on the total gross salary and salary-assimilated income of each employee, with no ceiling and no floor
employer_contributions.notes: This single rate is the whole employer side of a Romanian payslip, and it has been since 1 January 2018. Article 220^3(1) of the Fiscal Code states it in one sentence - 'Cota contributiei asiguratorii pentru munca este de 2,25%' - and article 220^4(1) defines the monthly base as the sum of gross salary and salary-assimilated earnings, with no ceiling written anywhere in the chapter. What makes Romania unusual is what that one rate buys. Article 220^6(4) splits the money five ways: 15% to the wage guarantee fund, 20% to the unemployment budget, 5% to the occupational accident and disease insurance system, 40% to the health fund for sick pay, and 20% to the state budget. Countries that charge an employer separately for accident insurance, unemployment and sick-leave funding collect all three here inside 2.25%. The 25% pension and 10% health contributions that also appear on a Romanian payslip are the employee's own, levied on the employee under articles 138(a) and 156; the 2018 reform moved them off the employer and they are not part of this figure.

source.name: Fiscal Code (Legea nr. 227/2015), articles 220^1 to 220^6, consolidated text of 8 August 2026 on the Ministry of Justice legislative portal

statutory_extras.name: First five days of sick leave - paid by the employer
statutory_extras.notes: A real employer cost that no percentage can honestly carry, so it is named here and left out of the total. Article 12 of Government Emergency Ordinance 158/2005 divides sick pay between two payers: 'de catre angajator, din prima zi pana in a 5-a zi de incapacitate temporara de munca', the employer from the first day to the fifth, and the national health fund from the sixth day onward. Every certified illness therefore starts on the employer's account, whatever the 2.25% has already paid into the health fund. What it costs you depends on how often your employee is ill, which is why it cannot be a rate; budget it as a small variable line rather than as nothing.

source.name: Government Emergency Ordinance 158/2005 on health insurance leave and allowances, article 12, consolidated text of 1 July 2026

statutory_extras.name: Disability employment quota - assessed on the legal employer's headcount
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is charged on a company's own headcount, not on one salary. Article 78(2) of Law 448/2006 requires any employer with at least 50 staff to fill 4% of its posts with disabled workers; article 78(3) requires an employer that does not fill them to pay the state, each month, either the national gross minimum wage multiplied by the number of unfilled quota posts, or at least half of that sum where the balance goes to buying goods and services from authorised sheltered workshops. Under an employer of record the legal employer is the provider, whose Romanian payroll is far past fifty people, so the levy is its cost and may be passed on: Deel's Romania page prints a flat 'Disability cost' of RON 162 a month per employee. Ask whether that line appears on your invoice.

source.name: Law 448/2006 on the protection and promotion of the rights of disabled persons, article 78, consolidated text of 31 August 2026

statutory_extras.name: Pre-employment medical certificate - required before the contract is valid
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a fee per hire, not a share of pay, and it is named because it is a condition of the contract existing at all. Article 27 of the Labour Code allows a person to be employed only on the strength of a medical certificate finding them fit for that work, and states in the next paragraph that failing to obtain one makes the individual employment contract void. Providers bill it separately; Deel's Romania page carries it at RON 240. Expect it once per hire, not monthly.

source.name: Labour Code (Legea nr. 53/2003, republished), article 27, consolidated text of 27 April 2026

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Romanian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code creates no thirteenth-month entitlement and no statutory holiday bonus. Romanian employers commonly add meal vouchers, private health cover, a performance bonus and a teleworking allowance, and Deel lists the last of these as a monthly line on its Romania page. None of them is compulsory. Treat all of them as market cost in a competitive offer, not as a legal charge.

source.name: Labour Code (Legea nr. 53/2003, republished), consolidated text of 27 April 2026 on the Ministry of Justice legislative portal

countries.notice_typical: At least twenty working days, the statutory minimum under article 75(1) of the Labour Code for dismissal on grounds of unfitness, professional inadequacy or redundancy. Contracts and collective agreements routinely set longer.

source.name: Labour Code (Legea nr. 53/2003, republished), consolidated text of 27 April 2026 on the Ministry of Justice legislative portal

countries.name: Serbia

assumptions.label: The hire is in their first year with this employer
assumptions.notes: Serbia adds a seniority supplement to pay rather than to the employer's contribution rates, so the ledger below is correct on day one and drifts upward afterwards. Article 108(1)(4) of the Labour Law entitles an employee to increased pay of at least 0.4% of the base for each full year of service completed with the employer, and the same article counts service with a predecessor employer and with entities related to the employer. It is a salary component, not a separate levy, which is why it is carried at zero here: a new hire has no completed years. Over a five-year engagement it adds about 2% to gross pay, and the contributions below then apply to the larger figure.

employer_contributions.name: Pension and disability insurance (PIO), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on a monthly base between the published minimum and maximum contribution bases
employer_contributions.notes: Article 44 of the Law on Contributions for Mandatory Social Insurance sets the headline pension rate at 24% and then splits it: where contributions are paid both out of and on top of the base, the rate is '14% for the persons referred to in article 7(1)(1) to (5) of this Law, and 10% for the employer'. So the 24% figure that appears in country comparisons is the combined rate, and the employer carries ten of those points. The base is bounded at both ends and the bounds are republished every year: the Republic Pension and Disability Insurance Fund states that the maximum monthly base in force from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2026 is RSD 732,820, and the minimum monthly base RSD 51,297, both published in Official Gazette No. 112/25. Those are carried here as annual figures of RSD 8,793,840 and RSD 615,564. The 2025 pair - RSD 656,425 and RSD 45,950 - is still shown on several provider pages, including Deel's Serbia page.

source.name: Law on Contributions for Mandatory Social Insurance, article 44, consolidated text published by the Tax Administration of Serbia, in application from 01/01/2026

employer_contributions.name: Mandatory health insurance, employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on the same bounded base as the pension contribution
employer_contributions.notes: The second and last employer line. Article 44 sets mandatory health insurance at 10.3% in total and 5.15% on each side when contributions are paid both out of and on top of the base, so employer and employee carry the same half. It runs on the same monthly base and the same 2026 floor and ceiling as the pension contribution. Together with the 10% pension share this gives a Serbian employer 15.15% of gross, which is the figure to use when comparing with a neighbour: Serbia's combined burden of 35.05% is slightly heavier than Latvia's 34.09%, but Serbia leaves 19.9 of those points with the employee while Latvia leaves 10.5, so the same gross salary costs an employer materially less here.

source.name: Law on Contributions for Mandatory Social Insurance, article 44, consolidated text published by the Tax Administration of Serbia, in application from 01/01/2026

statutory_extras.name: Unemployment insurance - withheld from the employee, not charged to you
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the employer does not pay it, and named because comparison tables routinely add it to the employer column. Article 44 lists unemployment insurance at 0.75% among the headline rates, and then says plainly that the unemployment contribution 'is paid out of the base at a rate of 0.75%' - out of the base means withheld from the employee's gross pay, unlike the pension and health lines, which are paid both out of and on top of it. An employer of record's invoice should show 15.15% of statutory charges, not 15.90%.

source.name: Law on Contributions for Mandatory Social Insurance, article 44, final paragraph, consolidated text in application from 01/01/2026

statutory_extras.name: Seniority supplement (minuli rad) - 0.4% of pay per completed year
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because a first-year hire has earned none of it, and named because it is the Serbian cost that grows on its own. Article 108(1)(4) of the Labour Law entitles an employee to increased pay of at least 0.4% of the base for each full year of service completed in employment with the employer, and the article adds that service with a predecessor employer under article 147 and with related entities counts too. It raises gross pay rather than the contribution rates, so it compounds: the 15.15% below then applies to the higher salary. Ask a provider how it handles the supplement on a long engagement, because it is a contractual minimum that a flat quote can quietly omit.

source.name: Labour Law of Serbia (Zakon o radu), article 108, editorially consolidated text on the official legal information system

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Serbian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Law creates no thirteenth-month salary. What it does create is a set of pay supplements in article 108 - at least 110% of the base for work on a non-working public holiday, at least 26% for night work and at least 26% for overtime - which are paid only when those hours are actually worked. A salaried engineering role normally triggers none of them, but they belong in the contract rather than in a surprise invoice.

source.name: Labour Law of Serbia (Zakon o radu), article 108, editorially consolidated text on the official legal information system

countries.notice_typical: Between 8 and 30 days where the contract is terminated because the employee is not meeting the required results or lacks the necessary knowledge and abilities, set by the employer's general act or the employment contract according to length of insured service, under article 189 of the Labour Law. During an agreed probation period, either side may terminate on at least five working days' notice under article 36, and the employer must give reasons.

source.name: Labour Law of Serbia (Zakon o radu), article 108, editorially consolidated text on the official legal information system

countries.name: Saudi Arabia

assumptions.label: Non-Saudi employee on a work visa and iqama
assumptions.notes: Almost every employer-of-record hire in Saudi Arabia is a foreign national, and that single fact decides the payroll. Article 5(b) of the Social Insurance Law keeps non-Saudi workers outside every social insurance branch except occupational hazards, so the 11% employer share of the annuities branch and the 1% employer share of unemployment insurance that a Saudi national costs simply do not arise. What the foreign hire costs instead is the end-of-service award, plus a set of per-head charges that no percentage can express. Nitaqat, the Saudisation quota system, is a hiring constraint rather than a payroll cost and is not modelled here.

assumptions.label: Basic pay plus housing allowance as a share of gross
assumptions.notes: Article 8(1) of the Social Insurance Law computes contributions on the basic wage, and lets the Regulations add other benefits and allowances to that base; in practice GOSI charges basic pay plus the housing allowance. This ledger models that base at 90% of gross, which is the share implied by Deel's own Saudi page: it offers employers either 2% of basic pay and housing allowance or 1.80% of the whole monthly gross as the equivalent flat figure. Raise this share towards 1 and the GOSI line rises towards the statutory 2%; it does not change the end-of-service award, which article 84 of the Labor Law computes on the whole wage.

employer_contributions.name: GOSI occupational hazards and additional compensations
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee and worker in the Kingdom, Saudi or foreign, on basic pay plus housing allowance up to SAR 45,000 a month
employer_contributions.notes: This is the only social insurance branch a foreign employee triggers. Article 28 of the Social Insurance Law makes the occupational hazards branch mandatory for 'all employees who work in the Kingdom' and 'all workers who work in the Kingdom', with no nationality condition, and article 29(1) sets the contribution at 'two percent of the contributory wage or salary', borne by the employer alone. Article 8(2) caps the contributory wage at SAR 45,000 a month, so SAR 540,000 a year. Two conditions can move the rate: article 29(1) lets the Board double it for an employer who refuses to comply with safety instructions, and article 29(2) lets the Council of Ministers amend it on an actuarial study. A Saudi national on the same payroll costs 11% for the annuities branch under article 15 and 1% for unemployment insurance under article 44 on top of this line.

source.name: Social Insurance Law, Royal Decree M/273 of 26/12/1445H (2 July 2024), Bureau of Experts official translation

employer_contributions.name: End-of-service award, first five years (provision)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, accruing from the first day and paid when the employment relation ends
employer_contributions.notes: Article 84 of the Labor Law: 'the employer shall pay the worker an end-of-service award equivalent to the amount of a half-month wage for each of the first five years and a one-month wage for each of the following years', calculated 'on the basis of the last wage', with the portions of a year owed in proportion to time served. Half a month a year is 4.1667% of annual pay, and that is the rate modelled here; from the sixth year it doubles to 8.33%, so a long tenure costs an employer twice what this line shows. The base is the wage, not basic pay: article 2 defines the wage as everything given to the worker for the work, and the 2024 amendment to article 61 requires housing and transport to be provided or paid as a cash allowance 'to be included in their wage'. Article 86 is the one lawful narrowing: the parties may agree to leave commissions and sales percentages out of the calculation. This is a provision, not a monthly payment: Saudi law does not require it to be funded month by month, which is why a provider's invoice and a company's own accounts can differ on when it appears.

source.name: Labor Law, Royal Decree M/51 of 23/8/1426H (27 September 2005), consolidated with its amendments, Bureau of Experts official translation

statutory_extras.name: Resignation discount on the end-of-service award
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it lowers a cost rather than adding one, and because no employer can plan on it. Article 85 of the Labor Law gives a worker who resigns one third of the award after two to five continuous years, two thirds after five to ten, and the whole of it after ten. Article 87 cancels that reduction where the worker leaves through force majeure, and for a female worker who ends her contract within six months of marriage or three months of childbirth. The practical consequence for a budget: the 4.1667% provision above is what a dismissal costs, and what a resignation costs is a fraction of it that depends on the calendar.

source.name: Labor Law, Royal Decree M/51 of 23/8/1426H (27 September 2005), consolidated with its amendments, Bureau of Experts official translation

statutory_extras.name: Work permit, iqama and repatriation costs
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because these are amounts per head, not a share of one salary, and they do not scale with pay. Article 40(1) of the Labor Law puts them all on the employer: 'the fees pertaining to the recruitment of non-Saudi workers, the fees for issuing and renewing residence permit (Iqama) and work permit, and the fines resulting from their delay, as well as the fees pertaining to change of profession, exit and re-entry visas, and return tickets to the worker's home country at the end of the relation'. Article 40(3) adds the transfer fee when a worker moves to a new sponsor. These are the charges that make a Gulf employer-of-record quote larger than its percentage suggests, and the reason a hire here takes weeks rather than days. Ask any provider which of them are inside its monthly fee and which are billed on.

source.name: Labor Law, Royal Decree M/51 of 23/8/1426H (27 September 2005), consolidated with its amendments, Bureau of Experts official translation

statutory_extras.name: Employer-provided health care
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a premium per head and per dependant, set by an insurer against the employee's age and cover, not a percentage of pay. Article 144 of the Labor Law requires the employer to 'provide his workers with preventive and therapeutic health care in accordance with the standards set forth by the Minister, taking into consideration whatever is provided for by the Cooperative Health Insurance Law'. Budget it as a real annual cost from day one, and as one that grows with the number of dependants rather than with pay.

source.name: Labor Law, Royal Decree M/51 of 23/8/1426H (27 September 2005), consolidated with its amendments, Bureau of Experts official translation

statutory_extras.name: Housing and transport, or an allowance in their place
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the amount is whatever the employer and employee agree, not a rate. Royal Decree M/44 of 8/2/1446H (12 August 2024) added paragraphs 5 and 6 to article 61 of the Labor Law, requiring the employer to 'provide appropriate housing for his workers, or pay adequate cash allowance in lieu of housing to be included in their wage', and the same for transport. Read the last six words: whatever the employer pays under this heading is part of the wage, so it lifts the base of the end-of-service award and, where it is the housing allowance, the GOSI base as well. This is the newest item on the page and the one most likely to be missing from guides written before 2025.

source.name: Labor Law, Royal Decree M/51 of 23/8/1426H (27 September 2005), consolidated with its amendments, Bureau of Experts official translation

countries.notice_typical: For an indefinite-term contract paid monthly, article 75 as amended in 2024 gives the employer a 60-day written notice period and the employee 30 days. Where the wage is not paid monthly, either side gives 30 days. Probation runs to 90 days and may be extended by written agreement to 180 days in total, excluding the Eid holidays and sick leave; termination inside probation carries no compensation and no end-of-service award.

countries.name: Sweden

employer_contributions.name: Old-age pension contribution (ålderspensionsavgift)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees; the only contribution still due for an employee who has turned 67 at the start of the year
employer_contributions.notes: Largest of the six statutory social contributions listed in chapter 2, section 26 of the Social Contributions Act, as amended by Lag (2025:1362). Section 27 of the same act limits the charge to this line alone once the employee has turned 67 at the start of the year, which is the rule behind the 10.21% band Skatteverket publishes for people born 1938-1958.

source.name: Socialavgiftslag (2000:980), chapter 2 section 26, as amended by Lag (2025:1362) - Sveriges riksdag

employer_contributions.name: Sickness insurance contribution (sjukförsäkringsavgift)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees under 67 at the start of the year
employer_contributions.notes: Funds the state sickness benefit. Separate from the employer's own duty to pay sick pay at 80% of salary for the first 14 days of an absence.

source.name: Socialavgiftslag (2000:980), chapter 2 section 26 point 1, as amended by Lag (2025:1362) - Sveriges riksdag

employer_contributions.name: Parental insurance contribution (föräldraförsäkringsavgift)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees under 67 at the start of the year
employer_contributions.notes: Funds the 480 days of parental leave shared between parents; the employer pays the contribution, not the leave itself.

source.name: Socialavgiftslag (2000:980), chapter 2 section 26 point 2, as amended by Lag (2025:1362) - Sveriges riksdag

employer_contributions.name: Labour market contribution (arbetsmarknadsavgift)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees under 67 at the start of the year
employer_contributions.notes: Funds unemployment insurance and active labour market measures.

source.name: Socialavgiftslag (2000:980), chapter 2 section 26 point 5, as amended by Lag (2025:1362) - Sveriges riksdag

employer_contributions.name: Survivors' pension contribution (efterlevandepensionsavgift)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees under 67 at the start of the year
employer_contributions.notes: Smallest of the pension lines; funds survivors' benefits.

source.name: Socialavgiftslag (2000:980), chapter 2 section 26 point 4, as amended by Lag (2025:1362) - Sveriges riksdag

employer_contributions.name: Work injury contribution (arbetsskadeavgift)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees under 67 at the start of the year
employer_contributions.notes: Flat national rate. Unlike Japan, Italy or Australia, Sweden does not vary the work injury contribution by industry risk class, so an office role and a construction role carry the same 0.10%.

source.name: Socialavgiftslag (2000:980), chapter 2 section 26 point 6, as amended by Lag (2025:1362) - Sveriges riksdag

employer_contributions.name: General payroll tax (allmän löneavgift)
employer_contributions.applies: Employers with a permanent establishment in Sweden
employer_contributions.notes: Set by a separate act from the six social contributions and paid to the state rather than to any insurance branch, which is why Sweden's headline 31.42% is 18.80% of social contributions plus this 12.62%. A foreign employer with no permanent establishment in Sweden pays only the 18.80%; an EOR hire runs through an established Swedish entity, so the full rate applies. From 1 April 2026 to 30 September 2027 a temporary measure (Lag 2026:100) halves this tax and the non-pension contributions for employees who had turned 18 but not 23 at the start of the year, on the part of pay up to SEK 25,000 a month, giving a blended 20.81%.

source.name: Lag (1994:1920) om allmän löneavgift, section 3, as amended by Lag (2025:1360) - Sveriges riksdag

statutory_extras.name: Holiday supplement (semestertillägg)
statutory_extras.notes: For a monthly-paid employee the salary keeps running during annual leave and a supplement of 0.43% of the monthly salary is added for each paid leave day taken. Over the statutory 25 days that is 10.75% of one month's salary, which is about 0.90% of annual pay - the figure carried here. Employees on weekly pay take 1.82% of the weekly salary per day instead, and employees with irregular pay can be settled under the alternative 12%-of-annual-earnings rule in section 16 b.

source.name: Semesterlag (1977:480), section 16 a, as amended by Lag (2009:1439) - Sveriges riksdag

statutory_extras.name: Occupational pension (tjänstepension) - contractual, not statutory
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero on purpose. Sweden has no statutory employer duty to fund an occupational pension: the Swedish Pensions Agency states that it is set in a collective agreement between an employer or employers' organisation and a union, or directly with the employee, and that it is not a given at private employers. Provider pages that add roughly 4.5% to Sweden's employer cost are quoting the ITP1 collective-agreement rate, which is a contractual commitment an EOR takes on, not a legal charge. Ask any provider in writing which collective agreement it applies before comparing quotes.

source.name: Pensionsmyndigheten - Det här är tjänstepension

countries.notice_typical: Statutory minimum one month for both sides; the employee's entitlement rises with service to two months (2-4 years), three months (4-6), four months (6-8), five months (8-10) and six months from ten years (Employment Protection Act, section 11).

countries.name: Singapore

assumptions.label: Employee is a Singapore citizen or PR (CPF applies)
assumptions.notes: Set to 0 for Employment Pass holders: no CPF, Skills Development Levy (SDL) only. Most EOR hires in Singapore are on an Employment Pass, so toggle this off unless the hire is confirmed as a citizen or permanent resident.

employer_contributions.name: CPF employer contribution (age 55 and below)
employer_contributions.applies: Singapore citizens and permanent residents only; see assumption employee_is_citizen_or_pr
employer_contributions.notes: 17% employer share applies to employees aged 55 and below earning above S$750/month, on Ordinary Wages capped at the OW ceiling of S$8,000/month (S$96,000/year) plus Additional Wages up to the annual limit. Employer CPF rate falls with age under the same official table: 16% (above 55-60), 12.5% (above 60-65), 9% (above 65-70), 7.5% (above 70). Rates in force from 1 January 2026 (CPF Board, Table 1). Does not apply to Employment Pass or S Pass holders.

source.name: CPF Board - CPF Contribution Rate Table from 1 January 2026 (Table 1, Singapore Citizens/PR)

employer_contributions.name: Skills Development Levy (SDL)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees working in Singapore, including foreign employees (Employment Pass, S Pass, Work Permit)
employer_contributions.notes: 0.25% of monthly total wages. Minimum payable is S$2/month for wages below S$800; maximum is S$11.25/month for wages above S$4,500 (modelled here as a floor/cap on the monthly wage base of S$800 / S$4,500, i.e. S$9,600 / S$54,000 a year). Payable for every employee regardless of nationality or CPF status, on top of CPF where CPF applies.

source.name: CPF Board - Skills Development Levy

countries.notice_typical: No fixed statutory length; Employment Act default when the contract is silent: 1 day (<26 weeks of service), 1 week (26 weeks-2 years), 2 weeks (2-5 years), 4 weeks (5+ years).

source.quote: These payments are not compulsory, unless they are in your contract.

countries.name: Slovakia

assumptions.label: Employee is not a person with a disability and does not draw an old-age, early old-age or long-service pension
assumptions.notes: Both change the ledger. For an employee with a disability the employer health rate halves to 5.5%. For an employee already drawing an old-age or early old-age pension the employer pays no invalidity insurance, and unemployment insurance does not apply either.

assumptions.label: Meal contribution paid on 234 shift days in 2026: 261 weekdays, less the 7 days of rest that fall on a weekday, less 20 days of leave
assumptions.notes: A declared modelling point, not a statutory figure. An employee who turns 33 during the year has 25 days of leave, which takes the count to 229; days of sickness or other absence take it lower again, because the contribution follows shifts actually worked for more than four hours.

employer_contributions.name: Sickness insurance (nemocenské poistenie)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees, up to the maximum assessment base
employer_contributions.notes: Section 130(b) of the Social Insurance Act sets the employer rate at 1.4%, the same as the employee's. The maximum assessment base for 2026 is EUR 16,764 a month, EUR 201,168 a year, and the Social Insurance Agency states that it applies to every social insurance fund except work-injury insurance. It is a ceiling on the base, not on the premium: the monthly maximum here is EUR 234.69.

source.name: Sociálna poisťovňa - Tabuľky platenia poistného od 1. januára 2026 (employer table and note 2)

employer_contributions.name: Old-age pension insurance (starobné poistenie)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees, up to the maximum assessment base
employer_contributions.notes: Section 131(1)(b) sets the employer rate at 14%. For an employee who saves in the second pillar, 4 points of it are passed on to the employee's pension fund in 2026; the Social Insurance Agency confirms the second-pillar rate stays at 4% this year. That is a split inside the 14%, not an extra charge, so the employer pays 14% either way.

source.name: Zákon č. 461/2003 Z. z. o sociálnom poistení, section 131, version in force from 1 September 2026 - Slov-Lex

employer_contributions.name: Invalidity insurance (invalidné poistenie)
employer_contributions.applies: Employees who do not already draw an old-age or early old-age pension
employer_contributions.notes: Section 132(b) sets the employer rate at 3%. It is a separate line from sickness insurance, and it is the one a cost table most easily drops: a provider table that shows 1.4% as 'disability insurance' has in fact printed the sickness line and left this one out. Section 128(3) exempts the employer for an employee who is already a pensioner.

source.name: Zákon č. 461/2003 Z. z. o sociálnom poistení, sections 128(3) and 132, version in force from 1 September 2026 - Slov-Lex

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (poistenie v nezamestnanosti)
employer_contributions.applies: Employers that also pay the short-time-work support premium, which covers an ordinary employment contract
employer_contributions.notes: Section 136(b) gives two employer rates: 0.5% for an employer that pays the premium financing short-time-work support, 1% for one that does not. Section 128(1)(g) makes that premium payable for every employee on an employment contract, so an ordinary hire sits on 0.5% here plus 0.5% on the next line; the total is 1% either way.

source.name: Zákon č. 461/2003 Z. z. o sociálnom poistení, sections 128(1)(g) and 136, version in force from 1 September 2026 - Slov-Lex

employer_contributions.name: Short-time-work support financing premium (poistné na financovanie podpory)
employer_contributions.applies: Employer, for each employee on an employment contract
employer_contributions.notes: Section 136a sets it at 0.5%. It funds the support paid to employers during short-time work, and it is the reason the employer's unemployment line is 0.5% rather than 1%. Cost pages that print a single 1% unemployment line are not wrong on the total; they are showing the older layout.

source.name: Zákon č. 461/2003 Z. z. o sociálnom poistení, section 136a, version in force from 1 September 2026 - Slov-Lex

employer_contributions.name: Guarantee insurance (garančné poistenie)
employer_contributions.applies: Employer, for each employee
employer_contributions.notes: Section 135 sets it at 0.25%. It funds wage claims when an employer becomes insolvent, and it is capped at the same maximum assessment base as the other social insurance funds: the Social Insurance Agency's note 2 lists guarantee insurance among the capped funds, and its table gives EUR 41.91 as the monthly maximum.

source.name: Sociálna poisťovňa - Tabuľky platenia poistného od 1. januára 2026 (employer table and note 2)

employer_contributions.name: Solidarity reserve fund (rezervný fond solidarity)
employer_contributions.applies: Employer, for each employee
employer_contributions.notes: Section 137(a) sets it at 4.75%, paid by the employer alone. It is the second-largest social insurance line after old-age insurance, and it is capped at the maximum assessment base: EUR 796.29 a month at most in 2026.

source.name: Zákon č. 461/2003 Z. z. o sociálnom poistení, section 137, version in force from 1 September 2026 - Slov-Lex

employer_contributions.name: Work-injury insurance (úrazové poistenie)
employer_contributions.applies: Employer, for each employee, on the full pay with no ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Section 133 sets a single employer rate of 0.8%, so there is no risk class to model: the rate does not depend on the provider's activity or on the job. It is the one social insurance line with no maximum base; the Social Insurance Agency marks it 'neobmedz.' in its employer table and states in note 5 that it is calculated on actual earnings because its base has no upper limit.

source.name: Sociálna poisťovňa - Tabuľky platenia poistného od 1. januára 2026 (employer table, notes 2 and 5)

employer_contributions.name: Public health insurance (zdravotné poistenie)
employer_contributions.applies: Employees without a disability, with no upper ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: Section 12(1)(d) of the Health Insurance Act still reads 10%, but the transitional section 38ezk sets the employer rate at 11% from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2027, continuing the 11% that applied in 2024 and 2025; the employee rate rose from 4% to 5% on 1 January 2026. VšZP, the state health insurer, prints the same 11% in its 2026 table and marks the maximum assessment base for employers as 'not set'. For an employee with a disability the employer rate is 5.5%.

source.name: Zákon č. 580/2004 Z. z. o zdravotnom poistení, sections 12(1)(d) and 38ezk, version in force from 1 July 2026 - Slov-Lex

employer_contributions.name: Statutory meal contribution (stravovanie zamestnancov)
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee working a shift of more than four hours, about EUR 3.84 per shift day, modelled at 234 shift days in 2026
employer_contributions.notes: A cost set by the Labour Code rather than by a premium, which is why it is missing from rate-only cost pages. Section 152 obliges the employer to provide a meal for every shift over four hours and to pay at least 55% of its price. A meal voucher must be worth at least 75% of the meal allowance for a 5 to 12 hour business trip, which has been EUR 9.30 since 1 December 2025, so at least about EUR 6.98. A teleworker whose employer runs no canteen receives the cash meal contribution instead, section 152(6)(d), at no less than 55% of that minimum voucher value, which is about EUR 3.84 a day. At 234 shift days that is EUR 899 a year, a flat sum whatever the salary, and it rises each time the ministry raises the allowance.

source.name: Zákonník práce (zákon č. 311/2001 Z. z.), section 152, version in force from 1 September 2026 - Slov-Lex; allowance: oznámenie č. 280/2025 Z. z.

statutory_extras.name: Mandatory social fund allocation (sociálny fond)
statutory_extras.notes: Counted in the total because it is a recurring percentage of pay that every Slovak employer must set aside. The Social Fund Act makes the employer allocate at least 0.6% of the gross wages it books each month to a fund that can only be spent on its employees; a profitable employer that is up to date with tax and insurance may allocate up to 1%. The allocation is a business expense, and the fund often pays the top-up on meal contributions, so it is money spent on staff rather than a levy paid to the state.

source.name: Zákon č. 152/1994 Z. z. o sociálnom fonde, sections 2 to 5, version in force from 1 January 2025 - Slov-Lex

statutory_extras.name: Employer-paid sick pay for the first 14 days (náhrada príjmu)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it follows absence rather than pay. Since 1 January 2026 the employer pays the first 14 days of a temporary incapacity, up from 10: 25% of the daily assessment base for days 1 to 3 and 55% for days 4 to 14, or up to 80% if a collective agreement says so. The Social Insurance Agency pays sickness benefit from day 15.

source.name: Zákon č. 462/2003 Z. z. o náhrade príjmu, section 8, version in force from 1 January 2026 - Slov-Lex

statutory_extras.name: Severance on redundancy (odstupné)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it depends on how the employment ends. Section 76 of the Labour Code pays it on termination for organisational or health reasons. After notice: one month's average earnings from two years of service, two months from five years, three from ten and four from twenty, with nothing under two years because the notice period covers that stretch. After a termination agreement for the same reasons: one month under two years, then two, three, four and five months at two, five, ten and twenty years.

source.name: Zákonník práce (zákon č. 311/2001 Z. z.), section 76, version in force from 1 September 2026 - Slov-Lex

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth-month pay
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because Slovak law does not create it. Summer and Christmas bonuses are common, but they come from a collective agreement or the employment contract, and when paid they count in full towards the social and health insurance bases.

source.name: Zákonník práce (zákon č. 311/2001 Z. z.), version in force from 1 September 2026 - Slov-Lex

countries.holidays_note: in 2026, with 8 May and 15 Sept suspended
countries.notice_typical: At least one month, and at least two months either way once the employment has lasted a year. An employer dismissing for organisational or health reasons gives at least three months after five years of service. Notice starts on the first day of the month after it is delivered and ends on the last day of the final month. Probation is at most three months, or six for a senior manager reporting to the statutory body, must be agreed in writing, and cannot be extended.

source.name: Zákonník práce (zákon č. 311/2001 Z. z.), version in force from 1 September 2026 - Slov-Lex

countries.name: Thailand

assumptions.label: Workmen's compensation main rate 0.2% (office and business services class)
assumptions.notes: The Workmen's Compensation Fund main rate runs from 0.2% to 1.0% of pay by business type, set by the ministerial notice of 21 February 2019. Modelled at the office and business-services grade, which is the lowest in that band, because the grade follows the employer's registered activity and an EOR registers as an office-based service business — the Social Security Office's own worked example puts a restaurant one grade above it. The base is capped at THB 240,000 a year per employee, so the whole line is THB 480 a year here and would be THB 2,400 at the 1.0% grade.

employer_contributions.name: Social security contribution (เงินสมทบประกันสังคม), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Section 33 insured employees; charged on monthly wages between THB 1,650 and THB 17,500
employer_contributions.notes: Five per cent in three pieces, all on the same capped base: 1.5% for sickness, invalidity, death and maternity and 3% for child allowance and old age, both from the 2012 ministerial regulation's schedule C in force since 1 January 2013, plus 0.5% for unemployment from the 2003 regulation in force since 1 January 2004. The ceiling is the whole story on an engineer's salary. It had been THB 15,000 a month since 1995; a ministerial regulation published in the Government Gazette on 12 December 2025 raised it to THB 17,500 from 1 January 2026, then THB 20,000 from 2029 and THB 23,000 from 2032. The employer's bill therefore stops at THB 875 a month, up from THB 750 in 2025.

source.name: Ministerial Regulation prescribing the minimum and maximum wages used as the base for calculating contributions of insured persons under section 33, B.E. 2568 (2025) — Government Gazette vol. 142, part 81 A, p. 5, 12 December 2025: not less than THB 1,650 and not more than THB 17,500 a month from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2028

employer_contributions.name: Workmen's Compensation Fund (กองทุนเงินทดแทน), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only work-injury cover; base capped at THB 240,000 of annual pay per employee
employer_contributions.notes: The Social Security Office states that the employer alone pays this fund, that the contribution is the year's total wages per employee capped at THB 240,000 multiplied by a main rate of 0.2% to 1.0% by business type, and that from the fifth year the rate is adjusted by the employer's own claims experience — up to 50% above the main rate for a loss-making record, down for a clean one. At the office class the whole line is THB 480 a year, under US$15.

source.name: Social Security Office notice on the criteria and method for calculating the loss ratio, with the accompanying explanation of experience-rated contributions — Government Gazette vol. 139, special part 290 D, p. 53, 14 December 2022: employer pays alone, annual wages capped at THB 240,000 per person, main rate 0.2–1.0%

statutory_extras.name: Provident fund contribution
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because no statute creates it. Thailand has no mandatory occupational pension on top of social security: a provident fund is voluntary, set up by agreement between employer and employees and typically 3% to 5% matched. Providers often quote one as part of a benefits package; that is a contractual cost, not a legal charge, so publishing it as law would publish a quote as the rule.

source.name: Ministerial Regulation prescribing the social security contribution rates B.E. 2555 (2012), schedule C — the statutory employer contributions are sickness/invalidity/death/maternity 1.5% and child allowance/old age 3%, with no further employer pension line

statutory_extras.name: Statutory severance pay on dismissal without cause
statutory_extras.notes: Real and large, but contingent rather than recurring, so it is named here and left out of the monthly on-cost. Section 118 owes severance only when the employer ends the contract, in six steps by uninterrupted service: 30 days of the last wage from 120 days to under one year, 90 days from one to three years, 180 days from three to six, 240 days from six to ten, 300 days from ten to twenty, and 400 days from twenty years. That first threshold is why probation periods in Thailand are usually written as 119 days. Budget for it as an exit cost, and ask the provider whether it funds the accrual or invoices it when the hire ends.

source.name: Labour Protection Act B.E. 2541 (1998) as amended to the Labour Protection Act (No. 7) B.E. 2562 (2019), official English translation published by the Department of Labour Protection and Welfare, section 118

statutory_extras.name: Statutory annual leave (6 days after one year)
statutory_extras.notes: Paid time inside the salary rather than an extra contribution. Section 30 gives an employee with one year of uninterrupted service annual holidays of not less than six working days a year, fixed in advance by the employer or by agreement, and lets the employer grant more from the following year; most provider contracts offer more, and a Thai employment contract usually sets 10 to 15 days. Sick leave is separate and paid for up to 30 days a year.

source.name: Labour Protection Act B.E. 2541 (1998) as amended to the Labour Protection Act (No. 7) B.E. 2562 (2019), official English translation published by the Department of Labour Protection and Welfare, section 30

countries.probation_note: no statutory maximum; severance from 120 days
countries.notice_typical: No fixed statutory maximum for probation, and no at-will termination: dismissal must rest on cause, and dismissal without cause requires notice of one full payment cycle — in practice one month — plus statutory severance that rises in steps with length of service once 120 days of work are complete. An employee resigns on the same one payment cycle of notice.

countries.name: Turkey

assumptions.label: The two-point Treasury support on the employer's pension share is left out of the total
assumptions.notes: Article 81(ı) of act 5510 has the Treasury cover part of the employer's pension share, but only while the employer files on time and owes SGK nothing in premiums, administrative fines, late-payment penalties or interest. It is a discount a buyer cannot verify from outside, and it was cut from four points to two with effect from 1 January 2026, so the ledger carries the undiscounted rate and names the discount instead.

assumptions.label: Role carries no added service time (fiilî hizmet süresi zammı), so the employer's pension share is 12%
assumptions.notes: Where a job qualifies for 60, 90 or 180 days of added service a year, the employer pays the whole of the difference: SGK publishes the employer pension share at 13%, 13.5% and 15% for those three cases. Office and software work is not among them.

employer_contributions.name: Invalidity, old-age and survivors' insurance, employer share (malûllük, yaşlılık ve ölüm)
employer_contributions.applies: Employees insured under article 4/1(a) of act 5510, at the ordinary rate with no added service time
employer_contributions.notes: Act 7566 of 4 December 2025 raised this branch from 20% to 21% with effect from 1 January 2026 and put the whole point on the employer, whose share went from 11% to 12% while the employee stayed at 9%. The same act cut the Treasury support in article 81(ı) from four points to two, so a compliant employer that files on time and owes SGK nothing pays 10% here rather than 12%; that support is conditional and is not applied in this ledger. The President may add up to six further points on the part of pay up to the floor for employers in particular provinces. The base runs between a floor of the monthly minimum wage and a ceiling of nine times it.

source.name: Sosyal Güvenlik Kurumu - İşveren Prim Oranları (rate table published 13 January 2026)

employer_contributions.name: General health insurance, employer share (genel sağlık sigortası)
employer_contributions.applies: Employees insured under article 4/1(a) of act 5510
employer_contributions.notes: Article 81(f) of act 5510 sets general health insurance at 12.5% of the premium base for people covered by both the short-term and the long-term branches, split 7.5% employer and 5% employee. It runs on the same floor and ceiling as the pension line.

source.name: Sosyal Güvenlik Kurumu - İşveren Prim Oranları (rate table published 13 January 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Short-term branches: work accident and occupational disease (kısa vadeli sigorta kolları)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees; the employee pays nothing towards this branch
employer_contributions.notes: Employer-only, and flat across industries since the risk-rated scale was abolished: article 81(c) of act 5510 sets one rate for everybody, raised from 2% to 2.25% by act 7524 of 28 July 2024, with power for the President to move it between 1.5% and 2.5%. A Turkish quote that varies this line by industry is quoting the pre-2013 system.

source.name: Sosyal Güvenlik Kurumu - İşveren Prim Oranları (rate table published 13 January 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance, employer share (işsizlik sigortası)
employer_contributions.applies: All employees; the state adds a further 1% alongside the employer's 2% and the employee's 1%
employer_contributions.notes: Collected with the social security premiums and on the same floor and ceiling, which SGK states in one sentence covering both. The employer's 2% is twice what the employee pays, and the state adds a matching 1% of its own.

source.name: Sosyal Güvenlik Kurumu - Prime Esas Kazanç Miktarları, 2026 limits (published 14 January 2026)

statutory_extras.name: Severance pay (kıdem tazminatı)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is contingent on how the employment ends, and it is the largest number a Turkish quote can hide. Article 14 of act 1475, kept alive by the 2003 Labour Act, gives 30 days' pay for every full year of service and a pro-rata amount for part years, but only where the employer terminates for something other than just cause, or the employee leaves for just cause, or for military service, retirement, the death of the employee, or a woman resigning within a year of marrying. A resignation without cause and a dismissal for cause pay nothing. Accrued in full it is 8.33% of annual pay, and the annual amount is capped at the highest civil servant's maximum one-year retirement bonus, a ceiling reset every January and July. Providers commonly hold a reserve or bill an accrual for it: ask which, and ask what happens to the money if the employee resigns.

source.name: İş Kanunu no. 1475, article 14, kept in force by article 120 of act 4857 - Mevzuat Bilgi Sistemi

statutory_extras.name: Payment in lieu of notice (ihbar tazminatı)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero for the same reason. Article 17 of the Labour Act lets either side end an indefinite contract by giving two, four, six or eight weeks' notice according to service, and the side that does not give notice owes pay for the notice period instead. An employer that wants an immediate exit therefore pays up to two months of salary on top of any severance.

source.name: İş Kanunu no. 4857, article 17 - Mevzuat Bilgi Sistemi

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth-month pay
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because Turkish law does not create it for the private sector. The Labour Act sets no thirteenth month or annual bonus; where one is paid it comes from the contract or a collective agreement, and it then counts in the premium base like any other payment.

source.name: İş Kanunu no. 4857, read in full for any bonus obligation - Mevzuat Bilgi Sistemi

countries.notice_typical: Two weeks for service under six months, four weeks from six months to a year and a half, six weeks from a year and a half to three years and eight weeks beyond three years, running from the day the notice reaches the other side (Labour Act, article 17). The periods are minimums and a contract may lengthen them, but the same length has to apply to both sides. An employer that wants the employee gone at once pays the notice salary instead. Probation may be agreed for at most two months, or four under a collective agreement, and either side may end the contract during it without notice or compensation.

countries.name: Taiwan

assumptions.label: Occupational accident insurance modelled at 0.25% (manpower brokerage and supply, the provider's class: industry rate 0.18% plus the flat commuting rate 0.07%)
assumptions.notes: The rate table in force since 1 January 2025, announced by the Ministry of Labor on 7 November 2024, has two columns: an industry rate running from 0.05% to 0.89%, and a single commuting-accident rate of 0.07% that every employer pays, for a combined premium of 0.12% to 0.96%. The rate follows the insured unit's registered business activity, not the worker's job, and under an employer of record the insured unit is the provider, so this page models the provider's class, as it does for Korea and Brazil: line 48, manpower brokerage and supply, reads 0.18% plus 0.07%, 0.25% in all. A provider registered under line 42, computer programming, consultancy and information services, would pay 0.05% plus 0.07%, 0.12% in all. The line is small either way: about US$69 a year at 0.25% on this page's example, about US$33 at 0.12%, and about US$264 at the top of the table.

employer_contributions.name: Labor insurance, ordinary accident premium (勞工保險普通事故保險費), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Employees covered by the Labor Insurance Act; charged on the monthly insured salary, which the official table floors at TWD 29,500 and caps at TWD 45,800
employer_contributions.notes: The headline rate is 11.5% of the insured salary and the employer pays 70% of it, which is the 8.05% used here. The Bureau of Labor Insurance publishes the rate calendar on its premium calculator: 10.5% from 1 January 2021, 11% from 1 January 2023 and 11.5% from 1 January 2025 (民國114年). The 70/20/10 split between employer, employee and central government is Article 15 of the Labor Insurance Act (https://law.moj.gov.tw/ENG/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=N0050001, amended 21 January 2026). The ceiling does most of the work on a professional salary: the insured-salary table issued by order of 21 November 2025 and in force from 1 January 2026 stops at TWD 45,800 a month for any total pay of TWD 43,901 or more (https://www.bli.gov.tw/Files/25661), so the employer's bill for this line stops at about TWD 3,687 a month.

source.name: Bureau of Labor Insurance — labor, employment and occupational accident insurance premium calculator, rate note: the ordinary-accident rate has been 11.5% of the insured salary since 1 January 2025, and employment insurance 1% since 2003

employer_contributions.name: Employment insurance (就業保險費), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Same insured salary as labor insurance, so the same TWD 45,800 monthly ceiling applies
employer_contributions.notes: One per cent of the insured salary, shared the same way as labor insurance, so the employer carries 0.7%. The Employment Insurance Act sets the rate band at 1% to 2% (Article 8) and refers premium sharing back to the Labor Insurance Act (Article 40); the rate has stood at the bottom of that band, 1%, since 1 January 2003. It is collected on the same bill as labor insurance, which is why provider quotes often merge the two into one line.

source.name: Employment Insurance Act, Articles 8 and 40 — the central authority sets the rate at 1% to 2% of the insured salary, and premium sharing follows the Labor Insurance Act

employer_contributions.name: Labor occupational accident insurance (勞工職業災害保險), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: Employer-only cover with its own insured-salary table: floor TWD 29,500 a month, ceiling TWD 72,800 a month
employer_contributions.notes: Since the Labor Occupational Accident Insurance and Protection Act took effect this cover has its own premium and its own, higher ceiling than labor insurance. The premium has two parts, an industry rate from 0.05% to 0.89% and a single commuting-accident rate of 0.07%, and the whole of it is borne by the insured unit; the insured salary is floored at the minimum wage (TWD 29,500 in 2026) and capped at TWD 72,800 (https://www.bli.gov.tw/0106048.html). Employers above a certain headcount are then experience-rated each year on their own claims record. Modelled here at 0.18% plus 0.07%, line 48 of the rate table (manpower brokerage and supply, the provider's class); see the assumption above.

source.name: Bureau of Labor Insurance — occupational accident insurance industry rate table, Ministry of Labor announcement Lao-Dong-Bao-San No. 1130085419 of 7 November 2024, in force from 1 January 2025: line 48, manpower brokerage and supply, industry rate 0.18% plus commuting rate 0.07%, 0.25% in all (line 42, software and information services, reads 0.12%)

employer_contributions.name: National health insurance (全民健康保險), employer share including the average-dependant factor
employer_contributions.applies: Employees of private businesses with a fixed employer (Category 1); insured amount floored at TWD 29,500 and capped at TWD 313,000 a month
employer_contributions.notes: The published rate is 5.17% of the insured amount and the employer carries 60% of it under Article 27 of the National Health Insurance Act — but the employer's share is not 60% of one premium. The NHIA charges the employer for the insured person plus an average number of dependants, set at 0.56 since 1 January 2024, so the employer pays 5.17% × 60% × 1.56 = 4.83912% whether or not this particular employee has any dependants. That is why the health line is the second largest in this ledger, and why it is easy to underestimate: reading 5.17% and taking 60% of it gives about two thirds of the real figure. The ceiling is high enough that most professional salaries are charged in full.

source.name: National Health Insurance Administration — premium contribution table (3) for employees of public and private enterprises with a fixed employer, in force 1 January 2026: rate 5.17% since 1 January 2021, employer share 60%, average dependants 0.56 (1.56 units) since 1 January 2024, grades from TWD 29,500 to TWD 313,000

employer_contributions.name: Labor pension contribution (勞工退休金), employer
employer_contributions.applies: Individual pension account under the Labor Pension Act; contribution wage capped at TWD 150,000 a month
employer_contributions.notes: Six per cent of the worker's monthly wage into an individual pension account, and the statute writes it as a floor — the employer's contribution shall not be less than six percent — so six is the minimum, not a negotiated rate. The contribution wage follows a grade table issued by order of 24 November 2025 and in force from 1 January 2026, whose top grade is TWD 150,000 a month (https://www.bli.gov.tw/Files/25709); this engine charges the salary itself up to that ceiling rather than rounding it to the nearest grade, which moves the line by at most a few dollars a month. It is the largest single line in this ledger at the example salary, and unlike labor and health insurance it is not shared with the employee.

source.name: Labor Pension Act, Article 14 (amended 15 May 2019): the pension borne by the employer shall not be less than six percent of the worker's monthly wage, graded by the Monthly Contribution Classification Table

statutory_extras.name: Arrear Wage Payment Fund (積欠工資墊償基金), employer only
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the amount is too small to show as a ledger line, not because the duty is missing: it is real, monthly, and paid by the employer alone. The rate is two and a half parts in ten thousand — 0.025% — of the labor-insurance insured salary, which is capped at TWD 45,800 a month, so the charge stops at about TWD 137 a year, roughly US$4. The fund advances unpaid wages, pensions and severance when an employer shuts down. It is billed on the same slip as the labor insurance premium, which is why it disappears inside provider quotes.

source.name: Regulations for the Contribution and Payment of the Arrear Wage Payment Fund, Article 3 (amended 20 May 2015): the employer contributes monthly at 2.5 per ten thousand of the total labor insurance insured salary

statutory_extras.name: Year-end bonus / profit allowance
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because no statute fixes an amount. Article 29 of the Labor Standards Act requires a business that closed its year in profit — after tax, after covering prior losses and after setting aside dividends and legal reserves — to pay allowances or a bonus out of what is left to workers who served the whole year without fault. That is a duty tied to profit, not a thirteenth month: it carries no rate, no floor and no effect in a loss-making year. Market practice around Lunar New Year is a separate matter and is usually written into the offer, so ask the provider what the contract promises before budgeting one or two months of pay.

source.name: Labor Standards Act, Article 29 (amended 31 July 2024): after the business year closes and taxes, prior losses, dividends and legal reserves are settled, allowances or bonus shall be paid out of the remaining net profit

statutory_extras.name: Statutory severance pay on employer-initiated termination
statutory_extras.notes: Real but contingent, so it is named here and left out of the monthly on-cost. Where the employer ends the contract on one of the statutory grounds, severance under the Labor Pension Act is half a month of average wages for every full year of service, pro rata below a year, capped at six months of average wages. Notice is separate: ten days after three months of service, twenty days after one year, thirty days after three years, or pay in lieu. Ask the provider whether it accrues this monthly or invoices it when the hire ends.

source.name: Labor Pension Act, Article 12 (amended 15 May 2019): severance of half a month of average wages per full year of service, pro rata for part years, not exceeding six months of average wages

statutory_extras.name: Employer supplementary health insurance premium
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because at this page's example there is no gap for it to bite on, but it is the charge most likely to surprise a first-time employer here. Article 34 of the National Health Insurance Act makes the employer pay a supplementary premium on the difference between the total salary it pays in a month and the insured amounts it declared for that month; Article 33 sets that rate at 2% at the start and has it move with the main premium rate, which the authority announces. The gap opens when a bonus is paid on top of the monthly salary, or when pay runs past the top grade of the health table — so a thirteenth-month payment carries a health charge for the employer as well as for the employee.

source.name: National Health Insurance Act, Articles 33 and 34 (amended 28 June 2023): the employer pays a supplementary premium on the amount by which salary paid exceeds the insured payroll amount for the month

statutory_extras.name: Statutory annual leave (7 days after one year of service)
statutory_extras.notes: Paid time inside the salary rather than an extra contribution. The Labor Standards Act grants three days after six months, seven after one year, ten after two, fourteen after three, fifteen after five, and one more day per year beyond ten years up to thirty. Unused days are paid out at the end of the year or on termination, so the entitlement turns into cash rather than lapsing.

source.name: Labor Standards Act, Article 38 (amended 31 July 2024): three days at six months, seven days at one year, ten at two years, fourteen at three years, fifteen at five years, rising to a maximum of thirty

countries.probation_note: none in statute; reasonable term by contract
countries.notice_typical: No statutory probation period: the Labor Standards Act has none, and its Enforcement Rules dropped their 40-day cap on 12 June 1997. The labour ministry's interpretation of 3 September 1997 accepts a reasonable probation agreed by contract, but dismissal during or at the end of it still follows the Act's ordinary notice and severance rules. Notice on employer-initiated termination runs ten days after three months of continuous service, twenty days after one year and thirty days after three years, with pay in lieu allowed; during the notice period the employee may take up to two paid days a week to look for work. Severance of half a month of average wages per year of service, capped at six months, comes on top where the ground for dismissal is a statutory one.

countries.name: Ukraine

assumptions.label: The employer is an ordinary payer, not a Diia City resident
assumptions.notes: This assumption is worth more money than anything else on this page. Part 14-1 of article 8 of the unified contribution law sets the contribution for a Diia City resident at the minimum insurance contribution on each insured person's salary - a flat amount, not a percentage - instead of 22% of actual pay. The minimum insurance contribution is defined in article 1 as the minimum wage multiplied by the rate, so in 2026 it is 22% of UAH 8,647, that is UAH 1,902.34 a month, whatever the employee earns. An employer of record is priced here as an ordinary payer at 22%, because Diia City residency is a status a company obtains for itself under the digital-economy law and carries qualifying conditions on activity, headcount and average pay that a provider hiring on your behalf will not normally meet for your role. If you are weighing an entity of your own, this is the line to model first.

employer_contributions.name: Unified social contribution (ЄСВ), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employee, on gross pay between one and twenty minimum wages a month; the employee has no contribution of their own
employer_contributions.notes: One contribution covers pensions, sickness, unemployment and work-accident cover, and the employee pays none of it: article 8(5) states that the unified contribution for the payers listed in article 4 'is set at 22 per cent of the base of assessment defined by article 7 of this Law'. The ceiling is where published figures for Ukraine go stale, and the law does not read the way most summaries say. Article 1(4) defines the maximum base as fifteen minimum wages, but that definition has been suspended for 2026 by the State Budget Law of 3 December 2025, and article 32 of that budget law sets the maximum base from 1 January 2026 at twenty minimum wages for everyone except military and police pay, which stays at fifteen. With the minimum wage fixed at UAH 8,647 a month by article 8 of the same budget law, the 2026 ceiling is UAH 172,940 a month, carried here as UAH 2,075,280 a year. Providers are still quoting the 2025 pair: Deel's Ukraine page prices the ceiling at UAH 160,000 a month, which is twenty times the old UAH 8,000 minimum wage. The floor is the other half of the rule: where the base is below one minimum wage the contribution is still computed on the full minimum wage, giving a minimum liability of UAH 1,902.34 a month.

source.name: Law of Ukraine No. 2464-VI on the collection and accounting of the unified contribution, article 8(5), consolidated text on the official parliamentary portal

statutory_extras.name: Contribution ceiling for 2026 - twenty minimum wages, not fifteen
