statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is a modelling rule rather than a charge, and named because it is the single most out-of-date number published about Ukrainian payroll. Article 32 of the Law on the State Budget of Ukraine for 2026 states that in 2026 the maximum base of assessment for the unified contribution equals twenty minimum wages from 1 January 2026, except for the pay of military personnel and police, where it equals fifteen. The same law fixes the minimum wage at UAH 8,647 a month. The ceiling therefore starts biting at about US$3,875 of monthly salary at the September 2026 accounting rate, which is above the example priced here, so the full 22% applies to this salary and the cap only matters for senior pay.

source.name: Law of Ukraine No. 4695-IX on the State Budget of Ukraine for 2026, articles 8 and 32

statutory_extras.name: Personal income tax and military levy - withheld, not added
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because both are withheld from the employee's gross pay rather than charged on top of it, and named because they are routinely added to Ukrainian employer-cost tables by mistake. The unified contribution is the employer's whole statutory bill; personal income tax and the military levy come out of the same gross salary the employee was promised. The practical consequence for an offer is that a Ukrainian gross figure converts to a noticeably smaller net than the same gross in a country where the employer carries part of the social burden, so compare net pay with a candidate, not gross.

source.name: Law of Ukraine No. 2464-VI, article 7, base of assessment for the unified contribution

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth month - not required by Ukrainian law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Labour Code creates no thirteenth-month salary and no statutory holiday bonus. Annual leave is paid at average earnings under the Law on Leave, with no separate holiday supplement. Bonuses and private health cover are contractual and normal in the Ukrainian technology market; price them as market cost, not as a legal charge.

source.name: Law of Ukraine No. 504/96-VR on Leave, article 6, consolidated text

countries.notice_typical: Two months for redundancy under article 49-2 of the Labour Code, which requires employees to be notified personally of a forthcoming release no later than two months in advance. An employee resigning from an open-ended contract gives two weeks under article 38. During martial law, article 5 of Law No. 2136-IX also allows dismissal while the employee is on sick leave or on leave, other than maternity and childcare leave.

source.name: Law of Ukraine No. 504/96-VR on Leave, article 6, consolidated text

countries.name: United States

assumptions.label: Employee works in California (state unemployment, training tax and workers' compensation priced at California rates)
assumptions.notes: Chosen on where software developers work, not on search volume. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' May 2025 Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics count 1,687,890 software developers (occupation 15-1252) in the United States, of whom 284,390 work in California (16.8%), against 163,880 in Texas (9.7%), 113,510 in New York (6.7%), 107,030 in Washington (6.3%) and 87,890 in Florida (5.2%). Social Security and Medicare apply at the same rates from one state to the next; the unemployment, training-tax and workers' compensation lines below change with the state. No local payroll tax is modelled: San Francisco's Payroll Expense Tax was repealed in full by Proposition F from 1 January 2021, and city gross-receipts or business-licence taxes are levied on the provider's revenue, not on a salary.

employer_contributions.name: Social Security (OASDI)
employer_contributions.applies: Employers, on wages up to the 2026 contribution and benefit base
employer_contributions.notes: 6.2% employer share on wages up to US$184,500 in 2026, so at most US$11,439 a year per employee. The employee pays the same 6.2% on the same wages, withheld from salary. The base changes each year with the national average wage index.

source.name: Social Security Administration - Contribution and benefit base (2026: $184,500; OASDI rate 6.2% each for employees and employers)

employer_contributions.name: Medicare (HI)
employer_contributions.applies: Employers, on all wages with no limit
employer_contributions.notes: 1.45% employer share on all wages, with no wage base limit. The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% on wages above US$200,000 is withheld from the employee only: Publication 15 states there is no employer share of it, so it is not in this ledger.

source.name: IRS Publication 15 (2026), Circular E, Employer's Tax Guide - Social security and Medicare taxes for 2026

employer_contributions.name: Federal unemployment tax (FUTA), net of the 5.4% state credit
employer_contributions.applies: Employers, on the first US$7,000 of each employee's wages in the calendar year
employer_contributions.notes: FUTA is 6.0% on the first US$7,000 of wages; an employer that pays its state unemployment tax in full and on time takes a credit of up to 5.4%, leaving 0.6%, or US$42 a year per employee. The credit is cut in a credit reduction state, and California is one: see the next line.

source.name: IRS Publication 15 (2026), section 14 - Federal Unemployment (FUTA) Tax

employer_contributions.name: FUTA credit reduction, California (2026 wages, at least)
employer_contributions.applies: Employers paying wages subject to California unemployment law, while California owes the federal unemployment fund
employer_contributions.notes: California owes the federal unemployment fund, so its employers lose part of the 5.4% FUTA credit, 0.3 point more for each year the advance stays unpaid: 1.2% for 2025 wages (Schedule A of Form 940 for 2025, US$84 a year per employee) and at least 1.5% for 2026 wages, US$105 a year per employee, the Department of Labor's potential 2026 reduction for the outstanding advance. The EDD's May 2026 UI Fund Forecast keeps the fund in deficit through 2027 (minus US$22.0 billion projected at the end of 2026), so the advance will not be repaid by 10 November 2026. The same Department of Labor table adds an estimated 3.8% benefit-cost-rate add-on, 5.3% in all (US$371), unless it is waived: it was waived for 2025, and the EDD's forecast assumes it is waived again for 2026. The final 2026 figure is set after 10 November 2026 and paid with the Form 940 for 2026.

source.name: U.S. Department of Labor, ETA - FUTA credit reductions (potential 2026 table dated 15 January 2026, republished 11 September 2026; historical table); California EDD - UI Fund Forecast, May 2026

employer_contributions.name: California Unemployment Insurance (UI), new-employer rate
employer_contributions.applies: Employers with California payroll, on the first US$7,000 of each employee's wages in 2026
employer_contributions.notes: A declared point inside a published range, not a floor. The EDD assigns new employers 3.4% for two to three years; after that the rate follows the employer's own claims history under Schedule F+ for 2026, from 1.5% to 6.2%. An employer of record is not a new employer and its experience rate is not published, so 3.4% on the US$7,000 wage limit, US$238 a year per employee, stands in for a figure between US$105 and US$434.

source.name: California EDD - Contribution rates, withholding schedules, and meals and lodging values (2026)

employer_contributions.name: California Employment Training Tax (ETT)
employer_contributions.applies: California employers whose UI reserve account balance is zero or positive
employer_contributions.notes: 0.1% on the first US$7,000 of wages in 2026, US$7 a year per employee. The EDD charges it when the employer's UI reserve account is zero or positive and shows 0.0% when it is negative, so a provider with a negative reserve pays nothing on this line. California State Disability Insurance (1.3% of all wages in 2026) is withheld from the employee and is not an employer charge.

source.name: California EDD - Tax-rated employers (ETT and SDI rates, 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Workers' compensation, California class 8859(1) (at least the pure premium)
employer_contributions.applies: California employers must insure; priced per US$100 of payroll by classification
employer_contributions.notes: Workers' compensation is an insurance premium, not a statutory rate. California's plan classifies a leased or provided worker 'as though the workers are employees of the client' (Uniform Statistical Reporting Plan effective 1 September 2026, Part 3, Section III, rule 7, Labor Contractors), so the class is the client's, not the provider's. For a client that develops software for others or sells standard software, that is 8859(1), Computer Programming or Software Development, whose payroll counts up to US$171,600 a year per employee. The approved advisory pure premium rate from 1 September 2026 is US$0.033 per US$100 of payroll: at least US$39.60 a year at the example salary. A pure premium covers expected losses and claim handling only; the WCIRB states that insurer rates are typically higher, so the premium actually billed is at least this figure. A client in another industry takes another class and another rate.

source.name: WCIRB California - Approved September 1, 2026 advisory pure premium rates (class 8859: 0.033) and Uniform Statistical Reporting Plan effective September 1, 2026

statutory_extras.name: Health coverage - no statutory premium, but a large employer must offer it or pay
statutory_extras.notes: No federal or California statute sets a health insurance contribution, so the total on this page carries none. Section 4980H applies to applicable large employers, those with an average of at least 50 full-time employees (including equivalents) in the prior year: they must offer affordable, minimum-value coverage to their full-time employees and dependents or risk a payment once a full-time employee gets a premium tax credit. For 2026 the IRS indexes the amounts to US$3,340 a year per full-time employee (minus up to 30) under 4980H(a) when coverage is not offered to at least 95% of full-time staff, and US$5,010 a year per employee receiving a credit under 4980H(b). Ask the provider which group plan it offers in California, what share of the monthly premium it bills to you, and whether that amount is inside or on top of its fee. For an order of magnitude, from a survey rather than a statute (KFF 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey): the average single-coverage premium was US$9,325 a year, of which covered workers paid US$1,440 on average, leaving about US$7,885 a year, about US$657 a month, to the employer; family coverage averaged US$26,993, of which workers paid US$6,850.

source.name: IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-26 (2026 adjusted amounts: $3,340 and $5,010); IRS Q&A on employer shared responsibility (ALE definition); KFF 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey (premium order of magnitude)

statutory_extras.name: Section 4980H - whose offer of coverage counts
statutory_extras.notes: Treasury regulations define the employer for section 4980H as the common-law employer (54.4980H-1(a)(16)), which is not necessarily the entity that runs the payroll. Whether an employer reaches 50 full-time employees (full-time equivalents included) is counted across its controlled group (54.4980H-1(a)(16)), and hours paid as income from sources outside the United States are left out (54.4980H-1(a)(24)). Where a staffing firm that is not the common-law employer offers coverage under its own plan on a client's behalf, the offer counts as the client's only if the client pays the firm a higher fee for an employee who enrols than for one who does not (54.4980H-4(b)(2)). Which entity is the common-law employer in an employer of record arrangement depends on who directs and controls the work; this page does not decide it. Ask the provider whether its fee is higher when the employee enrols in its plan.

source.name: 26 CFR 54.4980H-1(a)(15), (16), (24) and 54.4980H-4(b)(2), eCFR up to date as of 22 September 2026

statutory_extras.name: California paid sick leave - at least 40 hours or five days a year
statutory_extras.notes: Labor Code section 246 gives an employee who works in California for the same employer for 30 or more days within a year paid sick days, accruing at not less than one hour per 30 hours worked; an exempt professional is deemed to work 40 hours a week. The Labor Commissioner's guidance, updated 31 December 2025, is that since 1 January 2024 the employer must allow use of at least 40 hours or five days a year, whichever is more. Taken as paid time off inside the annual salary, it adds no cash cost and sits outside the total.

source.name: California Labor Code section 246; Labor Commissioner (DLSE) - Paid sick leave FAQ

statutory_extras.name: California State Disability Insurance - withheld, not charged to the employer
statutory_extras.notes: SDI, which also funds Paid Family Leave, is a withholding from the employee's pay: 1.3% of all wages in 2026, with no wage limit since 1 January 2024. It lowers the employee's net pay and adds nothing to the employer's cost.

source.name: California EDD - Contribution rates, withholding schedules, and meals and lodging values (SDI withholding rate 2026)

countries.holidays_note: federal list; not owed by private employers
countries.notice_typical: California employment with no specified term is at will: under Labor Code section 2922 it 'may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other', a section that fixes no length for that notice; the Department of Labor states that severance pay is a matter of agreement. Statute requires advance notice only for collective dismissals. The federal WARN Act applies to employers with 100 or more employees and requires 60 days' written notice of a plant closing (50 or more employees losing work at one site) or a mass layoff (at least 50 employees making up at least 33% of a site, or at least 500). California's own WARN Act applies from 75 employees and requires 60 days' notice of a layoff of 50 or more employees within 30 days.

countries.name: Uruguay

assumptions.label: Pension contribution ceiling taken at tope C, UYU 288,836 a month, its value for August and September 2026
assumptions.notes: The Banco de Prevision Social publishes its contribution ceilings every month on its Valores actuales page. For workers in the mixed pension system its Manual de materia gravada states that 'existe un tope de cotizacion, a los efectos de determinar el aporte jubilatorio patronal y personal', so the ceiling caps the employer's pension line as well as the worker's. It does not cap anything else: FONASA, the Fondo de Reconversion Laboral and the credit-guarantee fund are charged 'sin aplicar los topes definidos'. At UYU 288,836 a month the ceiling sits at about twice the example salary, so it does not bind here.

assumptions.label: Holiday bonus estimated at 3.8% of gross, below the figure for a single employee with no dependants
assumptions.notes: Ley 16.101 sets the salario vacacional at 100% of the net daily wage for each leave day, and the Ministerio de Trabajo defines that net wage as the nominal wage less the worker's social security contributions and income tax. Net pay depends on the employee's family situation, so the bonus cannot be read off a salary. At the example salary, a single employee with no dependants pays 19.6% in contributions and about 7.9% in IRPF under the BPS 2026 scale, which puts 20 days of net pay at 4.0% of annual gross; with a spouse and children it is about 3.9%. The page carries 3.8% so that the total stays a floor.

assumptions.label: The BSE work-accident premium is carried at zero, so the total below is a floor
assumptions.notes: Article 1 of Ley 16.074 makes accident and occupational-disease insurance compulsory. The premium is rated by the Banco de Seguros del Estado on the employer's own activity, which for an employee hired through a provider means the provider's classification, not the employee's job. No rate table is published on the BSE's accident-insurance page, so it is left at zero rather than guessed.

employer_contributions.name: Employer pension contribution (aporte jubilatorio patronal, BPS)
employer_contributions.applies: Industria y Comercio affiliation, on pay up to tope C of UYU 288,836 a month
employer_contributions.notes: The BPS Tasas page for Industria y Comercio, Trabajo Domestico and Civil: 'Aporte jubilatorio - Aporte personal (montepio) 15 % - Aporte patronal (desde 1/7/07) 7,5 %'. The worker's own 15% is twice the employer's rate. For workers in the mixed system the ceiling applies to both sides; the BPS values page sets tope C at UYU 288,836 a month for August and September 2026, which is the annual cap entered here (twelve months). Ley 20.130, for people whose first contributory job started on or after 1 December 2023, changes how the pension is calculated, not the contribution: the BPS manual notes it 'no implica un tratamiento diferencial en cuanto a las contribuciones'.

source.name: Banco de Prevision Social - Tasas (Industria y Comercio), with Valores actuales for the ceiling (updated 23 September 2026)

employer_contributions.name: Employer health contribution (FONASA, Seguro Nacional de Salud)
employer_contributions.notes: BPS, Tasas Fonasa: 'los aportes patronales con una tasa del 5 % y el Complemento de Cuota mutual (CCM) cuando corresponda'. The complement only arises when the worker's 3% basic contribution and the employer's 5% together fall short of the mutual-insurance fee for the people covered (CCM = beneficiaries x cuota mutual - 8%), which at the example salary they do not. The BPS manual states that FONASA is charged on all taxable pay 'sin aplicar los topes definidos', so there is no ceiling on this line. The worker adds 3% to 8% depending on pay, spouse and children.

source.name: Banco de Prevision Social - Tasas Fonasa

employer_contributions.name: Labour retraining fund (Fondo de Reconversion Laboral)
employer_contributions.notes: The BPS Manual de materia gravada, December 2024 edition: 'Las tasas que se recaudan por este fondo, a partir del 1.1.2019, segun lo establecido por el articulo 17 de la ley 19.689, son las siguientes: ... Dependientes 0,1 % [personal] 0,1 % [patronal]'. Older references to 0.125% predate that change. It funds retraining through INEFOP and is charged without a ceiling.

source.name: Banco de Prevision Social - Manual de materia gravada (December 2024 edition), Fondo de reconversion laboral (Ley 19.689, articulo 17)

employer_contributions.name: Wage-guarantee fund (Fondo de Garantia de Creditos Laborales)
employer_contributions.notes: The BPS Manual de materia gravada: the fund covers wages owed when an employer becomes insolvent, under Ley 19.690 and decreto 77/019, and 'la norma instituyo, ademas, una CESS de caracter patronal, que se calcula por una tasa de 0,025 % y que, desde 1.1.2019, corresponde aplicar sobre las remuneraciones de los trabajadores dependientes de la actividad privada'. It is charged to the employer only, without a ceiling, and comes to well under a dollar a month at the example salary.

source.name: Banco de Prevision Social - Manual de materia gravada (December 2024 edition), Fondo de garantia de creditos laborales (Ley 19.690)

statutory_extras.name: Annual complementary salary (aguinaldo)
statutory_extras.notes: The BPS Manual de materia gravada: the legal aguinaldo 'equivale a la doceava parte del total de los sueldos o salarios abonados en los doce meses anteriores al 1 de diciembre de cada ano', counting every cash payment of a remunerative nature but not the aguinaldo itself. For a fixed monthly salary that is one extra month a year; it is paid in two halves (the manual's 'medio aguinaldo').

source.name: Banco de Prevision Social - Manual de materia gravada (December 2024 edition), Sueldo anual complementario (aguinaldo)

statutory_extras.name: Employer contributions falling on the aguinaldo
statutory_extras.notes: The aguinaldo is taxable pay, so the pension, retraining-fund and credit-guarantee lines fall on it too, but not all of the employer bill does: the BPS manual states that it 'goza de una exoneracion del aporte patronal por el seguro de enfermedad (5 %) (articulo 4 del decreto 2/008)'. The charge on it is therefore 7.625% rather than 12.625%, and 7.625% of one twelfth of the year's pay is 0.635% of annual gross. The ceiling is applied to the aguinaldo separately, as an isolated payment (decreto 440/997), and does not bind at the example salary.

source.name: Banco de Prevision Social - Manual de materia gravada (December 2024 edition), Aporte al Fonasa y CCM; decreto 2/008, articulo 4

statutory_extras.name: Holiday bonus (salario vacacional, Ley 16.101)
statutory_extras.notes: The Ministerio de Trabajo: every private-sector worker receives 'una suma para el mejor goce de la licencia equivalente al 100 % del jornal liquido de vacaciones', paid before the leave starts, where the net daily wage 'es el que resulta de restarle al nominal los aportes de contribucion a la Seguridad Social y el impuesto a las retribuciones personales'. The BPS manual adds that it 'se encuentra exento de aportes a la seguridad social', so no contribution falls on it. Twenty days of net pay come to about 4.0% of annual gross for a single employee at the example salary and about 3.9% with a spouse and children; the page carries 3.8% as a floor. Collective agreements can set a more generous formula.

source.name: Ministerio de Trabajo y Seguridad Social - Salario vacacional (Ley 16.101), with the BPS IRPF 2026 scale (Comunicado R 5/2026)

statutory_extras.name: Work accident insurance (Banco de Seguros del Estado, Ley 16.074)
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because article 1 of Ley 16.074 makes the insurance compulsory but no statute fixes its price: the Banco de Seguros del Estado rates the premium on the employer's activity, and for a hire through a provider that is the provider's classification. The BSE's accident-insurance page publishes no rate table. Because it is left out, the total on this page is a floor; ask any provider to quote it.

source.name: Ley 16.074, articulo 1 (IMPO, Documento Actualizado, consulted 24 September 2026)

countries.holidays_note: paid; the rest are working days
countries.probation_note: none by law; case law accepts 90 days
countries.notice_typical: The Ministerio de Trabajo's page on dismissal of monthly staff sets out no notice period. What it sets out is the indemnity: 'remuneracion total correspondiente a un mes de sueldo por cada ano o fraccion de actividad, con un limite de seis mensualidades como maximo', owed without any minimum seniority ('no se exige antiguedad') and not owed for 'notoria mala conducta', which the employer must prove. That indemnity, rather than a notice period, is the number to model before a Uruguayan exit.

payments.name: Aguinaldo - first half (June)
payments.deadline: date fixed each year by the Executive (Ley 12.840 art. 1 sets payment within the ten days before 24 December)

payments.name: Aguinaldo - second half (December)
payments.deadline: date fixed each year by the Executive (Ley 12.840 art. 1 sets payment within the ten days before 24 December)

payments.name: Salario vacacional (Ley 16.101)
payments.deadline: before the start of the leave; the cash month depends on when the leave is taken

source.quote: Por sueldo anual complementario se entiende la doceava parte del total

countries.name: Vietnam

assumptions.label: Region I modelled: regional minimum wage VND 5,310,000 a month
assumptions.notes: Vietnam sets four regional minimum wages, and two things on this page depend on which one applies: the floor of the social-insurance base, and the ceiling of the unemployment-insurance base, which is twenty times the regional minimum. Modelled on Region I — the urban districts of Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, where almost every EOR hire sits — at VND 5,310,000 a month from 1 January 2026. Region II is VND 4,730,000, Region III VND 4,140,000 and Region IV VND 3,700,000. On a professional salary the choice changes nothing at all, because pay is far above the floor and far below the unemployment ceiling.

employer_contributions.name: Social insurance (BHXH), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Compulsory social insurance; monthly base floored at the regional minimum wage and capped at VND 50,600,000
employer_contributions.notes: Three funds in one line, all on the same base: 14% to the retirement and survivorship fund, 3% to sickness and maternity, and 0.5% to occupational accident and disease — 17.5% in total, against the employee's own 8%. The ceiling is the number to know: since 1 July 2026 the monthly base stops at VND 50,600,000, twenty times the reference level of VND 2,530,000 set by Decree 161/2026/ND-CP. In dollar terms that is about US$1,940 a month of pay, so a salary above roughly US$23,300 a year stops adding to this line — and the effective employer rate starts falling from there.

source.name: Vietnam Social Security (baohiemxahoi.gov.vn), 12 November 2025 — contribution rates from the base wage: the employee pays 8% to the retirement and survivorship fund; the employer pays 14% to the retirement and survivorship fund, 3% to the sickness and maternity fund and 0.5% to the occupational accident and disease fund; regional minimum wages under Decree 293/2025/ND-CP in force from 1 January 2026

employer_contributions.name: Health insurance (BHYT), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Same base as social insurance, so the same VND 50,600,000 monthly ceiling applies
employer_contributions.notes: The health premium is 4.5% of the same monthly wage that social insurance is charged on, and the decree splits it two thirds to the employer and one third to the employee — 3% and 1.5%. It rides on the social-insurance base, so it stops at the same VND 50,600,000 a month. Employers new to Vietnam often budget the 4.5% in full or halve it; neither is right.

source.name: Decree 188/2025/ND-CP detailing the Law on Health Insurance, as published by the Government's policy portal on 11 July 2025: the monthly contribution for employees equals 4.5% of the wage used as the basis for compulsory social insurance, of which the employer pays two thirds and the employee one third

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment insurance (BHTN), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Its own ceiling: twenty times the regional minimum wage, VND 106,200,000 a month in Region I
employer_contributions.notes: This is the line with the different ceiling, and getting the two confused is the most common error in Vietnamese cost models. The Employment Law sets the employer's contribution at no more than 1% of the monthly payroll of insured employees, with the state supporting up to 1% more, and caps the base at twenty times the regional minimum wage — VND 106,200,000 a month in Region I, more than twice the social-insurance ceiling. The wording is a maximum rather than a fixed rate, which is what allowed the rate to be cut during the pandemic; the full 1% is what is charged in the absence of a reduction decision. Note also that unemployment insurance is the branch that does not extend to foreign employees.

source.name: Vietnam Social Security (baohiemxahoi.gov.vn), 8 August 2025, on the Employment Law: under Article 33 the employee pays up to 1% of monthly wages, the employer up to 1% of the monthly payroll of employees participating in unemployment insurance and the state up to 1% more; under Article 34 the maximum wage used as the basis may not exceed twenty times the regional minimum wage at the time of payment

employer_contributions.name: Trade union funding (kinh phí công đoàn), employer only
employer_contributions.applies: 2% of the same payroll that compulsory social insurance is charged on, owed whether or not the workplace has a union
employer_contributions.notes: The charge that turns 21.5% into 23.5%, and the one most guides leave out. The Trade Union Law, in force since 1 July 2025, requires agencies, organisations, units, enterprises and cooperatives to pay union funding equal to 2% of the payroll used as the basis for compulsory social insurance for their employees. It is not union dues — those are 1% of pay and come from employees who join — and it does not depend on a union existing at the workplace: the employer pays it either way. Because the base is the social-insurance payroll, it carries the same VND 50,600,000 monthly ceiling.

source.name: Law on Trade Unions, Article 29(1)(b), passed by the National Assembly on 27 November 2024 and in force from 1 July 2025 (full text published by the Government's policy portal): union funding paid by agencies, organisations, units, enterprises, cooperatives and unions of cooperatives at 2% of the salary fund used as the basis for compulsory social insurance contributions for employees

statutory_extras.name: Tet bonus / 13th-month pay
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because no statute creates it. The Labour Code treats a bonus as money, property or other benefit the employer awards on the basis of business results and the employee's performance — discretionary by definition, and binding only once it is written into the contract, the collective agreement or the company's own bonus rules. Market practice around Tet is close to universal and usually amounts to a month of pay, which is why almost every offer here includes one; that makes it a negotiated cost rather than a legal one. Ask whether the provider's quote carries it and whether it is pro-rated for a part year.

source.name: Vietnam Social Security (baohiemxahoi.gov.vn) — contribution rules for compulsory social insurance, which set the employer's statutory charges at 14% + 3% + 0.5% with no thirteenth-month element

statutory_extras.name: Severance allowance on termination
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because for a normal hire after 2009 there is usually nothing left for it to cover. Severance under the Labour Code is half a month's pay for each year of service, but only for service that unemployment insurance did not cover — and unemployment insurance has been compulsory since 2009. So the allowance mostly bites for long-service staff hired before then, or for months where contributions were missed. What does apply to every hire is the notice period, and Vietnam has no at-will termination: dismissal must rest on a statutory ground.

source.name: Vietnam Social Security (baohiemxahoi.gov.vn), 8 August 2025, on unemployment insurance under the Employment Law — the compulsory branch whose coverage displaces statutory severance for the periods it covers

statutory_extras.name: Statutory annual leave (12 working days)
statutory_extras.notes: Read in the consolidated Labour Code published by the Office of the National Assembly (consolidated text No. 18/VBHN-VPQH of 2026, which folds in the three 2025 amending laws; Articles 113 and 114 are unchanged by them). Paid time inside the salary rather than an extra contribution: an employee with twelve months of service in normal working conditions is entitled to 12 working days of annual leave, 14 for young, disabled or arduous-work employees and 16 for the most hazardous categories, with one extra day for every five years with the same employer. Provider contracts often offer 15 days, so read the offer rather than the statute.

source.name: Labour Code 2019 (Law 45/2019/QH14), consolidated text No. 18/VBHN-VPQH (Office of the National Assembly, 2026), Article 113: 12 working days of annual leave with full pay for an employee with twelve months of service in normal conditions, 14 days for young/disabled/arduous-work employees and 16 for especially heavy, toxic or dangerous work, with Article 114 adding one day per five years of service

statutory_extras.name: New public holiday from 2026: Vietnamese Culture Day (24 November)
statutory_extras.notes: Worth knowing because every guide written before 2026 still says eleven public holidays. The National Assembly's Resolution 28/2026/QH16, in force from 1 July 2026, makes 24 November each year Vietnamese Culture Day, a paid day off for employees; the first one falls on Tuesday 24 November 2026, and the Ministry of Home Affairs has put forward two options for it — swapping the adjacent Monday to make a longer break, or taking the day itself. That takes the statutory count to twelve paid public holidays a year. It is not an extra cash cost, but it is one more paid day in a resourcing plan.

source.name: Government policy portal (xaydungchinhsach.chinhphu.vn), 13 January 2026: the National Assembly passed Resolution 28/2026/QH16 making 24 November each year Vietnamese Culture Day, on which employees are off with full pay; in force from 1 July 2026, first observed on 24 November 2026

countries.notice_typical: No at-will termination: an employer may end a contract only on a statutory ground, and notice depends on the contract type — at least 45 days on an indefinite-term contract, at least 30 days on a fixed term of 12 to 36 months, and at least 3 working days on a fixed term under 12 months. The employee resigning gives the same notice. Probation runs to a maximum of 60 days for a post requiring a college degree or above, 30 days for intermediate technical and skilled roles, 180 days for enterprise managers and 6 working days for everything else, and probation pay must be at least 85% of the rate for the job.

countries.name: South Africa

assumptions.label: COIDA is assessed at the Class A office tariff of 0.18%
assumptions.notes: The Compensation Fund assesses an employer by multiplying each employee's earnings, up to the prescribed maximum, by the tariff of the subclass the employer's business falls into. The tariffs are set by the Minister's Regulations on the Compensation Fund's Tariffs of Assessment (Government Notice 1282, Gazette 43959, 3 December 2020), which phased every subclass to its new rate by the 2025 assessment year: Class A, which covers finance, consultants, admin consultants and education services, is at 0.18%. That office tariff is what this page applies. Two consequences under an employer of record. The assessed employer is the provider, so the subclass and the claims record are the provider's, not yours: the same schedule puts subclass 1960, management and career agents, at 0.81%. And the Minister also prescribes a minimum assessment per employer - R1,621 a year - which a provider's South African payroll passes many times over, so it never shows up as a per-employee charge on your invoice.

employer_contributions.name: Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF), employer share
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on each employee's remuneration up to the earnings ceiling
employer_contributions.notes: SARS states the split and the ceiling in the same passage: 'The amount of the contribution due by an employee, must be 1% of the remuneration paid by the employer to the employee. The employer must pay a total contribution of 2% (1% contributed by the employee and 1% contributed by the employer)', and a contribution does not apply to remuneration exceeding 'R 17 712 per month (R 212 544 annually)' with effect from 1 June 2021. SARS spells out what that means in cash: 'the maximum contribution which can be deducted, for employees who earn more than R17 712 per month, is R177,12 per month'. This is the line that makes a South African professional hire cheap. The ceiling has not moved since June 2021 while salaries have, so the effective rate keeps falling: at the salary on this page the 1% is worth about 0.37% of pay, and at twice this salary it would be about 0.19%. Any page that prints '1% + 1% UIF' without the ceiling is describing a minimum-wage hire, not an engineer.

source.name: SARS - Unemployment Insurance Fund: contribution rate and earnings ceiling

employer_contributions.name: Skills Development Levy (SDL)
employer_contributions.applies: Employers whose total leviable payroll over the next 12 months exceeds R500,000, which an employer of record's South African payroll always does
employer_contributions.notes: SARS puts the rate plainly - '1% of the total amount paid in salaries to employees (including wages, overtime payments, leave pay, bonuses, fees, commissions and lump sum payments)' - and it carries no ceiling, which is why it overtakes UIF as soon as a salary passes about R17,712 a month. The threshold is the part worth understanding before you compare an EOR with your own entity: SARS exempts 'Any employer whose total remuneration subject to SDL (leviable amount) paid/due to all its employees over the next 12 month period won't exceed R500 000', and such employers need not even register. A company making its first one or two South African hires might sit under that line and owe no SDL at all. A provider's South African payroll never does, so the levy is always charged on an EOR hire even where a small entity of your own would owe nothing. Belgium's special unemployment contribution, charged because the legal employer has ten or more staff, works the same way.

source.name: SARS - Skills Development Levy: rate, base and R500,000 exemption

employer_contributions.name: COIDA assessment (Compensation Fund), Class A office tariff
employer_contributions.applies: Every employer, on each employee's earnings up to the prescribed maximum
employer_contributions.notes: The tariff is the Class A rate of 0.18% in Schedule A of the Regulations on the Compensation Fund's Tariffs of Assessment, made by the Minister under sections 97(2) and 83(1) of the Act (Government Notice 1282, Gazette 43959, 3 December 2020); Class A lists finance, beauty and hair salons, medical specialists, consultants, admin consultants, education services and organisations, all phased from their 2020 rates to 0.18% by the 2025 assessment year. No later tariff regulation was found. The subclass is the provider's, and the figure previously modelled here from a provider guide was 0.2%. The ceiling is read from the Minister's own notice. That notice, signed on 21 April 2026 under sections 83(8) and 83(2)(b) of the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act 130 of 1993 and published as General Notice 3910 of 2026 in Government Gazette 54577 of 24 April 2026, prescribes 'The amount of R668 000 per employee per annum as the maximum amount of earnings on which an assessment of an employer shall be calculated; this amount being effective from 1st March 2026', together with a minimum assessment of R1,621 for employers and R560 for domestic employers. It replaced the R633,168 ceiling that had applied from 1 March 2025, and the Minister re-prescribes the maximum by Gazette notice for each assessment year, so confirm the current figure before relying on it for a salary near the ceiling; at the salary on this page the ceiling does not bind. Unlike UIF and SDL, COIDA is assessed annually on a Return of Earnings rather than deducted monthly, so it appears on a provider's invoice as a spread cost or not at all.

source.name: Department of Employment and Labour - Regulations on Compensation Fund's Tariffs of Assessment, Government Notice 1282, Government Gazette 43959 of 3 December 2020 (Schedule A, Class A 0.18%)

statutory_extras.name: UIF employee share - deducted from pay, not an employer cost
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is the employee's money, and named because SARS describes the contribution as a total of 2% and several comparison pages read that as the employer's charge. The employer pays 1% and withholds another 1% from the employee, both stopping at the same R17,712 monthly ceiling, and remits 2% in one payment. Only the first 1% is your cost. The employer is the one who has to get the ceiling right in both directions, since over-deducting from an employee above the ceiling is a payroll error you would be liable to correct.

source.name: SARS - Unemployment Insurance Fund: the 2% total and how it is split

statutory_extras.name: COIDA minimum assessment - a floor on the employer, not on the salary
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because it is charged once per employer per year rather than per employee. The same ministerial notice that sets the earnings maximum prescribes 'A Minimum Assessment of R1 621 for employers with effect from 1st March 2026' and R560 for domestic employers. The ceiling rose for the 2026/2027 assessment year while this floor stayed at the same R1,621 it had the year before. For a one-person South African entity of your own this is the floor your COIDA bill cannot fall below, which matters when you model the entity route on a single hire; under an employer of record the provider's payroll clears it many times over and you never see it. It is the kind of small fixed amount that makes a first direct hire more expensive than a spreadsheet suggests.

source.name: Department of Employment and Labour - General Notice 3910 of 2026, maximum amount of earnings and minimum assessment (COIDA), Government Gazette 54577 of 24 April 2026

statutory_extras.name: Thirteenth cheque - not required by South African law
statutory_extras.notes: Carried at zero because the Basic Conditions of Employment Act creates no thirteenth cheque and no holiday bonus, although a December bonus is common enough in the South African market that a candidate may expect one. What the Act does require instead is annual leave on full remuneration and, where an employee works a public holiday they would ordinarily work, payment for that day. Treat a thirteenth cheque as a market cost in the offer, not as a legal charge, and say so explicitly in the contract if you are not paying one - a silence here is read locally as a yes.

source.name: Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997, Government Gazette No. 18491 of 5 December 1997

countries.notice_typical: Four weeks once the employee has a year or more of service, under section 37(1)(c) of the Basic Conditions of Employment Act; two weeks between four weeks and one year of service, and one week in the first four weeks. A collective agreement may shorten these periods, and section 37(3) forbids any agreement that requires a longer notice from the employee than from the employer. The Act sets no maximum probation period - probation is governed instead by the Labour Relations Act's Code of Good Practice, which requires it to be of reasonable length for the job and to be used for assessment rather than as a licence to dismiss.

scheduled_changes.note: Monthly wage ceiling rises to THB 23,000 from 1 Jan B.E. 2575 (2032), with no end date (employer maximum THB 1,150 a month; annual capped base THB 276,000 = 23,000 x 12, derived). Same secondary source and same caveat as the 2029 step.

pending.description: 2027 premium floor and ceiling (PEK alt/ust sinir): not published. The ceiling is 9 times the floor, and the floor is the monthly minimum wage, whose 2027 value has not been published at the research date. 2026 values read on the SGK page: floor 33,030 TL a month, ceiling 297,270 TL a month (ledger: 396,360 and 3,567,240 TL a year).
Minimum wage for 2027 (basis of the premium floor and ceiling): not published at the research date. The 2026 gross figure of 33,030 TL was announced by the labour ministry on 23 December 2025.

Treasury support of the employer pension share (art. 81(i) of act 5510): the consolidated text read on mevzuat.gov.tr states two points (footnote 149 of the consolidated text records the change from four to two by article 23 of act 7566), with no end date written in the paragraph. The ledger keeps the 12% employer share and does not apply the support, which is conditional on filing and payment. Act 7590 of 24 July 2026 also amended article 81 (in force 1 August 2026); its content was not read here.

Severance ceiling for the next period (the January 2027 value): not published at the research date. The ceiling is tied to the maximum retirement bonus of the highest civil servant; the 2026 amounts were not read.

Labor insurance ordinary premium rate: the act's schedule adds 0.5 point every two years from the year the rate reached 10% until 13%, but not when the insurance fund covers the next twenty years of benefits. BLI states 12.5% total (11.5% ordinary + 1% employment insurance) from 1 Jan 2025. If the next step applies on 1 Jan 2027 (year derived from the two-year cadence, not stated in any source read; 2027 BLI notice not read), the ordinary rate would be 12% and the employer share at 70% would be 0.084 (calculation, not a quote). Whether the fund condition suspends the step is not established, so the change is not recorded as enacted.

Monthly minimum wage from 1 Jan 2027: Minimum Wage Deliberation Council decided TWD 29,500 to 30,900 (hourly 196 to 205); the proposal still goes to the Executive Yuan for approval. The floor of the labor, employment, occupational accident and health insurance tables (TWD 29,500 today) follows the minimum wage, so the floor lines would move if approved.
Insured-salary grade table for 2027 (first grade follows the minimum wage; the TWD 45,800 ceiling): no 2027 table read; the BLI notice read concerns the 2025 revision.
2027 health insurance premium rate and grade table: the page read gives 5.17% from 1 Jan 2021 and no later change; no 2027 rate or table read.

Minimum wage 2027 in the draft State Budget Law: UAH 9,546 a month from 1 January 2027 (up from UAH 8,647), per a press article dated 15 September 2026 that cites the draft budget; whether the bill was registered or voted was not read, and the draft text itself was not read (secondary press report only). The ceiling of the unified contribution is a multiple of the minimum wage under the 2026 budget law (article 32), so it would move with it; the floor rule is not sourced in this file. Derived, NOT A CITATION: floor base 12 x 9,546 = UAH 114,552 a year; ceiling at twenty minimum wages 20 x 12 x 9,546 = UAH 2,291,040 a year. Whether the 2027 budget law repeats the twenty-wage ceiling was not read.
Maximum base 2027: the 2026 rule (twenty minimum wages) is set by the 2026 budget law for 2026 only; the 2027 rule is awaited with the 2027 budget law.

Social Security contribution and benefit base for 2027 (fiche: California, 6.2% employer share, 2026 base 184,500): the SSA page read today lists bases only through 2026; the 2027 base is set by the annual wage-index adjustment and is awaited (SSA announces it in mid-October with the cost-of-living adjustment; that timing is not stated on the page read).

FUTA credit reduction for California on 2026 wages, read from the cells of the Department of Labor xlsx 'Potential 2026 FUTA Credit Reductions' (row California): 1.5 % potential reduction for the outstanding advance, 0 % in the '2.7 add-on' column, 3.8 % in the 'BCR add-on' column, 5.3 % potential total. The table's footnotes describe the values as potential and preliminary (estimated from third- and fourth-quarter 2025 data), and say the BCR add-on can be waived and replaced by the 2.7 add-on. The reduction applies only if the outstanding advance is not repaid by 10 November 2026. Nothing here is enacted or final; the final figure is determined on 10 November 2026 and goes with the fourth-quarter deposit. Not an acquired value: the plugin must show it as awaited.
Payment timing of the 2026 credit reduction: it goes into the fourth-quarter deposit of the year.

California UI rate schedule and taxable wage limit for 2027: not published; the EDD page shows 2026 (Schedule F+, 1.5% to 6.2%) and says the schedule is determined annually. Employers' individual 2027 rates are mailed on the DE 2088 in December (EDD). The 3.4% new-employer rate is the figure read for 2026 only.
Individual notice of the contribution rate for the following year: mailed in December.
California ETT rate for 2027: not published; the page shows 0.1% for 2026 when the UI reserve account balance is zero or positive.

Ceilings (topes) of Ley 16.713 for 2027: BPS shows the current values (tope C UYU 288,836 a month, September and October 2026); no 2027 value is published yet and the date of the next adjustment was not found in a source read today.

Base de Prestaciones y Contribuciones (BPC) for 2027: BPS shows UYU 6,864 for September and October 2026 (the national minimum wage is shown separately at UYU 25,383, so the quoted creation text of Ley 17.856 no longer describes the current BPC level); no 2027 value published yet.

Executive reform line for 2026 (communique of 20 July 2026): early-retirement cause at 60 with 30 years of contributions, improvements to the individual-savings pillar, and the Asignación Única in the Rendición de Cuentas 2025 bill. The communique names no change to an employer contribution rate; the bills themselves were not read.

Regional minimum wage 2027: the Ministry of Home Affairs is consulting on a draft decree (official page dated 23 July 2026) that proposes Region I 5,700,000 VND/month from 1 Jan 2027 (Region II 5,080,000, III 4,450,000, IV 4,040,000), +7.8% on average, following a National Wage Council recommendation to the Government. Not a published decree and not enacted. It would move the unemployment-insurance ceiling (20x regional minimum wage) if adopted.
Draft table of monthly minimum wages from 1 Jan 2027 as reported in a secondary article dated 23 September 2026 that says the Ministry of Justice published the appraisal file. A draft, not a decree.

Reference level (mức tham chiếu) for 2027: the Government sets it and adjusts it on CPI, growth and fund capacity (Law 41/2024 Art. 7, secondary text). A VSS notice (9 July 2026) cites Decree 161/2026/NĐ-CP for a base salary level (mức lương cơ sở) of VND 2,530,000 from 1 July 2026 and uses it as the social-insurance floor and 20x as ceiling; no 2027 value found in any source read, so the 2027 ceiling is awaited. Decree 161/2026 itself was not read.

UIF monthly earnings ceiling: the SARS page still shows R17 712 per month (R212 544 annually) from 1 June 2021; no later ceiling or announced revision found in the sources read, so a revision is awaited, not ruled out.

COIDA maximum earnings for the assessment year starting 1 March 2027: the 2026-27 figure was gazetted on 24 April 2026 (about two months after its 1 March effective date); the 2027-28 notice is awaited.
COIDA minimum assessment for employers (R1 621 from 1 March 2026): the figure for 1 March 2027 is awaited with the next annual notice.
National minimum wage from 1 March 2027: the 2026 amendment (R30,23 per ordinary hour) was gazetted on 3 February 2026 for 1 March 2026; the 2027 amendment is awaited, typically around February.
